Outcomes will inform inclusive education, therapy, and policy, foster national and international collaboration, strengthen social connection and wellbeing, and position Australia as a global leader in accessible technology and inclusive music-making.
national-interest-test-statement:
This project advances Australia’s national interest by expanding equitable access to the arts and strengthening the creative economy. Musicians with disability remain significantly under-represented in professional music, despite national commitments to inclusion and cultural rights. Through the co-design of accessible instruments and collaborative frameworks, the project empowers artists with disability to lead creative innovation, enhances community wellbeing, and fosters cross-cultural connection.

Aligned with the 2023 Revive: National Cultural Policy, the Equity: Arts and Disability Associated Plan (2024), and NDIS reforms, the research provides evidence-based tools and strategies for embedding inclusion in artistic practice and education. By producing open-source technologies, professional performances, and transferable co-design methods, it delivers measurable cultural, educational, and economic benefits. The project will create new employment and training opportunities, attract international collaboration and cultural tourism, and show how inclusive design drives innovation across Australia’s $17 billion creative industries. Its outcomes will inform future cultural policy and research globally, building Australia’s long-term capacity in accessible technology, inclusive design, and creative leadership. It will enhance Australia’s reputation as a hub for equitable innovation and cultural diplomacy, promoting inclusion, creativity, and social cohesion at home and abroad.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Molecular innovations to defend wheat against stripe rust disease. The project aims to develop novel molecular strategies to protect wheat from harmful fungal diseases. Fungal pathogens cause some of the most devastating crop losses and are major threat to food security worldwide. The rapid evolution of fungal pathogens overcomes natural plant resistance and chemical fungicide, threatening the effectiveness of current control strategies. Managing these diseases is therefore a major challenge to agriculture. This project is expected to protect wheat with more effective genetic disease resistance and a novel class of chemical fungicide. These outcomes are expected to contribute to global food security by promoting sustainable agricultural practices and delivering substantial environmental benefits.
national-interest-test-statement: Global food demand is increasing rapidly. However global food production is under constant threat from devastating plant fungal pathogens. Wheat stripe rust disease is the most significant disease in wheat, leading to global losses of over 5 million tons of wheat annually, valued at around 1 billion USD. Australia is predicted to face severe stripe rust outbreaks, which may lead to 75% yield losses in non-resistant wheat varieties. Australia provides high quality food to local and global markets, therefore, will undoubtedly suffer severe economic consequences if afflicted by disease epidemics. This project is expected to provide novel and environmental benign genetic and chemical strategies to protect wheat from the stripe rust disease. Genetic control strategies provide an estimated national benefit of $1,500M/year to the production of Australian cereal crops. Fungicides is estimated to attribute to total $20 billion crop production annually in Australia. We aim to enhance these benefits through the project. The outcomes of the project are expected to have broad applications and significant commercial potential within the Australian grain industry. We will promote industry adoption of the novel strategies, which is expected to generate significant economic returns through improved agricultural productivity and royalties from seed and fungicide production. National crops would be better protected with sustainable strategies that are safe to the environment.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: New horizons in conformal quantum field theory: a unified approach. This project aims to develop a unified mathematical framework for the study of conformal field theories. Conformal field theories are quantum systems that behave the same at any scale. These systems are ubiquitous in modern physics including the study of statistical models and string theory. This project is expected to provide an innovative geometric framework which gives the first complete, rigorous description of conformal field theories, and in the process resolve long-standing mathematical conjectures. Anticipated benefits include significant new insight into conformal field theories and their applications, and new approaches to the rigorous study of quantum field theory, a central problem in 21st century mathematics.
national-interest-test-statement:
Quantum field theory is a fundamental pillar of 21st century physics. Despite many attempts, quantum field theory has defied a rigorous mathematical description. In contrast, the foundations of quantum mechanics have been understood for nearly 100 years. This project aims to significantly enhance our understanding of quantum field theory by providing a complete mathematical description of highly symmetric theories called conformal field theories. Conformal field theories model the behaviour of numerous modern physical systems, including string theories, critical lattice models, and edge states of topological phases of matter. Conformal field theories are linked to industry-led applications like topological quantum computation, which has the potential to reshape fundamental aspects of society, such as the cryptography that we rely on for basic activities like online shopping.

A successful outcome would significantly enhance fundamental knowledge in the physical sciences, reinforce Australia's role as a leader in the field, and lay the groundwork for domestic technological breakthroughs. The project provides training opportunities for students and junior researchers, bolstering Australia's readiness to engage with the technical challenges of the coming decades. The project also provides new avenues to engage with industry and government partners to apply the latest mathematical research to topological quantum computers and their underlying condensed matter states.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
current-admin-organisation: The University of New South Wales
announcement-admin-organisation: The University of New South Wales
grant-summary: Rethinking Immersive Digital Aesthetics for the Climate Crisis. This Project will investigate how immersive digital aesthetics can reshape the way we perceive and understand the climate crisis. It will advance creative research by exploring the experiential possibilities enabled by emerging immersive technologies in Media and Performing Arts, such as 3D visualisation, through a novel methodology integrating aesthetic, media, dramaturgical and climate theory. Expected outcomes include the first systematic theory of immersive digital climate aesthetics, grounded in the analysis of conceptual frameworks underpinning leading aesthetic practices. This research promises to effect a transformative shift in how art can embody and make tangible the human role in accelerating environmental change.
national-interest-test-statement: The Ipsos 'People and Climate Change 2025' report found that public motivation to act on climate change in Australia has declined by 13% since 2021, with many mistaking their active role as negligible. This Project tackles this misconception by examining how immersive digital aesthetics –enabled by technologies such as 3D visualisation and dynamic spatial sound– can make global warming tangible and human-climate feedbacks plausible. It investigates innovative yet critically overlooked practices in Media and Performing Arts that translate complex ecological processes into multisensory, emotionally resonant experiences that reframe humans and the climate as interdependent forces. By developing a new conceptual aesthetic framework, the Project will strengthen an emerging artistic paradigm and equip artists, curators and scholars with tools to render climate insight experientially compelling and accessible. This will enhance capacity for imaginative engagement and resilience – positioning Australia as a global leader in pioneering climate-focused art research. The Project will deliver open-access resources and convene public programs in collaboration with first-tier national and international collaborators such as ANAT and VRHAM! Digital & Immersive Art Biennale (Germany) – ensuring broad dissemination and real-world application by stimulating new aesthetic practices and public engagement with the climate crisis.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: The psychology of being informed in decision making . This project aims to develop a comprehensive framework and measurement tools for the concept of "being informed" in decision making. It will address critical gaps in our understanding of informed decision making by integrating advanced research methods and by accounting for human psychology, decision contexts, and sociocultural factors. Expected outcomes include increased knowledge of the psychology of informed decision making, as well as adaptable frameworks, tools, and recommendations for the public, experts, regulators, and policymakers. Potential benefits include promoting better decision making, reducing disputes in healthcare, financial, and legal settings, and improving communication across culturally diverse populations.
national-interest-test-statement: We routinely make important decisions about health, finance and legal matters in our lives, yet there are significant gaps between what experts and regulators intend and what the lay public understands. Via a mix of research methods combining qualitative and quantitative approaches, this project aims to fill critical gaps by developing a comprehensive framework and measurement tools to understand and improve informed decisions, factoring in human psychology, decisional contexts and sociocultural environments. Expected outcomes include increased knowledge of the psychology of informed decisions in a multi-cultural society, and the availability of an adaptable, implementable framework, tools, and recommendations for experts, regulators and policy makers. By informing stronger regulations and practices, this project may contribute to the adoption of evidence-based care, enhanced consumer protection, more rational investment decisions, fewer disputes in financial and legal settings, improved communication with culturally diverse populations, and greater public trust in regulators, experts and institutions. Long-term potential impacts include reducing public expenditure in health and legal systems and supporting market stabilisation through improved decisions and regulations. Outputs will be shared with research communities, Australian agencies, and international bodies (e.g., WHO), contributing to ongoing efforts to improve decision making in Australia and globally.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Turbulent Encounters: Particles, Droplets and Flow. This project aims to discover the fundamental mechanisms governing the interactions between droplets, particles and gases in highly turbulent three-phase flows. By integrating tomographic imaging with laser diagnostics and machine learning, this fellowship will lead to an urgently needed framework to define how these notoriously complex aerosol flows behave under practical conditions. The research outcomes are expected to lead to a new predictive framework, grounded in high-resolution experimental data, that can help to define the behaviour of these flows. This should provide significant benefits to areas ranging from microplastic transport assessment, to improving efficiency in chemical processes, coatings, and pharmaceuticals.
national-interest-test-statement: This project will focus on developing the necessary foundations to control and predict the behaviour of a particular type of aerosol flow known as a "gas-liquid-solid" flow or "3-phase" flow. These flows involve interactions between gas, solid particles, and liquid droplets and are a central aspect of defining the efficiency of processes ranging from pharmaceutical tablet coating to emissions reductions using chemical reactors. Right now, there is only a very rudimentary understanding of how these flows behave. Through the innovations proposed in this project, the expected outcome is a detailed understanding of 3-phase flows and a toolkit that can lead to the control and prediction of these flows. The project will lead to benefits which can include energy and water savings, improved prediction of pollutant dispersion, improved aerosol delivery device design, and better design guidelines for chemical reactors, all benefiting Australian communities, our environment, and the Australian economy.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Seeing by Choice: How the Brain Recognises and Remembers in a Digital World. This Future Fellowship research program investigates how the brain recognises and remembers images during self-paced scrolling, the dominant mode of digital information consumption. It combines sensitive human neuroimaging, behavioural measures, and computational models to identify neural mechanisms that determine what information captures our attention and enters memory. Outcomes will provide mechanistic accounts of recognition and memory in naturalistic, continuous input, and advance models linking human and machine vision. The program will train a new cohort of researchers in cognitive neuroscience, and has broad relevance for education, digital health and wellbeing, providing evidence-based principles to optimise digital environments.
national-interest-test-statement:
Our daily lives are dominated by scrolling through images and information on digital devices, yet we know very little about how our brains decide what content we notice, remember, or forget. This research program investigates the neural mechanisms behind recognition and memory in continuous, self-paced scrolling; an everyday behaviour that shapes our learning, decision-making, and well-being. Using cutting-edge brain imaging, behavioural testing, and computational modelling, we aim to reveal how attention and memory are allocated in real time and why some things stand out while other information is ignored.

Understanding these processes has broad benefits for Australia. In education, it can inform the design of digital learning tools that enhance retention and engagement. In digital health and well-being, it can guide evidence-based strategies to reduce information overload and support healthy social media use. The research also strengthens Australia’s research capacity by training emerging scientists in brain science. By linking human brain function with computer models, this research will position Australia at the forefront of innovative brain science producing insights and expertise that benefit science, the economy, and our society.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: The Leadership Imperative: Closing the Gap Through Indigenous Education . This project investigates how educational leadership can transform outcomes for Indigenous students in Australia. It addresses a critical gap by examining school leaders’ capacity to enact Indigenous education policy and foregrounding Indigenous youth voices. Through surveys, collaborative yarning, and policy mapping, the study will generate evidence to inform culturally responsive leadership practices. The findings will support systemic reform aligned with Closing the Gap priorities, elevate youth perspectives, and guide professional development for school leaders. Benefits include improved educational experiences for Indigenous students, strengthened leadership capacity, and enhanced policy-practice alignment across jurisdictions.
national-interest-test-statement: This project addresses a national priority by tackling persistent educational disadvantage among Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander students—Australia’s most underserved learners. Despite decades of reform and substantial investment, systemic inequities remain entrenched. This Indigenous-led research will generate urgently needed evidence about the role of school leadership in delivering culturally responsive education. By foregrounding Indigenous youth voices and examining leadership practices across jurisdictions, the project will inform policy and practice aligned with the Closing the Gap agreement. The findings will support professional development for school leaders, improve school-community relationships, and enhance educational outcomes for Indigenous students. The project’s multi-method design ensures relevance across diverse contexts, and its outputs—including plain-language summaries, media engagement, and policy briefs—will be accessible to educators, communities, and governments. The inclusion of Indigenous youth and researchers builds national research capacity and ensures the sustainability of impact. By strengthening leadership in Indigenous education, this project contributes to broader social and economic goals, including improved health, employment, and community wellbeing. It will help Australia meet its commitments to equity, reconciliation, and Indigenous self-determination, making a meaningful contribution to national progress.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Engineering Stealth Polymers for Improved Safety and Bioapplications. Stealth polymers are vital for controlling material-bio interactions in advanced technologies such as nanoparticle delivery systems. However, current stealth polymers can trigger unwanted immune responses, limiting their safety, reliability and performance. This project aims to apply innovative polymer chemistry to engineer next-generation stealth polymers with improved molecular design and immunological properties. The expected outcomes include advanced stealth polymers that extend the frontiers of polymer science and nanoparticle delivery systems. This should deliver significant benefits by advancing bio-related technologies and enabling applications in nanoparticle delivery, biosensing, and advanced surface coatings.
national-interest-test-statement: Stealth polymers are specialised materials that are designed to help prevent unwanted interactions between surfaces and biological components like cells and biomolecules. Stealth polymers work by forming a protective layer on the surface of materials, enabling reliable and durable performance in areas such as materials science, biotechnology, and nanotechnology. However, existing stealth polymers face key limitations that restrict their stability, compatibility, and broader applicability. This project aims to use innovative polymer chemistry to design and develop a new generation of stealth polymers with enhanced interfacial and biological properties. These new stealth polymers will have future applications in a wide range of areas such as nanoparticle delivery systems, biosensing, and surface coatings. The research will strengthen Australia’s capability in advanced polymer science and materials design, supporting the development of high-value materials for emerging industries including biotechnology, pharmaceuticals, diagnostics, and advanced manufacturing. The outcomes will position Australia as a global leader in high-performance polymer innovation, promote collaboration between academia and industry, and generate new opportunities for technology development and commercialisation across biotechnology and materials sectors.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Automating faces: Visual AI facial technologies and their impacts for youth. This Fellowship will investigate how the rapid rise of visual AI technologies in everyday life is impacting young people. Through world-first qualitative research, the project will generate new knowledge of the social and cultural implications of visual AI technologies that recognise and change faces. Using a cutting-edge youth-centred methodology and theories of visual digital culture, technologies and embodiment, this Fellowship will enhance Australia’s international research capacity to understand how visual AI technologies are changing how humans navigate identity. The Fellowship will provide significant benefits through informing new responses to support young people's safety, privacy, and wellbeing.
national-interest-test-statement: Visual AI technologies using facial scanning have developed rapidly and have quietly been implemented across all forms of facial biometric verification, and in all major visual social media platforms used by young people. These platforms collect and share substantial facial datasets drawn from users. These new technologies raise important questions regarding the meaning of identity and identification when it is performed by AI-integrated processes. The social and ethical impacts related to how facial technologies operate are significant, with risks for privacy and safety, and for exacerbating social biases and inequalities. This Fellowship addresses a vast gap in knowledge regarding the impacts of visual AI for young people’s identity construction, body image and wellbeing; and associated privacy and safety impacts relating to how young people’s facial data is used by key industries. This will create significant benefits by enabling Australians to understand the social, cultural and ethical implications of new facial technologies using visual AI. Through an innovative youth-centred methodology, and partnering with internationally-leading centres and key stakeholders from the technology and surveillance, beauty retail, and youth body image sectors, the Fellowship will deliver resources aimed at young people, parents, and teachers. This knowledge can be used to inform policies regarding the regulation and ethical use of visual AI.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Rearticulating housing crisis: land, debt and rent in the redeveloping city. This research explores how foundational housing relations are being reshaped by new forms of urban renewal in Australian cities. It will examine how land, debt, and rent interact to influence the role of public institutions, housing policy, and the lives of tenants. By combining land histories, detailed policy analysis and sector engagement, the project will explain how contemporary financial and governance changes are impacting housing crisis. This knowledge will support better decision-making by housing providers and expand advocacy for communities, leading to improved outcomes for people facing housing stress. The project will contribute to maturing public understanding about the broader forces shaping Australian cities into the future.
national-interest-test-statement:
This research investigates how housing in Australia is undergoing significant change driven by innovations in urban renewal, land ownership, and financial systems. Across the country, governments are redeveloping public housing through new financial partnerships and tenancy models, yet we know little about how these changes affect affordability, security, and the role of public institutions in providing housing. This project fills that gap by analysing how land, debt, and rent interact to create and remedy housing crisis conditions. Findings will produce knowledge that helps governments, housing providers, and communities make fairer and more effective policy decisions. It will benefit Australians by improving understanding of how housing systems operate, supporting reforms that increase housing security and affordability, and strengthening the public value of housing as essential infrastructure.

To ensure the research reaches beyond universities, findings will be shared through public forums, media articles, accessible online maps, and community engagement. The project will work with non-profit housing organisations, policy makers, and community groups, to make complex issues clear and relatable. By connecting research evidence with public debate and community advocacy, this work aims to influence national conversations about housing and help create a more just and sustainable housing system for all Australians.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Multiscale light-polarisation interactions for future actuation and sensing. This project aims to understand multiscale light‑polarisation interactions in solids to develop novel photostrictive materials that convert light directly into mechanical deformation. By building chemically validated, large‑box atomistic models, the project will advance knowledge of multiscale light–matter interactions and establish design strategies and standards for broadband, high‑performance photostrictive materials. These materials will enable wireless, stable, miniaturised actuators and sensors that overcome current limitations of complex circuitry and high energy consumption, significantly benefiting high-tech applications such as photonics, robotics, and quantum systems, positioning Australia for leadership in these emerging fields.
national-interest-test-statement: The emerging field of photonics, quantum computing and artificial intelligence requires miniaturised actuators and sensors capable of controlling mechanical displacements at the nanoscale. Existing actuation methods suffer from complex manufacturing processes and high costs for miniaturisation. This project will explore a new type of smart materials that provide a revolutionary solution to current actuating and sensing challenges. By directly converting light into mechanical deformation, these materials eliminate electrical contacts and enable wireless, low-cost, and miniaturised devices. Important applications of these actuators in robotics and biomedical imaging will improve Australian wellbeing and quality of life. Without the need for electrical circuits, the new devices significantly reduce energy consumption and electronic waste, contributing to environmental sustainability. To maximise impact, research results will be communicated through industry partnerships and collaborative networks. Through licensing new intellectual property to actuator and sensor developers, the project will drive advanced Australian technology and unlock potential for new devices across many sectors. In summary, the project will directly benefit Australian industries in robotics, biomedical devices, high-speed computation and communication, and quantum technologies, ultimately strengthening Australia's position in high-tech global markets and enabling a productive and innovative economy.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Timing it right: testing for climate change-driven pollination mismatches. This project aims to use native Australian plants and bees to test how climatic changes affect plant-pollinator interactions and the pollination services essential to natural ecosystems and the human food supply. Using an innovative experimental approach, this project expects to generate new knowledge about how warming alters plant and pollinator traits and the timing of their life events, both of which must match to sustain this mutualism. Expected outcomes of this project include knowledge about how pollination services provided by native bees in natural and agricultural communities will fare in changing climates. This should provide significant benefits, informing essential strategies to reduce threats to pollination in Australia.
national-interest-test-statement: Flowering plant and pollinating animal species can interact in ways that are mutually beneficial to both. In these interactions, plants gain pollen transfer and pollinators gain food. These interactions are essential for natural ecosystems and human food supply; about 90% of flowering plants and 35% of crops rely on animals for pollination. For these exchanges to persist, plants must flower at the same time of year that their pollinators are foraging. Similarly, certain traits of each partner, such as flower size and bee body size, must match. However, climate change may cause mismatches in the timing of life events and traits of organisms, leading to mutualism breakdown and extinction of interdependent species. This project will use native Australian plants and bees to experimentally test, for the first time, how warming throughout the life cycle affects plants and their pollinators in key areas. These include changes to major periodic events such as flowering; traits relating to shape, function and behaviour; and interactions and survival over successive generations. Findings will inform how changing climates affect native bee pollination in natural and agricultural contexts and are expected to provide environmental and economic benefits to Australians. Outcomes will be communicated to the public via popular press and other media outlets, and to relevant conservation and government bodies to inform essential strategies to prevent further threats to pollination in Australia.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Brain-Inspired Positioning for Fast, Energy-Efficient, Resilient Robotics. This project will develop the world’s first sub-millisecond, energy-efficient robot positioning system for reliable positioning in complex and resource-limited environments. It develops a novel brain-inspired approach where sensing and computation occur only when the scene changes, mirroring how neurons fire on meaningful events to maximise efficiency. By combining event-driven sensing with spectral processing, the system will achieve cooperative, ultra-low-latency positioning in challenging domains such as coral reefs, space, mine sites, and defence. Expected outcomes include new algorithms, open benchmarks, demonstrator platforms, and a national roadmap, strengthening Australia’s capability in safe, low-emission, long-duration autonomy.
national-interest-test-statement:
This project will develop fast, energy-efficient navigation systems that let robots and machines know where they are and move safely when satellite signals are weak or unavailable. Precise location is fundamental for autonomous vehicles, drones, underwater robots, and augmented-reality devices, yet current technologies are power-hungry and often fail indoors, underwater, and in remote or space environments. Using brain-inspired sensors and processors that work only when the scene changes, this research will create reliable, low-power positioning that enables robots to cooperate and share information even under limited communications.

Outcomes include new algorithms, open datasets, demonstrators, and a roadmap to help Australian industry and researchers adopt these advances. The project builds on established partnerships with the Australian Institute of Marine Science and Intel, and forms a new collaboration with Emesent, ensuring that innovations move rapidly from laboratory research to field-ready systems. Proof-of-concept marine and industrial deployments will demonstrate real-world impact.

By jointly advancing technology, industry capability, and researcher training, the Fellowship strengthens Australia’s position in sustainable robotics. The resulting systems will improve transport and infrastructure safety, enhance environmental monitoring, and bolster disaster-response capacity, while developing the next generation of skilled robotics researchers and industry leaders.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Heat-proofing crops by tapping into the superior genetics of wild relatives. This project will use state-of-the-art molecular and biochemical approaches to develop a novel framework that links unexplored photosynthesis genes in wild crop relatives to enhanced heat tolerance. Heat stress is a major and growing contributor to reduced crop yields globally, and current breeding efforts cannot fully engineer the necessary photosynthetic resilience into domesticated crops.  Expected outcomes include identifying the key gene mutations that determine photosynthetic heat tolerance and creating a molecular toolkit for enhancing photosynthesis. Benefits to agriculture include providing the knowledge necessary to breed heat-resilient crops, enabling more food to be grown with less water in the hotter climates of the future.
national-interest-test-statement: Across Australia and globally, rising temperatures pose an existential threat to crop productivity, with non-irrigated agriculture facing severe yield losses as warming progresses. Globally, crop yields are expected to decline by 5% for every 1°C of warming.  To safeguard Australia’s food security and agricultural sector, it is vital that we develop crops resilient to the hotter climates of the future. While traditional breeding has made advances, current efforts are unable to fully address the heat-sensitive biochemistry of photosynthesis – a key contributor to crop yield and the first process to fail as temperatures rise. The proposed project will use state-of-the art molecular and biochemical analyses to discover the naturally evolved, heat-resilient mutations in photosynthesis genes that enable wild crop relatives to grow in the extremely hot and arid environments of northern Australia. In doing so, the project will deliver specific genetic information and a molecular toolkit that will be shared with Australian breeders, enabling the specific targeting of multiple photosynthesis genes for heat improvement. This will provide Australia’s farming sector with superior, heat-resilient crop lines, directly contributing to the nation's food security and long-term economic stability in a warming climate.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Mapping opportunity: Transforming rural, first-generation university access. This project aims to investigate how ‘place’—including local culture, resources, and distance—shapes educational opportunity for first-generation rural and remote learners. Persistent inequities in higher education will be addressed by analysing how spatial, social, and structural factors intersect to influence participation. The project expects to advance knowledge through the innovative integration of geospatial mapping with theories of capability, capital, and spatial justice. Expected outcomes include a conceptual toolkit, practical resources, and policy translations to enhance university access and success. This should provide significant benefits by informing more equitable, place-based approaches to higher education participation.
national-interest-test-statement:
This project addresses one of Australia’s most persistent educational inequalities: the under-representation of rural, first-generation students in higher education. Despite decades of initiatives, these students remain far less likely than their urban peers to enrol in, persist with, or complete university. This gap cannot be explained simply by distance or aspiration but requires broader understanding grounded in the lived realities of learners.

Current outreach and support programs have had limited impact, as they often overlook how “place” (i.e., local culture, resources, and distance) shapes opportunity. This project addresses that gap by co-designing a new framework that combines geospatial mapping with insights from sociology and philosophy to better understand how rural, first generation learners navigate educational systems designed around urban-centric models of access.

By filling this critical knowledge gap, the research will benefit Australia socially and economically. Increasing higher education participation among rural cohorts strengthens communities, supports workforce development, and promotes national productivity and equity. Beyond academic dissemination, this project will produce a toolkit for policymakers and universities, outreach models and evidence-based resources. Findings will be shared through partnerships with university study hubs, educational providers, and government to ensure broad understanding, adoption, and lasting impact beyond academia.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Semiconductor-Fibre Composites for Extreme-Condition Wearable Sensors . This project aims to generate new understanding of the interactions between semiconductor soft structures and biosystems by testing their mechanical and electrical coupling under conditions of high sweat, corrosion, and high temperature. The knowledge gained will be used to develop next-generation wearable sensors that address major challenges of  performance degradation and material failure under extreme conditions. By engineering and seamlessly integrating semiconductor structures with reinforced-fibre composites, the resulting technology will enable reliable, long-term monitoring of bioelectric signals, stress, temperature and respiration, enhancing safety, performance, and resilience of Australian workers in extreme environments.
national-interest-test-statement: Wearable sensors are electronic devices attached to the human body that measure biophysical and vital signs such as respiration, motion, and temperature, providing crucial data on human health and performance. This project will develop next-generation wearable sensors using hybrid semiconductor and nanofibre composite materials. These innovations will enable ultrathin, lightweight, and durable sensors that conform comfortably to the skin, delivering continuous, reliable monitoring of biophysical signals in demanding and extreme environments. The outcomes have the potential to protect Australian workers exposed to extreme conditions across industries such as defence, mining, firefighting, and high-intensity sports. The new technology will enhance safety, resilience, and productivity while reducing risks associated with heat stress, fatigue, and injury, thereby supporting healthier, safer, and more resilient communities. By enabling real-time monitoring and assessment of health risks, this project will transform human performance and safety management. In addition, the project will generate advanced knowledge and high-performance sensing devices of interest to semiconductor and health technology companies, supporting the establishment of new Australian enterprises in wearable electronics. The outcomes will strengthen Australia’s sovereign manufacturing capabilities in semiconductors and composite materials, enhancing the nation’s competitiveness in the global market.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: From rain to riches: Surface processes behind Australia's mineral endowment. This project aims to uncover the geodynamic controls on burial, exhumation, and upgrading of Australia's critical and strategic minerals over the past 66 million years. It will employ state-of-the-art models of Earth's evolution to quantitatively link deep-mantle dynamics with surface processes, paleoclimate, and groundwater systems, integrating these models with diverse observational datasets across spatial and temporal scales. The outcomes will include quantitative reconstructions of Australia's physical and chemical weathering history, providing new insight into the distribution and economic viability of mineral deposits and strengthening national capability in exploration targeting.
national-interest-test-statement: Production of critical and strategic minerals is a cornerstone of Australia's economy, enabling the green-energy transition and underpinning national and human security. In those parts of the continent where deposits are exposed near the surface, despite a strong record of historical exploration, discovery rates have plummeted over the last two decades. Attention has therefore turned to the three-quarters of the continent where deposits are buried beneath other rocks. Successful exploitation of this vast new search-space represents a great prize that would give Australia a strategic edge on the geopolitical stage. Nevertheless, it comes with significant challenges and requires a paradigm shift in how we think about mineral systems. In particular, traditional economic geology does not consider processes such as landscape evolution and groundwater flow, which must now be better constrained using novel modelling strategies. Developing such a framework is the overarching aim of this proposal. Project outputs will pinpoint when and where conditions were optimal for deposit formation and preservation. By integrating insights into national resource assessments of all 36 critical and strategic minerals being undertaken through Geoscience Australia's Resourcing Australia's Prosperity initiative, this project will improve our capability to predict deposit locations in under-explored regions, increase exploration success, and inform government natural resource and land management.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Bridging Human and Mouse Tissue Immunity Using ‘Dirty’ Mice. Are laboratory mice too clean? Mouse models are a key component of our toolbox for understanding human immunity yet differ in key features that drive immune responses, such as genetics and microbiome. Microbes drive immune system development and disease responses. Consequently, specific pathogen-free (SPF) laboratory mice fail to mirror the human microbial experience. 'Dirty' mice exposed to diverse microbes closely mimic human immune conditions and show similarities in immune activation and composition. How microbial diversity influences this correlation is unclear. This project combines dirty mice and cutting-edge technology to explore how microbial diversity in dirty mice shapes cellular immunity, aiming to improve immunological models.
national-interest-test-statement:
Our bodies host diverse microorganisms, known as our microbiome, which train immune cells and are vital for our health. Laboratory mice are crucial for studying immune responses but are raised in near-sterile environments and possess immature immune systems that do not reflect the complexity of human immunity. To bridge this gap, we developed a microbially-diverse mouse model by transferring the microbiome from wild mice into lab mice, to better reflect human microbial exposure. This project will map the microbiome of these mice and define its impact on immune cell populations and tissue microanatomy. 

This project will enhance the understanding of immune responses and improve future applicability of research findings to humans. The project will produce refined animal models, which could lower the costs associated with future research on drug and vaccine trials. It will contribute to training the next generation of scientists and strengthening international collaborations. 

We will share our findings beyond academia through community talks, science festivals, and educational programs. We'll engage with healthcare professionals, consumers, and biotechnology firms via startup linkages and pitching bids. These efforts will help ensure our research is widely understood, applied and integrated into practice contributing to Australia's national interests and societal well-being.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Securing Antarctic Governance in an Era of Climate and Geopolitical Change. This project develops new approaches to address two crucial and interrelated challenges for Antarctic governance: the accelerating impacts of climate change and rising geopolitical tensions in the region. It responds to growing concerns about whether the Antarctic Treaty System can continue to govern effectively under these pressures. Drawing lessons from past environmental issues and geopolitical disputes in Antarctica, the project will examine how innovative negotiation strategies and scenario planning can help manage these challenges. Expected outcomes include a detailed mapping of the interests of key Antarctic states and a suite of targeted negotiation strategies to strengthen the legitimacy and effectiveness of the Treaty System.
national-interest-test-statement:
Australia claims sovereignty over 42% of Antarctica, a region central to our environment, security, weather systems, and economy. However, the region faces growing pressures from climate change and rising geopolitical competition that threaten its peaceful and environmentally protected status. The Antarctic Treaty System (ATS), the key framework underpinning stability in the region, is struggling to adapt to these challenges. A weakening of the ATS would directly harm Australia’s strategic, scientific, and environmental interests by increasing the risks of militarisation, mining, and industrial-scale fishing.

This project will strengthen Australia’s capacity to lead in Antarctic governance by generating new knowledge and practical policy tools to help the ATS respond to contemporary pressures. It will deliver negotiation strategies and scenario-planning frameworks to inform Australian government decision-making and strengthen diplomatic engagement. The outcomes will enhance national security, environmental protection, and Australia’s international standing, while also supporting civil society organisations involved in Antarctic science, conservation, and policy advocacy. The project directly contributes to implementing the Australian Antarctic Strategy and 20- Year Action Plan Update (2022) by advancing its goals of peace, environmental protection, and strategic leadership in the region.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Geonatural Archives as Engines of Regional Resilience. The project aims to strengthen environmental and socioeconomic resilience in regional Australia by activating geonatural archives, the preserved, lived, and recorded evidence of Earth’s environmental memory. It will contextualise and connect archives with regional and First Nations communities, build 3D digital twins, recover context that integrates palaeoenvironmental proxies, and design scalable sustainable repositories. The project expects to generate new knowledge supporting adaptation, conservation, and regional identities. Expected benefits include improved environmental foresight, diversified nature-tourism experiences, and stronger connection between geonatural sciences and regional communities across Australia and internationally.
national-interest-test-statement: Regional resilience is central to Australia’s future. As climate, industry and demographic pressures intensify, regional communities need new ways to sustain livelihoods, build identity and support wellbeing. This project investigates Australia’s finite and vulnerable 'environmental memory' - the combined record of natural and cultural histories preserved in landscapes, sediments, minerals, fossils, stories, documents and data. Targeted studies will elevate undervalued natural and geoheritage sites creating new assets for the "State of our Environment". It will provide avenues for regional tourism diversification supporting THRIVE 2030 and seek to improve local wellbeing and STEM equity supporting the National STEM School Education Strategy. It aligns with Net Zero 2050 by building new environmental baselines critical for conservation and climate-informed decision-making. It helps advance Closing the Gap in regional Australia through co-design with regional and First Nations communities and the return of context to culturally important heritage. Internationally, it will provide important cultural links between critical regional partners across the Southern Hemisphere, helping support regional strategies such as "Invested: Australia’s Southeast Asia Economic Strategy to 2040" and "COALAR Strategic Plan for engagement with Latin America". Pathways to a collective environmental memory will be co-created, tested and span the global south, servicing future generations.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Engineering Immobilised Biocatalysis for Bioplastic Monomer Production. Plastic waste increasingly threatens our environment. Biodegradable plastics, such as poly(lactic acid) (PLA), offer a sustainable alternative; however, their scalable production is limited by the supply of low-cost and renewable feedstocks. This project will develop enzyme-based biocatalysts within hydrogen-bonded organic frameworks (E-HOFs) to efficiently produce lactate, a key monomer for PLA, from renewable carbon sources such as carbon dioxide and ethanol. By integrating material and reaction engineering with data-driven optimisation, E-HOF's stability, activity, and durability will be enhanced, advancing scalable biocatalysis for sustainable bioplastic monomer production and supporting Australia’s circular manufacturing future.
national-interest-test-statement: Plastic pollution poses a major environmental challenge, driving the global shift toward biodegradable alternatives. Poly(lactic acid) (PLA), produced from lactate, is a promising substitute for petrochemical plastics. The global lactate market, which is essential to PLA production and other applications, is projected to exceed AUD 47 billion by 2032. Currently, industrial lactate production mainly relies on microbial fermentation or chemical synthesis, which is energy-intensive, involves toxic chemicals, and requires complex product separation. This project will develop enzyme-based biocatalysts within hydrogen-bonded organic frameworks to enable efficient and scalable lactate synthesis from renewable carbon sources. By converting waste carbon into useful products, it will lower the carbon footprint of lactate production, enhance resource efficiency, and support Australia’s transition to low-carbon industries. Outcomes will create opportunities for collaboration with Australian and global chemical and materials manufacturers, driving innovation in green technologies. This research also aligns with national priorities under the Net Zero Plan, contributing to climate resilience, job creation in sustainable manufacturing, and reinforcing Australia’s leadership in carbon-smart industrial transformation.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Array-on-a-molecule: a novel platform to measure metals in cells. The goal of this project is to develop a new and highly innovative method to determine metal concentrations within living cells by generating materials that contain multicoloured metal-sensitive elements. These new sensors will enable the first simultaneous imaging and quantification of metal ions for novel future applications across agriculture, medicine and the environment. This project will facilitate expanded collaborations with leading international researchers to uncover new knowledge about the cell biology of metals. The new methodology for imaging will underpin critical and urgent advances throughout biology, and the project will train a future workforce addressing future needs related to the impacts of metals on society.
national-interest-test-statement: Metals like iron, copper and zinc are essential for life, and imbalances in these can affect normal biological function. At the same time, toxic metals like chromium and cadmium, commonly encountered through mining and industrial activity, are harmful for plant, animal and human health. The central aim of this project is to design a transformative new method to determine the levels of these metals within the cells of living organisms; with immediate application in understanding the roles of both essential and toxic metal ions in biological processes. These new tools can be applied to a range of applications across agriculture, the environment and biomedicine; all of which are affected by the role of metals in biology. The new intellectual property arising from this project will benefit the Australian biotech industry, which is identified as being of strategic national importance and high economic potential, with breakthroughs of commercial significance patented and further developed as part of advancing the project’s commercialisation pathways. Critically, the research will also build frontier leadership in state-of-the-art technologies, including a multidisciplinary workforce of the future for roles in academia, government and biotech. In this project, knowledge transfer to labs and industry will leverage strong local and global partnerships, while public dissemination will capitalise on significant outreach networks and use diverse traditional and social media.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Certified Post-training for Pre-trained Models. This project aims to address the urgent problem of uncertified use of AI models through providing post-training certifications before their downstream usage. It will develop an advanced and reliable scheme of post-training methods for pre-trained AI models. This project will build new theories that guarantee a certified post-training scheme in various data drift situations through new data distribution measurements and data-centric learning frameworks. The outcomes should significantly improve the reliability of machine learning with benefits for certified AI use at scale.
national-interest-test-statement: Artificial intelligence (AI) models, such as ChatGPT, are increasingly used across Australian industries and government for data analysis, decision-making, and digital services. These models are often adapted after their initial training to suit a series of specific tasks, a process known as post-training. While post-training improves performance in targeted applications, current methods do not offer a way to certify when these adapted models can be trusted. This project will develop new techniques to formally certify post-trained AI models, helping users know when and how these systems can be reliably used. By improving the dependability of AI in complex and changing environments, the research will support safer and more transparent use of machine learning in business, government, and public services. The outcomes will deliver economic and commercial benefits by increasing public trust, improving the sustainability of data-driven systems, and supporting Australia’s growth as a reliable digital economy. Socially, it will help ensure AI systems are used responsibly and with confidence in areas such as healthcare, education, and public administration. Findings will be shared through an international public workshop focused on trustworthy post-training of large-scale models, ensuring broad engagement and practical uptake beyond academia.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: New light on ancient stars. This Fellowship aims to uncover the properties of the first stars and supernovae in the Universe, objects that profoundly shaped the Cosmos. Their signatures are preserved in the chemical compositions of the oldest surviving stars. Using state-of-the-art simulations and large observational datasets, this project will decode those signatures to reveal how the first stars formed, lived, and exploded. Understanding these earliest stars is essential to tracing the origins of the first galaxies, and will shine a light on our place in the Universe.
national-interest-test-statement: This project will contribute to answering how the first stars and galaxies transformed the Universe. This is one of the most fundamental questions of our cosmic origins, and forms part of one of the main questions in the Australian Astronomy Decadal Plan (2026-2035). The first stars were born thirteen billion years ago, well beyond the reach of the largest telescopes in the world, and exploded in powerful supernovae that transformed the early Universe. Traces of these supernovae can be found in the oldest stars alive today. The properties of the first stars will be determined to unprecedented accuracy through the most ancient stars known using data from Australian astronomical facilities. They will be interpreted through simulations on high performance computers using state-of-the-art software, promoting Australia as a global leader in observational astronomy, through leadership in large astronomical observational programmes, and in computational science, through the unique capabilities leveraged in this Fellowship. A deep understanding of the beginning of the Universe is at the core of Australian research in astronomy, and of profound cultural benefit to inspire interest in science and technology amongst young Australians.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Decoding the legacy of stressed sperm across generations. This fellowship aims to map how oxidative stress in sperm leads to poor embryo development and offspring fitness. Heat stress, age, and pollutants induce oxidative stress in sperm and damage the DNA carried by these cells. This project will generate the first high-resolution profile of the transgenerational effects of this damage in large animal species of agricultural & economic significance. It will leverage a unique combination of advanced reproductive biotechnologies, new sequencing methods and cross-disciplinary collaboration. This new knowledge will address a critical issue in reproductive biology relevant to all mammals, bolster genetic gain and climate resilience in our livestock, and help us understand how species adapt to change.
national-interest-test-statement:
The fertility of all male mammals is affected by heat stress, pollution and ageing. These factors can damage the DNA that sperm cells carry to the egg – resulting in offspring with compromised health. How this damage is passed on to the next generation is not yet known. This project seeks to understand this process and its effects on animal health. We will quantify how sperm DNA damage affects livestock productivity traits and investigate whether it is a hidden driver of how species adapt and evolve.

This work will help us to reverse the alarming fertility declines happening across species, to alleviate livestock productivity losses in the face of climate change and environmental pollutants, and to make our animal industries more productive and resilient. It may also support conservation of our native species. More broadly, it will contribute to public awareness that male fertility is an important issue with implications for the health of the next generation and will help to create future opportunities to address this growing concern. 

This project involves extensive collaboration with industry and this will offer a direct pathway for disseminating and adopting the recommendations coming out of this research. Capitalising on significant public and media interest in the subject of fertility, outreach activities will include high profile public engagement events and media outlets to ensure public access to and awareness of research outcomes.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Surface-Empowered Micro-Magnetofluidics. The project aims to develop a technology that enables the efficient manipulation of microparticles within complex fluids encountered in environmental water treatment, analytical testing and biological screening applications. By exploiting tailored surface topographies and interfacial fluid dynamics, the project will generate new knowledge of surface-mediated particle transport and establish innovative manipulation strategies and prototype devices for high-throughput, scalable particle and fluid processing. The project expects to train young scientists and provide significant benefits to Australia’s strategic priority areas, including biotechnology, water purification, environmental remediation, and miniature medical robotic technologies.
national-interest-test-statement:
Biomedical screening, analytical testing, and environmental remediation increasingly rely on the ability to manipulate microparticles in fluid flow. This capability is crucial across diverse applications, for instance, in isolating rare cells from bodily fluids at high throughput, or removing microplastics, heavy metals, and water-borne pathogens from wastewater. However, manipulating microparticles in such settings remains challenging, as existing methods often assume fluid behaviours that differ markedly from those of real biological and environmental fluids.

This project will develop a next-generation manipulation technology that exploits engineered surfaces and magnetic fields to enable high-throughput and efficient handling of magnetically functionalised particles in complex fluids. It will advance understanding of particle–surface interactions in microscale flows and apply this knowledge to design innovative devices with strong commercial potential for Australian biotechnology and water treatment industries, both of which are expanding rapidly in global markets. Expected outcomes include prototype systems for large-volume bioparticle isolation and water purification, contributing in the future to enhanced healthcare and environmental sustainability in Australia. Project outcomes will be actively disseminated through participation in industrial exhibitions, public engagement activities, and media outreach.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
current-admin-organisation: The University of New South Wales
announcement-admin-organisation: The University of New South Wales
grant-summary: Uncovering the Enhancer Regulatory Code of Animal Development. This project aims to understand the evolution of critical non-coding DNA sequences that control the timing and location of gene expression, known as enhancers, across animals. Enhancers evolve rapidly and are thus hard to identify. Using innovative computational and experimental approaches, the project will investigate how enhancers and their gene regulatory networks evolve. Expected outcomes include the identification of conserved enhancers, their associated regulatory networks, and the development of strategies to understand and predict enhancers. These results will establish a framework for interpreting the non-coding genome and clarify the fundamental principles of developmental gene regulation and evolution.
national-interest-test-statement:
We have now sequenced thousands of animal genomes, yet for most species we still do not know what the majority of their DNA does. These sequences do not code for proteins and make up the ‘non-coding genome’— which includes the regulatory code that determines which genes turn on in each cell type. Regulatory elements underpin why a cell becomes a muscle cell vs a neuron vs a hepatocyte, yet in nearly all species they remain unannotated. This is now the central frontier in animal genomics. Without understanding these elements, we cannot reliably predict the consequences of genetic variation in animals or humans.

This project will develop new experimental and computational approaches to identify regulatory elements across diverse animal species and determine how they function. This has the potential to transform our ability to explain why species respond differently to environmental stress, why some individuals are more susceptible to disease, and how regulatory changes drive adaptation. 

The outcomes of this work will build national capability in genomics and AI, and create a foundation for broad future applications in sustainable agriculture, precision medicine, conservation genetics, and bioengineering. The project will train researchers in cutting-edge genomic technologies and machine learning, skills in high demand across both academia and industry.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Next-Generation Aqueous Zinc Batteries for Australia’s Energy Security. This project will develop safe and cost-effective zinc–bromine batteries that use water-based electrolytes and abundant Australian materials. This technology eliminates toxic bromine formation, offering a safer and cheaper alternative to lithium-ion batteries, which are fire-prone and reliant on imported critical minerals. By addressing key challenges in performance optimisation and large-size manufacturing, the project will deliver reliable, scalable energy storage systems. These innovations will reduce dependence on foreign supply chains and enhance national energy security, helping to lower living costs, minimise environmental risks, and position Australia as a leader in clean, sovereign technologies vital for a secure net-zero future.
national-interest-test-statement:
This project will develop next-generation aqueous zinc–bromine batteries for affordable, large-scale energy storage. Lithium-ion batteries dominate the market, but they are costly, flammable, and reliant on imported critical minerals. In contrast, aqueous zinc–bromine batteries use water-based electrolytes that are intrinsically safe, cost-effective, and non-flammable. They can also leverage Australia’s abundant zinc resources, strengthening Australia’s energy independence and supply chain resilience. Through innovations in battery design and manufacturing, the project will overcome limitations of existing technology and deliver industrially relevant prototypes. 

The project will benefit Australia by contributing to the country’s clean energy transition and net-zero emissions targets. Other benefits include lower renewable energy integration costs, lower household energy bills, and improved safety for communities. By enabling deeper adoption of solar and wind power, the new technology will reduce greenhouse gas emissions. It will also benefit rural and remote regions by providing reliable off-grid storage and greater resilience to power disruptions.

Translation of research outcomes beyond academia will occur through industry collaboration and alignment with government initiatives like the Cheaper Home Batteries Program (2025). The outcomes will also be shared with the broader community through media, social media, and outreach events to promote clean energy awareness.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Old shells, new data: high-resolution archaeology of the Great Barrier Reef. This project aims to understand long-term Indigenous interactions with the Great Barrier Reef via reconstructing a 6500-year history of marine shellfish use from coasts and offshore islands. The project will generate high-resolution, paired records of seasonal resource use and environmental change using novel multi-proxy analyses from key island archaeological sites. These unprecedented records will not only provide pre-European baseline data essential for managing the Great Barrier Reef social-ecological system, but also a deep-time history of Indigenous marine lifeways and connections to Sea Country to be appreciated by all Australians.
national-interest-test-statement: This project will uncover how Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples sustainably managed marine resources along the Great Barrier Reef over the past 6,500 years. By analysing ancient shell remains with advanced scientific methods, it will produce the first combined high-resolution records of seasonal shell fishing practices and environmental change in this region. These findings will provide vital new knowledge of how Indigenous communities adapted to past climate variability, including El Niño events, and how their cultural practices shaped long-term resilience. The research will benefit Australia by strengthening Indigenous-led management of Sea Country and providing new scientific baselines for sustainable fisheries and reef conservation—critical as the Great Barrier Reef faces climate change, coral bleaching and growing environmental pressures. Beyond cultural and environmental gains, the project will enhance Australia’s global leadership in climate science, archaeology, and Indigenous-engaged research, while training the next generation of researchers in emerging and innovative techniques. Findings will be shared widely through co-produced publications with Indigenous partners, community workshops, heritage reports, and open-access articles. Results will also be communicated to policymakers, reef managers, schools, and the public, ensuring the project delivers lasting cultural, environmental, and social benefits for all Australians.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
current-admin-organisation: The University of New South Wales
announcement-admin-organisation: The University of New South Wales
grant-summary: Unlocking the full potential of wide-bandgap perovskite for photovoltaics. This project aims to advance next-generation photovoltaic technologies based on wide-bandgap perovskites by expanding the understanding of crystallization kinetics and anisotropy-driven defect management to improve device efficiency and stability. It expects to generate new knowledge on structure–property relationships by decoupling bulk orientation and surface-exposed facets to overcome the performance bottleneck. Expected outcomes include advanced synthesis protocols, improved solar cell performance, and pilot-scale module demonstrations, bridging laboratory innovation and industrial deployment. This will strengthen Australia’s leadership in advanced photovoltaics while contributing to national clean energy strategies and net-zero goals.
national-interest-test-statement: This project will develop new approaches to improve the efficiency and stability of wide-bandgap perovskite solar cells, a promising next-generation solar technology that can maximising the value of Australia’s abundant solar resource by supporting building-integrated photovoltaics for power-generating windows and facades and enable perovskite/silicon tandem solar cells that overcoming the efficiency limits. Despite rapid progress in their development, these devices remain limited by excessive voltage losses, unsatisfactory operational stability, and a lack of manufacturing consistency. The research will advance fundamental understanding of how wide-bandgap perovskite films grow and how defects form, which are key barriers to overcome the challenges. By focusing on crystallisation control and material anisotropy, the project will deliver advanced fabrication methods and tailored interface treatments, enhancing both efficiency and durability while validating scalable film deposition compatible with industrial processes. These outcomes will accelerate the commercialisation of next-generation photovoltaics, directly supporting Australia’s transition to affordable clean energy while strengthening advanced manufacturing. The project will reinforce Australia’s leadership in renewable energy innovation. Over the long term, it will stimulate local industry growth, create skilled jobs, and contribute to global net-zero targets through sustainable and cost-effective solar technology.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Efficient fault-tolerant quantum logic for utility-scale quantum computing. A worldwide effort is underway to design and build useful quantum computers. Progress in quantum error correction has disrupted existing roadmaps with the promise of a faster path to scaling up. This project aims to lay the foundation for utility-scale quantum computing by inventing fault-tolerant protocols for universal quantum logic that approach the limits of achievable efficiency. This will lead to new architectures for useful quantum computers that unlock the full potential of available quantum hardware. Expected outcomes include designs for new, more efficient, fault-tolerant quantum logic gates. Our results will pave the way to a new era of technological discovery driven by useful quantum computers.
national-interest-test-statement: This project will develop a new foundation for the design of future utility-scale quantum computers. By inventing new techniques for drastically improving the efficiency of fault-tolerant quantum logic we will set the stage to scale up quantum computers from the first generation through to broad utility. This addresses a gap in the Australian research landscape in pushing state-of-the art techniques for efficient fault-tolerant quantum computation to meet the specifications of quantum hardware. This project has the potential to generate massive benefits to Australia's economy and technology ecosystem by enabling the development of useful quantum computers. This will drive progress in Australia's quantum computing industry which is projected to be worth $6 billion and generate 20,000 new jobs over the coming two decades. The utility-scale quantum computers that this project lays the groundwork for promise revolutionary new approaches to cryptography and the simulation of chemistry and materials science. Realising this new computational paradigm will benefit Australia’s national security, environmental technologies, and high-tech economy. The results of our research will be presented to the international quantum research community at academic and industry conferences. This will promote the broad adoption and translation of our research across the quantum ecosystem, setting the stage for the global quantum computing research effort to scale up and achieve utility.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Data-Driven Material Discovery for Next-Generation X-ray Scintillators. This project aims to develop faster, brighter X-ray detectors by integrating high-throughput screening, machine learning, and multimodal microscopy to discover low-defect two-dimensional perovskites and scale them into flat-panel and flexible devices This project will generate new knowledge on defect-controlled scintillators through an innovative, data-driven discovery-to-device pipeline. Expected outcomes include practical design rules, an open structure–property database, and prototypes validated for non-destructive testing and security. This should provide significant benefits in real-time, higher-contrast, lower-dose imaging and strengthen Australia’s sovereign capability in advanced sensors and manufacturing, and researcher training.
national-interest-test-statement: This project will deliver safer, faster X-ray scintillating materials for X-ray detection and imaging in airports, industry, and the environment by creating a new type of bright, rapid radiation detectors made from two-dimensional perovskites. These materials can be manufactured at low temperature and printed over large or flexible areas, reducing cost, energy use, and supply risks compared with current scintillating crystals. This means clearer images at lower radiation doses for objects, quicker screening at borders, and better inspection of critical infrastructure and manufactured parts. For the first time, this project will link data-driven discovery with advanced multimodal microscopy and real-world radiation imaging device testing, transforming Australia’s national facilities and partnerships into practical benefits for the community. Outcomes include working detector prototypes, open design rules, and a searchable materials database that local companies and research groups can use to accelerate innovation, research and development, and technology commercialization. The project will also train new scientists and engineers in areas critical to  security, space, health and clean industry. By building sovereign capability in advanced sensors and creating tools that reduce dose, cost, and imaging time, this project will deliver broad economic, social, and environmental value for Australia while opening new opportunities for international collaboration.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Enabling Predictive Modelling of Photoactivated Molecular Systems. This project aims to develop a computational chemistry toolkit with robust, freely available methods for accurately modelling molecular processes after light absorption, including how molecules interact with one another after exposure to light. These developments expect to overcome limitations of current methods, enabling predictive, more reliable simulations to guide experimentalists and computational chemists alike. Expected outcomes include improved workflows to design solar cells, molecular switches, and photochemical reactions. Given computational chemistry's central role across disciplines, this work should provide broad significant benefits and advance the computational design of future technologies.
national-interest-test-statement: Computational chemistry is a rapidly growing field that offers a more sustainable and cost-effective approach to chemical research.
