This project will boost Australia’s expertise in computational chemistry by creating reliable, freely accessible methods to accurately simulate molecular processes and chemical reactions. This includes how molecules interact after absorbing light. These processes are fundamental to many technologies, such as light-responsive materials used in solar energy systems and chemical reactions triggered by light. Current methods struggle to fully capture these complex events, leaving an important gap this project will close. By improving the ability to predict and design solar cells, molecular switches, and light-driven chemical reactions, this research will play a key role in Australia’s shift towards clean energy and sustainable technologies. It offers economic and commercial benefits to Australia by driving innovation in renewable energy, pharmaceuticals, and advanced materials. To maximise national benefit, results will be shared through free software, encouraging collaboration between computational and experimental chemists, including those in industry. The project will train future computational chemists, thus strengthening Australia’s expertise. New methods and results will be promoted widely to ensure they advance Australia’s scientific, economic, and environmental goals.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Centring children in the housing crisis. Housing is central to children’s present and future well-being—a well-being threatened by the current housing crisis that disproportionately affects households with dependent children. Despite this, children are relatively invisible in relevant housing and policy conversations. This Fellowship aims to produce a new body of national data, as well as international and interdisciplinary comparative evidence, to better understand the impact of housing on child well-being. Using novel qualitative and quantitative approaches that foreground children’s input, outputs co-developed with key stakeholders are expected to deliver new insights and an actionable roadmap for housing and other policy responses to optimise child well-being equitably.
national-interest-test-statement: The housing crisis is one of the foremost challenges facing Australia. More and more people are struggling to secure and maintain housing that is affordable, suitable, and stable. Households with children are at the frontline of these issues, and its impact on children is powerful - affecting their links with schools and healthcare, their development, relationships, risks of experiencing poverty, and more. Despite this, the impact of the housing crisis on children has yet to feature adequately in research or policy. This research will utilise novel mixed methods and international comparison to fill this gap, identifying the consequences and means of mitigating the impact of housing on children's well-being. These insights will have economic and social benefits for Australia, including improved productivity and health for the children involved and society more broadly. Research impact will be maximised via the production of policy briefs and summaries aimed at policy makers, peak bodies, and the public. This topic is of global relevance and importance, with many other countries facing similar challenges. This Fellowship will therefore place Australia at the forefront of tackling this important challenge, as well as producing benefits for Australia's children in the present as well as the future.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Incommunicado detention and predatory justice in Indonesia, 1965–today. This project aims to map the evolution of incommunicado detention—the mechanism through which an estimated tens of thousands of civilians are tortured, murdered or disappeared every year in Indonesia—as a predatory form of law and order over the past 60 years. It investigates how and why this illegal practice became embedded in Indonesia’s justice system and develops innovative, evidence-based tools for redress. Integrating historical, qualitative, and quantitative methods, the project will produce the most comprehensive record of these abuses to date and create a secure digital platform to strengthen legal aid coordination, advance understanding of illiberal governance, and inform new, data-driven strategies to prevent human rights abuses.
national-interest-test-statement:
Every year, it is estimated that tens of thousands of Indonesians are detained in secret by police, military, and intelligence officials—cut off from lawyers, families, and doctors, and often tortured, disappeared, or killed. This project investigates how this illegal practice, known as incommunicado detention, became entrenched in Indonesia’s justice system, and develops practical tools to help end it. By mapping over 60 years of cases and building a secure digital platform for legal aid and human rights workers, the project will strengthen local capacity to prevent abuse and seek redress. 

Working in close partnership with Indonesian human rights organisations, the project supports Australia’s broader diplomatic and aid priorities in the region, particularly with Indonesia, our most important regional neighbour. It will enhance the effectiveness of Australia’s governance and human rights assistance programs by providing reliable, data-driven insights into how legal and policing institutions operate on the ground. By advancing justice, transparency, and the protection of human rights in Indonesia, the project contributes directly to a more stable, accountable, and resilient Indonesia—helping to safeguard the long-term relationship between our two nations. It will also build lasting local research and advocacy capacity, ensuring that Indonesian partners can continue this work independently and sustainably into the future.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Left and right in contemporary Australian democracy. This project aims to understand the left and right in contemporary Australian democracy. Australian democracy is structured around a political left and right, although we do not understand what this means to Australian citizens. This project will generate the most comprehensive map of contemporary Australian political attitudes among citizens and elected representatives, using surveys and interviews. Expected outcomes include the development of a multidimensional understanding of the political preferences of contemporary citizens, to move beyond left-right models. This is expected to strengthen democratic responsiveness by equipping politicians and policymakers with an understanding of the preferences of Australian citizens for government.
national-interest-test-statement: Evidence from surveys shows that Australian citizens are increasingly dissatisfied with politics and don't trust politicians. In particular, the attitudes and preferences of many citizens no longer align with those of Australia's major political parties. Democracy has traditionally been organised around ideas of a political 'left' and 'right'. These left and right labels persist today, although we know little about what they mean to cotemporary Australians. This project will provide the most comprehensive map to date of Australians' political attitudes and beliefs. The attitudes of citizens and politicians will be compared to evaluate how well politicians represent the broader community. This is important to Australia's democracy as it will enable citizen political preferences to be communicated to those who make political decisions. This can make Australia's democracy more responsive to citizens. The research outcomes will be published in accessible reports to communicate findings to policymakers, the media and citizens. The research findings will be shared with government departments, political parties and civil society organisations. The aim of the project is to strengthen Australian democracy by giving Australian citizens a greater voice.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Scaling Intelligence: Ultra-Efficient Adaptation for the Next-Gen AI Models. This project develops scalable methods to make adapting large AI models efficient. Modern large AI models are highly effective at handling broad tasks. Yet, applying them to critical fields like healthcare requires substantial adaptation with private data, which can be very slow due to heavy communication load. We propose new methods to significantly reduce communication traffic for adaptation while maintaining model accuracy and reliability. Expected outcomes include novel methods, an open-source prototype and evidence-based guidelines for practical adoption. By lowering infrastructure cost, saving energy, and enabling safe collaboration across machines, this project will make advanced AI more accessible, practical and sustainable.
national-interest-test-statement: This project will enable large AI models to specialise for privacy sensitive fields such as healthcare and finance by creating communication-efficient, distributed adaptation methods. This allows models to learn from sensitive private data, which is currently inaccessible, making them more accurate and practical for these critical domains. Our project develops novel distributed optimisation techniques that dramatically reduce the amount of data that needs to be shared while maintaining the AI’s accuracy and reliability. The benefits to Australia are threefold: first, it will lower the costs of running AI services by reducing network traffic and preventing Internet congestion; second, it will enable AI systems to scale efficiently across many devices, from smartphones to Internet-of-Things sensors, supporting wider adoption by Australian industry; and third, it will improve the quality and speed of AI-powered services, enhancing experiences in applications such as online decision support tools, and healthcare systems. To ensure the research has real-world impact, we will release open-source tools and prototypes, provide practical demonstrations, publish results in accessible formats, and collaborate closely with industry partners. By doing so, this project will strengthen Australia’s leadership in safe, efficient, and privacy-conscious AI technologies, delivering tangible benefits to both research and industry while supporting innovation, economic growth.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: A New History of Appetite Since 1945. After World War II changes in the global food system, accelerating consumer capitalism, and new ideas about body, brain and mind vastly altered the stakes of eating in prosperous societies. This Fellowship will produce a new history of appetite since 1945, responding to the rise of GLP-1 agonist medications like Ozempic. Using novel empirical materials, it will investigate changes to the understanding and regulation of appetite, producing vital new knowledge about how historical forces have shaped our fundamental urge to eat. Expected outcomes include a critical historical framework for understanding current controversies over the medical control of appetite and new methods for historians studying the nexus of biology, politics and culture.
primary-field-of-research: 5002 - History and Philosophy of Specific Fields
national-interest-test-statement: The urge to eat is central to human experience but has received comparatively little attention from historians. This Fellowship creates important and timely knowledge regarding changing ideas about appetite and its consequences in the second half of the 20th century. Using a novel set of sources, it investigates how appetite and its relationship to eating behaviour became a key concern for governments, commercial entities, health authorities and individuals during this period, and thus develops a new case study for historians studying the relationship between biology, politics and culture. The project will benefit the Australian community by providing crucial historical context for the emergence of obesity and food insecurity as national health priorities, including the current and sometimes controversial efforts to address obesity through the medical control of appetite via bariatric-metabolic surgeries and new GLP-1 agonist medications like Ozempic. Knowledge about the recent history of ideas about appetite and the attempts to control it will also enrich public discourse on a topic of significant contemporary concern and individual experience. Understanding of this project outside academic audiences will be maximised through the project’s strategic communication plan, which includes extensive Open Access publications, media articles, a publicly-accessible project website, and regular interactions with the food policy and related sectors.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Exploring the Birth of Belief: Early Ritual Activity in Northern Arabia. How did early belief or religious systems develop and spread? This project aims to investigate this question through a study of Neolithic ritual structures known as mustatils. Only identified in the last 10 years, mustatils represent one of the earliest cohesive and widespread ritual landscapes in the world. By employing new scientific techniques, this project aims to identify the origin and geographic spread of the mustatils, as well as changes in ritual activity and belief throughout the life of this tradition (c. 5300-4200 BCE). The expected outcomes of the project include a greater understanding of how early belief systems developed, spread, and changed over time, particularly during periods of climatic and environmental deterioration.
national-interest-test-statement: Home to one of the world’s youngest populations, with more than 50% aged under 25, Saudi Arabia is a key partner in the Australian Higher Education and Research sphere, and a growing area of Government priority. This project will strengthen the bilateral relations between Australia and Saudi Arabia through an investigation of Saudi Arabia’s earliest known belief system. Additionally, as Australia faces the social and environmental disruptions of the climate change, understanding how earlier societies adapted to past climatic and environmental change is critical. This project will generate new knowledge on how an early belief system was impacted by environmental change, providing insight into human adaptation and behaviour during an era of rapid aridification. Assessing the impact that these changes may have had on belief and social cohesion, is crucial to Australia and the globe as we enter a new era of climatic and environmental instability. This research and understanding will strengthen resilience and build insight into future social and metaphysical challenges for both Australian and international communities. The project will support early-career researchers and foster long-term collaboration between Australian and international scholars and stakeholders, delivering lasting social and cultural benefits. Project outcomes will be shared through academic outputs and engagement with local communities and governments.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Connecting with Country: Indigenous creative practice research. The project aims to build Indigenous pathways in the cultural sector through a Connecting with Country framework. Investigating the intersections between practice-led research and Indigenous ways of knowing, the project expects to generate new knowledge about that agency of Indigenous mark making and how the cultural sector can build ethical relationships with Indigenous knowledges, cultures and creative practice. Expected outcomes include new models for exhibition development and Indigenous engagement in museums and galleries. This will provide significant benefits including advancing the agency of Indigenous practitioners, communities and knowledge holders within the cultural sector and improved training for Indigenous researchers.
primary-field-of-research: 4501 - Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Culture, Language and History
national-interest-test-statement: This project aims to transform the way the Australian cultural sector engages with Indigenous knowledges, cultures and creative practice. It addresses a critical gap in how the cultural sector disregards Indigenous conceptions of connecting with Country and aims to shift established practices in museums and galleries. Addressing the ambition of the National Cultural Policy, the project will advance the agency of First Nations peoples in the sector and elevate Indigenous understandings of Country to demonstrate the crucial place of First Nations stories at the centre of Australia’s arts and culture, thus benefiting the cultural life of all Australians. Working with communities, industry and institutions, it will provide a range of real, impactful benefits including innovating new models for exhibition development and Indigenous community engagement and holistic approaches to cultural heritage management to better reflect the lived experience of Indigenous peoples. The project will train Indigenous post graduate students in practice-led research and build the capacity of Indigenous artists, communities and knowledge holders to take on leadership roles in the cultural sector. It will maximise these impacts through communicating results across multiple platforms, including public exhibitions in museums and galleries, and by publishing key texts in the field.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Southern Ocean Heat and Mixing: Can Antarctic Sea Ice Recover? Antarctic sea ice has reached record lows in recent years, raising urgent questions about its potential recovery and implications for Australia and the global climate. This project will estimate how much heat from the deep ocean reaches the surface and drives sea-ice loss. It will fill critical knowledge gaps through new ocean turbulence measurements under Antarctic sea ice, combined with existing data to deliver the first clear picture of ocean heat exchange between deep waters and sea ice. Outcomes will clarify the ocean's role in driving sea-ice decline and whether recovery remains possible. Benefits include improving climate models and sea-ice predictions, and strengthening Australia's science expertise and international collaborations.
national-interest-test-statement:
Antarctica plays a critical role in regulating the global climate and holds key natural and economic resources that are closely linked to the fate of its sea ice. Over the past decade, Antarctic sea ice has reached record lows, and it is unclear whether it will recover. Major knowledge gaps remain in understanding the ocean’s role in this loss and specifically, how much heat from the deep ocean reaches the surface and melts sea ice. In addition, climate models struggle to produce accurate Antarctic sea-ice projections. This project will address these gaps by providing new ocean turbulence measurements under Antarctic sea ice, focusing on the under-observed East Antarctic region. By linking these turbulence measurements to the transport of heat from deep waters to sea ice, it will reveal how likely Antarctic sea ice is to recover from recent record lows and improve confidence in sea-ice projections.

This project will build new Australian capability to measure ocean turbulence under sea ice and deliver essential knowledge to understand and predict sea-ice change. Its findings will inform policy makers, improve climate models, and strengthen national preparedness for environmental and economic risks linked to Antarctic change. Through collaborations with national and international partners, and proactive communication via public talks, media, and policy briefings, outcomes will be shared widely to maximise impact beyond academia.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Solar-Driven Tandem Catalysis for Low-Carbon Alkene Production. This project aims to advance sustainable alkene production by developing multifunctional photothermal catalysts that simultaneously activate propane and carbon dioxide through tandem catalysis. By integrating adaptive active sites within a photothermal ensemble, this project will enable synergistic C–H and C=O activation and dynamic hydrogen transfer under mild, solar-driven conditions. It expects to generate new knowledge in light-induced charge redistribution and hydrogen mediation using an innovative catalytic approach. Expected outcomes include design principles for durable, low-carbon catalysts, delivering significant benefits through reduced industrial emissions and enhanced national capability in sustainable chemical manufacturing.
national-interest-test-statement:
Propylene is a vital chemical feedstock and the world’s second most used polymer precursor, yet current production relies on fossil-fuel heat, causing high energy demand and substantial emissions. This project will develop a solar-driven catalytic process that converts propane and carbon dioxide into high-value propylene with markedly lower energy input and near-zero emissions. By integrating renewable solar energy with advanced catalyst design, the research addresses the urgent need for low-carbon, high-efficiency chemical manufacturing.
The project directly supports Australia’s 2024 National Science and Research Priority 'Transitioning to a net zero future', and aligns with the National Reconstruction Fund focus on 'Value-Added Manufacturing' and 'Renewable Energy Technologies'. It advances the Clean Energy and Low-Emissions Technology Roadmap and Australia’s Net Zero by 2050 commitment.
Outcomes will enable on-shore, solar-powered propylene production, reduce reliance on imports, cut industrial emissions, and create new pathways for sovereign capability and circular-carbon manufacturing. Knowledge generated will be transferable to other alkene and hydrocarbon conversions, broadening impact across the chemical sector. The team will apply open-science principles, share datasets through repositories, and engage industry, government, and policy stakeholders via workshops to accelerate translation and adoption.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Towards Real-World 3D Point Cloud Understanding. This project aims to advance real-world three-dimensional (3D) data understanding by developing a new artificial intelligence (AI) framework for denoising, reconstruction, and large-scale foundation learning from unlabelled data. It will generate new knowledge in 3D spatial intelligence through innovative machine learning methods designed for complex, real-world 3D data. Expected outcomes include novel algorithms and a large-scale foundation model that improve robustness, accuracy and generalisability in 3D understanding. The project will strengthen Australia’s leadership in spatial AI and support applications across robotics, autonomous systems and digital twins.
national-interest-test-statement:
This project will strengthen Australia’s leadership in artificial intelligence (AI) for three-dimensional (3D) spatial data. It will develop new methods for cleaning, reconstructing, and interpreting 3D data captured by sensors such as LiDAR, drones and cameras. Current technologies often struggle with real-world conditions that involve noise, missing information and complex environments, limiting their reliability and use. The research will fill this critical gap by creating advanced algorithms and a first-of-its-kind AI foundation model that can learn from large, unlabelled 3D data, greatly improving accuracy, adaptability and scalability. 

The outcomes will lead to major national benefits, including safer and more efficient mining operations, smarter monitoring of cities and infrastructure, and advances in autonomous systems, robotics and digital-twin technologies. These capabilities could also enhance environmental monitoring, disaster response and sustainable urban planning, supporting national resilience and economic growth. 

The project’s results will be shared through open-source tools, collaborations with industry and government, and public demonstrations. By strengthening national expertise and advancing new technology development, this project will help position Australia as a global leader in next-generation artificial intelligence.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: The faults in our stars. Spectroscopy is among the most powerful tools for understanding stars, but it is held back by imperfect models. Those shortcomings lead to systematic errors that cascade through nearly all astronomical measurements, and undermine our understanding of how planets, stars, and galaxies form and evolve. This project will achieve stellar parameter and chemical abundance measurements ten times more precise than current methods, answering fundamental questions about star cluster homogeneity, element creation processes, how convection and magnetic fields alter spectra, and rare stellar phenomena. It will launch a new era of precision spectroscopy and establish Australia as a world leader in stellar astrophysics.
national-interest-test-statement: Australia has invested heavily in telescopes and surveys to study stars, including the Australian-led GALAH survey. However, current methods of analysing starlight use simplified models, leading to systematic errors that undermine our understanding of how stars, planets, and galaxies form. This research will develop new computational techniques to dramatically improve the accuracy of stellar measurements, combining physics-based models with modern data analysis. This project delivers significant benefits to Australia. It maximises the value of existing infrastructure—billions of dollars spent on telescopes and surveys—by extracting more reliable information from data already collected. The advanced data analysis skills developed through this research prepare students for high-value careers in finance, data science, risk management, and engineering. The research cements Australia as a world leader in computational data analysis and stellar astrophysics, building on our existing strengths in survey design. Results will be shared through school visits, public science events during National Science Week, and media engagement, inspiring the next generation of scientists. By transforming how we analyse starlight, this work helps answer fundamental questions about our cosmic origins while training Australia's future workforce in cutting-edge analytical methods.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Drivers of El Niño-Southern Oscillation changes under future climates. This project aims to uncover drivers of future changes of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO). This project expects to leverage an unprecedented set of simulations, combined with a range of techniques such as targeted climate model experiments, traditional data analysis, and deep learning. Expected outcomes of this project include understanding ENSO’s evolution under two contrasting futures: one where greenhouse gas emissions continue to rise, and one where net-zero is achieved. This should provide significant benefits such as improving preparedness and understanding of ENSO-driven extremes, which will reduce economic and societal costs and inform evidence-based policy to strengthen Australia’s resilience in a warming climate.
national-interest-test-statement: Australia’s climate is strongly influenced by the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO), which drives droughts, floods, bushfires, and major shifts in rainfall and temperature. Understanding how ENSO will change as we face two possible futures, one where greenhouse gases continue to rise and another where the world transitions to net zero emissions, is critical for managing Australia’s water resources, agriculture, infrastructure, and disaster preparedness. This project will use an unprecedented suite of climate model experiments to determine the physical mechanisms that drive ENSO change and to assess how ENSO behaviour evolves across a range of future scenarios. By identifying when and why ENSO may intensify or weaken, the research will provide vital information to improve long-term climate projections and risk assessments for Australia. The outcomes will directly support government and industry planning in sectors such as emergency management, agriculture, and energy, and strengthen Australia’s leadership in climate science. The project will also train the next generation of Australian climate researchers, build national expertise in advanced climate modelling and artificial intelligence, and enhance international collaboration on climate prediction.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Ultrathin 2D Hollow Nanoassemblies for Wearable Biosensing. This project aims to develop a new class of ultrathin biosensors from hollow plasmonic nanoparticles. It is expected to address key knowledge gaps and long-standing challenges in biochemical sensing and materials science by unlocking previously inaccessible internal surfaces of metal nanoparticles and elucidating how these nanostructures govern plasmonic behaviour and sensing performance under static and mechanical deformation. Expected outcomes include new knowledge in plasmonics and biosensing and the establishment of a transformative wearable biosensing platform with broad applicability. This will significantly benefit Australia’s emerging sectors in personalised healthcare and advanced manufacturing and drive high-value industry growth.
national-interest-test-statement: Wearable biosensors represent a critical frontier in next-generation personalised healthcare. Surface-Enhanced Raman Scattering (SERS) biosensors enable rapid, label-free detection of biomolecules through their characteristic Raman signatures. However, transitioning from current rigid or colloidal SERS sensors made from solid nanoparticles to future flexible, wearable devices requires filling key knowledge gaps in understanding and engineering ultrathin SERS substrates for biochemical sensing. This project focuses on unlocking the hidden internal atomic surfaces of metal nanoparticles to develop a new SERS platform that is ultrathin yet mechanically robust, highly sensitive, and compatible with soft biological interfaces for dynamic biomolecule detection. Building on CI Shi’s pioneering work in cell-like nanoreactor arrays, ultrathin SERS sensors assembled from hollow nanoparticles will be engineered with independently tunable internal and external surfaces to reveal how internal architectures govern sensing performance. This will advance the fundamental understanding of biosensing mechanisms, establish new plasmonic material design principles, and develop a transformative wearable SERS platform adaptable to various biomolecules and surface types. The outcomes will be shared with collaborators and medical research centres to promote wearable biosensors for future real-world personalised healthcare, enhancing Australia’s competitiveness in this rapidly growing field.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Holding Country, Facing Crisis: Aboriginal Men’s Ceremonial Futures. This project addresses critical socio-cultural challenges facing central Australian Aboriginal communities. In partnership with Anmatyerr & Arrernte communities, this project examines how ceremonial knowledge and practice functions as a critically important Indigenous social institution. The research investigates connections between living ceremonial practice, archival collections, and contemporary social life to understand how Aboriginal men draw upon ceremonial knowledge to navigate 21st-century challenges. It will generate new theoretical frameworks about the value and state of ceremonies, create community-controlled archives, provide evidence-based policy recommendations, and mentor Aboriginal researchers through collaborative training.
primary-field-of-research: 4505 - Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples, Society and Community
national-interest-test-statement: This research delivers critical socio-cultural and economic benefits to Australia by documenting how Aboriginal communities in central Australia use ceremonial knowledge to respond to 21st century challenges, including high incarceration rates, social dislocation, and cultural disruption. With 84% of Northern Territory prisoners being Aboriginal men, understanding community-grounded solutions is a matter of national urgency. Aboriginal men across central Australia are struggling to maintain ceremonial practices that bolster identities and create support networks, yet these initiatives receive little attention or institutional support. This project documents these practices and their effectiveness, providing the evidence needed to develop policies that support successful community-driven approaches. Beneficiaries include Aboriginal communities, who will gain greater recognition for their innovative solutions and preservation of contemporary ceremonial knowledge; Australian taxpayers, who will benefit from more cost-effective social programs; government agencies, which will receive practical guidance for culturally appropriate policies; and future generations, who will be supported by stronger policy frameworks that promote Indigenous-led community development. To maximise understanding and adoption beyond academia, outcomes will be communicated via community outreach and collaborations, policy reports, national and international workshops, media engagement and online content.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Rewilding, resistance, and belonging in Alpine landscapes. This project aims to investigate why rural communities resist conservation efforts, focusing on how belonging and place ownership shape responses to environmental change. Using two emblematic cases – the return of wolves in the European Alps and debates over wild horses in the Australian Alps – it expects to generate new knowledge about how rural conflicts become focal points for struggles over identity, heritage, and environment. Expected outcomes of this project include new insights into the roots of mistrust in environmental decision-making. This should provide significant benefits, including a deeper understanding of bridging divides between conservation goals and rural communities and guidance for more socially sustainable policies.
national-interest-test-statement: Australia faces urgent environmental challenges, particularly in Alpine regions, where wild horse management debates highlight tensions between scientific conservation goals and community values. Building inclusive, trusted environmental decision-making is essential to address climate change and ecological decline. This project will explore why some rural communities resist environmental policies, even when ecological harm is evident, filling a critical gap in understanding public engagement with environmental decision-making. By comparing wild horse management in the Australian with wolf reintroduction in the Austrian Alps, the project will uncover the social factors shaping community responses, offering insights for more inclusive policy solutions. Through public exhibitions, a photo essay book, and workshops with conservation practitioners and rural leaders, findings shared will highlight the deep values Australians attach to landscapes and animals, ensuring these perspectives inform future decisions. By equipping policymakers with socially grounded strategies for conserving fragile alpine ecosystems, it will enable the public’s voices and values to actively shape environmental policy. This will lead to benefits including the strengthening of both public trust and democratic participation processes, offering pathways to more inclusive, and effective environmental decision-making for Australia’s future.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Reconfiguring Criminal Law in the Climate Crisis. The fellowship aims to address a critical gap in understanding of how criminal law is used to respond to environmental harm. It investigates the rapid expansion of environmental criminalisation in Australia and beyond, examining its legal, social, and political impacts. Through case studies in New South Wales, Vanuatu, and the International Criminal Court, the project will reveal how criminal law is reshaping environmental governance and justice. Anticipated outcomes include new insights to guide fairer and more effective legal and policy responses. The study will deliver significant benefits for Australia: strengthening environmental protection, supporting regional partnerships, and contributing to global efforts for environmental justice.
national-interest-test-statement: This project investigates how criminal law is increasingly being used to tackle environmental harm in Australia and beyond. Around the world, governments, courts, and campaigners are turning to criminal penalties to respond to problems like pollution, deforestation, and biodiversity loss. To date, there is no critical research investigating this trend. This project addresses that gap by examining how environmental harm is criminalised in Australia, New South Wales, how Pacific nations such as Vanuatu are leading calls for new international environmental crimes, and how global campaigns are pressing for environmental harm to be recognised as an atrocity crime at the International Criminal Court. The research will benefit Australians by providing clear, evidence-based insights into criminal law's use and effectiveness as a tool for environmental protection. Its findings will help shape fairer and more effective policies for safeguarding Australia’s unique ecosystems, supporting climate resilience, and strengthening regional partnerships with the Pacific and beyond. To ensure impact beyond academia, the project will share results through public reports, podcasts, targeted workshops with community and policy groups, and media engagement. This will make the findings widely accessible, encourage public debate, and support law reform and advocacy efforts that aim to secure a more just and sustainable environmental future for all Australians.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: The Gender of International Law Today: Genocide and Crimes Against Humanity. This project examines how international law responds to feminist critique through two contemporaneous legal processes: genocide cases at the International Court of Justice and negotiations for a new United Nations treaty on crimes against humanity. It aims to identify how these processes reflect or ignore women’s and LGBTI+ experiences, and how feminist actors have shaped them. Diverse feminist critiques are considered, including liberal, racial, and ecofeminism. The findings will guide governments with a stated commitment to 'gender mainstreaming' in international law, including Australia, on how to achieve that aim in today's legal and political landscape.
national-interest-test-statement:
This project addresses the urgent problem that international law is primarily shaped by male perspectives, limiting its capacity to protect women, girls, and LGBTI+ people. Despite states’ pledges to “gender mainstream” their legal systems, feminist critiques reveal that structural inequalities persist and that international law often fails to respond to the lived realities of those most affected by violence and discrimination. By analysing current genocide cases before the International Court of Justice and negotiations for a new UN Convention on Crimes Against Humanity, this research fills a major gap: no integrated feminist study has yet examined how these parallel legal processes reflect or resist diverse feminist critiques.

The project directly benefits Australia’s national interests by strengthening its leadership in advancing gender equality and human rights through international law. These are key priorities in Australia’s foreign policy and national research agenda. It will produce practical guidance for government lawyers and civil society, enhancing Australia’s ability to engage effectively in UN treaty processes. Beyond academia, the outcomes will enrich public understanding of international justice, inform gender-responsive policy and legal practice, and contribute to social, cultural, and environmental resilience by embedding feminist and Indigenous perspectives in global governance.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Deciphering Local Chemical Order for Next-Generation Alloy Innovation. This project aims to establish local chemical order, which profoundly shapes the performance of multi-principal element alloys, as a predictive and controllable design parameter for next-generation alloy innovation. By integrating advanced microscopy with atomistic modelling, it will elucidate the physical origins, dynamic evolution, and tunability of atomic ordering, and quantify its role in governing mechanical behaviour and defect kinetics. The research will deliver a quantitative and transferable framework that defines a new paradigm for sustainable alloy design. Expected outcomes will advance fundamental knowledge and enhance Australia’s capability to engineer high-performance materials for aerospace, energy, and manufacturing sectors.
national-interest-test-statement: This project will unravel the atomic-level rules of local chemical order in multi-principal element alloys, a new frontier in structural materials offering extraordinary potential for demanding applications. Local chemical ordering is a subtle but critical phenomenon that governs the exceptional strength, toughness, and durability of these alloys, yet its origin, tunability, and impact remain poorly understood, limiting their full technological potential. This research will address this critical knowledge gap by establishing a predictive and quantitative design framework that enables tailored properties and accelerates the transition to more sustainable and energy-efficient systems. Beyond multi-principal element alloys, the knowledge and insights generated will be highly transferable to a wide range of advanced alloy families, amplifying impact across Australia’s key industries and delivering long-term economic and environmental benefits. This project directly supports Australia’s national priorities in aerospace, advanced manufacturing, energy, mining, and the emerging hydrogen and space industries, where high-performance materials are essential. The research findings will be promoted through industry partnerships and public engagement, ensuring rapid uptake and translation. This project will strengthen Australia’s global leadership in materials and manufacturing innovation, advancing national resilience, sustainability, and economic competitiveness.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: AI companions and Monetisation of Youth Loneliness: Reducing Harm by Design. This project aims to unpack a poorly understood yet highly consequential phenomenon: the monetisation of youth loneliness through AI companions and chatbots. By partnering with a youth advisory group, this innovative research explores the full lifecycle of AI companions; design strategies used to target and engage lonely youth; their lived experiences; parental attitudes; and the AI regulatory landscape. Expected outcomes include better understanding of AI companions, new ethical AI design frameworks, guidance for parents negotiating digital access at home; and actionable advice for policymakers debating platform age restrictions. This will bring significant benefits to Australians and a growing AI industry by improving AI design for youth.
national-interest-test-statement: Nearly 43% of Australian youth aged 15–24 report feeling lonely, and 35% turn to AI companion chatbots for comfort. However, these platforms operate on a "freemium" model, locking deeper emotional engagement behind paywalls, potentially exploiting vulnerable users. While the Australian government’s proposed age restrictions for users under 16 may apply to AI companions, this alone does not address the broader impacts. It is crucial for our national interest that the harms caused by design in AI companions are better understood and to ensure that young people are empowered—not excluded—in shaping these technologies. International research to date has been largely focused on algorithmic and psychological impacts. This project uses a design lens. By partnering directly with young people, the research will investigate how interface features in AI companions are designed and how they shape youth lived experiences within a social, technical, and regulatory environment. Methods include platform audits, in-situ longitudinal ethnography with youth/families, industry interviews, workshops and a policy hackathon. The goal is to uncover harmful industry practices that manipulate young Australians who use AI to alleviate their loneliness and inform future applications where AI companions might be suitable, e.g. educational and therapeutic purposes. The project will produce academic outputs, practical tools, and videos to spark public debate and inform ethical AI design and policymaking.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Unravel chemicals-microbiome interactions to fight antimicrobial resistance. Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a pressing global threat; however, little is known about how complex mixtures of chemicals influence the emergence of AMR in real microbial communities. This project will develop platform technologies to uncover the molecular and ecological mechanisms underlying chemical–microbiome interactions, harnessing machine learning to predict AMR risks from chemical mixtures. Outcomes will provide a national, open-access dataset of high-risk chemical combinations and their AMR effects. This project will establish Australia as a leader in AMR–chemical risk assessment, delivering environmental, social, and economic benefits while strengthening national resilience to global AMR challenges.
national-interest-test-statement:
This project addresses the urgent challenge of antimicrobial resistance (AMR), a leading global threat with profound implications for water and soil environments. While growing evidence suggests environmental pollutants promote the spread of AMR, most research has focused on the effect of a single pollutant on a single bacterial species. Real-world environments contain complex mixtures of pollutants acting on diverse microbial communities. This project will fill this critical knowledge gap by uncovering how pollutant mixtures shape AMR emergence, developing machine learning tools to predict risks, and identifying intervention strategies that mitigate AMR spread by targeting key pollutants and leveraging resilient microbial taxa.

The outcomes will deliver significant benefits to Australians. Environmentally, it will guide pollution management and protect natural ecosystems. Socially and economically, it will support safer communities by reducing the risk of AMR transmission through water, soil, and food systems, helping to alleviate pressure on healthcare. Commercially, it will generate predictive tools and risk assessment frameworks that can be adopted by regulators, water utilities, and industries to ensure safe and sustainable practices.

Outcomes of this project support Australia's National Antimicrobial Resistance Strategy - 2020 and Beyond. Research findings will be translated through peer-reviewed publications, media releases, public presentations and policy briefs.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Infrastructural Diplomacy and the Future of Global Health Governance. Global health governance is at a critical turning point as multilateral institutions lose legitimacy, making regional partnerships essential for shared health challenges. This project aims to develop a new governance approach by examining how the Asia-Pacific forges innovative biomedical collaborations beyond international law, conventional science diplomacy, and North–South frameworks. It will illuminate how non-state actors navigate scientific, technological, regulatory, and epistemic forms of infrastructural diplomacy and apply these insights to design tools that promote greater equity. The project’s outcome will strengthen Australia’s capacity for regional biomedical collaboration, offering a governance model with global relevance.
national-interest-test-statement: As traditional multilateral institutions like the World Health Organisation face declining influence, Australia is navigating a changing landscape of global health governance. This project bridges law, diplomacy, and bioscience to examine how international health cooperation is increasingly shaped through “infrastructural diplomacy”, where countries gain influence not through formal treaties, but by financing and building biomedical facilities, laboratory networks, and health systems in partner countries. Focusing on the Asia–Pacific, the research sheds light on the growing role of non-state actors (research institutions, technology companies, pharmaceutical industries and NGOs) in shaping how health is governed. Through partnerships connecting Australian, Indonesian, and Chinese research centres, and a cross-sectoral regional workshop guided by an international advisory board, the project will deliver practical insights with lasting impact. These activities will strengthen pandemic preparedness and build Australia’s capacity to shape health governance in our region. The outcomes directly support Australian Government Science and Research Priority 2 (healthy and thriving communities) and Priority 5 (secure and resilient nation), while delivering on DFAT’s commitments in Southeast Asia. By contributing to SDG 10 (reduced inequalities) and SDG 16 (inclusive and strong institutions), this project positions Australia as a leader in science diplomacy and equitable governance.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Families and Net-Zero Transport Transitions. This project aims to accelerate net-zero transport transitions in households with children. It moves beyond technology to examine how everyday routines, collective values and political realities shape travel choices. Combining qualitative methods with hybrid choice modelling, it applies the Practice-Institution-Community Framework, engaging families and decision-makers to generate new knowledge on travel behaviour determinants and pathways to net-zero mobility. Expected outcomes include strategies for planners and policy-makers, a robust evidence base for policy and community action, and a tested framework for mobility research—advancing Australia’s net-zero progress and delivering lasting environmental, social and economic benefits.
national-interest-test-statement:
Australia’s transport sector is on track to become the nation’s largest source of emissions by 2030. Road transport accounts for 86% of these emissions, with passenger cars alone responsible for 42%. In addition, congestion currently costs Australia $19 billion annually, and road trauma $27 billion. While vehicle electrification is essential for climate targets, current EV uptake is too low, and embedded energy in manufacture too high. Our ambitions for an Australia that is net-zero, equitable and economically resilient will also require reductions in car travel – in some cities by up to 40%.

This net-zero project develops culturally attuned, community-led and policy-ready interventions to support families in net-zero transport transitions. By learning from households in Scandinavia and the UK, and engaging parents, policymakers, and communities in co-design, it will generate practical, politically feasible strategies to shift everyday travel behaviour. The result will be timely, evidence-based solutions to reduce the multiple negative externalities of transport systems, as well as a replicable and globally relevant research framework for net-zero transitions. 

The project is, itself, a showcase of net-zero research practice, directly supporting Australia’s climate goals while enhancing economic resilience, public health, and social equity.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: A novel process-based flood risk assessment framework for Australia . This project aims to develop a novel framework for flood risk assessment in Australia. This project will generate significant new knowledge in understanding flood geneses and develop improved techniques for estimating both current and future flood risk. The expected outcomes will lead to enhanced flood resilience across Australia. Over one million private properties, or about one in 10 homes, have some level of flood risk in Australia. This project will reduce future damages associated with flooding that are currently projected to increase.
national-interest-test-statement: The economic loss due to flooding just on the east coast of Australia in February and March of 2022 totaled US$6.6 billion. With the economic loss due to flooding only projected to increase insurance experts and economists continually rank extreme weather events as the top economic risk. Regulators now also require organisations to disclose their climate related risk exposure. There is a pressing need to quantify flood risk, but there remains a lack of practical methods to quantify how flood risk will change into the future. This research would quantify the drivers of flooding across Australia and link these drivers to the state-of-the-art climate model projections to develop a novel and robust methodology to estimate current and future flood risks across Australia. The proposed approach would allow the augmentation of existing historical flood estimates for the future, while also deriving new and improved estimates of both current and future flooding. Key barriers to adoption would be overcome through strong collaborations with research and industry leaders.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Coffee lifeworlds in a changing climate. This project aims to uncover how multispecies approaches offer new ways of intervening in the relations between agriculture, sustainability, climate justice and resilience at a time of intensifying ecological degradation and vulnerability. It does so through a case study of coffee in Timor-Leste, the country’s second largest export and primary income source for over a third of the population. Anticipated outcomes include a stronger understanding of the transforming biocultural relationships underpinning agrarian lifeworlds, landscapes and livelihoods. This will enrich Australian and global transdisciplinary debates on multispecies justice and inform policy to enhance the resilience of agrarian systems amid growing climactic uncertainty.
national-interest-test-statement: This project aims to generate stronger ethnographic and interdisciplinary understandings of the transforming biocultural and multispecies relationships underpinning Timorese coffee landscapes and livelihoods in the face of urgent development needs, ongoing post-conflict recovery efforts and rising climate unpredictability. Australia has been at the forefront of international support for the neighbouring state of Timor-Leste since its independence. The project aligns with Australia’s sustained commitment to supporting Timor’s stability, prosperity and development as Timor's largest aid and security partner. It also aligns with the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) Australia-Timor-Leste Development Partnership Plan 2025-2030 and DFAT Australia Pacific Climate Partnership, both of which hold an explicit and cross-cutting focus on climate change adaptation and resilience. Planned non-scholarly outputs including an industry report, museum exhibition, news and media features and public talks will translate the project’s findings into improved policy and practice, in support of a resilient, just and community-led approach to coffee production in Timor-Leste and beyond.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Sustaining Emergency Fire Management in Times of Crisis. This project addresses the critical need to understand the future of Australian fire management in the face of climate change and political and economic crises. By examining the sector's social dimensions and its engagement with forms of collaboration and sharing the research will uncover hidden vulnerabilities and opportunities key to sustaining this vital emergency infrastructure. Utilising a unique ethnographic approach across multiple sites, the project will develop conceptual tools for understanding and justifying emergency management systems. It will also provide insights to enhance Australia’s resilience, national security, and environmental protection, ensuring a more effective and sustainable approach to future emergencies.
national-interest-test-statement: This project is in the national interest because it will inform critical national policy and strategic planning for fire and emergency management. As climate change intensifies bushfire events and seasons, improving understanding of and capacity for coordinated emergency management is essential to protect Australia's people, economy, and national security. The project fills key knowledge gaps in how Australia collaborates domestically as well as with countries such as the United States and Canada , examining the cultural, political, and economic factors that shape these sectors and their resource sharing. The findings will directly inform policy and practice, enabling Australia to proactively and collaboratively develop and diversify its emergency response, ensuring a more coordinated, effective, and sustainable approach to environmental protection and national security. Through industry engagement, project workshops, and outputs, this research will actively foster utilisation by the fire and emergency management sectors. Specifically, a policy report will be delivered directly to sector leadership, and key findings presented at sector conferences. Insights from international collaborations will be proactively shared to strengthen national resilience strategies. It will also cultivate a skilled cohort of researchers to forge new social science expertise, positioning Australia at the forefront of global climate-adapted fire and emergency management.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Mito-nuclear drivers of biodiversity revealed by wild bees. This project aims to advance understanding of the evolutionary processes that generate and maintain biological diversity. It will combine molecular and field studies of Australia’s unique native bee fauna to reveal how interacting mitochondrial and nuclear genes affect hybridization in natural populations and thus drive the evolution of new species. The expected outcome is new knowledge of how coevolving genomes shape the macro diversity of our natural world. The project is also expected to benefit the commercial use of native bees as pollinators of crops, and the conservation of wild bees in Australia’s tropical ecosystems.
national-interest-test-statement: This project will develop new understanding of the processes that affect the genetic integrity of wild flora and fauna populations, informing efforts to manage and protect the natural world. Using field-based and genomic approaches in wild populations of Australian bees, the project will reveal how interactions between different genomes in the same cell – mitochondrial and nuclear – can impede hybridization in nature and produce global patterns in biodiversity. The project expects to deliver new knowledge of the molecular basis of species boundaries, with potential to guide diverse endeavours in agriculture, biosecurity and conservation. By working with Australia's wild bees, this project also expects to produce new knowledge that supports the commercial use of native stingless bees in crop pollination by informing beekeeping practices and developing guidelines for native bee breeding. Native bees can contribute to a resilient horticulture industry, with 70% of crops grown in Australia aided by bee pollination and bee pollination estimated to contribute >$4 billion to the economy each year. This project will also raise public awareness of the importance of native pollinators to Australian ecosystems and food production. These benefits will be shared with beekeepers, horticulture industry and the wider Australian community via workshops, public talks and articles, and media engagement.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: A causal analysis of extreme speech and political violence. This project aims to investigate the relationship between extreme speech and incidences of politically motivated violence in Australia. Despite the rising risk of harmful speech, conspiracy theories and propaganda online, little is known about how internet culture produces physical violence. This project will attempt to map escalation towards violence in the texts and images that represent the ideologies associated with violent action. It seeks patterns of emergence to inform co-design interventions to protect and prepare civil society. Additional outcomes include a cultural-historical archive of extremist discourse, new analytical methods, counter extremism media and contributions to both public and policy debates on free expression.
national-interest-test-statement: Politically motivated extremism and violence pose a growing threat in Australia. Recent warnings from security agencies highlight the risk of harmful speech, conspiracy theories and propaganda online. While much research focuses on individuals or groups, this project takes a new approach. It treats extremism as a communication process and examines how certain ways of speaking and sharing ideas create conditions that make violence more likely. The research will map the links between extremist language and acts of violence to help communities, governments and civil society recognise early warning signs and respond more effectively. It would benefit Australians by providing better tools to understand and counter extremist threats. This would contribute to national security, help to protect vulnerable groups often targeted by extremist, and support social cohesion in a time of democratic strain. Beyond academia, the findings will be shared through workshops with community organisations, social workers, youth programs and law enforcement. Practical resources, such as an intervention manual and digital tools, will be co-designed with stakeholders. Public reports, media outreach and open-access databases will further ensure that the knowledge created is widely accessible and usable.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: The formation of blood flow patterns in the central nervous system. Understanding how the vascular system supplies blood to the neurons is crucial to comprehending how the central nervous system works. Blood delivery is achieved by the formation of blood flow patterns or differences in blood flow between vessels. However, how these flux patterns are generated is completely unknown. This project aims to investigate the mechanism behind the formation of blood flow patterns in the visual pathway (i.e., brain, optic nerve, and retina). The expected outcomes include new knowledge related to the formation of blood flow patterns obtained with methods of imaging only available at the University of Melbourne. This project will establish the conceptual framework for future studies on basic neurovascular function.
national-interest-test-statement: Function of the brain and eye are dependent upon the precise delivery of oxygen and nutrients from the bloodstream. This is achieved by highly accurate blood distribution, which ensures that the right amount of oxygen is delivered to every nerve cell or neuron. Accordingly, each vessel carries a different volume of blood, producing “blood flow patterns” or differences in how blood flows between capillaries. Although this concept is accepted within neuroscience, how blood flow patterns are generated remains a fundamental question that is largely unresolved, despite being crucial for understanding how our brains and eyes work. This project aims to discover the primary mechanisms behind the formation of blood flow patterns. This fundamental knowledge advance will deliver ground-breaking insights into neurovascular research and reinforce Australia’s leadership position in the field. The outcomes of this work will be a major knowledge advance that will enable the establishment of a conceptual physiological framework for how communication occurs within neurovascular networks. Future studies to address neurovascular communication dysfunction, which affects an estimated 10.6 million Australians with an economic burden of >$74 billion, would leverage this fundamental knowledge and address this Australian Science and Research Priority. Outcomes from this work will be communicated to the general community through radio, television, and social media interviews.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Towards Building Scale Phytosystem Biofiltration for Cleaner Indoor Air. This project aims to develop, evaluate and apply biotechnology-driven phytosystem biofilters for building-scale air purification. Specifically, it will determine whether phytosystems can wholly or partly replace mechanical ventilation to provide economical, high-quality indoor environmental management; establish the air handling capacity required per unit indoor volume; and assess the energy reduction potential of HVAC-integrated or retrofittable phytosystems. Expected outcomes include the advancement of the fundamental science of air-bioremediation, and the delivery of strategies for large-scale deployment, thus creating a much stronger economic driver for this Australia-led innovation.
national-interest-test-statement: This project will develop, evaluate and trial phytosystem biofilters integrated with ventilation systems for building-scale air purification. It will identify the mechanisms underlying botanical air pollutant biofiltration, optimise system design and airflow capacity, and assess energy efficiency and indoor environmental quality outcomes under varied conditions. It addresses the growing gap in Australia’s ability to remove harmful indoor air pollutants efficiently and sustainably. As our cities become denser, energy-intensive ventilation systems are increasingly inadequate for providing healthy indoor air, while contributing heavily to national energy consumption. By advancing the fundamental science of air-bioremediation, generating performance benchmarks, and trialling scalable deployment strategies, the project will deliver practical solutions for healthier, low-energy buildings. These findings will underpin the creation of a set of best-practice design and implementation guidelines, ensuring reliable integration of botanical biofilters into retrofitted ventilation systems for sustained indoor air quality improvement. The fellow supported by the program brings award-winning science communication, which will be used to disseminate results via national media platforms, and social media to the Australian public. The outcomes will strengthen Australia’s position as a global leader in air-bioremediation innovation and create significant economic drivers for industry adoption.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
current-admin-organisation: The University of New South Wales
announcement-admin-organisation: The University of New South Wales
grant-summary: Intelligent green porous structural design for active carbon removal. This project aims to develop lightweight green structures using carbon-absorbing concretes for achieving net zero. The innovation lies in the deep learning-enhanced intelligent structural design, using graded porosities to improve load carrying capacity and air permeability for mitigating carbon footprints efficiently. By generating new insights into permeability-strength balance via tailoring porosities, this project will address the limitation of carbon removal in existing designs due to low air permeability. This will accelerate the transformation of civil industries toward zero emission, promote the economic growth and create jobs in green and smart construction, driving environmental sustainability and emerging market expansion.
national-interest-test-statement:
This project will pioneer new techniques to design next-generation green structures with carbon-absorbing concretes for active carbon removal, transforming Australia’s high-carbon construction sector into an emission-free industry, as a vital part of Net Zero Plan. Achieving large surface areas and high air permeability is critical for effective carbon absorption, which is not feasible through existing design approaches. The proposed structures will bridge this gap with innovative graded porosities to deliver mechanical robustness and superior carbon removal efficiency, while reducing material consumption. Such structures are deep learning-driven for efficient analysis and design, and can be 3D printed for direct and scalable implementation.

The outcomes will promote the emerging market of green concretes in Australia with job creation and GDP growth; benefit the transformation of civil industry towards sustainability, digitalisation, efficiency, and safety; address the challenges of labour and resource shortage in Australian rural areas; save costs in both labour and material and support fast construction; positively influence the social wellbeing with enhanced natural ventilation and urban cooling; and protect the environment.

To maximise the impact, the project will develop in-house software and demonstrate the cost and environmental benefits to end-users. Findings will be disseminated through conferences, media engagement, and academic and industrial collaborators.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Activity and passivity: Spinozist philosophical insights for our time. This project aims to investigate fundamental questions of human agency: when are my desires just passively 'from the outside' and when do they count as active and 'really mine'? Developing underappreciated theoretical resources from the great 17th century philosopher Spinoza, the project will generate new knowledge about Spinoza's philosophical system and new knowledge in political philosophy concerning individual and collective agency. Expected outcomes include a novel Spinozist theoretical paradigm for political philosophy, and enhanced research capacity through the development of an Early Career Researcher network. This should provide significant benefits, such as building our democratic resilience.
primary-field-of-research: 5002 - History and Philosophy of Specific Fields
national-interest-test-statement: Being human involves both activity–acting from one's own power–and passivity–being under the influence of external forces. But as societies face dramatic technological progress and rising democratic disaffection, our understanding of activity is under pressure. Individually, citizens ask, which of my attitudes are just 'from outside', which are 'really me'? Collectively, democracies take citizens' expressed desires as authoritative, even though those desires are shaped by broader forces. While scholars have critically investigated power and agency, none have yet been able to conceptualise passivity without paternalistically pointing to hidden true interests. Nor has the distinctiveness of Spinoza's non-paternalistic approach been appreciated. The project will produce the first comprehensive study of Spinoza's theory of activity and passivity, then bring the Spinozist approach to bear on contemporary puzzles of power and agency. The Spinozist paradigm will provide unique resources for diagnosing and responding to individual and collective passivity, and thereby will advance Australia's democratic resilience. The project will train the next generation of researchers in cutting-edge methods of historically-informed political philosophy. Communication of research outcomes in public-focussed discussions and articles will engage the community in reflection on the ethical and political challenges of dependence on external forces.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: 2D-Lipid Nanoparticles: A New Platform for mRNA Delivery to the Brain. This project aims to develop a novel two-dimensional (2D) lipid nanoparticle (2D-LNP)-based platform for the delivery of mRNA to the brain. By combining organic synthesis and large-scale lipid formulation screening, lead 2D-LNP candidates with superior mRNA transfection and ability to transport across the brain barriers, including blood brain barrier and adhesive extracellular matrix, will be constructed and systemically validated. Expected outcomes include novel LNP formulations, new insights at the nanoparticle-neuron interface, and an effective mRNA delivery platform for genetic modulation in the brain. This project is also expected to generate patents that deliver economic benefits to Australia's biotech and pharmaceutical industries.
national-interest-test-statement:
Messenger RNA (mRNA) delivery technology has transformed the biotechnology landscape. Despite the remarkable success of existing lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-based systems, efficient mRNA delivery to the brain remains a substantial challenge due to the complex neurobiological environment and multiple physical barriers, including the blood–brain barrier and the dense, adhesive extracellular matrix. Inspired by the superior fluid mobility of disc-shaped red blood cells, this project will pioneer a novel disc-like, two-dimensional LNP (2D-LNP) platform designed to enhance mRNA transport to the brain, particularly into regions that remain inaccessible with current delivery technologies. 
We will integrate rational organic synthesis with large-scale lipid formulation screening to identify lead candidates and rigorously evaluate their delivery performance in vitro and in vivo. Economically, the discoveries from this project will underpin the development of a patentable mRNA delivery technology with strong potential for industry uptake and impact, offering a powerful and commercialisable tool for genetic engineering in the brain. These innovations will strengthen Australia’s international standing in RNA technology and catalyse the creation of new pharmaceutical and biotechnology ventures. 
Alongside high-quality scholarly outputs, the project’s key advances will be broadly disseminated to end-user communities and the public through workshops, outreach activities, and media engagement.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Enhancing spin-electric coupling for quantum technologies. Electric fields enable the rapid and low-energy execution of quantum operations on quantum bits, and crucially, can be employed in high-density quantum circuits. However, we do not know the rules for designing materials to enhance the effect of electric fields. This fellowship aims to utilise quantum chemistry methods to identify structures that exhibit strong coupling to electric fields, and then experimentally verify the effects. Key outcomes will include development of design guidelines for enhancing electric field control of quantum materials and a new device to measure electric field control of the quantum states of molecules. Benefits include accelerating the commercial development of quantum devices in Australia.
national-interest-test-statement:
Australia has been a global leader in quantum technologies for decades. There is a concerted national effort to translate this strong research background into a competitive high-technology industry, which has received substantial support from government funding. Developing such an industry would significantly benefit Australia’s economy by generating high-quality jobs and bolstering the country's sovereign defence capabilities. As such, this fellowship addresses the "Building a secure and resilient nation" National Research Priority.
Quantum technologies, such as computing, sensing, and encryption, require the ability to set, and measure, individual quantum bits. This is usually achieved with microwaves, but these exist on the centimetre scale, meaning that we cannot exploit the nanoscale dimensions of quantum bits to build high-density quantum circuits. This project will develop fundamental knowledge in how to use electric fields to directly interact with electron spins, and thus overcome this limitation.
