By developing knowledge and techniques to optimise quantum materials for computing and communication, this project will enhance the value of Australia’s investment in quantum technologies. With numerous commercial and national players in the quantum tech sector, finding ways to improve quantum materials will provide Australia with a significant competitive advantage.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
current-admin-organisation: The University of New South Wales
announcement-admin-organisation: The University of New South Wales
grant-summary: Digital Twins in Defence and the Transformation of Military Knowledge. This project aims to investigate how digital twins—dynamic computer models linking simulations with real-world systems—are transforming military knowledge by integrating and coordinating data collection, simulation, and prediction. Under AUKUS, Australia has committed to their use in defence but the implications for military knowledge and decision-making are not yet understood. Combining archival and empirical methods to create analytic frameworks and tools, the project will generate and translate new knowledge about their limits, risks, and possibilities on and off the battlefield. This should benefit Australia by ensuring that public scrutiny and democratic accountability keep pace with the rapid adoption of digital twins in defence.
national-interest-test-statement:
Australia's defence increasingly depends on advanced technologies to generate knowledge and inform decision-making. Digital twins are at the centre of this transformation: dynamic, data-driven models that couple computer simulations and predictions with real-world systems. Through partnerships such as AUKUS, digital twins are reshaping how military knowledge and decisions are made yet there is very little public understanding or democratic scrutiny of their implications.

This project will deliver the first major social study of defence digital twins, tracing their historical origins and analysing their contemporary adoption in Australia, the United States, and the United Kingdom. By examining how these technologies are developed and deployed, the research will generate vital insights into how they transform military knowledge and what that means for how Australia plans and conducts war.

The project will directly benefit Australia and Australians by ensuring that public investment in defence innovation is matched by transparency and civic oversight. Through public events, media engagement, and accessible resources, it will foster informed democratic debate and strengthen Australia’s reputation as a leader in socially responsible and globally engaged research on security and technology. This work will help safeguard democratic values while building national capacity to critically assess emerging technologies that influence defence and society more broadly.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: A Biocultural Approach to Knowing Ground Parrot Country. The project takes a biocultural approach to restoring Ground Parrot Country. It will test the efficacy of evidence briefs for incorporating Traditional Knowledge and Western science and guide management decisions. Field research will include assessing the efficacy of vegetation management techniques to restore grassy heaths, evaluating fire impacts on threatened mammals, exploring the efficacy of artificial refuges to improve outcomes for threatened species in burnt landscapes, and assessing phytophthora management outcomes for biodiversity. Aligning Western science with Eastern Maar's knowledge and priorities, demonstrates an Indigenous-led pathway to meeting global biodiversity targets while upholding free, prior and informed consent.
national-interest-test-statement: To avert the global biodiversity crisis, harnessing the ecological knowledge of Indigenous communities is essential. This project implements a biocultural values-led landscape ecology research program focused on the care of a species of cultural significance to the Eastern Maar in Southern Australia. The Eastern Ground Parrot is no longer present in Gadanabud Country, and restoring Ground Parrot Country is a research priority of the local community. The project builds on existing work in the region to understand the capacity of heath & scrubland in Gadabanut Country to support populations of Eastern Ground Parrots, while balancing other ecological values and fire risk. It will provide an applied demonstration of how cultural values and Traditional ecological knowledge can be integrated into a research program. Such integration has great potential to improve biodiversity in landscapes while supporting a range of values, leading to environmental benefits not just from this project but from future ecology research projects. Outcomes of this project will be shared with land management agencies and government departments in the Otway region, and have implications for the management of natural values nationally and internationally.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Terahertz Integrated Secure Communications and Sensing for 6G and Beyond. This project aims to develop transformative theories and signal processing solutions for terahertz integrated secure communications and sensing, a breakthrough paradigm for sixth-generation and beyond wireless systems. It will create fundamental models, analytical frameworks, and practical design guidelines to enable simultaneous ultra-fast secure transmission and highly precise sensing -- a capability largely unexplored to date. Such innovations will establish new foundations for intelligent, multifunctional connectivity to support emerging applications such as smart industry and autonomous transportation, driving a transformation in the telecommunications sector and boosting industrial productivity for our intelligent society beyond 2030.
national-interest-test-statement:
Sixth-generation (6G) and beyond communications are recognised as a Critical Technology in the National Interest, with immense potential to boost Australia’s economy and revolutionise industries beyond telecommunications, including smart manufacturing and transportation. Two emerging 6G capabilities -- Immersive Communications and Integrated Sensing and Communications -- will enable unprecedented services that combine ultra-fast data transmission and ultra-accurate sensing. Achieving these capabilities requires harnessing the terahertz (THz) frequency band and ensuring communication security to realise the social and economic benefits of 6G. However, this area is largely uncharted.

This project addresses this gap by developing new theoretical foundations and signal processing techniques for THz integrated secure communications and sensing. It will position Australia at the forefront of the next telecommunications revolution, strengthening national capability in the 6G and beyond era. Collaborating with experts in control, computing, and industry partners like Optus, the project will foster innovative, high-impact applications that demand both secure transmission of massive data and precise sensing. Examples include 1) digital twins for smart factories, boosting Australia’s manufacturing quality and reducing production costs, and 2) intelligent navigation for smart roads, enhancing traffic safety and saving over a thousand Australian lives lost annually to car accidents.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Trophic signals: monitoring ecosystem services through carrion use. This project addresses a critical gap in our ability to quantify the economic and ecological value of biodiversity by developing a novel framework to measure the ecosystem service of scavenging. While there is global interest in quantifying the benefits of healthy ecosystems, current methodologies are limited in their ability to assess services provided by animals. This research will pioneer a new approach to measure the efficiency of carcass removal by both vertebrate and insect scavengers. Expected outcomes include the development of a standardised tool to monitor ecosystem function that will enable land managers and policymakers to make informed decisions on maintaining intact food webs amidst ongoing biodiversity declines.
national-interest-test-statement: Australia's economy and well-being depend on healthy ecosystems, which provide essential benefits like clean air and water. However, our ability to monitor these natural services, especially those provided by animal communities, is severely limited. This project addresses that critical gap by pioneering a cost-effective and feasible method to track the vital ecosystem service of scavenging. This research will help us understand how animal communities including birds and insects keep our landscapes clean by rapidly recycling nutrients from carcasses. Ultimately, the project will equip Australian land managers and policymakers with clear indicators and a decision framework to incorporate animal diversity/function into policy or practice. This will ensure we can protect our biodiversity and maintain healthy, functional ecosystems in the face of global environmental change, benefiting all Australians.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Books that Change You: Modernist Teachings, Textual Pedagogics. This project explores how modernist authors sought to reinvent teaching through literature. It offers the first comprehensive study of the interplay between pedagogical activity and literary creativity in modernism. It examines the pedagogical dynamics of modernist writing worldwide, moving beyond Eurocentric perspectives. The project establishes a global history of literary pedagogy and a new methodology for studying it. Outcomes include an interactive digital resource for mapping these affiliations and illuminating how literature models new ways of thinking and learning. The project offers vital insights for educators, researchers, and readers by reimagining education and literature today.
national-interest-test-statement:
This project investigates how modernist writers used literature as a form of teaching, developing what is termed here textual pedagogies—creative ways of making readers think differently and question accepted ideas. It fills a major research gap by revealing how authors in the early twentieth century experimented with new modes of learning and knowledge across cultures, including links with First Nations, African American and Caribbean writers. By documenting these global pedagogies, the project will place Australia within a broader history of educational and literary innovation.

The research will benefit Australians culturally and socially by inquiring into how literature fosters critical reflection, empathy and imagination – skills vital for education, civic engagement and social cohesion. It also strengthens Australia’s reputation as a leader in the humanities through international collaboration and digital innovation.

To promote and translate outcomes beyond academia, the project will create an interactive open-access website mapping the relationships between writers and their teaching practices from around the world, providing resources for educators, students and readers. Public talks, media engagement and partnerships with cultural institutions and online reading communities will further extend its impact, supporting a national appreciation of how reading shapes thinking and learning in everyday life.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
current-admin-organisation: The University of New South Wales
announcement-admin-organisation: The University of New South Wales
grant-summary: Understanding temporal inequity and its societal impacts in Australia. This project aims to understand how the unequal distribution of time affects people and social groups in Australia by conceptualising and developing a novel framework and measurement index for temporal inequity. The project expects to generate new knowledge in the area of social determinants of health and ageing using an innovative interdisciplinary approach combining social theory, national public datasets, and policy co-design. Expected outcomes include a validated index, open data tools, and policy guidance to measure and reduce time poverty and its impacts. This should provide significant benefits, such as informing fairer work, care, and ageing policies to enhance wellbeing in more equitable ways across Australia’s ageing population.
national-interest-test-statement: This project addresses a growing challenge in Australia: the unequal distribution of time. Many people, especially women and carers, struggle to balance paid work, unpaid care, and rest. Their lack of time erodes wellbeing and contributes to stress and social isolation, which translates into poorer health outcomes with increasing age. Yet Australia has no national measure to quantify temporal inequity and its social and economic costs. This project will fill that gap by developing and applying the Temporal Inequity Measurement Index (TIMI), leveraging national public datasets. The research directly supports the Australian Government’s "Measuring What Matters" Framework (2023), the Fair Work Act (2023-24), and the Gender Equality Strategy (2024), each of which calls for better data on unpaid work, time use and wellbeing. The outcomes will benefit Australians by helping governments and employers design fairer work, care, and ageing policies by enabling measurement where time poverty and its impacts are greatest. It will guide policies that promote health, strengthen families, boost workforce participation and build more inclusive communities. The results will be translated beyond academia through an open data tool and policy briefings for government agencies, such as Treasury and the Department of Social Services. A communication campaign “Making Time for Wellbeing” will engage the general public in understanding how time contributes to a healthier and more equitable future.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Australia’s Tiananmen Generation and Its Remaking of Chinese Culture    . This project situates the cultural products of Australia's Tiananmen Generation in their proper central place in our country's recent history. Accessing the Chinese-language culture produced by the Tiananmen Generation between 1986 and 2001 will show how Chinese migration shaped Australia's image in the world's most-spoken mother tongue. Cultural products made by migrants in Chinese literature, press, and theatre offer a novel view of Australian culture and society from a cohort hungry for expression. However, most of what they wrote and performed remains behind a language barrier, unread and unstudied. With this project, a wider Australian public can access and appreciate what the culture of Chinese migrants has brought to this country.
national-interest-test-statement: Australians need and have a right to genuine access to culture created in any of this country's languages. The multilingual corpus of this country’s culture helps us unlock the many diverse experiences of which our society is comprised. One of the largest and oldest migrant languages in Australia is Chinese, and the men and women who came from mainland China starting from the mid-1980s represent a large, distinct, expressive, and influential group. This project looks at what they wrote and performed in Chinese in various genres, including fiction, theatre, radio plays, and the daily Chinese press. These creative works help us to understand how they reflected on, critiqued, and processed the world they had just left as well as the lives they were building in their new home. This project is especially beneficial because through translation it will provide the means for teachers, students, and general readers to get to know the perspectives and talents of the migrants who came from China to Australia (1986-2001) and consider what that body of work means for Australian culture, identity, and history.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Processable Microporous Membranes for High Temperature Hydrogen Separation. This project aims to develop novel processable microporous membranes to address key challenges in membrane fabrication and practical hydrogen separation, including membrane processing, defect control for scalable manufacture, thermal and mechanical stability. By utilising highly processable metal-organic framework (MOF) glasses, the project will deliver defect-free membranes that operate robustly at high temperatures. Expected outcomes include new fabrication methods for ultrathin MOF membranes, enhanced understanding of hydrogen transport in amorphous microporous networks, and scalable membrane modules. The project will advance Australia’s leadership in sustainable hydrogen technologies and contribute to low-emission manufacturing.
national-interest-test-statement:
Australia has committed to becoming a global hydrogen leader by 2050, producing up to 30 million tonnes annually and building regional hydrogen hubs to drive clean energy exports and industrial decarbonisation. To realise this vision, the country requires cost-effective, energy-efficient hydrogen purification technologies that can operate at industrial conditions. Conventional methods including pressure swing adsorption and cryogenic distillation are energy-intensive and unsuitable for emerging low-emission manufacturing processes.

This project aims to address this critical research gap by developing novel processable microporous membranes that can efficiently separate hydrogen under industrial working conditions. This project is expected to deliver high-performance membranes, scalable membrane fabrication techniques, and stable membrane modules for continuous operation. By enabling more efficient hydrogen purification, this project will strengthen Australia’s position in the global clean-energy supply chain, reduce emissions from heavy industry, and create economic opportunities within hydrogen hubs and regional manufacturing precincts. This project will leverage Australian industry partners to commercialise the developed membranes after the successful completion. The technical outcomes of this project will also be extended to related separations in key Australian hydrogen sectors, including green-ammonia production, hydrogen-based steelmaking, and clean-fuel synthesis.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Indigenous Language Reclamation in Aboriginal Early Childhood Education. This project addresses Indigenous language reclamation in Australian Aboriginal early childhood education by conceptualising a new framework - translingual yarning pedagogy. This innovative framework will combine Western and Aboriginal practices and ways of knowing to advance knowledge in applied linguistics and Aboriginal early childhood education. The expected outcomes of strengthening Aboriginal community-led theory and practice will enhance health and wellbeing, and support the preservation and revitalisation of Aboriginal languages and cultures. By prioritising Aboriginal community leadership, this project will build the resilience of Aboriginal children, families, communities and languages.
national-interest-test-statement: This project advances Indigenous language reclamation in Australian Aboriginal early childhood education by developing an innovative framework - translingual yarning pedagogy. It addresses a critical gap in applied linguistics and Aboriginal education, where Aboriginal children’s linguistic realities are frequently overlooked. By embedding translanguaging pedagogy within Aboriginal practices of yarning, the project will generate new knowledge that strengthens Indigenous language preservation and educational equity. The research will deliver wide-ranging benefits. Socially and culturally, it will reinforce Aboriginal community-led theory and practice, revitalise endangered languages, and preserve cultural heritage. Improved engagement in Aboriginal early childhood education will also enhance long-term wellbeing, health, and life opportunities for Aboriginal children. To maximise impact beyond academia, the project will collaborate closely with Aboriginal communities, educators, and policymakers. Outcomes will be translated into accessible toolkits, workshops, and community resources. Crucially, the project will sustain the curriculum across Aboriginal schools nationwide, ensuring scalability and continuity. It will also establish online language documentation and archival initiatives, and produce books and culturally relevant resources for Aboriginal children. These strategies will ensure lasting, transformative impact in education and community practice.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Universities, freedom of speech and protest: A transnational history. This project uncovers the transnational history of current debates about free speech, academic freedom and protest rights on university campuses across the Anglosphere. With the university’s traditional role as the site of free inquiry and expression seemingly under threat, this project will be the first to examine how this discourse has developed transnationally since the 1960s. Focusing on Australia, the UK and the US (plus Canada and New Zealand), the project will use archival material and oral histories to explore the notion of the university as a contested space. The project will deliver outputs that will provide historical insight to higher education policy and greater understanding of how competing voices on campus have been managed.
national-interest-test-statement:
Universities have become ground zero for debates about free speech, academic freedom and protest globally, with threats being viewed as coming from above (governments or industry) and below (students or activists). However much of this debate has been ahistorical and confined to nation-based narratives. This project will place events on Australian campuses in a historical and transnational context, in comparison with Britain and the US. It will be the first transnational history of free speech, academic freedom and protest across the Anglosphere. It will use archival material, generated by students, universities and policymakers, as well as oral histories and witness seminars, to explore the history of how universities have long been contested spaces.

The project will benefit Australians by highlighting the important role that universities play in liberal democracies as sites of free expression and inquiry. It will expand our knowledge of how threats to free speech and academic freedom have been addressed in the past and how these freedoms have been protected. It will use the recent past to historically inform contemporary debates about social cohesion and freedom of speech in Australia and elsewhere. 

Beyond academic outputs, the project will deliver an open access policy-oriented report and public facing website, with oral history transcripts, primary source documents and educational resources about free speech and academic freedom at universities.

grant-summary: Symmetry in action: novel tools to harness abstraction. Group theory is the mathematical study of symmetry. Groups are best judged by their actions and this project will investigate fundamental questions about how infinite groups act. These questions relate to orderability and rigidity, invertibility, and quantified finite presentability. Symbolic computation, especially the novel application of techniques from computer science such as SAT solving, is key to this project's approach. Expected outcomes include the resolution of major open problems. This project will benefit Australia's strength in pure mathematics research.
national-interest-test-statement: Mathematics underpins modern science and technology such as telecommunications, artificial intelligence and meteorology. A crucial notion both in applications and internal to pure mathematics is that of symmetry. For example, symmetry is central in crystallography, a branch of science linking biology, chemistry and physics. The mathematical subject called group theory studies symmetry through algebraic language. This project will address fundamental gaps in our knowledge of group theory, specifically about how algebraic and geometric aspects of symmetry are connected. This will be achieved through novel application of ideas and tools from different areas of mathematics and theoretical computer science. This keeps Australia at the forefront of research in this crucial subject. The students and early-career researchers in the project will receive in-depth training. This will ensure Australia remains globally competitive and has capacity in quantitative skills. Outreach activities such as public lectures will spread knowledge to a broad audience and increase public understanding of fundamental research.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Making it Count: Closing the Data-Action Gap for Global Gender Equality. Across the world, governments rely on data to advance workplace gender equality, yet progress remains uneven. Counting inequality has not been enough to drive change. This project will transform how gender equality is measured and realised by showing how reporting systems can move from mechanisms of compliance to catalysts for reform. Through comparative research across Australia, France and the United Kingdom, it will generate a transformative framework for gender-data governance globally. Expected outcomes include best-practice guidelines for inclusive data collection, new theoretical insights into how data systems shape equality, and a Global Gender Data Summit uniting experts to drive lasting, systemic and inclusive reform worldwide.
national-interest-test-statement: Around the world, governments and employers are using data to track progress on gender equality. They count pay gaps, promotions, and leadership roles in the hope that measurement will lead to change. Yet despite this growing focus on data, inequality remains. Reporting too often serves compliance needs rather than informing action or reform in workplaces. Understanding how to make gender equality data meaningful and effective is now vital for Australia and other countries aiming to build fairer workplaces. This research will compare gender equality reporting systems in Australia, France, and the United Kingdom to find out why some approaches work and others fall short. It will show how data can be designed and used to create genuine progress rather than compliance alone. The findings will help Australian employers and governments make better use of gender data, supporting the national gender equality strategy and improving fairness and opportunity at work. Results will be shared widely through public reports, media engagement, and a Global Gender Data Summit, ensuring that lessons reach policymakers, businesses, and the wider community. By improving how we measure and act on gender inequality, Australia can lead global efforts to build more inclusive, productive, and equitable workplaces.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Thalamic circuits underlying the sense of touch. This project will define how parallel somatosensory pathways from the spinal cord and brainstem converge and are integrated in the thalamus to encode our tactile world. Using cutting-edge genetic, imaging, and circuit-mapping tools to trace and test these pathways with unprecedented precision, the research will link cellular circuits to network dynamics and behavioural output. By resolving how ascending signals are integrated and transformed within the thalamus, the project will establish a unifying framework for how the brain constructs mechanosensory representations—advancing understanding of perception, and facilitating progress across sensory neuroscience, neural network models and engineering, and brain–machine interface research.
national-interest-test-statement:
Touch is fundamental to our experience of the physical world. These sensations are mediated by several skin receptors that are sensitive to the different physical features we encounter, from gentle caress to strong and potentially damaging events. Together, touch receptor signals must all be processed, integrated, and reassembled in our brain. Current models treat different receptor signals as independent channels, only combining to produce a coherent sensory experience at the highest brain level known as the cortex. This proposal builds on recent discoveries to generate a new model, where the spinal cord and brainstem act as preprocessing hubs, before a central brain region called the thalamus assembles information into a coherent sensory representation that is shared with the cortex.
Experiments combine several advanced neuroscience techniques to deliver fundamental knowledge on how touch signals are transformed into sensory perception and action. The results will be relevant to many fields, including sensory and social neuroscience, motivation, decision making, brain-inspired engineering, and neuroscience-based knowledge economies like sensory prosthetics. Communication of these findings will support Australia’s international standing and advance the broader public’s appreciation of touch and brain function. Inclusion of students in experiments ensures these future leaders are trained in the leading-edge technologies required to advance our understanding of brain function.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Radically Reinventing Light-Driven Synthesis for Chemical Recycling. This project aims to overcome the limits of light-driven chemistry in order to break strong chemical bonds, the main impediment to recycling common plastics. The project will generate new knowledge in sustainable chemical synthesis and demonstrate how challenging high-energy reactions can be driven with low-energy light by instead harnessing the energy stored within chemical additives. Expected outcomes include replacing precious metal catalysts with earth-abundant alternatives and improved methods of chemical recycling, converting common pollutants into useful chemical building blocks. It will guide more sustainable industrial processes and provide significant economic and environmental benefits.
national-interest-test-statement: Plastic is ubiquitous in modern Australia, with 4 million tonnes of waste generated in 2024. While our generated waste grows every year, recovery and recycling remained steady at only 14% in 2024. Existing methods cannot keep up with demand, are costly, inefficient, and generate products of low quality with limited market demand. This project aims to drive the chemical breakdown of plastics by converting visible light into usable energy, similar to the process of photosynthesis in plants. Importantly, this approach avoids relying on precious-metal catalysts. Instead, it uses sustainable alternatives to release the energy stored in simple molecules. This project will benefit Australians by providing sustainable methods to recycle plastic waste. The new technology will be shared with industry and government agencies responsible for managing plastic pollution. The project is expected to generate follow-on economic benefits by converting end-of-life plastic back into simple chemical building blocks, accelerating a circular plastic economy. It will also make use of Australia’s abundant solar energy resources. Beyond scientific publications, project outcomes will be promoted through University media and shared with policy makers within government and industry as well as the national media.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Citizen-making in the 21st Century: The Ethics of Demographic Renewal . This project aims to assess the ethics of demographic renewal, the process by which new citizens join a political community over time. Low fertility rates around the world raise the question of whether it is legitimate and ethical for liberal democracies to adopt pro-natalist polices, thereby encouraging citizens to have more children than they would otherwise. This project expects to generate new knowledge in political philosophy and public policy by developing a new theory of family formation policies. Expected outcomes include an improved understanding of the costs, risks, and benefits of different approaches to demographic renewal. This will provide significant societal benefits, such as tailored policy recommendations for Australia.
national-interest-test-statement: This project addresses the social and economic challenges posed by declining fertility rates around the world, a phenomenon known as depopulation. It explores the ethical dimension of this challenge by developing a theory of legitimate family formation policies for liberal democratic states, one that considers the interests of citizens and non-citizens, as well as the interests of current and future generations. The project will generate significant benefits for Australia by guiding government action in the area of demographic renewal. It will demonstrate that economic factors are only one part of the equation, and that demographic renewal policies must be compatible with gender equality while also creating the conditions for achieving environmental and global justice. The project will deliver cultural benefits by highlighting the complex ethical considerations involved in this policy area and enriching public discussions on depopulation. One of the main outputs will be the publication of a report with public policy recommendations, produced in collaboration with the think tank Think Forward. The project will also influence public policy through public philosophy pieces and a podcast series. These outputs will help Australia respond to depopulation without imposing moral costs on current citizens and without imposing unfair burdens on future citizens, thereby supporting healthy and thriving communities and contributing to building a secure and resilient nation.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Radically Changing Polymers: Embedding Function and Degradability. Radical polymerisation is the main form of plastic fabrication in both fundamental science and industry; but the polymers it yields are non-functional, with non-degradable all-carbon backbones. This project aims to establish a synthesis platform that can build various desired functionalities into the backbone, and targets for on-demand degradation. The polymers would be accessible for disintegrating in response to a specific enzyme, or light of a specific wavelength. These outcomes should be usefully translatable for industrial radical polymerisation, in applications such as styrofoam, adhesives, 3D printing, and dental fillings: with economic and environmental benefits from embedding new functionality, and facilitating breakdown and reuse.
national-interest-test-statement: Modern dental fillings, styrofoam cups, and many 3D-printed objects have one thing in common: they are all produced through a chemical process called radical polymerisation. This accounts for 45% of the world’s plastic fabrication. The process builds materials as long chains of polymers that unfortunately cannot be readily altered, which is why styrofoam is virtually non-degradable under normal environmental conditions. While reinforcing Australian research capability in a vital and economically significant field, this Future Fellowship project aims to deliver a chemistry that can beneficially alter the fundamental building blocks but still relies on the same well-established fabrication techniques. Plastic materials made using this new synthesis platform would interact with targets as required, rather than being inert; and some could degrade in the presence of a specific enzyme or a specific kind of light. As it is based on the existing process of radical polymerisation, the newly developed technology will have the same full range of applications: scientific, industrial, commercial, medical, and so on. But now, on-demand disintegration of the styrofoam cup, many 3D-printed objects, and even dental fillings becomes possible. A filling could be replaced without drilling. Adhesives could be produced that unstick by a convenient designated process: enabling delamination for clean and efficient waste recycling, contributing to a circular economy for lasting environmental benefit.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Enabling a novel photothermal catalytic system for green ammonia synthesis. This project will develop advanced photonic-plasmonic catalysts and efficient photothermal reactors to explore new pathways for producing ammonia from sunlight, nitrogen, and hydrogen under mild conditions. By integrating porous nitride frameworks with oxide and metal components, it will strengthen coupling between light, heat, and reactants to enable effective nitrogen activation. The research will deliver crucial new understanding of how light and heat promote chemical conversion and advance pathways for ammonia synthesis beyond conventional thermal processes. It will drive new catalyst and reactor design, open new opportunities for photothermal catalysis, and support Australia’s transition toward clean energy and sustainable industries.
national-interest-test-statement:
This Fellowship research focuses on new ways to synthesize ammonia using sunlight, nitrogen, and hydrogen under mild conditions. Ammonia is essential for food production and is also an emerging energy carrier. In industry, it is mainly produced through the fossil-fuel-intensive Haber–Bosch process, which releases significant carbon emissions. By developing porous plasmonic materials and designing solar-powered photothermal reactors, this project will generate the discoveries and technology breakthroughs needed to advance ammonia production with much lower energy use and without direct greenhouse gas emissions.
Australia has abundant sunlight and strong expertise in catalysis and materials research, making it exceptionally well placed to lead in solar-driven chemical processes. The outcomes of this Fellowship will lay the groundwork for next-generation renewable energy conversion and future green ammonia technologies – contributing to national priorities across clean energy, Net-Zero, and advanced manufacturing. Further, students embedded in this innovative research will bolster Australia’s materials science and clean energy workforce.
Project findings will be shared openly with other researchers, and with industry and broader audiences, through publications, workshops, and outreach activities, with IP protection and licensing considered where there is commercial potential. These plans aim to maximise Australian benefit through a tiered strategy of knowledge transfer.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary:
Taming the Phase Energetics of Disordered Perovskite Semiconductors. The on-going expansion of new semiconductor technologies which source, detect and control light has reshaped human existence. Promising next-generation optical materials exist, known as halide perovskites, however they are typically unstable under real-world operating conditions. This project aims to understand and control the
fundamental mechanisms of destabilisation through several different crystal engineering strategies and demonstrate stable light-emitting and -detecting device prototypes. The expected outcomes include the realisation of new stabilisation methods which align with the scaled production of functional perovskite thin-film devices, which will directly impact the future success of these materials and related technologies.
national-interest-test-statement: According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), Australia’s dependence on non-renewable energy generation – like the burning of coal and natural gas – has seen no significant decrease in the past ten years, which contributes directly to global warming. Further, approximately 20% of the electricity is used for lighting loads. This project will help develop a next-generation optical material, known as halide perovskite semiconductors, which are cheap and easy to make, as well as capable of effectively converting light into electricity, and electricity into light. While these materials are relatively new to this area of science and have shown great promise, they suffer from stability issues which have thus far hindered real-world applications and widespread adoption. This project aims at developing new and innovative ways of making these materials stable and demonstrate their functionality within working device prototypes. Market-relevant intellectual property will be secured under an Australian banner via project outcomes that are compatible with existing semiconductor industry standards. This will help claim Australia’s position within the competitive scientific spotlight, open emerging optoelectronics markets, and allow device engineers to move beyond older semiconductor technologies, like silicon, which have become stagnant with respect to realising the National Interest of ever more efficient and energy conservative optical devices.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Toughing out drought: identifying molecular mechanisms for plant survival. This project aims to identify genes that enhance drought survival in conifers (cone-bearing trees), focusing on radiata pine, Australia’s most widely planted softwood species. With climate change intensifying drought severity, understanding how trees survive water stress is critical to future-proofing Australia’s $23b forestry industry. This project expects to characterise hormone dynamics, effects of drought memory on vascular development, and genes underpinning drought resilience using advanced imaging and sequencing. Expected outcomes of this project include identifying molecular markers for drought resistant varieties. This should provide significant benefits for Australia’s forestry breeding programs, guiding plantation hardiness.
national-interest-test-statement: Australian forestry systems and iconic ecosystems are under threat from increased drought severity and frequency due to climate change, exacerbating the critical timber shortage. Trees provide invaluable environmental, social and cultural benefits, as well as significant economic value, supply chain security and carbon capture. Conifers are the oldest surviving tree lineages in Australia and play a key role in our $23b forestry industry, supplying the structural timber market. Despite their importance, the genetic and physiological traits underlying drought resistance in conifers remain poorly understood. This project will investigate how conifers, especially the drought-sensitive dominant forestry species radiata pine, respond to drought at the molecular level. By uncovering the biological mechanisms underlying drought resilience, the findings will help to identify genetic markers to guide breeding and selection of hardier varieties, accelerating the development of climate-ready forestry systems. This will support sustainable plantation planning in drier regions, timber supply security, and long-term industry viability. To maximise impact and national benefit, findings will be shared widely with forestry industry partners – Tree Breeding Australia and the Radiata Pine Breeding Company – for rapid implementation into breeding programs, the international research community, and the broader public, through talks, media outreach, social media and open-access publications.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Next-Generation Lithium-CO2 Batteries: From Greenhouse Gas to Clean Energy. Lithium-CO2 (Li-CO2) batteries represent a transformative technology capable of directly converting greenhouse gases into clean electricity with high energy densities, offering a promising pathway toward carbon neutrality. However, their practical development has been hindered by major challenges, including low capacity, poor efficiency, and limited stability. This project aims to develop new functional composite solid-state electrolytes with gradient structures, to produce stable, efficient, and durable Li-CO2 batteries, using industrial flue gas as feedstock. This project is expected to facilitate the commercialisation of next-generation Li-CO2 batteries and to develop energy storage devices to benefit both the economy and environment.
national-interest-test-statement: Australia’s transition to net-zero emissions requires new technologies that can both store renewable energy and reduce carbon pollution. This project will develop solid-state lithium-CO2 (Li-CO2) batteries that can directly capture and convert CO2 from industrial flue gas into stored electrical energy. It addresses a major gap in the nation’s energy and climate strategy: CO2 cannot be directly utilised to generate clean electricity, and existing capture methods are costly and inefficient. By designing functional composite solid-state electrolytes, this research aims to create safe, high-efficiency batteries that operate across wide operation conditions and release pure CO2 on charging for conversion to high-value chemicals and fuels (CO, ethylene, ethanol) through a tandem electrocatalysis process, achieving a closed-loop carbon-energy cycle. The outcomes will benefit Australians through clean energy storage, reduced emissions, and new economic opportunities in sustainable manufacturing and carbon recycling industries. Beyond academia, the project will engage industry partners, government agencies, and the wider community through prototype demonstrations, public science communication, and collaboration with clean-energy initiatives. These activities will accelerate the translation of research outcomes into commercial applications, supporting Australia’s leadership in carbon-neutral energy technologies, and contributing to its long-term environmental and economic resilience.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Build Back Better? Threats and Opportunities for Vaccination Governance. This project investigates post-pandemic threats to vaccination governance arising from politics, policies, and institutions. It aims to understand how governments react and prepare. The project focuses on Australia, France, Italy and the US, which share many features of vaccination governance. The goal is to develop a framework for interpreting threats, opportunities, and responses. This supports researchers and policymakers to address emergent problems including right-wing resistance; non-implementation of policies; and governments leading anti- vaccination activities. Outputs include journal articles; a book; policy briefs; “roadshow” presentations; a stakeholder workshop; and translations of findings-in-progress during data collection.
national-interest-test-statement: Resistance towards vaccination policies threatens societies and economies in Australia and abroad, posing challenges for routine governance and situating us poorly for future pandemics. Overseas, political leaders are directly mobilising public institutions to discredit vaccines and empower proponents of misinformation; in the US, governments are also dismantling policies that drive uptake of childhood vaccines. These measures fracture the social order in which vaccinations protect the functioning of educational institutions, workforces and businesses. Australia’s strong bipartisan immunisation policies not make us immune from such threats. Our far right is already mobilised against vaccines following the pandemic; policies also face risks from not being implemented on the ground. Australia needs to prepare. This project examines threats to vaccination governance at political, policy and institutional levels. It engages in comparative research across 4 high-income countries (Australia, France, Italy and the US) to explore government capacities and strategies to manage threats. The project also investigates new opportunities for vaccination governance, engaging with Australia’s Centre for Disease Control and exploring how US states are standing up new technical advisory groups. Project findings and recommendations are shared iteratively with Australian government departments and agencies.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Decoding the neuromuscular mechanisms of locomotor energetics across scales. Movement is our most prized possession. This project aims to decode the neuromuscular mechanisms that govern the energetic cost of movement across structural, spatial, and temporal scales. Via integrating experiments, models, and bio-inspired devices, the project expects to generate new knowledge of how neural control, muscle–tendon structure, and body size interact to shape locomotor efficiency across species and the human lifespan. Expected outcomes include new energetic models to predict energy use and bio-inspired assistive devices to improve movement efficiency. This will benefit science, industry, and society by driving innovations that enhance human performance, restore mobility, and inspire next-generation wearable technologies.
national-interest-test-statement: Movement is something we often take for granted—until we lose it. Understanding how muscles convert energy into motion holds the key to improving movement efficiency and creating technologies that keep people moving and communities thriving. This fellowship will reveal how neural control, muscle-tendon structure, and body size interact to determine the energy required for movement across different animals and as humans age. By integrating experiments, computer models, and wearable assistive devices, the project will generate new knowledge critical to our understanding of energy use during everyday movements. The outcomes will provide insights for robotics and bioengineering industries, which may support the design of exoskeletons and prosthetics that reduce movement costs in older adults, enhance mobility in people with neuromuscular disease, or improve athletic performance. By creating more accurate energy models, this research could improve health monitoring technologies, such as smart watches, to more carefully track the calories we burn to move. By integrating animal models with innovations in human biomechanics, muscle and neurophysiology, and computational modelling, this project positions Australia to lead world-class discoveries in comparative biomechanics, revealing how animals, past and present, move efficiently. To ensure the research has widespread impact, outcomes will be shared through scientific publications, industry collaborations and community engagement.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Liquid Metal Based High Entropy Catalysts. This project aims to explore and design advanced catalysts for key reactions of economic and environmental significance, including the manufacture of ammonia, methane coupling with carbon dioxide and hydrogen synthesis, by harnessing the properties of liquid metals. The project expects to generate new knowledge in understanding how liquid metals can be used in synthesis and how the composition of complex alloy catalysts affects their activity. The expected outcomes are new catalysts that will support the transition towards sustainable chemical industries. This project should benefit Australia in tackling big challenges like emissions reduction, minimising energy consumption and turning greenhouse gases into valuable products.
national-interest-test-statement:
This project will examine and develop new materials to address two critical problems that our society is facing: greenhouse gas emissions and the sustainable production of useful chemicals. One of these is ammonia, a core ingredient of fertilisers and a hydrogen storage medium.
Producing ammonia requires hydrogen and a lot of energy, leading to the release of vast amounts of carbon dioxide. This project will create new systems for manufacturing both ammonia and hydrogen. A further platform chemical that will be produced is ethylene which is used for making plastics. This project will develop a new pathway to produce ethylene that uses the greenhouse gases carbon dioxide and methane as starting materials. All three investigated reaction products, namely hydrogen, ammonia and ethylene, will employ a new range of catalysts that will be produced with the help of liquid metals. All catalysts will contain several active chemical elements which can act in unison, and by doing so, boost performance and make chemical reactions more efficient. This will help Australia to meet its ambitious climate targets by turning greenhouse gases into products and facilitating the production and storage of hydrogen. By leveraging existing and new links with industry, the results from this project are expected to be adopted by the fertiliser production industry, the natural and biogas industry and the emerging hydrogen industry.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Structural basis of choline transport throughout the brain. The brain relies on a constant nutrient supply to function properly. Choline is one such essential diet-derived nutrient: it is crucial for generating new brain cells, insulating neurons, and supporting blood vessel formation. However, it remains unclear how choline crosses the brain’s protective barrier to deliver these vital benefits. This Fellowship aims to uncover how choline moves into the brain and between its cells, and expects to generate new knowledge that will benefit our understanding of brain development and healthy brain health. The outcomes should provide fundamental insights into nutrient transport across the blood-brain barrier.
national-interest-test-statement:
Choline is an essential nutrient that must be obtained through the diet (e.g., from eggs, fish, and broccoli). It is a recommended supplement during pregnancy to support foetal brain development, and an adequate choline supply remains critical throughout life to support cognitive function and healthy aging. 
This Fellowship aims to uncover how choline is transported into the brain and between its millions of cells to provide fundamental insights into its roles in development and lifelong brain health. While well beyond the scope of this Fellowship, these discoveries may inform future research into disorders such as Alzheimer’s disease, which is linked to reduced brain choline levels. By 2050, an estimated 1.2 million Australians will be living with Alzheimer’s disease, imposing a substantial economic burden projected to exceed $17 billion annually. The knowledge generated through this project may also open new avenues for delivering drugs into the brain – a long-standing bottleneck in neurotherapeutic development that contributes to the $74 billion annual economic burden of brain disorders in Australia. Finally, this Fellowship will provide a platform for training the next generation of Australian scientists in Nobel Prize-winning techniques and enhance Australia’s research capacity through international collaborations.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Understanding how heat drives human aggression. There is evidence of a strong relationship between excess heat and human aggression, but how and why this happens remains unanswered. As such, Australia is not ready to tackle the increases in aggression that are occurring as climate change accelerates extreme heat events. This project aims to answer how and why excess heat increases aggression by leveraging digital technology to collect real-world data on heat and human behaviour. This project expects to generate critical new knowledge in an underaddressed area of climate change impacts, enabling significant benefits such as allowing policymakers to optimise mitigation strategies to reduce and prevent heat-related aggression.
national-interest-test-statement: Climate change is now inevitable: the question for policy makers is how to mitigate the worst effects, which include the impacts from heatwaves and other excess heat conditions. Humans have long made the connection between increased heat and aggression, yet ethical and practical challenges in this field of research mean there is no evidence around how and why heat drives aggression. This knowledge gap means that Australia is not properly prepared for the climate-change induced heat changes that are steadily worsening. This project will leverage new technology that can collect data on human behaviour and heat in the real world, as it happens, in order to unpack this relationship. We will collaborate with front-line aggression workers (e.g. mental health clinicians, first responders, family and domestic violence services) and climate change policy officers, to interpret and contextualise research findings.  The findings will be the essential evidence base needed to develop future heat-specific interventions, including in homes, on the roads, in workplaces, and in public health warnings, which will be valuable to Australia socially and economically, as increased likelihood of aggression and associated violence has substantial personal, societal, and economic harm. Results will be disseminated through media engagement, public lectures, and direct targeted outreach with frontline services, ensuring the research outcomes reach the Australian communities most likely to benefit.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Collaborative Intelligence: Harnessing Foundation and Specialist Models. This project aims to develop an innovative collaborative intelligence framework that integrates the broad knowledge of large foundation models with the rapid adaptability of specialist small models to deliver accurate, reliable, and efficient solutions. The research will advance knowledge discovery and model design by exploring the general knowledge embedded in foundation models to help specialist models adapt quickly to specific domains, thereby significantly reducing the demand of large datasets and intensive computation. The expected outcomes will benefit a wide range of applications, such as combating emerging misinformation and abnormal events, and accelerate the sustainable adoption of advanced technologies across Australian industry.
national-interest-test-statement:
This project is developing a system that combines large, general-purpose artificial intelligence (AI) models with smaller, specialised ones. These models work together using a method called collaborative intelligence to deliver accurate results while using less energy. Current foundation models are powerful but often impractical for Australian industries due to their enormous data and computation demands in training. Addressing this critical gap, this research will pioneer methods that reduce dependence on massive data and costly infrastructure, enabling AI systems to be affordable and tailored to Australia’s needs. 
The outcomes will benefit several key sectors: In healthcare, the research will advance novel methods that can be later applied to develop early diagnosis and prevention tools. In society, it will strengthen Australia’s ability to address the growing risks of misinformation from emerging digital media, protecting communities from misunderstanding and harmful influence. In industry, the framework will lower the cost and barriers to adopting advanced technologies, particularly for small and medium-sized enterprises. 
To maximise the impact of the research beyond academia, findings will be shared through industry partnerships, training workshops, public outreach activities and collaboration with government organisations, enabling Australian businesses, communities, and policymakers to directly benefit from the project’s outcomes.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Palaeoclimate Constraints on High Latitude Climate Sensitivity. The mismatch between climate models and observations undermines confidence in climate prediction. This project aims to determine why climate models of past warm periods consistently underestimate temperatures at high latitudes compared to geological evidence. Using the best analogue for the climate expected by the end of this century—the Pliocene (~3.2 million years ago)—this project tests the three leading hypotheses for data-model mismatch. It develops and employs novel and established climate methods at well-dated Arctic sites for targeted data-model comparison. The insights gained will reduce uncertainty in climate sensitivity, helping to predict climate tipping points and guiding climate change mitigation and adaptation.
national-interest-test-statement:
Australia’s future climate resilience—in a nation prone to drought, fire, flood, and sea-level rise—depends on accurate climate prediction. A major source of uncertainty in climate prediction is how sensitive the high latitudes are to greenhouse gas concentrations. Most tipping points for abrupt, self-reinforcing climate change involve high latitude processes, thus high latitude uncertainty affects Australian climate projections. Climate models disagree with reconstructed Arctic warmth in past warm periods, and it is not known why.

This project addresses why climate models and data disagree on Arctic warming. It examines three potential causes by applying palaeoclimate tools to a warm period in Earth’s past, analogous to conditions expected by 2100. By reducing uncertainty at high latitudes, and so in prediction, this research supports climate-informed planning for infrastructure key to Australia’s climate resilience, such as water storage, flood mitigation and coastal protection, and enhanced projections of ecosystem change for conservation management. These outcomes will benefit Australian communities, industries and policymakers preparing for climate extremes, with project findings to be shared across diverse media for wide reach. 

Australia looks to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) to shape our climate policy. Project results will directly inform the IPCC and uptake by climate modelling networks will impact both policy and climate model development.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
current-admin-organisation: The University of New South Wales
announcement-admin-organisation: The University of New South Wales
grant-summary: Biocatalytic Reticular Chemistry for Environmental Remediation. This project aims to develop highly active and selective biocatalytic reticular frameworks for per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) remediation via a novel solvent- and energy-free synthesis strategy integrated with enzyme immobilization. It tackles key limitations of current biocatalysts, including non-biocompatible synthesis methods, limited substrate selectivity, and reduced catalytic efficiency. The anticipated outcomes will advance manufacturing, environmental remediation, and nanotechnology, directly supporting Australia’s transition to a net zero future and the protection and restoration of its environment, while reinforcing the nation’s global leadership in advanced materials and sustainable environmental technologies.
national-interest-test-statement: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are persistent synthetic pollutants linked to chronic diseases such as kidney disease and testicular cancer. Widely used in firefighting foams, stain-resistant coatings, and non-stick cookware, PFAS are now common in Australian waterways, drinking water, surface water and groundwater. Current treatment technologies often fail to fully remove them, posing ongoing health risks. This project aims to revolutionise environmental remediation technologies by developing advanced biocatalytic materials capable of simultaneously capturing and degrading harmful PFAS. It will deliver breakthroughs in nanomaterial design, offering sustainable, cost-effective, and reliable solutions to improve water, soil, and air quality. These outcomes align with Australia’s multi-billion-dollar investments in modern manufacturing and environmental remediation, directly contributing to the nation’s transition to a net zero future and environmental protection. To commercialise these disruptive biocatalytic nanomaterials, I will pursue licensing agreements with Australian manufacturing and water treatment industries, enhancing Australia’s global leadership in advanced materials and sustainable environmental technologies.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
current-admin-organisation: The University of New South Wales
announcement-admin-organisation: The University of New South Wales
grant-summary: New generation of strategic models to evaluate new mobility technologies. The pandemic fundamentally disrupted transport patterns through widespread remote work, rapid growth in e-shopping, and unsustainable energy use, revealing urgent gaps in current infrastructure models. This project advances transport modelling theory by creating flexible and efficient formulations that better capture how agents and systems interact. By integrating diverse multimodal data, it delivers adaptable modelling specifications, moving beyond prefabricated ones. Importantly, the framework can incorporate information from all types of data sources, ensuring evidence-based policy and guiding the right investment strategies. The outcome is a transformative modelling method equipping planners with resilient, future-ready decision tools.
national-interest-test-statement:
Travel patterns have shifted dramatically in recent years. The pandemic accelerated wprk from home, boosted online shopping, and reshaped travel demand, while new technologies such as electric vehicles and the prospect of autonomous transport are rapidly changing how people and goods move. Yet, the planning tools we currently use are limited and cannot fully account for these realities. Existing approaches often rely on a single model specification, which risks producing results that are too narrow or sensitive to small changes in data.
This project will create a flexible and adaptive modelling framework that better reflects today’s complex transport systems and the choices people make within them. It will draw on a wide variety of data sources and incorporate multiple competing model specifications, ensuring more reliable and robust results. With this capability, contemporary issues such as carbon pricing, alternative fuel taxation, and strategies for building sustainable, efficient, and user-friendly cities can be assessed with greater confidence.
Importantly, the models developed through this project will be open-source, allowing transport agencies to adopt or integrate them into the existing systems. By providing planners and policymakers with tools that reflect real-world behaviour and rapid technological change, this project will support evidence-based decisions and guide investments toward resilient, future-ready urban transport systems both in Australia and globally.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Fire, rock art and the Indigenous creation of Country . Fire is an essential partner in human life. By centering fire as cultural practice linked to rock art, this project seeks insight into how Indigenous people used fire to create, mark and maintain Country and rock art estates from deep time until today. By braiding Archaeology, Indigenous Knowledge and GIS Story Mapping at six rock art landscapes in northern Australia and southern Africa I will reposition our perception of fire as a growing global threat, to being an artefact, ally and ancestor. This insight reformulates problematic nature-centric government fire management practices relevant to rock art management. Outputs will include interactive fire archaeology maps, oral knowledge recording apps, micro-credentials, and public outreach.
national-interest-test-statement: Fire is a growing threat to Australian and global cultural heritage – especially rock art. But fire is also an artefact and ally. Work with Indigenous partners and government officials at six rock art cultural landscapes in northern Australia and southern Africa, including two UNESCO World Heritage Sites, will show the long history of how fire was used to create rock art images, sites and narratives. This research will advance our understanding of hunter-gatherers as large-scale land managers and ecoscapers from deep time until today. Collaborative work will directly address national science and research priorities and fill crucial gaps in climate change heritage management policies by contextualising fire as a cultural and a natural phenomenon. Mapping sites and recording fire stories will aid inter-generational learning using bespoke micro-credentials that recognise existing skills and upskill Rangers, youth and land managers as next generation heritage leaders. Multi-way learning will be supported with interactive heritage recording and risk assessment maps and apps. This research will pioneer measurements to cost carbon credits and offsets for field and lab work, while measuring the mental and cultural health of project participants. Scientific findings will be centrally housed in a public web-based Story Map, with monthly communication through a project blog, radio, television, social media, National Science Week, and at on-Country workshops for schools and communities.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: A nature repair plan for agricultural productivity and biodiversity. This project aims to produce an evidence-based plan to restore Australian agricultural regions to maximise agricultural productivity and biodiversity conservation, in line with international commitments. This is urgently needed to address biodiversity decline, land degradation and threats to Australian and global food security. Expected outcomes include detailed knowledge of the relationships between cover of native vegetation, insect-eating bat and bird communities and their capacity to deliver control of crop pests; and a detailed map pinpointing where restoration would be of greatest benefit. Significant benefits include enhanced agricultural productivity, reduced reliance on pesticides, and biodiversity conservation are expected.
national-interest-test-statement: Ongoing land degradation and environmental decline threaten the living systems on which we depend, namely agriculture and native ecosystems. In addition, Australia is heavily reliant on pesticides to produce our food, which poses serious threats to both environmental and human health. The Australian Government has recognised that a nature repair plan is needed for biodiversity, and to meet global commitments. However, the optimal design for nature repair that would boost the health of our native ecosystems and increase food security, and reduce our need for pesticides, is not yet known. This project aims to investigate the relationship between native vegetation and agricultural productivity, and the native vegetation configurations that support native animals such as bats and birds to control agricultural pests. By determining the ideal amount and arrangement of native vegetation, recommendations can be made on where to focus on native vegetation repair. This project will be designed and implemented in partnership with farmers, natural resource managers and state government to design a nature repair plan with needs of all stakeholders in mind. Expected economic benefits include substantial reductions in crop pest damage and reduced input costs. Expected environmental benefits include repair of degraded landscapes and greater conservation of biodiversity in agricultural landscapes.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Water-Proof: Exporting Australian water expertise to the world since 1949. This project aims to deliver the first comprehensive history of water in Australian foreign aid since 1949, analysing how past initiatives can inform present and future programs and policies. This project expects to generate new knowledge in understanding Australia’s evolving role in global water aid and how historical experience can shape ethical, sustainable, and effective development practices. Expected outcomes of this project include new historical insights and policy tools to strengthen the design and delivery of Australian water aid. This should provide significant benefits, such as enhancing policymaking, capacity-building to improve regional water security, and reinforcing Australia’s leadership in tackling the global water crisis.
national-interest-test-statement: Australia has a long history of supporting water security in our region. Despite this, our expertise in water management is often overlooked and underutilised in international development responses. Sharing this knowledge can help address global water security challenges, promote climate-resilient development, and strengthen regional ties. Using archival methods and interviews to study the development and impact of Australian water aid projects since 1949, this project will identify the challenges and opportunities associated with delivering water aid programs overseas. It will document how Australian water expertise has worked in the past with key partners (Papua New Guinea, Indonesia, India, Jordan and Viet Nam), and synthesise guidance to support future responses. Domestic and international workshops with representatives from government and the humanitarian sector, a virtual exhibition, and public reports and policy forums will transfer the project’s lessons to guide the next wave of policy development in water aid. Through its uptake in government and the humanitarian sector, this knowledge exchange will build urgently needed capability, delivering water aid programs that are cost-effective and fit for purpose. By cementing Australia’s leadership in water security, this project will help to safeguard the liveability of our region and strengthen climate-resilient development in the Indo-Pacific.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Characterising the neuromuscular junction to modulate muscle function. This project aims to characterise the neuromuscular junction, a highly specialised region where the nervous system connects to, and communicates with skeletal muscle. We will characterise changes in this communication to understand how these mechanisms modulate and impact muscle function. This is significant because a fundamental understanding of the mechanisms controlling skeletal muscle function has extremely broad benefits in fields ranging from exercise-, life-sciences, and anti-ageing to agriculture and meat production.
national-interest-test-statement: A fundamental understanding of the mechanisms controlling skeletal muscle function is a critical research question that has broad applications and massive financial potential to the Australian economy. This project introduces a new paradigm by studying and targeting the neuromuscular junction, a specialised and small region that connects the nervous system to skeletal muscle. Using brand-new technology to study this unique region that is available only to my research team, we have identified several exciting new mechanisms that appear to be vital for the communication between neurons and skeletal muscle. This project seeks to expand our knowledge and investigate if we can manipulate these mechanisms to modulate muscle function. This is highly relevant to settings of muscle wasting and Australia’s ageing population as maintaining skeletal function is key to movement and healthy ageing. This fundamental knowledge could also lead to better livestock production and athletic performance. We will share our results at national and international conferences, in leading journals and in community media outlets, social media and public events.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Building climate adaptation capacity through frontline workforce knowledge. This project investigates how frontline workers in Australia develop and apply practical knowledge about climate risks to support households and communities. Workforces routinely exposed to extreme weather, energy poverty and infrastructure failures develop place-based adaptive practices that formal adaptation planning overlooks. Focusing on home-based care and municipal maintenance workers, the research examines how adaptive knowledge and skills develop and circulate across different sectors and contextual conditions. Outcomes include a co-designed toolkit for integrating workforce knowledge into adaptation governance, evidence-based recommendations for supporting workers, and new understandings of climate adaptation as everyday work.
