national-interest-test-statement: As climate impacts intensify, Australia needs adaptation strategies that build on existing community capacities. Yet little is known about the knowledge and skills workers develop while managing climate risks daily at household and community scales. Home-based care and municipal maintenance workers routinely face climate and energy challenges – from extreme heat and energy poverty to infrastructure failures – generating practical, place-based adaptive responses often overlooked in formal planning. This project focuses on these frontline workforces to understand how they develop and apply practical knowledge of climate risks to support vulnerable households and communities. The research benefits Australia by documenting how workers respond to climate vulnerabilities across diverse regional contexts, how this knowledge circulates within and between workforces, and what organisational and geographical conditions enable or constrain adaptive capacity. Findings will provide evidence to better support essential frontline workers and strengthen Australia’s capacity to respond to intensifying climate impacts. Outcomes include improved understanding of the adaptation work already embedded in essential services, and co-designed approaches for integrating frontline workforce knowledge into adaptation governance. These outcomes will be shared with care organisations, local councils and government agencies, ensuring research informs adaptation planning.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Intelligent Platform for Wastewater Emission Control. This project aims to address fundamental issues with current models for simulating nitrous oxide (N2O) emissions in biological wastewater processes. This project expects to generate new knowledge in the area of hybrid N2O modelling and integration of machine learning algorithms. Expected outcomes include an intelligent platform that enables water utilities to optimise operations for real-time reduction of greenhouse gases from sewage treatment processes. This should provide significant benefits, supporting the water industry to maximise infrastructure utilisation, underpinning net-zero emission goals by 2050.
national-interest-test-statement:
Nitrous oxide (N2O) is a potent greenhouse gas with a global warming potential 273 times that of carbon dioxide. The wastewater sector is the second-largest contributor to global N2O emissions, accounting for up to 90% of the total carbon footprint of sewage treatment plants. However, emission reduction in sewage treatment plants is hindered by a lack of reliable modelling tools for reliable long-term emission simulation and effective real-time decision-making. 

Utilising real-time plant data enables the creation of a digital solution - N2O soft sensors - as an alternative to expensive physical N2O sensors. By integrating this hybrid model into treatment plant systems, a comprehensive decision-making framework can be established, enabling water utilities to optimise their operation in real-time

The newly developed intelligent platform will provide tools and operational guidance for real-time process optimization, supporting the Australian and global water industry in achieving net-zero emission goals by 2050 and advancing the scientific foundation for hybrid modelling framework in the general bio-process field.

The research outcomes will be shared widely through the strong collaboration the team has with wastewater industries nationally to support policy makers, environmental regulators, and practitioners. Broadly, press releases, public lectures, public seminars, and various social media channels and online science blogs, will be used to disseminate the outcomes.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Building Financial Resilience Against Manipulative Digital Design. Australians’ ability to make considered choices online is increasingly undermined by manipulative “dark nudge” designs (e.g., false urgency, hidden costs), that exploit cognitive biases and drive over spending. This project addresses this pressing issue by generating new knowledge on how different consumer groups respond to digital dark nudges, informing the design and testing of behaviourally informed, personalised interventions. Outcomes include innovative digital tools that enhance informed decisions and build transferable skills for navigating coercive online platforms. This research will bring an innovative, preventative approach to inclusive consumer protection policy and practice, advancing digital capability and financial wellbeing.
national-interest-test-statement:
Financial stress affects over one in three Australians and costs the economy about $45 billion annually through lost productivity, reduced savings and higher health and welfare demand. As online shopping, gambling and gaming expand, people are increasingly exposed to manipulative design practices that push them to spend more than they intend. Despite rising global concern, there is little empirical evidence on how to equip consumers to recognise and combat these influences.
This Fellowship will address the critical knowledge gap and develop new digital tools to help Australians make more informed and confident online decisions. The tools will allow people see a clear picture of their spending, learn how digital platforms influence their choices and build everyday skills to manage money wisely. Unlike existing tools, this will offer personalised, real-time support via an interactive dashboard tailored to users’ goals and contexts based on their own spend data. The tools will be co-designed with consumers and professionals to ensure they are practical, accessible and relevant, especially for young people and lower-income households most affected by financial stress, producing system-wide benefits. 
The findings will be shared with government, regulators, and financial counsellors via white paper, a cross-sector symposium, project website, and professional social network, supporting more ethical digital environments and strengthening Australia’s financial and digital resilience.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Dynamic Cloaks in Nonplanar Mechanical Metamaterials. This project aims to develop programmable mechanical invisibility, known as cloaks, in nonplanar metamaterials with controlled nonlinear behaviours, which can shield internal areas against external disturbances under diverse dynamic loading conditions. While cloaking strategies remain largely confined to static regimes, limiting their practical impact, the project will use a dynamic framework to integrate the design and manufacturing of metamaterials for switching tasks in response to a determined stimulus. The outcomes will establish a new paradigm of programmable mechanical cloaks with broad impact in soft robotics, aerospace, impact protection, and adaptive infrastructure beyond the reach of conventional manufacturing.
national-interest-test-statement: This project will create new knowledge in advanced manufacturing by developing materials that can make certain parts of a structure protected from forces and vibrations, so protected regions remain undisturbed, even under variable loads and conditions. Current cloaking technologies only work in limited fixed static settings, which restricts their use. Using advanced additive manufacturing, this project will design and develop dynamic cloaks that adapt their behaviour in real time, shielding structures from stress, vibration, or impact while maintaining performance. In aerospace and defence, cloaking materials could protect sensitive equipment and improve safety. In healthcare, they could make implants and protective devices that distribute forces more evenly and reduce failure risks. In civil and infrastructure applications, cloaking could help create safer, longer-lasting materials that resist shocks and extreme conditions. In the long term, it will help produce customised solutions locally, such as wearable devices for aged care and protective materials for defence. This approach will reduce waste, shorten supply chains, and enable sustainable production, aligning with Australia's priorities in advanced manufacturing. This project will help strengthen Australia’s position in programmable material technologies globally and, through collaboration with industry partners and public engagement, could be translated into real-world products for Australian industries.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Exploiting bacterial nickel dependence for antibacterial agent discovery. Nickel is important for the ability of bacteria to cause disease. This project aims to provide a detailed understanding of how nickel is imported into bacterial cells and will generate new knowledge about how nickel and other metals are transported across cell membranes. Other expected outcomes of this work include enhanced national capacity in advanced microscopy and membrane protein methods through training of emerging researchers. By investigating novel antibacterial targets, this work could lead to the future development of new antibacterial therapies, delivering economic and social benefits across healthcare, agriculture, and biotechnology sectors.
national-interest-test-statement: Bacteria have developed ways of protecting themselves against current antibacterial agents, resulting in antibacterial resistance. This is a growing challenge for various sectors, including health and agriculture, and new ways of treating and preventing infections are needed to aid in our fight against bacterial infections. One promising approach is to target the systems bacteria use to bring nickel into their cells, as nickel is important for their survival. This project will generate fundamental knowledge about how bacteria uptake nickel, laying the foundations for future development of new antibacterial agents that target this process. The development of new antibacterial agents will have substantial economic and social benefits for Australia. For example, they would reduce the burden of resistant infections in healthcare, which in 2020 caused over 1,000 deaths and cost the economy an estimated $470 million. The outcomes from this project will be shared with other researchers who may build upon the findings, the public, and the health and agriculture sectors through standard and social media.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Next-Gen Cyborg Insects: From Neuromechanics to Real-World Navigation. Collapsed buildings, dense vegetation and fragile ecosystems create environments that current robots cannot navigate. This project aims to investigate how insects sense instability and adapt movement in complex terrain to develop small, low-power cyborg insects for search and rescue and environmental monitoring. It is expected to generate new knowledge on the sensory and neural mechanisms that support climbing, stabilisation and obstacle negotiation. Desired outcomes include neural, biomechanical and behavioural datasets that inform adaptive control systems. Benefits include improved emergency-response capability, low-disturbance ecological monitoring and advances in insect neurobiology and biohybrid robotics.
national-interest-test-statement: Australia faces increasing challenges in disaster response and environmental conservation as extreme weather and habitat pressures intensify, and many critical environments, such as collapsed buildings, unstable rubble, dense vegetation and fragile ecosystems, remain inaccessible to current technologies. To address this limitation, this project aims to develop cyborg insects that combine insects’ natural agility with miniature sensors to navigate confined and hazardous spaces, while also uncovering how insect nervous systems detect instability and adapt movement in complex terrain. By linking biological insight with engineering design, the research is expected to generate new understanding of sensory and neural mechanisms and produce low-power cyborg insect systems capable of detecting survivors, heat, gas leaks and structural hazards in places unreachable by drones or robots. These advances will support terrain-aware control systems, validated prototypes and datasets for future innovation in robotics and environmental sensing. Together, these outcomes will strengthen Australia’s search-and-rescue capability, benefiting Australia's Disaster Assistance Response Team (DART), which faces significant risk during overseas deployments, and provide new tools for low-disturbance ecological monitoring. The project also builds sovereign capability in advanced manufacturing and biohybrid robotics while training Australia’s first specialists in this emerging field.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Metabolic and post-translational rhythms in circadian physiology. Circadian clocks operate in all body tissues, coordinating physiological processes. Yet it remains unclear how these tissue clocks communicate. This project aims to investigate how metabolism regulates 24-hour rhythms in protein secretion to coordinate physiological processes. Using molecular, imaging, and computational approaches, the research will test how rhythmic glycogen breakdown, a key energy store, keeps different organs in sync. Expected outcomes include a new understanding of how circadian clocks organise physiology, as well as open datasets and novel computational tools for rhythm analysis. This should provide benefits through new intellectual property and by strengthening Australia’s leadership in circadian metabolic research.
national-interest-test-statement: Circadian (24-hour) clocks, or body clocks, are present in every tissue and regulate most aspects of daily life, including the timing of sleep, food intake, and metabolism. Recently, we discovered a new metabolic mechanism that we suspect enables different organs to synchronise their daily activity. This discovery underscores key gaps in our understanding of how body clocks communicate across organs to maintain physiological balance. This project will fill those gaps to provide fundamental insights into how biological timing sustains health and homeostasis. Understanding these mechanisms may lead to strategies for mitigating the effects of circadian disruption, a condition that commonly affects shiftworkers (15-20% of the workforce in industrialised societies) and contributes to major health burdens, including metabolic disorders or cancer. This may include the discovery of new druggable targets to address circadian disruption. The project will establish new computational tools and open-access datasets, enhancing national research capability in systems biology and quantitative physiology. It will also equip the next generation of researchers with highly transferable skills integrating molecular, imaging, multi-omics and AI approaches, valued across academia, industry and government. Through existing industry partnerships and support from the commercialisation team at UniQuest, new intellectual property from this work will be promoted to Australia’s biotechnology sector.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Illuminating photosynthesis with far-red light . This project aims to enhance the energy use and productivity of certain plants by improving their capacity to harvest far-red light wavelengths in the shaded deeper layers of leaves and canopies. Scientific advances it generates, concerning how expanding the spectrum of light available for efficient photosynthesis can boost growth and yield, should include valuable new insights into plant biology and strategies for increasing canopy photosynthesis in economically vital crops, giving up to 26% yield enhancement without additional agricultural inputs or environmental costs. Among expected broader benefits are increased farm profits, responsible use of agricultural resources, and enhanced food security in Australia’s climate-challenged future.
national-interest-test-statement: Australia’s agricultural sector contributes $71.5 billion to the economy, with crops accounting for 35% of all agriculture, fisheries, and forestry production. Yet over a quarter of crop productivity is lost in the plant canopies, where lower leaves receive too little light. This is especially serious for crops like sorghum, maize, and sugarcane; their complex internal leaf anatomy restricts light penetration, and they use a specialised pathway called “C4 photosynthesis”. To safeguard food security, rural livelihoods, and our competitiveness in global markets, we need new strategies to enhance productivity without deploying extra land, water, or fertiliser. This project tackles the challenge by adapting a protein from shade-adapted plants to improve light capture in deeper canopy layers. It will generate urgently needed fundamental knowledge of the bottleneck that restricts C4 crops’ productivity at low light. It points forward to sustainable ways of offsetting yield losses and improving efficiency in the use of essential resources, reducing agriculture’s environmental footprint. Beyond agriculture, the outcomes will advance global plant models – an integral part of climate change mitigation strategies – by delivering insights into C4 biology. I will use my industry connections to communicate the findings to farmers, breeders, government, and researchers – building the necessary research workforce, and new pathways for action, to translate our findings for real-world benefit.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Taking charge: new quantum electro-optical interfaces for diamond devices. This project aims to realise new breakthroughs in room-temperature electrical readout of quantum systems and establish new single-photon emitters for quantum networks. Using recently developed methods for controlling electronic environments in quantum materials, the project aims to address critical problems impeding the electronic and photonic integration of quantum systems. Expected outcomes include a definitive understanding of quantum optoelectronic processes applicable to a wide variety of platforms, the fastest ever room-temperature electrical qubit readout to date and noise-immune spin-photon interfaces. The expected benefits should enable major strides towards electro-photonically interfaced qubits that have real-world applications.
national-interest-test-statement:
Australia is a global leader in quantum technologies. By 2045, this field is expected to contribute to 35,000 jobs
and $6.1 billion to the economy. This project is about finding new ways to interact with quantum objects in
materials using electronics and light. It addresses a key gap in our knowledge of how quantum systems can be
simultaneously integrated with electronics and light, using new methods of imaging and measurement that detect
the flow of electric charges through an operating device, such as a prototypical quantum computer or
magnetometer. By comparison, existing methods are inefficient, cumbersome and stand in the way of scaling up
these quantum technologies to their full potential. The outcomes of this project will help to develop new solutions
to critical bottleneck problems in the miniaturisation and optimisation of quantum devices. Improving our
understanding of quantum technology will have significant benefits for Australia economically and commercially.
This project will inform the development pathway for the next generation of laboratory based quantum
technologies transitioning into industrial applications. The outcomes of this project will be disseminated to the
public as open-access publications with accompanying general-audience pieces for significant results. This
project has good prospects for the development of intellectual property with potential for commercial applications,
and as such will be protected through the lodging of appropriate patents.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Nociceptor–Immune Regulation of Tissue Repair and Regeneration. This project will investigate how sensory nerves influence the body’s ability to heal after injury. We recently discovered that these nerves actively grow into damaged tissues and communicate with immune cells to promote repair and regeneration, revealing a completely new process of healing. Building on this breakthrough, the project will define how nerves enter injured tissues, identify the detailed signals that control recovery, and test whether this mechanism also operates in the heart after injury. The findings will transform our understanding of how the nervous and immune systems cooperate to drive tissue healing, strengthen Australia’s leadership in this emerging field, and provide knowledge with broad relevance across biology.
national-interest-test-statement:
This project will uncover how sensory nerves and the immune system cooperate to repair damaged tissues. By defining the mechanisms that allow nerves to guide immune responses and release pro-healing signals, the project will generate fundamental knowledge with direct relevance to tissue repair in skin, muscle, and the heart. Effective repair after injury is critical for maintaining independence and recovery capacity, particularly in Australia’s ageing population where healing strongly affects quality of life and ability to remain active and productive.
The research will consolidate Australia’s international leadership in regenerative biology, building on discoveries made here that established neuro-immune modulation during tissue healing as a new field. It will create high-value resources, including genetic models, transcriptomic datasets, and training in advanced methods. These resources will be openly shared, accelerating discovery across Australian laboratories and providing enduring benefit to the research community.
In the longer term, knowledge generated by this project can underpin future technologies that improve tissue healing strategies. By linking discovery research to potential applications, the program will open opportunities for Australian innovation and partnerships with industry. More broadly, it will enhance Australia’s global reputation as a leader in regenerative biology, contributing to national capability, wellbeing, and economic competitiveness.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Constructing Gender Justice: How to Build Back Better After Conflict. The project will investigate the ways in which social justice, especially for women and marginalised groups, can be designed into public spaces, homes and infrastructure when communities are rebuilt after war. Using innovative research techniques and drawing on the work of architects, activists and artists, it will generate new knowledge on how power operates in reconstruction efforts and how legal rights to reparation can be leveraged. The project will establish national academic leadership in a critical field, build capacity in early career researchers, enhance the capacity of donors such as Australia to meet gender equality targets in aid work, and, through a toolkit to support community activism, advance progress towards gender justice.
national-interest-test-statement: War destroys homes and cities, and reconstruction costs billions of dollars. Building back after conflict should aim to create the conditions for sustainable peace. This includes building for social justice – ensuring that environments meet the needs of all their inhabitants. Australia is a global leader in promoting gender justice, but DFAT struggles to achieve its gender equality targets in post-conflict development projects when other investors and local governments prioritise profit over progress. This matters because fair societies are less likely to go to war, reducing the ongoing costs to donors of conflict and development. This project will work through existing networks of civil society groups and policy makers in Australia and elsewhere to generate practical guidance on rebuilding for social justice. It will draw lessons from in-depth research with affected communities, donors, architects and policy makers involved in, or excluded from, major post-conflict reconstruction projects in four countries: Solomon Islands, Sri Lanka, Colombia and Lebanon. Findings will be distributed through an innovative online toolkit for war-affected communities and donors, as well as workshops and policy reports for DFAT and United Nations agencies, detailing specific ways in which the aid sector can work with communities to support peace through just reconstruction. This will enhance the efficiency of Australia’s aid spending and advance progress towards its gender justice goals.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Integrating Ancient and Modern Genomics to Decipher Human Evolution. This project will generate unprecedented genetic data to explore the rich and complex history of human settlement across Wallacea and Sahul. Using state-of-the-art approaches from population genetics and ancient DNA analysis combined with high-quality genomic data from present-day populations, this research will investigate >1 million years of human evolution by integrating genetic information with archaeological and fossil evidence. This research will uncover the lost histories of the diverse and now-extinct hominin groups and ancient human populations that once inhabited this vast geographical region that witnessed some of the most important chapters in the prehistory of humanity.
national-interest-test-statement:
This project will uncover new knowledge about the identity and evolutionary history of ancient human groups that once lived across Island Southeast Asia, New Guina and Australia - regions central to understanding over a million years of human evolution - and their connection to the ancestors of contemporary Indigenous Australians and Torres Strait Islanders. Working with world-leading researchers, the project will place Australia at the forefront of global human evolutionary science and strengthen its leadership in genomic research.
By applying advanced ancient DNA and population genetics techniques, it will reveal how people migrated, adapted, and interacted across this key region. The project will directly benefit Australia by expanding national expertise in genomics and computation, creating highly skilled research roles, and training the next generation of scientists in cutting-edge methods. It will also enhance cultural understanding by illuminating Australia’s deep human past and foster respectful dialogues and engagement with Indigenous communities.
The findings will be communicated to the scientific community, but also disseminated through public lectures, online documentaries, and community engagement programs that promote shared knowledge and respect for cultural heritage. This inclusive approach will ensure the project’s discoveries reach the broader Australian public and contribute to national identity, cultural understanding, and scientific innovation.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: From Data-Hungry to Data-Smart: Efficient, Safe and Adaptive Robot Learning. This project aims to create the next generation of learning robots, enabling robots that can learn new skills from a few human demonstrations, adapt to new situations, and respond safely when unexpected events occur. It addresses key knowledge gaps, as current systems require large amounts of data and struggle in changing real-world environments. The project will deliver open-sourced implementations of new mathematical models and algorithms that make robot learning more data-efficient, safe, and adaptable. This will benefit Australia by advancing reliable and more capable robotics for homes, hospitals, agriculture, and industry, supporting productivity, safety, and sovereign capability.
national-interest-test-statement:
Australia faces growing skill shortages in manufacturing, agriculture, construction and aged care. Robots that learn directly from people could help and take on repetitive, physically demanding and time-consuming work, allowing humans to focus on higher-value tasks. However, current robots are expensive and difficult to train, often requiring hundreds of human expert demonstrations for simple tasks and struggling to operate safely in new situations.

This project will develop and open-source new methods that allow robots to learn efficiently, safely and with minimal data, directly from humans. This will make robotics more capable, trustworthy and affordable, enabling even small and medium Australian businesses to benefit without relying on overseas foundation models or infrastructure.

The outcomes will strengthen Australia’s capability in robotics, machine learning and AI, supporting local industry and startup growth. The project will work with Australian businesses, policymakers and the public through open-source software, demonstrations and outreach to ensure broad uptake of the developed technology. Together, these advances will support national priorities in productivity, workforce resilience, advanced manufacturing, improve workplace safety and contribute to a strong, independent and competitive Australian robotics sector.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
current-admin-organisation: The University of New South Wales
announcement-admin-organisation: The University of New South Wales
grant-summary: Leveraging Social-Emotional Motivation to Enhance Adolescent Development. Social-emotional skills and wellbeing decline during adolescence, a trend that has worsened in recent years. New research has identified social-emotional motivation, defined as adolescents’ belief in their ability to shape their social-emotional experiences, as a key driver of positive development. This project will advance understanding of social-emotional motivation and its protective role in supporting developmental outcomes in adolescence. This knowledge will be used to create evidence-based practice and policy insights tailored to schools and broader systems, enabling them to better foster positive social-emotional and academic development among young people across Australia.
national-interest-test-statement: Poor social-emotional development in adolescence can lead to long-term challenges such as lower educational attainment, higher unemployment, and increased mental health issues. These impacts have costs to both individuals and society as a whole. Alarmingly, many countries including Australia are now witnessing declines of up to 19% in a wide range of social-emotional development outcomes among adolescents such as drops in relationship skills and wellbeing. Despite ongoing efforts, current research and interventions have struggled to reverse these trends. Evidence now highlights motivation as a critical lever for change. Social-emotional motivation refers to an individual’s belief that they can positively impact their social-emotional experiences. When adolescents hold this belief, it fuels their willingness to engage and grow, leading to positive development. This project will extend understanding of social-emotional motivation and its protective role among adolescents. Findings will inform evidence-based guidelines for schools and broader systems to strengthen adolescents’ development. By supporting social-emotional motivation, this research will deliver social and economic benefits to Australia, such as helping to reduce the projected $350b deficit to Australia’s GDP from suboptimal social-emotional development. To maximise impact, outcomes will be shared widely through practice and policy briefs for teachers, school leaders and policymakers.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Risk into Resilience: Mitigating Housing Bubbles and Navigating Turbulence. This project aims to build a more resilient Australian financial system by addressing two key sources of instability: speculative housing bubbles and market turbulence. It will develop the first method to assess policies that mitigate speculative bubbles and pioneer high-frequency techniques to detect market direction. Expected outcomes include new theory for explosive processes that define bubbles, empirical evidence on housing policy effectiveness, advances in high-frequency econometrics, and adaptive trading strategies for investors. The project will equip regulators with more effective policy tools, enable superannuation funds to better protect retirement savings, and position Australia as a global leader in financial econometrics.
national-interest-test-statement:
This project will help Australia build a stronger, more resilient financial system by tackling two major sources of instability: speculative housing bubbles and market turbulence. Housing bubbles drive prices beyond reach for many Australians and put families, banks, and the economy at risk when they burst. Market turbulence, often triggered by global events, can erode retirement savings and undermine confidence in the financial system. Both issues affect millions of Australians through house prices, job security, and superannuation balances.

The research will create new tools that allow policymakers to evaluate whether interventions, such as interest rate increases, are effective in preventing bubbles before they grow into crises. It will also provide superannuation funds and other institutional investors with real-time signals on market direction, helping them protect Australians’ retirement savings during periods of turmoil. Findings and tools will be shared through workshops, open source software, and media outreach to ensure broad understanding, practical adoption, and lasting impact.

By delivering clear evidence on whether and how policymakers and investors should act, the project will strengthen Australia’s ability to manage financial risks, stabilise housing markets, and safeguard long-term wealth. It will also enhance Australia’s international leadership in financial risk management, contributing to economic security and prosperity for the Australian community.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
current-admin-organisation: The University of New South Wales
announcement-admin-organisation: The University of New South Wales
grant-summary: Advancing Air-Humidity Energy Harvesting: Beyond Moisture Constraints. This project aims to develop next-generation energy harvesting technology that converts moisture energy into electricity to power Internet of Things (IoT). The goal will be achieved through engineering the interactions among functional materials, water molecules and mobile ions. The project is expected to advance the fundamental understanding of electricity generation and degradation mechanisms, while addressing challenges in conversion efficiency, stability, and environmental resilience. The expected outcomes include a new class of materials capable of ultralong lifetimes and high energy output across diverse environments. Its success will transform existing technologies and open new opportunities for self-sustainable IoT applications.
national-interest-test-statement: Australia’s transition to net zero requires clean, reliable, and locally manufactured energy technologies. Current Li-ion batteries pose safety risks and require frequent recharging, whereas conventional energy harvesting methods rely on intermittent stimuli such as light and heat. This project aims to develop an innovative technology that harvests energy from moisture, creating a new sustainable energy source beyond traditional methods. By engineering material compositions and interfaces, the project will enable continuous, all-weather energy generation for Internet of Things (IoT) application, reducing the influence of climate, geographic location, and daily fluctuations while lowering maintenance and installation requirements. The proposed technology offers safe, low-cost, and maintenance-free energy for applications in remote monitoring, mining, agriculture, and health care, where battery replacement is costly or impractical. The outcomes will reduce reliance on imported and toxic minerals and lower maintenance costs across key industries such as agriculture and environmental monitoring. Economically, the project supports the growth of Australia’s advanced materials, printing, and electronics industries while creating high-skill jobs and intellectual property in a globally emerging field. Long-term benefits include direct support for Australia’s National Science and Research Priorities by advancing sovereign energy technologies and contributing to national net-zero goals.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Monetising Data - The Growth and Governance of AI Dataset Markets. This project aims to investigate the ways that AI turns data into money. AI training datasets are extremely valuable, but how they are commodified and transacted in markets, and who gets to benefit from the value they produce are poorly understood. That lack of insight makes it impossible to regulate dataset markets for Australian economic interests. Through empirical and conceptual research, this project expects to produce knowledge about the rules and commercial practices shaping the AI data economy and will propose new data governance principles for datasets. The benefit will be to enable regulation of AI training dataset markets in service of Australian creatives and data workers, and ensure a resilient and sovereign technology sector.
national-interest-test-statement: Global, multi-billion-dollar AI training dataset markets are emerging to power AI development. Australian creative communities use these markets to monetise their work in the digital economy, and Australian software companies use them to acquire specialised datasets to train AI models for specific skills and purposes. But these marketplaces operate with very little public or regulatory scrutiny. Industry actors are independently setting the rules for how datasets are constructed, the information provided when they are transacted, and whether they abide labour, licensing, or quality requirements. Through systems of self-regulation, they exert private control over marketplaces in ways that exploit creatives and digital workers, and transfer the value of Australian data holdings to international firms. The lack of insight into dataset market rules has become a critical knowledge gap because those rules determine who can produce value from datasets and how that value is distributed. This project therefore proposes the first focused study of AI training datasets as a new type of digital commodity and dataset markets as sites for value creation and distribution. The goal is to produce knowledge resources for government and industry actors that will encourage confident participation in this new frontier of the digital economy, and to identify pathways for governing dataset creation and exchange that support a sovereign software industry serving Australian economic interests.

grant-summary: Probing the dark sector with precision atomic sensors. This project aims to identify novel signatures of dark matter and the origin of the matter-antimatter asymmetry -- two of the most important unsolved problems in contemporary science -- and to develop novel methods to search for these effects in atomic systems. Expected outcomes include improved sensitivity to parameters associated with dark matter and discrete fundamental symmetries by up to several orders of magnitude. The project will advance knowledge in fundamental atomic and astroparticle physics, enable ground-breaking discoveries of physics beyond the Standard Model of particle physics, build international collaborations, and train the next generation of Australian scientists in priority areas and at the cutting-edge frontier.
national-interest-test-statement:
This project aims to provide new information about the nature of dark matter (which makes up 85% of all the matter in our Universe) and the origin of the predominance of matter over antimatter, which are two of the most important unsolved problems in contemporary science. Leveraging recent developments in quantum technologies, I will pave new ways in which precision atomic systems can be used to probe the dark sector, promising up to several orders of magnitude better sensitivity than conventional approaches.

The project synergises with numerous fields within applied science and technology prioritised in Australia’s National Quantum Strategy (2023) and National Science and Research Priority 5: Building a secure and resilient nation (2024). Precision atomic systems are vital in navigation, valuable resource and minerals exploration, medicine and defence, bringing enormous benefits to Australia’s security, economy, commercial activity and society.

This project will strengthen Australia’s ties to major laboratories and universities around the world and will advance Australia’s global standing in fundamental physics research. Training the next generation of scientists and leaders will enable Australia to thrive in a competitive global environment into the 21st century. Open-access publication of research outcomes, combined with public outreach activities, will bring benefit to Australia’s social and cultural fabric by invigorating the public’s interest in fundamental science.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Building Australia’s national gesture dictionary. This project aims to document Australia’s national ways of gesturing, providing the first detailed documentation of the multimodal features of Australian English. This will focus on gestures that can be used without speech (emblems). This project will incorporate our gestural history and the rich influence of diverse communities on this gestural lexicon, including migrant Australians, regional Australians and Auslan signers. This research can benefit Australia by providing a cultural record, as well as a sovereign digital database of Australian gesture for technical application. This project will use computer vision methods as part of data collection and analysis, exploring novel methods of processing and presenting gestural data.
national-interest-test-statement:
This project provides the first digital documentation of Australia’s national gesture lexicon. New digital methods offer an unprecedented opportunity to understand how we communicate. This project incorporates our gestural history and the rich influence of diverse communities on this gestural lexicon, including migrant Australians, regional Australians and Auslan signers. 

This research can benefit Australians by providing a cultural record, analogous to the Australian National Dictionary that exists for words. By systematically documenting gesture, the knowledge can be fed into emerging AI tools that have the potential to transform human communication and advance intercultural understanding within and beyond Australia. As more computers include visual gestural input, we need to ensure data sovereignty so that Australians can make use of these systems. 

Methods developed in this project can be used to improve the documentation of the gesture repertoires of communities across Asia as international cultural influence flattens traditional practice. The tools can also be used to improve navigation of the existing Auslan dictionary. 

Central to this project is the promotion of research outcomes beyond academia. I draw on my extensive experience creating public engagement materials to bring all Australians into data collection and presentation. This includes accessible digital and print versions of the gesture dictionary.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Building community climate wellbeing amid multitemporal climate distress. This project will deliver the world’s first qualitative study of multitemporal climate distress—how past disasters, present disruptions, and future imaginaries intersect to shape lived experience. Using an innovative weather-responsive ethnography and interdisciplinary environmental humanities framework, it will document the affective, relational, and imaginative factors that enable disaster-impacted communities to respond collectively and constructively to the knowledge that climate crisis will worsen in future. Its bottom-up, community-led approach will identify everyday strategies that can support community climate wellbeing, and will amplify community efforts to strengthen climate adaptation, social cohesion, and environmental justice.
national-interest-test-statement:
Australian communities have already experienced repeated catastrophic climate disasters in recent years, and science indicates this will intensity in future. Yet little is known about how disaster-impacted communities experience the worry that can arise when thinking about future climate scenarios, nor how these communities can support themselves emotionally and culturally in this context.  

This project addresses two critical national needs. Firstly, building knowledge and recognition of the emotional experiences of living amid cascading and compounding climate crises, and the flow on social, cultural and political impacts of this. Secondly, understanding the emotional, relational, and imaginative practices that can contribute to community climate wellbeing, and how community organisations can support and amplify these practices. 

The research will benefit Australians socially and culturally by uncovering practical, bottom-up strategies that embed emotional support into everyday community life, reducing the need for clinical services. Strengthening these approaches will help communities adapt, maintain cohesion, and prevent the worst impacts of climate distress.

To maximise public impact, a national summit with community leaders, a blog and podcast series, and easy-to-follow guidelines will be delivered. These outputs will help Australians prepare for and adapt to climate challenges in ways that protect mental health and foster social cohesion.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Building the Foundations of Federated Agentic AI. Building the Foundation of Federated Agentic AI aims to develop a new framework that enables various intelligent systems to work together safely, efficiently, and responsibly. The project will create a framework that enables many user-governed AI agents to collaborate, learn from one other, and adapt to human needs while ensuring data privacy, security, and autonomy. By delivering open-source tools, scalable techniques, and practical applications, the research will generate new knowledge in distributed and agentic AI, strengthening Australia’s leadership in trustworthy, privacy-preserving AI, and driving innovation across healthcare, business, finance, and smart technologies to build a resilient, inclusive digital economy.
national-interest-test-statement:
Agentic AI—autonomous intelligent systems capable of making decisions, taking action and adapting to new situations without constant human intervention—are rapidly advancing worldwide, including in Australia. With the rise of modern AI infrastructure, including advanced hardware, cloud computing and generative AI models, industries including healthcare, retails and mobile services are increasingly developing agentic AI tools to automate workflow and enhance productivity.
 
However, a key limitation persists: current agentic AI models cannot accumulate knowledge or self-improve collaboratively over time. This project will overcome this barrier by establishing new theoretical and computational frameworks that enable AI agents to share experiences, adapt to dynamic environments and build collective intelligence within a federated structure.
 
These innovations will empower Australian companies to develop intelligent, privacy-preserving applications where data remains securely on users’ devices while still benefiting from shared intelligence across organisations. The outcomes will support personalised services such as recommendation, business intelligence and decision support without comprising user privacy. To enable understanding and potential adoption of the project's outcome, findings will be shared with industry stakeholders through open-source toolkits, public seminars and industrial meet-ups, thus driving the growth of a responsible AI-driven digital economy in Australia.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1

announcement-admin-organisation: The University of New South Wales
grant-summary: Revealing the Infancy of Stars and Planets across our Galaxy. The first few million years of stars' lives are crucial to star and planet development. This project aims to understand the connection between the environments where stars are born and the evolution pathways of the dusty disks that surround them during their infancy. By combining observations from world-class satellites TESS and Gaia, this project will produce a novel map of newborn stars within our Galaxy. Expected outcomes include new insights into the physical processes that shape the terrestrial disk regions and determine disk longevity, ultimately impacting their ability to produce planets. This project directly aligns with the aims of the Decadal Plan for Australian astronomy and will enhance Australia's leadership in space astronomy.
national-interest-test-statement:
Understanding how stars and planets form is central to understanding our place in the Universe and addressing two fundamental questions of humankind: "How did we get here? Are we alone?" Our current knowledge is fragmented, with key gaps on how newborn stars gain their mass and its effect on the growth of planets in the dusty disks that surround them. By combining observations from world-class telescopes in space and on Earth, this project will map the demography of stellar nurseries within our Galaxy and generate new knowledge on the progression of star formation, the dynamics of stellar mass growth, and the life spans of protoplanetary disks in different environments.
This project addresses one of the "questions for a new decade" put forward by the Decadal Plan for Australian astronomy of the Australian Academy of Science. Benefits to Australia include an immediate return on government investment in the Rubin Observatory and bolstering Australia's international leadership in space-based astronomy. This research will produce new advanced software for the analysis of time-dependent signals that will be made public for cross-disciplinary applications, from academia to finance. It will also train Australian students in highly in-demand skills like programming, statistical data analysis, data visualisation and problem-solving. For maximum impact, research outcomes will be published in open-access journals and disseminated through public lectures, press releases and media forums.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Reducing the sexual precarity of migrants in the workplace. The project aims to investigate and reduce workplace sexual violence experienced by migrants through a mixed-methods, five-country comparative study. It will create a unique database of 1,000 court cases and conduct 100 trauma-informed interviews with survivors and legal professionals. Its significance lies in revealing how visa status, legal systems, labour policies and cultural norms contribute to sexual precarity, offering evidence-based reforms. Expected outcomes include new data, scholarly publications, and policy reports to inform governments and international agencies. The benefits include enhanced legal protections, improved trauma-informed policy design, intergovernmental cooperation, and strengthened support for migrant workers.
national-interest-test-statement: Despite their essential contribution to Australia’s economy, migrants experience disproportionate rates of workplace sexual violence. This project aims to transform understanding of how immigration and employment systems contribute to workplace sexual violence and harassment experienced by migrants in Australia and comparative countries. It will develop new conceptual and data frameworks to explain how visa status, employment regulation, sector of employment and gender interact to heighten sexual precarity and restrict access to justice. The project will deliver the first comparative legal database on migrant experiences of workplace sexual violence, identify high-risk industries and legal and policy pain points, and provide actionable reforms for state and federal governments, unions and employers. The research will strengthen Australia’s social and economic wellbeing by promoting safer and fairer workplaces, reducing the human and financial costs of sexual violence, and enhancing Australia’s reputation as a global leader in ethical immigration and labour practices. Translation will occur through sustained engagement with policymakers, legal practitioners, unions, industry and international non-government bodies to ensure findings are adopted in legislative, institutional and workplace reforms that deliver lasting national impact. Working directly with victim-survivors in a trauma-informed fashion will ensure the legitimacy and sensitivity that such a project demands.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Click for care—quality, safety, & equity in digital care platforms. This project aims to investigate how gig-economy digital care platforms—apps connecting care workers with aged, disability, and childcare recipients—are transforming how care is experienced and valued. Using innovative digital methods, interviews, and co-design, the project expects to generate new knowledge about how platforms impact care quality, safety, and equity for workers, recipients, and informal (family) carers. Expected outcomes include world-first evidence guiding new policies and strategies to address regulatory gaps and challenge structural care devaluation. This should provide significant benefits, including to strengthen protections, enhance care quality and safety, and improve the sustainability of Australia's care sector.
national-interest-test-statement:
Australia faces a predicted shortage of 285,000 care workers by 2049-50—a crisis rooted in the systemic devaluation of and chronic underinvestment in care work. Digital care platforms like 'Mable' are rapidly filling this gap, charging fees to connect millions of care workers with recipients. Yet they operate largely unregulated within government-funded systems like the National Disability Insurance Scheme, while government policy remains silent on platform care. We do not know if care platforms genuinely help or simply hide problems like worker exploitation, compromised care quality, and safety risks behind a technological veneer.

Drawing on my expertise in social policy and care inequities, this research critically examines how care platforms affect workers, recipients, and informal carers in combination—a dynamic not yet studied. The project aims to assess whether platforms improve flexibility and care quality, or deepen inequalities for Australia's most vulnerable.

The benefits are significant: protecting Australia's $100+ billion care economy, advancing fairness for all giving and receiving care, and reshaping how we value care. Findings will inform Fair Work protections, the National Carer Strategy, and new regulations—preventing exploitation while exploring how platforms can support quality care. Expected outputs include policy reports, platform guidelines, parliamentary submissions, and public seminars—ensuring findings shape regulation and drive social change.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: The periodic table of quantum correlations and applications. This project aims to develop the periodic table for quantum correlations and its applications in quantum computation and quantum communication by employing techniques from algebraic geometry and nonlinear optimisation. This is a paradigm shift in how we think, organise, teach and ultimately utilise quantum correlations. Expected outcomes of this project are a new conceptual framework to classify quantum correlations, efficient and optimal protocols for quantum communication and quantum computing. This should provide significant cost-reducing benefits to the design and implementation of quantum technologies, and a comprehensive battery of tests to assist the discovery and development of further theories of Nature beyond quantum theory.
national-interest-test-statement: Quantum theory has led to ground breaking technologies such as semiconductor electronics, solid-state lasers, magnetic resonance imaging and the global positioning system. The second quantum revolution promises to transform computing and communications in ways that can inform new drug discoveries and safeguard our critical cyber infrastructure. This project directly contributes to Australia's cybersecurity and national quantum strategy by addressing a key theoretical and technical obstacle. It will provide a new conceptual and classification framework for quantum correlations in terms of their utility in various applications. This will translate into more efficient and precise control of quantum systems, which will lead to the next generation of information processing technologies. To maximise understanding and future adoption beyond academia, I will engage with industry and government partners, as well as popular media platforms, and provide accessible workshops and briefings to support translation and uptake.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Data-informed mitigation of agricultural nitrogen pollution. Substantial loss of nitrogen from fertilisers undermines agricultural productivity and damages the environment. Identifying critical zones and times of nitrogen pollution is vital for targeted action, yet current approaches lack the precision and scalability needed for site-specific management. This project aims to integrate data-driven insights with nitrogen process understanding to build a new fusion model for revealing and managing vulnerable zones and times of nitrogen loss. Expected outcomes include a suite of soil- and climate-specific response patterns and parameters for reliable, scalable forecasting, enabling diagnostics and decision-support to enhance nitrogen efficiency, curb pollution and foster resilient Australian agriculture.
national-interest-test-statement: Nitrogen fertilisers are indispensable for food production, yet 50% or more of the nitrogen applied to agricultural systems is lost to the environment. These losses reduce farm productivity, damage ecosystems, and affect human wellbeing in Australia and globally. Accurately predicting where and when nitrogen losses are especially high (“hot spots” and “hot moments”) is essential for developing effective, site-specific interventions. However, conventional approaches often fail to capture the spatial and temporal variability of nitrogen losses, which is critical for soil-climate-crop specific mitigation. Here, better targeted, adaptive nitrogen management will be developed by integrating data-driven analytics with modelling of nitrogen loss processes that respond differently under varying environmental and production systems. This innovative approach will enable the creation of pollution-risk maps that pinpoint where mitigation resources should be prioritised and provide the foundation for advanced decision-support tools delivering precise, data-driven recommendations for sustainable agriculture. These advances are expected to increase profitability, lower greenhouse gas emissions, protect waterways, and reduce the environmental and social costs of fertiliser use in Australia. Project outcomes will be shared widely with researchers, industry stakeholders, and policymakers, strengthening Australia’s leadership and impact in digital agriculture and environmental stewardship.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Computational and experimental analysis of microbial community dynamics. This project aims to uncover the unique principles that shape ‘local’ microbial communities that reside within the greater gastrointestinal tract. It will develop computational models that can explain complex ecosystem dependencies and predict how these communities assemble and persist. Advanced microfluidic systems will be used to investigate host‑specific niches and community states, identifying the factors that stabilise or shift populations, for example the transient role of host diet as a short‑term driver of ecological change. Outcomes include new ecological knowledge and predictive modelling tools for microbial evolution, with benefits for biotechnology, sustainable agriculture, and strengthen Australian research leadership.
national-interest-test-statement:
This project will develop innovative strategies to understand, restore, and manage microbial ecosystems. By integrating ecological theory, advanced microbial culturing, and complex systems modelling, it will generate foundational knowledge and new approaches that strengthen and expand nationally significant industries. The research will examine ecological niches within host‑associated microbiome communities and the environmental and host factors that shape microbiome composition.

Microbial ecosystems underpin Australia’s agricultural and environmental systems, are essential for sustainable production and ecosystem management, and have broad applications in industrial biotechnology. The knowledge generated will deliver direct economic benefits through efficiency gains in existing applications, refinement of fermentation and biotechnology processes, and development of new opportunities. It will also improve ecological understanding for applications across diverse commercial and environmental settings.

The research will be communicated widely beyond academia. Ongoing engagement with biotechnology, leveraging established industry connections, will maximise application and impact. Public engagement through Monash University outreach and national and international media will ensure broad dissemination and awareness.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: How Family Traditions Shape Gender Psychology in Australia and Beyond. This project aims to uncover why progress toward gender equality in Australia remains slow by investigating how cultural family traditions—such as who belongs, who moves, and who inherits—become internalised and shape wellbeing, emotion, and autonomy. Combining national surveys, social media data, family studies, and modelling, it will reveal how these norms persist or change across generations. The project expects to generate new interdisciplinary knowledge linking family systems and gender psychology, producing open data, refined theory, and practical insights. Outcomes should provide significant benefits by informing more inclusive, culturally grounded policies that advance wellbeing and accelerate progress toward gender equity.
national-interest-test-statement: From housing and eldercare to domestic violence prevention and family law, Australian gender equity policies often assume a narrow idea of what a “normal” family looks like. These assumptions can clash with the realities of migrant and Indigenous communities, leading to mismatches, marginalisation, and policy failure. What is missing is a clear understanding of how deep-rooted family practices—such as traditional cultural norms around ancestry and marital residence—shape gender roles and expectations in contemporary Australia. Without this understanding, gender equity policies risk targeting symptoms rather than understanding causes. This project aims to address that gap by clarifying how family practices shape gender attitudes and core aspects of psychological life. In doing so, it hopes to provide a new framework for culturally sensitive, evidence-based responses to gendered inequality that show how entrenched norms might be shifted to promote equity for all Australians. Findings will be shared through policy briefs, public reports, and workshops, including a Knowledge Exchange with culturally and linguistically diverse community leaders, service providers, and policymakers. Public talks and media engagement will help make the results accessible and relevant to everyday life, and collaborations with service providers will help translate them into practice.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Reconceptualising harm reduction for young people. This project aims to develop an innovative approach that will reduce the harm related to young Australians’ drug use. It is expected to generate urgently needed new knowledge on the relationship between the priorities that currently guide harm reduction responses and young people’s own concerns about and experiences of drug harms. Through a collaborative process involving novel theory, sophisticated methods and consultation with experts, service providers and young people, the project intends to produce new responses that engage directly with young people’s perspectives, making them more relevant and effective. Anticipated benefits include reduced drug-related harm among young Australians and a lower overall drug-related burden of disease.
national-interest-test-statement: Illicit drug use accounts for around 3% of Australia’s total disease burden, costing about $16.5 billion annually. Young Australians are a priority population, with approximately 800,000 aged 18–24 (35%) and 200,000 aged 14–17 (13.3%) reporting drug use in 2022–23. The drugs they consume most often are cannabis, ecstasy, cocaine, hallucinogens and ketamine. Increasingly common and alarming detections of lethal synthetic opioids (such as nitazenes) in substances not typically linked to overdose (e.g., cocaine and ketamine) highlight the importance of finding more effective responses to youth drug use. Harm reduction – the third pillar of Australia’s National Drug Strategy – aims to minimise drug-related harm rather than eliminate use. Yet, young people are often sceptical about harm-focused messaging and express a need for resources that address the diversity of drug use experiences, including harms. This project will use innovative methods and collaboration between harm reduction experts, youth researchers and young people themselves to generate new data on and insights into youth drug use. Outcomes will include a new youth drug use response framework and related implementation resources, disseminated to key stakeholders, advocacy groups and communities through webinars, lay summaries and media engagement. By building a more responsive and evidence-informed framework, this project aims to reduce drug-related harms and costs and ultimately save young lives.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: A New Transasymptotic Framework for Partial Differential Equations. This project will create powerful new tools that overcome barriers in mathematical modelling using approximation methods, enabling the exploration of complex phenomena previously beyond reach. By leveraging cutting-edge ideas from asymptotics and complex analysis it will accurately describe subtle hidden influences and sudden behaviour shifts in nonlinear models of complex real-life systems. Expected outcomes include the creation of a rigourous asymptotic framework for mathematicians and scientists to tackle nonlinear differential and difference equations arising from realistic physical models. Benefits include sharper predictive tools for Australian industry to design effective optical instruments and mitigate chaotic shocks in waveguides.
national-interest-test-statement: Real-world systems, from ocean waves to black hole interactions, can undergo sudden, dramatic changes when hidden effects accumulate and erupt without warning. Yet current approximation methods break down just when accurate prediction is most needed, because they treat each effect separately and miss the buildup of complex and nonlinear interactions between them. This project will create a new mathematical framework to reveal these hidden influences and follow their growth as they reshape system behaviour in realistic models. It will provide scientists and engineers with a reliable cost-effective predictive tool to improve the design of practical technologies used in advanced manufacturing. By enabling the study of realistic models instead of oversimplified ones, the method will improve modelling predictions across science and engineering. Immediate benefits include support for Australian priorities in advanced manufacturing for upcoming net-zero transitions, achieved through better predictive modelling of laser response, waveguide stability, and energy loss in particle-based components. The project will strengthen existing links between mathematicians, physicists, and engineers, and create new connections between these disciplines through public lectures and outreach. Its success will position Australia at the forefront of global research in cutting-edge mathematics, with flow-on benefits to science, technology, and industry.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Towards quantum telescopes for extremely high-resolution imaging. This project aims to combine world-leading Australian optical and quantum measurement technologies with machine learning and near-term quantum memories to demonstrate the world’s first quantum interferometer telescope. This project expects to demonstrate that quantum detectors can feasibly link optical telescopes, separated by hundreds of kilometres, to achieve extremely high-resolution imaging. Expected outcomes are the demonstration of technologies for practical quantum telescopes that will enable imaging resolution more than 20 times better than any existing telescope. This will provide significant outcomes for astronomy, space situational awareness, and defence.
national-interest-test-statement: Due to recent large Government investments in space exploration, Australia has become a world leader in telescope technology. We now have numerous excellent telescopes, but there is significant scope to improve the quality of the images that they generate. This project will develop technology that will result in the generation of images that are 1000 times clearer, which will allow us to study planets outside of our solar system, the behaviour of black holes, and the origins of star systems like our own. This technology will also have more immediate economic and practical benefits to Australians by enabling better satellite imaging for Earth observation such as crop monitoring and resource exploration, as well as better imaging and tracking of spacecraft and space debris in Earth’s orbit, safeguarding satellites we use for communications, navigation, and disaster response. This work will further Australia's standing both as a world-leader in advanced astronomy instrumentation and as a leading innovator in measurement science and quantum technologies. Adoption of the outcomes of this work will be through work with the international astronomy community, and with defence who will be able to use the improved imaging technology to keep critical satellites safe from collisions with space debris.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
current-admin-organisation: The University of New South Wales
announcement-admin-organisation: The University of New South Wales
grant-summary: Understanding and Predicting Resilient Nature-Based Stormwater Systems. This project aims to establish the scientific basis for maintaining the long-term functionality and safety of nature-based systems as critical urban infrastructure for managing stormwater. It expects to generate new understanding of how system structure, maintenance, and environmental stresses drive long-term performance and contaminant behaviour, through integrated field, pilot, and laboratory studies with predictive modelling. Expected outcomes include new design principles and hybrid models for forecasting performance, maintenance, and risk. This will deliver significant benefits by enabling evidence-based design and management of resilient stormwater assets that protect waterways and enhance the climate resilience of Australian cities.
national-interest-test-statement: Australia’s cities face growing challenges from urban flooding, stormwater pollution, and climate extremes. Nature-based stormwater systems—such as rain gardens and constructed wetlands—are being built within our cities to capture and clean stormwater, cool cities, and protect waterways. However, these living systems can degrade over time, reducing their performance and creating long-term maintenance and safety concerns. This project will establish the scientific foundation for maintaining the long-term functionality and safety of these systems as vital urban infrastructure. It will generate new evidence on how design, maintenance, and environmental stresses influence performance and pollutant build-up, and develop predictive tools to guide timely maintenance and reduce costs. The outcomes will help governments, councils, and water utilities design and manage stormwater assets that deliver reliable flood protection, cleaner waterways, and greener neighbourhoods. In partnership with industry, professional bodies, and policymakers, the research findings will be shared through open data, industry conferences, and targeted practitioner engagement to ensure practical adoption and strengthen Australia’s resilience to climate and water challenges.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Electrochemical Modulation of Oxygen Activity for Metal Oxide Synthesis. This project aims to develop and validate a novel electrochemical method capable of generating ultra-high oxygen pressures to synthesise metal oxides. By systematically elucidating reaction mechanisms and optimising key parameters, it will establish the fundamental principles governing this new electrochemically activated solid-state synthetic route. These extreme conditions enable the discovery and precise control of oxide materials with unique structures and exceptional functionalities for clean energy conversion, efficient catalysis, and durable electronic devices. The gained understanding and knowledge will accelerate optimization of this method and facilitate its broad application in designing next-generation functional materials.
national-interest-test-statement:
This project aims to develop a new way to create metal oxide materials that are essential for technologies such as batteries, catalysts, and electronic devices. It uses an electrochemical approach applying electricity to drive chemical reactions so that these materials can be formed under extremely high oxygen pressures. These unique conditions will enable scientists to design and precisely control oxide structures, leading to materials with exceptional performance and durability for clean energy and advanced technologies.
Australia faces major challenges in reducing emissions, improving energy efficiency, and developing sovereign capability in advanced materials. Many critical technologies from fuel cells, electrolysis cells, batteries, and electronics, depend on special metal oxides. By pioneering methods to design and control such materials, this project will provide the new knowledge and platforms needed for breakthroughs in sustainable technologies.
To promote research outcomes beyond academia, we will collaborate with industry partners and government, ensuring practical application and commercial viability. By demonstrating a prototype platform, we will translate research findings into real-world solutions. We will also engage in public forums, industry conferences, and media outreach to increase visibility, encourage adoption, and contribute to Australia's clean energy future.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: The School Infrastructure Gap: Choice, Opportunities, Leadership, Equity. This project aims to transform how Australia plans and invests in school infrastructure by building the first national data system linking facilities and educational equity. Combining geospatial mapping, AI-enabled data collection, surveys and case studies, it will show how infrastructure disparities shape school choice, student opportunity and principals’ work. Outcomes include a public School Facilities Dashboard, an equity standards guide, and a needs-based investment framework. The project will deliver lasting national benefit by improving transparency, guiding fairer investment, and ensuring a future where every child learns in a safe, well-resourced school.
national-interest-test-statement: This project addresses a critical gap in Australian education policy by developing the first comprehensive evidence base on the distribution, quality, and effects of school infrastructure.
