With no national framework for capital investment, responsibility remains fragmented across states and sectors, reducing both efficiency and equity in spending. By delivering new public data infrastructure, the research will promote transparent and cost-effective investment in school facilities, ensuring taxpayer funds are directed where they have the greatest impact. It will provide data-driven tools for governments to improve planning and prioritisation of capital works, strengthen accountability through greater transparency about how facilities shape educational opportunity and parental choice, and reduce the financial and administrative burden on principals by limiting reliance on inequitable fundraising practices and identifying schools most in need of public investment. Aligning with the National School Reform Agreement, the project will generate robust, accessible evidence to guide future infrastructure policy and investment, supporting long-term productivity, social cohesion, and equitable, high-quality education for all Australians.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: 2D High-Entropy Catalysts for Green Hydrogen. This project aims to develop new, low-cost, and efficient catalysts for producing green hydrogen, a clean energy source vital for a carbon-neutral future. By combining theoretical calculations, advanced materials design, and atomic-level engineering, the research will create two-dimensional high-entropy oxides materials with superior activity and durability for water splitting. The project will provide new insights into how these catalysts work and demonstrate their use in practical hydrogen production systems, helping to make sustainable hydrogen energy more affordable and scalable for future clean energy technologies.
national-interest-test-statement: This project will support Australia’s transition to a clean, secure, and sustainable energy future by advancing the science and technology of green hydrogen production. Hydrogen is vital for decarbonising heavy industries, transport, and chemical manufacturing. However, current technologies depend on expensive, scarce noble-metal catalysts, limiting scalability. This research will develop next-generation, low-cost, durable catalysts based on two-dimensional high-entropy materials to enable efficient water splitting. Integrating theoretical calculations, atomic-level design, and advanced characterization, the project will establish new catalyst design principles and accelerate renewable energy innovation. The outcomes will support the Australian Government’s National Hydrogen Strategy by strengthening national capability in clean hydrogen production and export. To maximise understanding, translation, and adoption, findings will be shared through collaboration with industry partners, participation in government-led hydrogen initiatives, and engagement with the broader energy sector and public via workshops, media, and outreach activities. In the long term, this research will reinforce Australia’s global leadership in green hydrogen, drive economic growth through advanced manufacturing, and contribute to national emission-reduction goals, generating environmental, industrial, and social benefits.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Conversion and Holy War on an Islamic Frontier: The Qarakhanids of Xinjiang. This project investigates how legends of the Qarakhanid dynasty—the first Turkic steppe rulers to embrace Islam—were transformed into Sufi hagiography and vernacular literature in Central Asia. Focusing on the Tazkira-i Uwaysiyya and related texts, it traces how these narratives of conversion and holy war adapted to new imperial and cultural settings from the sixteenth to nineteenth centuries. Combining philology, historical analysis, and digital mapping of shrines, the project recovers an endangered manuscript tradition in Xinjiang. In doing so, it illuminates Islam’s eastern frontier while preserving sources now imperilled by cultural repression and destruction.
national-interest-test-statement: This project will advance Australia’s national interests by strengthening relationships with Central Asian countries and enhancing understanding of a strategically significant region. In an area where Australia has limited official engagement, scholarly collaboration offers a cost-effective and credible means of constructive involvement. By diversifying Australia’s international research networks, the project supports government priorities to expand engagement beyond the Indo-Pacific and deepen ties across Eurasia—an emerging hub of energy production, transport connectivity, and geopolitical competition. The project will enhance Australia’s capacity to interpret and respond to religious and cultural policies in Xinjiang, a region central to Australia’s wider relationship with the People’s Republic of China. It will provide policymakers, diplomats, and journalists with authoritative research and analysis, improving the quality of Australia’s engagement with China and its regional partners. By documenting an endangered Islamic manuscript tradition, the project contributes to the preservation of global cultural heritage in line with Australia’s commitments to human rights and freedom of religion and belief. Supporting a PhD student from the region will foster lasting people-to-people ties, while Australia’s visible role in protecting Islamic heritage will generate goodwill and bolster its reputation among Muslim-majority countries worldwide.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Neuroeconomics of Risk and Delay: Redefining Theory and Improving Decisions. This project studies how the brain’s limits combined with economic conditions affect people’s economic decisions. Traditional economics assumes people have stable preferences, but in reality choices are shaped by cognitive capacity, which declines with age and can be disrupted or enhanced. By combining neuroeconomics modelling with economics experiments, the project will advance economics by revealing how economic conditions together with cognitive limits influence risk-taking and patience. The outcomes will provide evidence from controlled experiments for new foundations for economic theory and generate practical insights to improve policies on savings, ageing, obesity, workplace safety, and climate action.
national-interest-test-statement:
Australians decide daily about saving, investing, eating, exercising, and environmental protection. These decisions determine our long-term health, wealth, and well-being. Yet people struggle with short-sighted choices—such as failing to save for retirement or prioritising immediate pleasures over future benefits. This project will uncover how the limits of the human brain and economic conditions together shape such behaviour.

The findings will generate broad benefits for Australia. In an ageing society, understanding how cognitive decline affects decision-making will support new tools to help older adults maintain financial security and independence. With two-thirds of adults overweight or obese, the research will identify how cognitive limits contribute to suboptimal health behaviours and suggest strategies that promote sustainable lifestyle choices. The project will also explain why people undervalue long-term climate risks, informing more effective environmental policy.

Beyond immediate applications, this project strengthens Australia’s research leadership in economics and neuroscience. It will train the next generation of researchers and attract international collaboration, positioning Australia at the forefront of global efforts to understand and improve human decision-making. The outcomes will help build a healthier, fairer, and more resilient nation.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: How are immune responses to cellular RNA kept in check? Sensing of double-stranded RNA, a hallmark of viral genomes, is an ancient cellular mechanism for detecting infection. How endogenous RNAs evade this surveillance remains poorly understood. This project aims to uncover how cells regulate endogenous dsRNA to prevent aberrant immune sensing, using innovative models and approaches. The research will yield transformative insights and intellectual property with broad applications in health and agriculture. It will strengthen international collaborations and national RNA research networks, delivering new tools, datasets, and training to bolster Australia’s leadership in RNA biology.
national-interest-test-statement:
Innate immunity is the body’s frontline defence against infection, detecting common pathogen features and is highly conserved across evolution. A key challenge for cells is distinguishing harmful viruses from their own nucleic acids, which can share molecular signatures like double-stranded RNA. This project will investigate newly identified pathways that help cells balance antiviral responses with avoidance of self-reactivity. Understanding this fundamental biology is essential for tackling autoimmune disease, chronic inflammation, and viral susceptibility in health and agriculture.
By leveraging specialised models and expertise developed over the past decade, this project will strengthen Australia’s leadership in RNA biology and innate immunity. It aligns with priorities in Australia’s RNA Blueprint (Department of Industry). Advancing foundational knowledge could inform development of RNA-based therapeutics and novel immunomodulatory drugs—global markets valued at USD$12.2B and USD$217.7B, respectively.
The project will enhance Australia’s position at the forefront of RNA research and generate significant new knowledge. Training researchers at the RNA–immunity interface will expand our skills base amid growing demand, as RNA therapeutics rapidly evolve. Outcomes will be shared via open-access publications, media, stakeholder engagement, and public outreach to maximise visibility and impact.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
current-admin-organisation: The University of New South Wales
announcement-admin-organisation: The University of New South Wales
grant-summary: OmniSB: Sovereign Agent-guided Foundation Model for Virtual Cells. This project will develop OmniSB, a world-leading artificial intelligence (AI) platform for spatial biology. Using a novel AI-based approach, OmniSB will learn from large-scale gene and cell data to map tissue structure, identify cell types and interactions, and reveal how biological conditions alter these patterns. It will enable virtual experiments that predict cellular responses, accelerating discovery and hypothesis generation. The project will deliver open-source tools, datasets and training resources to empower Australian researchers and strengthen Australia’s global leadership in spatial biology and AI. Expected benefits include advances in health, agriculture and biotechnology through next-generation biological modelling.
national-interest-test-statement:
This project delivers a sovereign Australian capability in advanced biological artificial intelligence. It will build OmniSB, a national AI platform that can read complex spatial biology data, where genes, proteins and metabolites are active in real tissue, and turn it into actionable biological insight. This matters for Australia for four reasons.

First, it supports national security of biological data. Australia currently depends on overseas, proprietary systems to analyse spatial genomics data. OmniSB will be developed, hosted and maintained in Australia, ensuring that sensitive biological data, including data from agriculture and biosecurity, can be analysed domestically.

Second, it creates critical research infrastructure. OmniSB will be released with open software, benchmarks, and explainable outputs, enabling Australian labs and facilities to interpret spatial data without needing to build their own AI stack.

Third, it builds workforce capability. The project will train Ph.D researchers and early-career scientists in foundation models, spatial biology, and trustworthy AI, directly addressing national priorities in sovereign AI and advanced manufacturing of high-value bio-technologies.

Finally, it supports long-term innovation in health, biotech and agriculture by enabling virtual cells and virtual biopsies for discovery and screening, accelerating research while reducing experimental cost and time.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Molecular Insights into Cross-Species Transmission of Influenza A virus. This project aims to understand how avian influenza viruses adapt to jump from birds into mammals. Highly pathogenic avian influenza has a devastating impact on Australia’s poultry industry and poses an emerging threat to the cattle industry and wild bird populations. The project will generate new knowledge in Influenza cross-species transmission through interdisciplinary approaches and international collaborations. Expected outcomes include identifying molecular markers for host adaptation to improve early detection in biosecurity and public health programs. The results will provide significant benefits for agriculture, conservation, the economy, and health in Australia, while expanding fundamental knowledge of influenza and glycobiology.
national-interest-test-statement:
This project aims to uncover key molecular differences in the neuraminidase protein of avian and bovine (cattle) influenza viruses. The ability of fast-spreading, highly contagious influenza viruses to cross species barriers represents an existential threat to global biodiversity, livestock industries, and public health. Our capacity to monitor and mitigate this threat is limited by a lack of understanding of the precise mechanisms by which avian influenza adapts to and infects mammals.
Through interdisciplinary approaches and international collaboration, this research will provide fundamental insights into how avian influenza viruses evolve to infect new mammalian hosts. This resulting knowledge will enable more effective surveillance programs to detect early adaptive changes in circulating viruses, anticipate and mitigate to future panzootic (animal pandemics) events, and inform vaccine development. The research will deliver both economic and environmental benefits in line with the goals of Australia’s biosecurity system—critical to maintaining livestock industries while simultaneously protecting our unique wildlife from exotic infections.
Outcomes will be disseminated through national biosecurity and industry networks. Research data will be made publicly available in open-access repositories and communicated through media engagement and scientific conferences. This proposal aims to inform nationally coordinated responses and future policy developments.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Conditioning wildlife for resilience to shifting fire regimes . This project aims to enhance wildlife resilience to increasingly intense fire regimes. Through innovative behavioural experiments, it will determine whether fire-adaptive traits are genetically inherited or environmentally acquired and develop targeted strategies to protect vulnerable species from fire-driven extinction. By uncovering the evolutionary and behavioural foundations of fire adaptation, the project will predict the ecological consequences of fire spreading into new ecosystems, including World Heritage areas. Expected outcomes include insights into how animals adapt to fire and practical tools to reduce extinction risks. Benefits include improved capacity to predict and safeguard ecosystems under future fire conditions.
national-interest-test-statement: As climate change accelerates and land use shifts, fire is spreading into ecosystems where it once scarcely occurred, placing billions of animals at risk. Megafires are devastating landscapes globally, and a key vulnerability is fire naïveté—when species lack evolutionary experience with fire, leaving them unprepared and highly susceptible. Like prey naïveté, which has driven extinction waves worldwide, this vulnerability threatens Australia’s No New Extinctions policy under the Threatened Species Action Plan and could erode confidence in the $136 billion Nature Repair Market. This project will map the prevalence and causes of fire naïveté across World Heritage areas and determine whether fire-adaptive traits are inherited or learned. It will test strategies to condition wildlife against fire naïveté, reducing extinction risk in an increasingly flammable world. The research will deliver environmental and societal benefits by improving biodiversity resilience, informing conservation policy, and strengthening regional research capacity. Building on an exceptional record of science communication, the project will promote its outcomes through partnerships with land managers, Traditional Owners, and government agencies, and through targeted media, education, and outreach initiatives to maximise understanding, translation, and adoption beyond academia.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Digital Diets: Tracking the dietary impact of online food marketing. This innovative longitudinal study investigates how exposure to unhealthy food marketing in online media influences Australian children’s diets over time. Using screen recordings and AI-powered image recognition, the project will quantify unhealthy food marketing exposure and assess its impact on dietary intake, food attitudes and food purchases. The study evaluates the effects of Australia’s new social media age restrictions, comparing cohorts with varying access to online platforms. By capturing real-time marketing exposure and dietary outcomes, the study will generate critical evidence to inform equitable policy reform and protect children from harmful digital marketing, addressing a major gap in global obesity prevention efforts.
national-interest-test-statement: Marketing normalises unhealthy foods and encourages overconsumption, leading to poor diets and excess body weight. Protecting children from the impacts of unhealthy food marketing has been identified as a priority intervention for childhood obesity prevention by leading health agencies and the Australian Government. Yet Australian regulations to protect children from this marketing are vastly inadequate. Effective regulations have been stifled due to a lack of local evidence linking children’s marketing exposures to diets and a lack of sustained civil society pressure for policy reform. This project aims to quantify the extent of Australian children’s everyday unhealthy food marketing exposures on digital media and the influence of this marketing on their diets. It will contribute to national and global policy dialogues for limiting children’s exposure to unhealthy food marketing. Outcomes will include world-first evidence on the long-term effects of contemporary food marketing on children’s diets. This evidence will be critical in countering the prevailing industry arguments that marketing does not influence consumption and that the existing industry self-regulatory codes of practice for responsible marketing to children are adequate. Project outcomes will be widely disseminated to policy stakeholders, including through partnerships with civil society organisations and leaders, and through the dissemination of policy briefs and direct engagement with decision-makers.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Neural architecture of spatial working memory: from neurons to networks. This project aims to investigate the mechanisms the brain uses to store information in working memory across multiple scales of brain activity - from populations of cells to interactions across brain areas. This project expects to generate new knowledge about how the brain keeps track of information flowing across brain networks using novel techniques and capacity. The interaction across these networks of brain areas is critical for cognition, including working memory. The expected outcomes include new knowledge about how the connections across brain areas lead to cognition. Understanding these mechanisms will provide significant benefits such as enriching the development of neural engineering projects like prosthetics and computer vision.
national-interest-test-statement: Cognitive behaviours are controlled by competing inputs that the brain must parse and integrate. The overarching aim of this project is to understand how the brain takes in multiple sensory inputs, holds them in working memory, and integrates them to guide behaviour. Working memory is a useful behaviour for studying communication across brain areas because we know that it is stored across a network of brain areas, yet we have little understanding of how information is communicated and integrated across brain areas.  This project tackles that question from multidisciplinary approaches to untangle how the populations of cells -  both within and across brain areas, store and retrieve items from working memory. This project aims to determine the computational strategies the brain uses to support cognition. This project will increase our understanding of how our brains guide behaviour. The aims of this project do not study or address any diseases. However, we know that even in healthy brains, working memory degrades as we age. Understanding the mechanisms of working memory will give insights into future research to support healthy aging. This project will generate a foundational dataset that we intend to make publicly available, to be shared with other researchers, as well as industry and clinical partners.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Transforming Equity and Private International Law: A New Framework. The Project addresses a critical gap that currently leaves cross-border disputes unpredictable and unfair due to the lack of a comprehensive framework bridging equity law and private international law. Adopting an innovative methodology, it will develop a holistic model of equity law, and use it to transform private international law in Australia. It aspires to bring Australian law in line with global standards, creating a more coherent structure for cross-border litigation. It will generate benefits to Australia by enhancing legal predictability, attracting international litigation work currently diverted to competing jurisdictions, while positioning Australia as the preferred Asia-Pacific hub for cross-border dispute resolution.
national-interest-test-statement: This Project tackles a serious problem in Australia’s legal system for handling disputes involving overseas parties or foreign laws. Poorly developed rules connecting equity law and private international law have created significant uncertainty, undermining the predictability and global competitiveness of Australian law. Resolving these disputes fairly and predictably is essential for ensuring justice in a globalised world. This Project will develop a holistic, contextualised model of equity law by adapting modern understandings for Australia’s needs, and use it to reform private international law rules, ensuring greater alignment with global standards. The impact on Australians will be meaningful — improving the clarity and reliability of legal outcomes in cross-jurisdictional disputes, increasing the efficacy of legal resolutions, and enhancing Australia’s reputation as a global leader in international commerce and dispute resolution. A comprehensive roadmap for legislative and judicial reform will be widely shared through media and online channels, and direct engagement with policymakers and regulatory bodies will ensure the research helps to shape future legal frameworks. These efforts will not only transform legal practice but also influence critical policy reforms, empower communities, protect rights, and ultimately cement Australia’s leadership in global legal standards while delivering a more just, reliable, and forward-thinking legal environment for all Australians.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Producing multi-Carbon Chemicals via Tandem Carbon Capture and Electrolysis. This project aims to develop a streamlined “capture–electrolysis” process that uses blended liquids to absorb CO2, tandem catalysts, and a liquid-fed electrolyser powered by renewable electricity to make multi-carbon products such as ethylene. It will turn industrial carbon emissions into chemicals without gas purification and contribute new knowledge on how blended solutions and catalysts work together, define rules for C–C bond formation in solution, and deliver validated solvent–catalyst pairs and an integrated system. Expected outcomes include lower emissions, a home-grown renewable pathway to critical feedstocks, and a strengthened national clean-energy supply chain, providing benefits through enhanced manufacturing capability.
national-interest-test-statement:
Australia’s path to net-zero and a secure domestic supply of basic chemicals requires the adoption of efficient carbon capture and utilisation (CCU) technologies. Today’s CCUs are separate processes: carbon emissions are first stripped and purified—adding huge energy and cost (~4.2 GJ or ~$60–120 per tonne)—and then converted in gas CO2 electrolysers that often clog with salts and electrolyte flooding. This project resolves the gap by creating a tandem capture–electrolysis pathway. New blended absorbents will also serve as the reaction medium, tailored electrocatalysts will turn captured CO2 into multi-carbon products, and a liquid-fed electrolyser will connect directly to capture units, powered by renewable electricity.

National benefits include lower emissions, reduced reliance on imported feedstocks, and growth of clean manufacturing jobs in regions hosting emission-intensive plants. Deliverables include validated solvent/catalyst “recipes” and a capture-to-product module, strengthening sovereign capability and positioning Australian IP for commercial translation with industry partners. The Fellowship will also train Honours, PhD, and early-career researchers, building the skilled workforce needed for Australia’s clean industry transition. Outcomes will be translated through RMIT’s industry networks via workshops and demonstration days, pilot collaborations, contributions to standards, and outreach through industry forums to drive adoption across Australian plants.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Community Led Reclamation of Kulin Nations Star Knowledge. This project aims to deliver the first comprehensive study of the Star Knowledges of the eastern Kulin Nations of Victoria. It will revitalise and integrate Indigenous and scientific understandings of the sky to reveal links between land, stars, and ecological systems to better understand local seasons, climate patterns, animal behaviour, and food economics through cultural practice. Outcomes will inform sustainable land management, guide light pollution reform, and advance Indigenous-led tourism and education. The project strengthens Indigenous self-determination, builds economic capacity, trains future leadership, and contributes to National Research Priorities and Closing the Gap targets through transformative, community-driven research.
primary-field-of-research: 4506 - Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Sciences
national-interest-test-statement: Aboriginal Elders teach that the land is reflected in the sky; to understand how our world works, we need to look to the stars. Traditional star knowledge was deeply impacted by the ongoing effects of colonisation, particularly in Victoria, where star knowledge is highly fragmented. This project will fill this gap by researching astronomical knowledge systems of the eastern Kulin Nations, the lands on which 20% of Australia’s population live and work. This will be done in a collaboration with the Taungerong, Wurundjeri, and Bunerong communities, at their invitation. The project will develop seasonal calendars and star maps for cultural education that will inform the development of tourism activities that reflect cultural priorities, as well as government policy to safeguard access to dark skies. This will build capacity and open career pathways for Aboriginal tour guides and public education programs, providing social, economic and cultural benefits for Aboriginal communities and peoples. It also addresses the Australian government’s policy on Closing the Gap and ensuring First Nations’ cultures and languages are supported. The education materials developed through this program will both support and inform the Australian National Curriculum’s approach to teaching/learning Indigenous history and science.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Advanced Microscopy on Antiferroelectric Phase Transition and Fatigue. This project aims to uncover the atomic-scale mechanisms of electric-field-induced phase transitions and fatigue in lead-free antiferroelectrics (AFEs). Using advanced in-situ biasing/heating electron microscopy and nanoscale property characterisation, it will directly visualise phase transition pathways, electric dipole rearrangements, and defect formation. Such insights will elucidate the fundamental processes of energy storage and reveal how defects and repeated cycling drive fatigue, establishing design principles for the development of efficient and durable capacitors. The outcomes will advance the development of high-performance, lead-free AFEs, supporting clean energy, electric vehicles, and Australia’s advanced manufacturing.
national-interest-test-statement: Lead-free antiferroelectrics offer an eco-friendly pathway for advanced capacitors. Yet the electric-field-driven transition from the antiferroelectric to ferroelectric phase, which is central to energy storage, release, and fatigue, remains poorly understood. This project addresses this critical knowledge gap by applying cutting-edge in-situ electron microscopy and nanoscale property measurements to directly reveal dipole rearrangements, phase transition pathways, and defect evolution. The outcomes include identifying the fundamental causes of energy loss and fatigue and establishing design principles for efficient, durable capacitors. These findings will accelerate the development of high-performance, lead-free energy storage devices vital for clean energy technologies, electric vehicles, and next-generation electronics. The knowledge generated will strengthen Australia’s capability in advanced manufacturing and energy storage, driving economic growth and supporting progress toward net-zero emissions.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Building resilience without resistance in microbial communities. The aim of this project is to investigate the impact of antimicrobial fluctuations on microbial communities, and how community dynamics feed back on the evolution of resistance. Most pathogens are embedded within ecological communities, yet we have limited understanding of the role that off-target species play in regulating resistance evolution. Through a close integration of experiments and mathematical modelling, this project expects to uncover the dominant processes shaping microbial stability and adaptation under fluctuating stress. This should provide significant benefits including a stronger foundation for the development of ecology-based strategies for antimicrobial use and the design of probiotic consortia.
national-interest-test-statement: Antimicrobial resistance is a major global threat to human, animal and environmental health. Yet most research focuses on antimicrobials and pathogens in isolation, overlooking the ecological context in which resistance evolves. Microbial communities underpin essential processes in animal hosts, soils, and waterways, but we know little about how environmental variability, such as nutrient fluctuations, interacts with antibiotic exposure to impact the stability of microbial communities and the evolution of resistance. This project addresses that gap by integrating mathematical modelling and experiments in a tractable animal model to reveal how the timing of antimicrobial and nutrient pulses shapes resistance evolution in microbial communities. The findings will provide foundational knowledge to strengthen Australia’s capacity to manage microbial ecosystems that support environmental, animal, and human health. To maximise impact beyond academia, we will share findings through open data and modelling tools, collaborate with research networks, and engage with government and industry forums focused on antimicrobial stewardship and biosecurity.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Small nucleus, broad influence: the Locus Coeruleus in brain states. This project aims to reveal the central processing mechanisms of the brain: one of the most fundamental challenges in science. This project expects to develop innovative technologies to to uncover the foundations of neural communication through the meticulous manipulation of a key brain region: the Locus Coeruleus. Expected outcomes of this project include state of the art microscopy approaches, avenues for the development of adaptive models in artificial intelligence, high impact publications, and international collaborations. The anticipated benefits are the high-quality training of the Australian workforce and further establishment of Australia as a leader in microscopy, neuroscience and artificial intelligence.
national-interest-test-statement:
This project aims to advance Australia’s intellectual leadership in neuroscience, imaging, and computational analysis. More specifically, this project will reveal how specific brain regions tune and adapt to environmental demands. The outputs of this research will establish fundamental principles of neural function that are essential for understanding cognition, perception, and adaptive behaviour. It will also provide crucial information for the development of more efficient, flexible, and robust computational architectures.
This project is expected to advance Australia’s leadership in neuroscience and technology by uncovering how brain networks operate, training a new generation of researchers in cutting-edge imaging and computational methods, and strengthening national research capacity and international reputation. 
Results and their impact will be communicated to broad audiences through public outreach, media engagement, and educational initiatives, including engagement with schools, science events, and public lectures to enhance the understanding of brain research in the community.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Mycorrhizal matchmaking: predicting the right place, practice, and plant. This project advances sustainable agriculture by predicting and testing beneficial partnerships between crops and mycorrhizal fungi—soil organisms that enhance plant nutrition, growth, and stress tolerance. Using advanced molecular and statistical techniques with national-scale spatial mapping, field studies, and glasshouse experiments, it will identify which fungi are suited to which regions and crops, and which deliver the greatest benefits. The project’s outcomes will enable targeted “mycorrhizal matchmaking” to reduce fertiliser and pesticide reliance, support soil biodiversity, and improve productivity—strengthening environmental and economic resilience in Australian farming under a changing climate.
national-interest-test-statement:
Australia’s cropping systems rely heavily on fertilisers and pesticides, costing farmers billions of dollars each year and contributing to soil degradation, pollution, and greenhouse gas emissions. This project will help reduce that dependence by harnessing one of nature’s most effective partnerships—between plants and beneficial soil fungi called mycorrhizas. These fungi improve crop nutrition and resilience, but their effectiveness varies across different soils, climates, and crops, meaning most farms are not reaping their benefits.
This research will map which fungal communities are best suited to Australia’s major crop-growing regions, determine how agriculture influences their survival, and test whether targeted inoculation can improve crop nutrition, yields, and resistance to disease. By identifying the “right place, practice, and plant” for effective mycorrhizal partnerships, the project will deliver the scientific foundation for nature-based farming innovations.
Outcomes will include tools and guidelines to help farmers apply native soil fungi to increase productivity, reduce fertiliser and pesticide use, and restore soil biodiversity. The project will strengthen national food security, enhance farm profitability, and reduce agriculture’s environmental footprint—advancing Australia’s leadership in sustainable, low-emission agricultural innovation.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Advancing Fairness-aware Personalisation Algorithms. This project addresses the unfairness inherent in personalisation algorithms that underpin today's online services and recommender systems, particularly as it impairs marginalised user groups. The knowledge to be generated concerns fairness, scalability, and interpretability of personalisation models. The expected outcomes include a new personalisation paradigm that moves beyond traditional data-driven designs, and facilitates fair, accurate, and transparent personalised predictions across user groups via knowledge-grounded reasoning and bias-aware optimisation. These outcomes will fill an important digital equity gap, and strengthen Australia's leadership in developing trustworthy and socially responsible artificial intelligence solutions.
national-interest-test-statement: As the algorithmic backbone of today's online services, personalisation models provide tailored user experiences that counter information explosion. However, these models are known to underperform for minority users where interaction data is limited and where scaling to diverse marginalised communities is difficult. Furthermore, the models act as a blackbox that amplifies user distrust. This project will establish a new personalisation paradigm to fill this research gap. The work involves developing a novel user demand modelling process that is less reliant on historical interactions yet fully reflects the nuanced need of minority users. Knowledge-grounded reasoning and bias-aware optimisation make the paradigm inherently interpretable and scalable-by-design to ensure minorities find the predictions trustworthy and so the model can efficiently scale to different user groups. This project will advance the field of fairness-aware personalisation algorithms, positioning Australia as a global leader in equitable data science research. These new ethical artificial intelligence products will enhance trust, satisfaction, and retention among marginalised communities, directly contributing to revenue growth across sectors reliant on personalised digital services. The project outcomes will also address society's concerns about bias and discrimination in automated systems, ultimately contributing to a fair, trustworthy, and socially responsible digital ecosystem in Australia and beyond.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Digital twin housing for affordable and sustainable homes. This project aims to analyse digital twin technology for affordable and sustainable housing, using a critical social science approach. This project expects to generate new knowledge in the fields of geography, housing and the built environment by examining how digital tools and data practices are already transforming apartment design, delivery, management and their real-world impacts. Expected outcomes include new conceptual models of digital twin deployment and clear digital maturation pathways for the housing sector. This should provide significant benefits, such as improved housing productivity and performance to support National Cabinet’s ambitions for affordable quality supply, and Infrastructure Australia’s Digital by Default agenda.
national-interest-test-statement: Australia urgently needs more sustainable and affordable housing, yet business as usual approaches underperform due to low productivity and limited innovation. This project aims to assess the potential for digital twin technology to support more affordable, sustainable homes through new technical capabilities in design, delivery and operations. Digital twins are digital replicas of real buildings that support data-sharing and advanced decision-making. This project examines how digital twins are transforming the way apartments are designed, built, managed and experienced. This project will produce new evidence on the social, economic and environmental impacts of digital twin housing (such as better team coordination, reduced costs, fewer errors and lower emissions), and will trace where benefits and risks fall among stakeholders, including renters. The project will bring together government, industry and community groups to co-design a roadmap for responsible digital twin deployment across the apartment housing sector. This will help guide and de-risk digital transformation in housing for public servants, developers, architects, planners, builders, and housing asset owners and operators. Moreover, it will support high-quality design, faster and more efficient delivery and improved long-term performance in the apartment sector, with clear benefits for households.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Comprehensive Analysis of Singularities in Geometric Flows. Geometric flows are powerful and proven ways of advancing mathematics (e.g. solving the Poincaré Conjecture), science (e.g. modelling the spread of bushfire and diseases) and technology (e.g. designing and processing semiconductors). This project aims at a comprehensive study of the central and pressing problem of singularity formation in Ricci flow and mean curvature flow by describing the shapes and determining the stability of singular solutions. This project will generate new and significant results in singularity analysis with many benefits: enriching the understanding of geometric flows at and past singularities, deepening the theory of geometric flows and enhancing their applications in mathematics, science and technology.
national-interest-test-statement: Curvature occurs everywhere at all scales from the cosmological spacetime to the molecular interfaces. Geometric flows such as Ricci flow and mean curvature flow are powerful ways of finding optimal shapes and thus hold profound theoretical and versatile practical implications. Ricci flow, with its celebrated resolution of the Poincaré Conjecture, holds great promises in demystifying the four-dimensional geometry and topology. Mean curvature flow is used to design and process semiconductors, sharpen images in computer vision, and model the spread of bushfire and diseases, all of which hold strategic importance to Australia’s national interest in security, development and well-being. By proposing original ideas and innovative approaches to tackle the central problem of singularity analysis in geometric flows, this proposal is poised to achieve results with far reaching consequences in theories and applications. The mathematical findings will significantly expand and deepen our knowledge base of geometry, topology and nonlinear partial differential equations. The findings will also help us devise efficient and cost-effective methods in crafting advanced materials and semiconductors, rendering medical images, and managing wildfire, just to name a few. The proposed project attracts talent around the globe and trains the next generation of innovators and researchers in Australia, thereby maintaining Australia’s international lead in science and technology.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Molecular insights into plant-like transporters in eukaryotic metabolism. This project aims to define how GPR155 PIN transporters, newly discovered relatives of plant auxin transporters, function in insects and animals as cholesterol sensors and regulators of metabolism. By integrating cryo electron microscopy, biochemical assays, cross species structural comparisons and machine learning, it will uncover how these ancient membrane proteins bind small molecules, switch conformations and engage metabolic signalling complexes. The research will deliver foundational insight into transporter evolution and metabolic sensing, advance molecular imaging capabilities and position Australia as a global leader in structural biology and cellular metabolism.
national-interest-test-statement:
This research will investigate a newly discovered family of membrane transporters, known as GPR155 PIN transporters, which help cells detect and respond to cholesterol. Although these proteins share structural features with hormone transporters found in plants, they have evolved new roles in animals as key regulators of cellular metabolism. Their importance in cholesterol sensing is only beginning to be understood, and we do not yet know how they recognise small molecules or activate growth-related pathways in response to cholesterol. This project will fill that gap by revealing how these transporters evolved, how they function at the molecular level, and how they connect cholesterol sensing to broader metabolic control.

Understanding this mechanism will offer future insights into how cells regulate energy use and growth, especially in relation to conditions such as cardiovascular disease, obesity and age-related decline. It will strengthen Australia’s leadership in structural biology and metabolism research. Results will be shared through publications, public communication, and scientific conferences. By building national capability in advanced imaging and molecular discovery, this project will deliver long-term economic, health, and research benefits to Australians.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Physiological pathways controlling immune cell function in the gut. This project aims to uncover how communication between the nervous and immune systems maintains gut health. It will investigate how lifestyle factors such as diet, disrupted circadian rhythms, and stress alter these neuroimmune circuits and how their disruption affects tissue function. Expected outcomes include new knowledge of the physiological pathways that regulate immune balance and the identification of nerve-based strategies to control inflammation. The benefits include advancing bioelectronic medicine and informing future non-drug treatments to reduce chronic inflammatory disease in humans and animals, improving health and productivity.
national-interest-test-statement: Barrier tissues such as the intestine are constantly exposed to environmental changes and daily challenges from the food we eat. To stay healthy, the gut must rapidly detect these changes and respond with precision. Communication between the nervous and immune systems is central to this process; however, we still lack a clear understanding of how immune cells and nerves interact to sense environmental change and coordinate these responses. How disruption of this dialogue leads to chronic inflammation also remains unknown. This project fills that gap by mapping the neuroimmune circuits that sustain intestinal health and defining how lifestyle factors such as diet, circadian disruption, or chronic stress alter these circuits and reprogram immune responses. The knowledge generated will enable the development of next-generation, non-drug therapies that use gentle nerve stimulation to control inflammation and restore immune balance, a promising approach known as bioelectric immunomodulation. This strategy could greatly reduce the burden of chronic inflammatory diseases affecting millions of Australians. It will strengthen Australia’s biotechnology and advanced-manufacturing sectors through innovation, partnerships, and skilled jobs. Our findings will be shared through public talks, clinician workshops, media engagement, and consumer forums to support translation.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Planetary Civics: Innovations in Regenerative Stewardship and Governance. This project aims to investigate how communities and governments advance regenerative stewardship as a concept and practice for climate adaptation and resilience. It expects to develop new socially innovative governance frameworks and implementation mechanisms that bridge local action with global climate and biodiversity goals. Working with communities, civic and Indigenous leaders, policy experts and industry partners, the outcomes include the co-design of participatory processes that strengthen community climate resilience across borders. Expected benefits include supporting communities to adapt to global climate risks, protecting biodiversity and cultural heritage, and improving water security, planetary health and community wellbeing.
national-interest-test-statement: This project will address one of Australia’s most urgent national challenges—how to restore ecosystems and strengthen community resilience under accelerating climate change. It will develop practical frameworks for stewardship and governance that connect local action with global climate and biodiversity goals. By centring Indigenous custodianship and socially innovative community-led action, the project fills a major research gap in understanding how regenerative stewardship can be embedded across governance practices to drive implementation at the local scale. The research will deliver environmental and social benefits by improving the policy, planning, and management of Australia’s rivers, coasts, and urban ecosystems, supporting community-led adaptation to droughts, floods, and coastal change. It will provide tested governance models, participatory tools, and monitoring and evaluation metrics that support communities to adapt to climate risks while protecting biodiversity, cultural heritage, and water security. The project findings will be disseminated through co-design community tool-kits led by local and Indigenous leaders, policy translation labs and dialogues with universities, government and industry to build national capacity in regenerative design and governance. This research is essential for fostering cultural and behavioural shifts in climate action, enhancing stewardship capabilities, and strengthening Australia’s resilience against climate change.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Iron ore assisted gasification of biomass for green ironmaking. This project aims to develop a novel iron ore assisted biomass gasification process that co-produces high-quality syngas and pre-reduced ore for the direct reduced iron process. This process integrates biochar steam gasification and steam reforming of volatiles with iron ore reduction, addressing major challenges associated with syngas quality and catalyst deactivation in conventional catalytic biomass gasification processes. The expected outcomes include key fundamental knowledge and process development that are essential to this technology. The successful completion of this project will bring significant benefits to Australia’s energy and iron industries, and foster the growth of the biofuel sector in Australia's rural and regional areas.
national-interest-test-statement: Australia has committed to achieving net zero emissions by 2050 under the Long-Term Emissions Reduction Plan, and has recently updated its 2035 target to a 62–70% reduction below 2005 levels. Decarbonising heavy industries such as ironmaking is recognised as a national priority under the Future Made in Australia agenda. This project directly supports that goal by developing a novel iron ore assisted biomass gasification technology, which enables the co-production of high-quality syngas and pre-reduced iron ore with deposited carbon as excellent feedstocks for green ironmaking in the direct reduced iron process. The proposed process integrates biochar steam gasification and steam reforming of volatiles with iron ore reduction, where iron ore serves as both a reactant and a catalyst. It addresses key challenges associated with syngas quality and catalyst deactivation in conventional gasification processes. By coupling renewable biomass resources with local mineral feedstocks, this technology provides a low-emission, energy-efficient, and cost-effective pathway to decarbonise Australia’s iron industry. The outcomes of this project will strengthen Australia’s capability in renewable energy and green metal manufacturing, advancing the national ambition of becoming a renewable energy and green metal export superpower. It also aligns with the Future Made in Australia and Made in WA visions by leveraging domestic resources and innovation to create sustainable industrial value chains.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Shifting sands record the dynamic evolution of the East Antarctic Ice Sheet. Deep under the Antarctic Ice Sheet, sediments form slippery environments that control where and how fast glaciers flow. This project aims to investigate sedimentary basins underlying vast sectors of East Antarctica most vulnerable to ice-sheet instability and rapid change. By unlocking this sedimentary archive through innovative analytics and models, this project expects to generate new knowledge of Antarctic tectonics, landscape evolution and ice-sheet history. Expected outcomes include comprehensive geological datasets that refine ice-sheet configurations for past warm climates. This should provide critical benchmarks for ice-sheet simulations, helping to reduce future sea-level rise uncertainty and inform adaption measures.
national-interest-test-statement: Understanding how Antarctica’s ice sheets respond to a warming climate is critical for predicting future sea-level rise. This project will use samples and data from East Antarctica to investigate how the geology of vast low-lying basins influences ice-sheet behaviour today and during past warm climates, which are analogues for our future. Through existing partnerships with collaborative international Antarctic working groups, this research will be used in studies that predict ice-sheet behaviour and reduce uncertainty in sea-level projections. The outcomes will help understand future sea-level rise risk from East Antarctica, assisting governments and communities plan for coastal protection and climate adaptation. This is especially important for Australia and our Pacific neighbours, where rising seas threaten homes, infrastructure, and ecosystems. The research also strengthens Australia’s leadership in Antarctic science and contributes to national priorities in climate resilience and environmental protection. To ensure broad impact, the project will share results through open-access databases, public talks, and collaboration with government and international agencies. It will also train the next generation of geoscientists, helping build national capability in a field identified as a critical skills gap. This work will inform policy and help Australia prepare for the environmental challenges ahead.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: New Frontiers in Privacy-Preserving Cryptography. This project advances the next generation of privacy-preserving cryptography—technologies that safeguard how digital information is shared, verified and protected across interconnected systems. Current approaches cannot balance privacy with accountability and will soon be exposed to the risks of quantum computing. The research will create adaptive cryptographic frameworks that enable controlled, verifiable and long-term secure digital communications. As governments and industries worldwide accelerate the transition to quantum-safe standards by 2030, this project will place Australia at the forefront of building trustworthy, privacy-preserving and resilient digital infrastructures essential for future national security and prosperity.
national-interest-test-statement: Australia’s future prosperity relies on the security and privacy of its rapidly expanding digital ecosystem. As almost every aspect of life—from health and finance to government and industry—depends on data, protecting this information while allowing its secure and useful use has become a national priority. Privacy-preserving cryptography offers the scientific foundation for achieving both security and privacy simultaneously. However, current approaches remain limited, particularly in enabling privacy-preserving disclosure and controlled linkage of information across systems. This project will develop new theoretical foundations and practical frameworks that overcome these limitations and support Australia’s coordinated transition to quantum-safe digital infrastructure by 2030. The outcomes will deliver novel cryptographic mechanisms resistant to quantum-era attacks and directly applicable to Australia’s critical digital infrastructure. They will strengthen cyber resilience, support trusted data sharing, and inform future national and international standards. The project will also build Australia’s research and training capacity in advanced cryptography—identified as a critical technology for national security and economic growth. Through collaboration with industry, government, and academic partners, the results will accelerate innovation, foster sovereign capability, and help position Australia as a global leader in privacy-preserving and post-quantum security technologies.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Unravelling Lubrication Layer Mechanism for Durable 3D Printed Concrete. This project aims to develop new knowledge and tools to enable durable and sustainable automated construction using 3D printed concrete. It will investigate how a thin layer of material that forms during printing around the pipe affects the strength, durability and long-term performance of printed structures. The research will support the use of low-carbon and recycled materials in construction by improving our understanding of how these mixes behave during printing. The outcomes will help advance automated building methods, reduce environmental impacts and provide practical guidelines to support safer, greener and more affordable buildings and infrastructure in Australia.
national-interest-test-statement: Rapid urbanisation and population growth are increasing the demand for affordable, sustainable housing. 3D printing technology, including 3D printed concrete, has emerged as a promising tool for the automation of construction and offers potential for faster, more efficient, and economical building processes. Yet,the full potential of 3D concrete remains unrealized due to limited understanding of key material behaviours. The lubrication layer that forms during 3D printing of concrete plays a critical role in its structural integrity and long-term durability. This project will investigate the formation and impact of the lubrication layer through experimental testing, modelling, and optimization to improve the reliability of 3D printed structures. The outcomes will deliver economic benefits by enhancing construction productivity, reducing costs, and creating high-skilled jobs in advanced manufacturing. Environmentally, it will lower the carbon footprint of construction, reduce waste, and potentially support the use of recycled materials. Socially, it will improve access to affordable housing, enable rapid infrastructure deployment, and support customised solutions for diverse and remote communities. Findings will be communicated through workshops with industry partners, practical demonstrations, media channels including social media, and open-access resources to ensure impact beyond academia and translation into real-world applications.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Decoding cellular bioelectricity via stochastic electrochemistry. This project aims to introduce an advanced screening tool for the analysis of tiny signals that are naturally generated in all living cells by cellular ion transport. The project expects to generate significant new knowledge about ion channel dynamics by combining innovative light-activated and stochastic electrochemistry techniques.  Expected outcomes include enhanced capacity to decode and manipulate cell signalling patterns in dynamic systems and driving biosenors and diagnostics innovation. This should provide significant benefits such as advancements in biomedical innovations such as biosensors, point-of-care devices, and drug screening technologies, offering transformative benefits for public health and wellbeing.
national-interest-test-statement:
This project addresses a critical, unresolved question in bionics: how do living cells communicate through bioelectrical signals at the level of ion channels? Ion channels are central to controlling cellular function, homeostasis, and responses to environmental stimuli, yet their role in intercellular interaction remains poorly understood.
By developing a technology platform that integrates ultra-sensitive electrical detection, electroactive biointerfaces, advanced microscopy, and pattern recognition, this fellowship will allow the direct observation of ion-channel–mediated bioelectrical signalling with unprecedented precision. This capability will open new avenues in basic biology, diagnostics and bioelectronics.
For Australians, the project seeds innovations in health-monitoring devices, biosensors, personalized diagnostics, and electroceutical therapies. These technologies align with national priorities in advanced health technologies and data-driven biotechnology. In the medium term, the platform enables earlier disease detection, lower-cost diagnostics, and adaptive bioelectronic interfaces. 
To maximize translation and uptake beyond academia, the project will (i) disseminate data and algorithms openly via a cloud-based repository; (ii) engage with industry, clinical partners, and start-ups for technology uptake; (iii) present results in accessible media (e.g. public outreach, policy briefings). This strengthens Australia’s capacity and leadership in health technologies.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: The Ties That Bind: A Legal History of the Australian Family Across Time. The family and the law are two of our most important social institutions, yet we have no history of how their relationship has evolved across time in Australia. This project fills this gap by providing the first legal history of the Australian family from the colonial period to the present. Bringing innovative, interdisciplinary methods in law, history and biography to bear upon the question of how the family has been shaped by law as well as subjectively experienced, it will advance national and international knowledge by analysing the socio-cultural context of court records offering a new history of an area of law that affects more people, and is more contested, than any other. Outputs include a searchable database, a podcast and a book.
national-interest-test-statement: From the colonial period to the present day, the legal status of the family has been at the centre of political debate - whether it be Governors enforcing marriage in the eighteenth century, feminists campaigning for equal divorce laws in the nineteenth century, recognition of the stolen generations in the twentieth century, or the marriage equality referendum in the twenty-first century. While Australians largely agree that the family is among our most important social institutions - ‘the natural and fundamental group within society’ in the words of the Family Law Act, how the law imagines, defines, buttresses or proscribes conjugal and familial relations is a topic of endless discussion. Yet in the absence of a comprehensive history of the relationship between law and the family, we conduct these debates in a fog. This project will remedy this deficit in national knowledge by providing the first history of the legal regulation of the family from the colonial period to the present. It will unearth previously unexamined records of court hearings and analyse them using innovative interdisciplinary methods in law, history and biography to explain how the family has changed over time, how it was subjectively experienced, and how it was regulated by law. It will also make this research accessible to the community through producing a digital database of historical court cases concerning the family, a high quality podcast, and an engaging and inclusive scholarly book.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Development of novel ultrahigh-strength steels with additive manufacturing. This project aims to address the long-standing embrittlement problem of high-carbon, hard and high-strength steels by leveraging the micro-melting and rapid cooling features of metal 3D printing with grain refinement strategies. Using this innovative approach, the research expects to develop cost-effective ultrahigh-strength steels with performance comparable to or even exceeding the currently expensive benchmark steels. Expected outcomes include new printable steels with exceptional properties and new scientific knowledge to understand the breakthrough in alloy design enabled by metal 3D printing. These should deliver lower-cost, energy-efficient, and more sustainable steels with enhanced properties for various industry sectors.
national-interest-test-statement:
This project will support Australia’s transition to advanced and sustainable manufacturing by developing cost-effective ultrahigh-strength steels using metal 3D printing. Steels underpin all industrial sectors, and current high-strength steels rely on complex, energy-intensive processing or heavy alloying with resource-critical elements, which limit sustainability. By leveraging the rapid melting and cooling features of metal 3D printing in conjunction with well-established grain refinement technology, this project addresses the long-standing trade-offs between strength, ductility, and manufacturability in steels. The research establishes a new strategy to design and produce new and better steels with 3D printing.

These advances will reduce manufacturing costs, lower carbon emissions, and improve energy efficiency through material and weight reduction, enabling Australia to directly produce high-performance, high-value-added steel components. The research aligns with the Future Made in Australia and Green Metals initiatives, strengthening sovereign capability, industrial resilience, and sustainable materials innovation.

The Fellowship will enhance Australia’s global reputation in advanced materials and manufacturing by strengthening national expertise in metal 3D printing and alloy design, training future researchers, fostering industry collaboration, and driving long-term innovation in sustainable, high-value steel production.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Representation-Based Learning and Control: from Theory to Applications. Intelligent robotic systems have immense potential to transform industries but still struggle to interpret and act on complex, high-dimensional sensor data—such as images, sonar, and LiDAR. This project addresses this challenge by integrating representation learning with model-based control, developing control strategies that efficiently exploit multimodal sensory information while achieving strong generalisation across diverse tasks and environments. The outcomes will include both theoretical advances and practical algorithms, with a focus on vision-based control. These innovations will enhance productivity, reduce costs, and improve safety across key Australian industries, including mining, agriculture, and manufacturing.
national-interest-test-statement: Australia stands at the forefront of a robotics revolution, where intelligent robotic systems can transform industries by performing complex tasks in unpredictable environments. However, current systems struggle to reliably interpret vast streams of sensor data—like images, sonar, and LiDAR—especially in dynamic or unfamiliar settings. This project addresses that gap by developing new control algorithms that combine advanced learning techniques with control theory, enabling robots to incorporate multimodal sensors and perform safely and efficiently across diverse tasks. The research will benefit Australians by improving productivity, reducing costs, and enhancing safety—particularly in sectors like mining, agriculture, and manufacturing. It will also support environmental goals by enabling more efficient resource use and reducing waste. Two real-world robotic demonstrators will accelerate technology adoption and showcase practical applications in manufacturing and deep-water exploration, supporting Australia's global competitiveness in robotics. Beyond academia, findings will be shared through workshops and media outreach to engage industry, policymakers, and the public.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Clonally resolving the differentiation of blood stem cells to T cells. This project will study how blood stem cells decide to become different types of T cells, which are vital parts of the immune system. Using new single-cell tracking and gene expression analysis tools, it will uncover how these cells develop and what controls their fate. The project will create new knowledge about how immune cells form and provide useful methods for other areas of biology. Because T cells are important in all vertebrates, the findings could improve animal health, support biosecurity, and strengthen Australia’s innovation in agriculture and biotechnology.
national-interest-test-statement: T cells are a crucial part of the immune system and have key roles in the defence against various environmental challenges. Despite the importance of T cells, there is a major gap in understanding the biological process by which stem cells makes the fate decision to become T cells instead of other types of blood cells. We previously developed a powerful tool to track how individual cells develop over time. By combining this tool with other cutting-edge technologies, we can analyse the genes that are active in each individual cell and identify those that are likely to govern the processes that lead to cell fate decisions. The knowledge gained from this research has the potential to advance Australia's capabilities in fundamental cell biology, immunology, and biotechnology. This research has broad-reaching impact in Australian industries including agriculture in enhancing disease resistance in livestock and strengthening biosecurity from emerging biological threats. The project will build national research capacity by training researchers in advanced genomics and computational biology, supporting Australia's next generation of STEM leaders. It will also foster international collaboration and enhance Australia's reputation for excellence in fundamental science. We will make all publications accessible to the public through open access platforms and communicate our research findings through media engagement to inform and benefit the wider public.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Engaging Communities in the Ethics of Experimental Reproductive Technology. This fellowship aims to promote responsible use of experimental reproductive technologies in Australia by building a transferable model for effective community engagement. The project will develop a theoretical framework for understanding the role of the community in governance decisions about reproduction, and build a novel methodology for ethically informed use of reproductive technologies. Major outcomes include a robust framework for responsible innovation in reproductive healthcare that balances individual and community interests. The anticipated benefits include community engagement tools, ethical guidance to support inclusive regulation and public outreach models to foster democratized knowledge and ethical decision-making.
national-interest-test-statement: From conception through pregnancy, there are now a suite of experimental reproductive technologies in development that will shape reproductive decisions in Australia, as well as what counts as human reproduction. These technologies are scientifically and clinically ground-breaking but high-stakes in terms of societal impacts. Australia has no ethical or regulatory roadmap, at a time of increasing public controversy about commercialised reproductive tools that are outpacing ethical considerations. This fellowship will comprise the first community-engaged investigation and governance model for preparing Australians for the imminent introduction of three high-stakes technologies across the spectrum of reproductive intervention. Through collaborations with those at the forefront of these advancements across five countries, Australia will be brought to the forefront of responsible use of experimental reproductive technologies. Outcomes will benefit all Australians through public engagement mechanisms that bring together different stakeholder perspectives and knowledge so that tomorrow’s families are informed and prepared for technologies that are no longer just science fiction.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Fuelling the Brain: Neuronal Fatty Acid Metabolism in Energy and Cognition. The brain needs vast energy to think, learn and remember. The prevailing view is that neurons derive energy solely from dietary sugars. A recent breakthrough by the applicant has challenged this long-held view, revealing that endogenous fats play a critical role in powering neurons. Using advanced imaging and multiomics, this project aims to reveal the mechanisms underlying this uncharacterised pathway, specifically the role of lipid enzyme Ddhd2, and how it supports neuronal function, integrates with other brain energy systems, and changes with ageing. This is expected to establish a transformative conceptual framework for brain energy metabolism, guiding innovative strategies to support brain health and deliver wide-ranging benefits.
national-interest-test-statement:
Tiny in size, huge in demand – the brain is 2% of your weight but consumes 20% of your energy to keep its neurons communicating, enabling vital functions like thinking, memory, and movement. These neurons are believed to acquire all their energy from sugars in our diet. However, applicant’s recent research challenged this long-standing view, demonstrating that neurons are not fuelled solely by sugars, and instead also rely on fats that are produced within the body itself, to power their energy and function.

The aim of this project is to characterise this newly identified fat-based neuronal energy pathway and understand its role in maintaining brain health and cognition throughout life.

The outcomes are expected to provide groundbreaking understanding of the brain’s metabolic adaptability, redefining how neuronal communication is powered, and informing strategies to support healthy brain ageing. A deeper understanding of lipid-based energy use in the brain could inform how diet and metabolism influence cognitive function across the lifespan, knowledge that could guide future evidence-based public health and nutrition strategies to support brain health in Australia’s ageing population.

The project will position Australia at the forefront of this conceptual revolution in neuroscience. Further benefits will come from advancing Australia’ capability in advanced imaging and multiomics providing world-class training opportunities for the next-generation of scientific leaders.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: How our cells age: Discovering the Molecular Networks that Control Ageing. The project aims to uncover how and why ageing-related changes occur by identifying key molecular switches that drive decline across multiple tissues in humans. The project expects to generate new knowledge of the molecular control of ageing using big data, advanced computational modelling and molecular analyses. Expected outcomes include discovering key ageing-related molecules, understanding their roles across tissues, and creating the world’s first open-access web tool (AgeMap) to map molecular ageing networks. These outcomes will transform our understanding of fundamental biological processes across lifespan.
national-interest-test-statement:
