This project aims to uncover novel molecular indicators of the ageing process in multiple tissues, including those which predict ‘faster’ ageing to provide a framework for future tailored ‘good health’ prescriptions that can help Australian’s “Age Well”. This will lead to a better understanding of how humans respond to changing environments during their lifetime, keep Australians healthier for longer reducing healthcare and economic burdens.
 
The National Action Plan for Critical Technologies cites the need for enhanced genome and genetic sequencing and analysis capacity. Our novel and publicly accessible analyses, data sets, and freely available webtool, will promote Australia’s expertise in this area, building the capacity of researchers and enabling use of the data by health practitioners.

Beyond academia, outcomes of this research will be communicated to aged-care professionals, exercise scientists, and industry partners to assist developing targeted healthy lifestyle interventions aiming to slow down ageing across different tissues. The outcomes of this project will therefore have significant economic and social benefits to the community. We will also leverage Monash science communication support to promote the utility of our resource to the broader community, incl. webinars analogous to how the human genome project captured the wider scientific interest.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Harnessing hybrid particles for on-chip generation of quantum light. This project aims to investigate a novel platform based on the hybridisation of light and matter for the efficient generation of quantum light from a semiconductor chip. The project expects to generate new knowledge on the role of light-matter hybridisation in semiconductors in quantum light generation, providing insights across different areas of physics, from semiconductors to quantum optics. Expected outcomes include novel methods for generating complex quantum light from a microscopic device. This should provide significant benefits such as opening up the ability to design and implement on-chip quantum light sources, which are the critical component in realising robust, scalable, and compact light-based quantum devices.
national-interest-test-statement: Quantum technology is poised to transform many aspects of our lives. It can provide ultrasensitive sensors that detect diseases before symptoms appear, a highly secure digital world safe from cyber threats, and powerful computers that can accurately predict the weather. Australia is at the forefront in developing these cutting-edge technologies, with the National Quantum Strategy projecting a $9 billion economic boost and over 50,000 jobs by 2045. However, to realise this potential, we must urgently overcome key technical barriers, such as miniaturisation and deployability. Delaying investment risks falling behind in a fast-moving global quantum race. This project tackles these challenges head-on by developing a promising platform for generating complex quantum light from a microscopic chip, which is essential for scalable, on-chip quantum technologies. The project will provide a significant step towards advancing quantum optical and materials technologies, laying the foundation of quantum polaritonics as a new platform for fundamental quantum studies and applications. It will help fill highly skilled jobs by providing world-class training at the ANU's unique environment for the next generation of quantum scientists. The domestic capabilities and new knowledge developed through the project will enable Australia to maintain its position at the forefront of innovations in quantum science and technology.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Fast radio bursts as tracers of baryons, galaxies and the evolving Universe. This project aims to understand the origins and environments of fast radio bursts at high redshift and use them as tools to study galaxy evolution and the distribution of matter in the universe. By combining precise radio positions with deep optical and infrared observations, we will measure host galaxy properties and explore how local and global galactic environments influence the bursts. The outcomes will map the distribution of baryons across cosmic time, test progenitor models, provide a framework to interpret and test the implications of the highest redshift population, and position Australia as a world leader in high-redshift FRB astronomy.
national-interest-test-statement:
High-redshift fast radio bursts (FRBs) are emerging as powerful probes of the intergalactic medium, baryon distribution, and galaxy evolution during the peak epochs of star formation. By assembling the first well-characterised high-redshift FRB population using the MeerKAT and ASKAP telescopes, combined with targeted optical and near-infrared follow-up using the JWST, this research will establish FRBs as precision cosmological tools and provide insights into the formation and evolution of galaxies across cosmic time.

Australia’s leadership in FRB discovery and localisation, coupled with access to world-class facilities including JWST, Keck, VLT, and the SKA pathfinders, ensures that this project leverages national infrastructure and expertise to generate high-impact science outputs. The project also strengthens international collaborations, enhances Australia’s global reputation in radio astronomy, and builds a skilled workforce trained in cutting-edge observational techniques, multi-wavelength analysis, and cosmology. The outcomes will contribute to national priorities in scientific excellence, innovation, and STEM capability, demonstrating Australia’s leadership in transformative astronomy research with global impact.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: RAMP-dependent modulation of the calcium sensing receptor. This project will uncover how small accessory proteins called receptor activity-modifying proteins (RAMPs) shape the structure and behaviour of the calcium-sensing receptor, a key molecule that enables cells to detect and respond to their environment. Using advanced imaging and mass spectrometry, the research will reveal new principles of how receptors assemble, move, and communicate within cells. These discoveries will deepen understanding of how complex signalling networks function and create new opportunities for innovation in biotechnology, structural biology, and molecular medicine.
national-interest-test-statement: This project will explore how small partner molecules, known as receptor activity-modifying proteins (RAMPs), influence the three-dimensional shape and communication of a key calcium-sensing receptor that helps the body maintain calcium balance. Receptors are specialised proteins on the surface of cells that act like switches, detecting chemical signals and triggering specific cellular responses. While RAMPs are known to adjust how some receptors behave, their broader role in controlling receptor three-dimensional shape and signalling remains unknown. By uncovering how these partner molecules fine-tune receptor communication, this research will reveal new principles of how cells regulate and adapt to their environment. Using Australia’s advanced imaging and protein-mapping technologies, the project will strengthen national research capability and train future scientists in structural biology and receptor pharmacology. The discoveries will provide a foundation for future advances in biotechnology and medicine, informing how receptor function can be modulated in health and disease. Research outcomes will be shared openly with academic, clinical, and industry partners, ensuring the findings are widely understood, translated, and used, enhancing Australia’s reputation and capacity for world-leading discovery science.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
current-admin-organisation: The University of New South Wales
announcement-admin-organisation: The University of New South Wales
grant-summary: An Atomic-Resolution Quantum Sensor for Quantum-Emergent Magnetism . This project will develop a novel atomic-resolution quantum sensing microscopy technique based on single spin defects in atomically thin crystals. These quantum spins act as ultra-sensitive probes of electronic, magnetic, and superconducting properties, at the atomic level. Addressed by a quantum microscope, we will control and read out individual spins to uncover new forms of magnetic, correlated, and topological order in quantum matter. The outcomes of this fellowship will deepen our understanding of quantum materials and create pathways toward next-generation error-resilient quantum technologies that will strengthen Australia’s research and innovation capacity.
national-interest-test-statement:
This project will advance Australia’s leadership in quantum science by developing quantum-coherent sensing microscopy with atomic-resolution. Leveraging on atomically-confined spins in 2D crystals, this project will enable sensing of quantum-emergent magnetic phenomena, using a uniquely sensitive quantum microscope. The quantum sensing enabled discovery of novel topological and correlated phases of quantum matter promise to underpin next-generation error-resilient quantum hardware.

The outcomes directly address the Australian National Quantum Strategy priorities to build sovereign capability in quantum devices, materials, and sensing. By integrating world-leading expertise at UNSW with the Institute for Basic Science (Korea), this work will establish Australia’s first atomic-scale electron-spin-resonance platform for atomic-resolution quantum sensing microscopy.

The project will train highly skilled researchers in quantum science, helping grow the national quantum workforce and supporting Australia’s ambition to be a top-tier quantum nation by 2030. The resulting sensing and control technologies have potential applications in low-power computing, defence, and advanced manufacturing, providing social, economic, and strategic benefits through scientific sovereignty and long-term innovation leadership.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Logics for Quantitative Reasoning. This project aims to develop new many-valued logics to help machines reason about data that is scored with numbers, probabilities, security access levels, etc. This is a significant issue since a great deal of information we handle in daily life comes in this form. This project expects to improve how we ask questions of complex databases by producing novel techniques and explore how much time and memory computers need to answer them. This has potential for applications in AI, secure data access and disease tracking, among others.  The expected outcomes are novel logical tools for understanding and optimizing queries.  Benefits include the development of distinguished expertise in Australia to lead in logic for advanced data technologies.
national-interest-test-statement: Australian society heavily relies on collecting and manipulating vast amounts of data, from health records to financial transactions. Yet current database systems struggle to handle questions that go beyond simple yes/no answers —such as how often  a certain kind of event occurred,  what level of access is needed to view certain data, or what level of trustworthiness the data has. The project aims to develop new logical systems that allow for more expressive and secure data querying, using advanced mathematical structures called semirings. In future,  these tools will lead to long-term benefits impacting how we track disease spread with databases, manage sensitive information, and explain decisions made by Artificial Intelligence systems in a humanly intelligible manner — such as why a person was denied a bank loan. The outcomes will support Australia’s priorities in advanced information systems, as outlined in the 2023 List of Critical Technologies. By collaborating with global leaders in academia and industry (specifically,  IBM Research in the USA) the project could help shape the next generation of database languages. Furthermore, engagement with industry partners to facilitate real-world adoption will be ensured through inclusion of the VP Research of Relational AI (one California-based company that has adopted the semiring paradigm in their commercial database product) in the two workshops of the project.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Reaction Hijacking: A Novel Approach to Inactivate Essential Enzymes. Antimicrobial resistance poses an urgent and growing threat to our society. This project aims to elucidate the molecular basis of a groundbreaking inhibition strategy targeting a family of essential enzymes involved in protein synthesis, aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, in malaria parasites. In this unusual mechanism, the enzymes are induced to synthesise their own inhibitors. Uncovering the principles behind this process will generate new insights to guide the design of parasite-selective inhibitors and the identification of novel enzyme targets. The outcomes will advance fundamental understanding of parasite biology and lay groundwork for future industry partnerships, positioning Australia to lead in the expanding global anti-infective market.
national-interest-test-statement: Antimicrobial resistance, including resistance to antimalarial drugs, has become a significant global burden, both economically and socially. It claims millions of lives each year and leads to substantial productivity loses. Climate change is predicted to expand the range of malaria-carrying mosquitoes into Northen Australia, and a warmer climate may also increase the risk of new cases through imported infections, leaving Australia increasingly vulnerable. The urgent need for breakthrough drugs with novel mechanisms of action and a low potential for resistance has never been more pressing. This project aims to uncover the molecular basis of a new strategy for inhibiting essential enzymes by leveraging the microorganism’s own cellular processes against itself. This mechanism, termed “reaction-hijacking”, enables the simultaneous targeting of multiple enzymes, thereby reducing the risk of resistance development. The findings from this research could pave the way for the downstream development of new anti-infectives in the future, enhancing health protection for Australians while positioning the country to benefit economically from the global antibiotics market. The project outcomes will provide powerful new tools in chemical biology and deepen our understanding of the novel inhibition mechanism, offering promising new therapeutic options for infectious diseases.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: The next frontier in fundamental physics: atoms as probes of the universe. Despite its successes, the Standard Model of particle physics leaves several deep mysteries unsolved, including the matter-antimatter asymmetry and the nature of dark matter. This project aims to combine atomic physics, particle phenomenology, and astrophysics to push the boundaries of fundamental physics using low-energy high-precision atomic methods. By developing highly sensitive approaches, such as utilising networks of atomic clocks, this will enable the search for previously undetectable forms of dark matter and probe for violations of the Standard Model. Expected outcomes include advances in precision atomic measurements and significant contributions to the global search for new physics, expanding knowledge in fundamental science.
national-interest-test-statement: This research aims to address some of the most pressing questions in fundamental science by using atomic systems to probe the mysteries of dark matter, fundamental physics, and potential deviations from the Standard Model. By developing innovative atomic techniques, the project not only deepens our theoretical understanding but also drives practical advancements in precision measurement. Advancements in precision quantum sensing and the development of atomic clocks will further fuel technological breakthroughs in areas such as telecommunications, navigation, and quantum computing. Furthermore, this project fosters international collaboration, positioning Australia as a leader in cutting-edge research and innovation in fundamental physics. Engaging students and early-career researchers through mentoring and training will help develop the next generation of scientists, enhancing Australia’s scientific workforce, with a particular emphasis on developments for precision measurements, scientific computing and data analysis. The proposed research aligns with Australia’s goals of promoting scientific excellence, driving technological innovation, and contributing to economic growth, and aims to further Australia’s standing in the fields of atomic, astroparticle, and fundamental physics.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Deciphering metabolite-mediated immunity. This proposal aims to define key mechanisms of metabolite-mediated immunity. In mammals, T cells are a major component of the immune system, playing diverse roles in physiology including mediating responses to cellular stress, clearance of infection and tumours, and in the maintenance of homeostasis. How T cells detect small metabolites, and which metabolites are detected, however, remains poorly understood, and this represents a major gap in our understanding of a major feature of immunity. This project will decipher this biology, thereby accelerating discovery in immunity and life sciences more broadly. This work will be applicable to diverse vertebrate species and will thus have implications in biodiversity, agriculture and biosecurity.
national-interest-test-statement: This research investigates how the immune system (the body's defence system) detects and responds to metabolites (small molecules) produced by the body under cellular stress. It focuses on a specific type of white blood cell called T cells, which use special sensors (receptors on the cell surface) to detect these stress signals. Using cutting-edge immunological and biochemical techniques, the project aims to 1. identify which metabolite stress signals T cells can detect and 2. discover new ways in which T cells respond to these signals. This work will fill an important gap in our understanding of how our immune system works. It will also create new tools for studying how different stress signals affect the fundamental biological process of metabolite-mediated immunity. The findings could lead to innovations in biotechnology which may contribute to advancing agricultural practices, help fight infectious diseases, and improve Australia's biosecurity. Beyond academic outputs, research outcomes will be promoted via public lectures and collaborations with industry partners.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Understanding avian heat adaptation and its developmental drivers. This project aims to understand avian adaptation to rising temperatures under climate change and the potential for prenatal exposure to an acoustic signal of heat to accelerate this adaptation. It will provide significant new insights on heat impacts on animal physiology and the strategies of heat resilience that animals have evolved. Expected outcomes include an extensive dataset on organismal and cellular heat-resilience and thermoregulation capacity, and an assessment of the genetic and developmental drivers of heat tolerance in birds. Benefits include improving our capacity to predict climate change impact, alleviating heat insults in species of ecological or economic importance, and understanding sound and noise impact on development.
national-interest-test-statement:
Birds are essential to ecosystem functioning (seed dispersal, insect management), and human-nature
interactions, including in urban environments. Yet, birds are especially vulnerable to increasing temperatures
under climate change. This not only threatens global biodiversity, but also the Australian poultry industry, yielding
over $5 billion annually. Currently, we do not know whether and how birds may adapt to high temperatures, in
order to persist in the coming decades and centuries. This innovative project will establish how avian heat-
tolerance may be improved by warning embryos about heat threat using prenatal sounds (i.e. heat-calls), and
thereby alter their development. This fascinating strategy is well documented in the desert-adapted Australian
zebra finch, but other species have not been investigated. Using novel methodologies and field data, this project
will aim to predict species vulnerability to climate change, based on heat-calling occurrence, and will test a nature-
based and economical tool for alleviating heat-stress for conservation and poultry production purposes. Because
of the birds’ strong ecological, social, cultural and economic values, this project will benefit Australia in all of these
areas. The project will involve poultry welfare specialists, conservation agencies and bird hobbyists. Its findings
will be communicated to the broad Australian public via news articles, radio interviews, short videos, and school
and community outreach activities.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: New ways forward in the theory of turbulent heat and momentum transport. This project aims to advance our understanding of intricate mechanisms behind heat and momentum transport in turbulent flow, using a new class of exact coherent structures (solutions of the Navier–Stokes equations). It targets valuable insights into how transport processes are influenced by flow conditions, including fluid properties and wall characteristics. Expected outcomes include computational tools and predictive models to enable rapid estimation of turbulent transport without relying on experiments or simulations. Among the project’s expected economic and environmental benefits is support for optimal design of power plants and heat exchangers – reducing fuel consumption, and helping in the effort to lower carbon dioxide emissions.
national-interest-test-statement: Movement of fluids in what is called turbulent transport has many practical consequences, by influencing the transfer of heat and the overall degree of resistance to flow. This in turn affects the efficiency of a huge range of infrastructure and devices in daily use. Despite decades of research into turbulent transport, its fundamental mechanisms remain unclear – leaving the design of products involving fluids (either liquids or gases) reliant on costly experiments, and large-scale simulations across many operating conditions. This project addresses that knowledge gap in the theory of turbulent transport, through innovative mathematical approaches. It will deliver powerful new computational tools to estimate conditions leading to optimal transport. Efficient optimisation of turbulent transport is essential for improving the performance of power plants and heat exchangers (such as air conditioners and refrigerators), reducing fuel consumption, operational costs, and carbon dioxide emissions, with significant economic, environmental benefits. The project will build research workforce and capacity for Australia, and its findings will be shared in national and international workshops with experts in engineering, physics, and mathematics. This will bridge the gap between theoretical research and practical applications, while the project’s outcomes will be integrated into next-generation turbulence transport prediction models, delivering reliable tools for industrial use.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Accelerated multiscale modelling with physics–data Informed upscaling. The project aims to reveal the mechanism driving the upward migration of water and fine particles in soils under oscillatory deformation—a long-standing problem causing cargo liquefaction in ships and mud-pumping hazards in railways. It is expected to develop a multiscale, multi-physics framework that links fine-scale processes to large-scale predictions with high accuracy and quantified uncertainty. Expected outcomes include next-generation numerical models and innovative upscaling techniques that transform understanding of these phenomena and enhance transport and infrastructure safety. The new computing tools will accelerate model development and maximise computational performance, benefiting diverse scientific and engineering fields.
national-interest-test-statement:
Mining and agriculture together accounted for about two-thirds of Australia’s exports and roughly 14% of GDP in 2024. These industries are vital to national prosperity and employment, with most products transported by rail to ports before being shipped overseas via bulk carriers. However, both rail and maritime transport face a shared threat: under oscillatory deformation, water and fine particles within rail embankments or ship cargo migrate upward against gravity, leading to mud pumping in railways and cargo liquefaction in ships. More than 300 mud-pumping sites have been identified along the NSW coastal rail network, costing millions of dollars annually in maintenance. Cargo liquefaction has caused 23 major vessel capsizes between 2013 and 2022, resulting in the loss of 104 seafarers. However, the underlying mechanism remains poorly understood.
This project will address this critical gap by developing advanced computational tools and next-generation multiscale models for accurate prediction and effective mitigation. The findings and tools will be shared with industry partners—including rail authorities, contractors, maritime regulators, and mining and shipping companies—through workshops and technical briefings to enhance infrastructure resilience, reduce maintenance costs, and prevent catastrophic shipping incidents. The project will deliver major savings for industry and government, contributing directly to national priorities in building a secure and resilient nation.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary:
The Quantum Smithy: Crafting Iron into molecular FeQubits. Quantum computing promises a revolution by solving complex problems beyond the reach of classical computers.
However, fundamental particles, Quantum bits (Qubits), are extremely fragile and suffer from short Qu-lifetimes. They rely on geopolitically sensitive rare-earth elements, and require handling under bulky cryogenic conditions, limiting real-world use.
By confining iron in rigid macrocyclic scaffolds this project will develop 'FeQuBits' as a molecular solution, achieving stronger spin coupling and improved manufacturing.
Through proven synthetic routes, in-situ characterisation, and collaborations for on-surface read-out, Australia's resources can be utilized to advance Australia’s Quantum materials capability.
national-interest-test-statement:
Australia’s ability to build next-generation quantum technologies depends on materials that are affordable, abundant and reliable. Yet many current quantum systems rely on rare-earth or critical-metal elements whose supply is geopolitically constrained and costly, and requires bulky cryogenic systems to handle their fragile nature. Hence, Quantum bits (QuBits) face critical barriers to practical application for a broad customer base. 
This project will develop iron-based molecular FeQubits. By confining iron into rigid macrocyclic structures, a defined surface orientation and well-defined redox-switchable quantum states can be achieved. This defined approach increases the signal intensity, and reduces errors during the read out of quantum states. Those enhanced properties will be confirmed by integrating them into prototype read-out architectures.
Because iron is widely available and low-cost, the outcomes will support a domestic quantum-materials supply chain, reducing dependence on imported critical materials. Beyond academia, the results will be shared with industry partners in quantum technology and national measurement labs, and methods will be translated via open-access protocols and collaborative workshops. In this way the research will contribute to Australia’s economic resilience, technological sovereignty and global competitiveness in quantum science.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Geometric Theory of Wave Propagation. A wave equation is a mathematical model describing how waves evolve in time. These equations predict how waves of diverse types - from gravitational waves in space to seismic waves in the earth - travel, scatter, and interact with their environment. This project will use a powerful new mathematical framework, non-elliptic Fredholm theory, to solve previously inaccessible problems in wave propagation, including the construction of global spacetime Feynman propagators, nonlinear scattering matrices, and a non-elliptic index theory.  Key benefits include new fundamental knowledge in mathematical analysis and training a new generation of Australian researchers in these powerful, cutting-edge techniques.
national-interest-test-statement:
This project uses advanced mathematics to examine the behaviour of waves.  Being fundamental research, the models are quite broad, and apply to both familiar waves, such as water waves, sound waves, and electromagnetic waves (like light and X-rays), and also to more exotic waves that arise in quantum mechanics.  The models developed will help in the detection and evaluation of wave signals, and therefore have many potential industrial applications, including to optics, materials science, engineering and chemistry, potentially leading to significant commercial benefits for Australian industries in these sectors.
Indeed, analysis of wave signals is a crucial component of communication infrastructure, geophysical imaging, and medical imaging.  The specific advancements related to inverse problems have potential use cases in X-ray tomography and cosmology.   It will strengthen existing collaborations between Australian and International researchers in the United States, Italy, and Japan, and help maintain Australia’s strong research profile in pure mathematics. The outcomes of the project will be communicated to the public via public lectures, presentations, and articles in University of Melbourne media outlets such as Pursuit and the Conversation.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: First Breath: Evolutionary Origins of Air Breathing in Early Vertebrates. Today >37K vertebrates breathe air to survive, including humans. However, the drivers, conditions and timing of when air-breathing first evolved in terrestrial animals (tetrapods) remains unknown. This project aims to address this long-standing evolutionary problem using world-class fossils and rare specimens of iconic ‘living fossils’ (Indonesian coelacanth and Australian lungfish). The evolutionary drivers of air breathing will be revealed by synthesising 3D scan data with a novel analytical approach to identify anatomical proxies of air-breathing function in living and fossil animals. The research will also drive new insight for enhanced conservation efforts for these endangered Australasian species, and strengthen international links.
national-interest-test-statement: One of the greatest steps in evolution was the transition from water to land, an event that ultimately gave rise to all terrestrial animals (tetrapods) including humans, today. A major obstacle in this evolution was learning how to breathe air. This project investigates how, when and why vertebrates evolved to breathe air, by integrating data from exceptional fossil records and unique Australasian animals known as ‘living fossils’. It aims to generate landmark discoveries to improve our understanding of this transition, and inform on the structure of the respiratory system of all tetrapods today with lasting potential for veterinary and respiratory biomedical insight. The project also offers significant new knowledge gains in the fundamental anatomy of two endangered species, and how animals have adapted to radically novel environments. For Australia, the suites of discovery science delivered from this Fellowship will bolster museum and digital collections, provide insight guiding conservation efforts, and enable the application of breakthrough digital imaging and analytical capabilities across multiple research areas. Key outreach will involve leveraging my extensive media and engagement profile to promote better public understanding and scientific literacy of evolution, and new appreciation for iconic species within Australasia’s unique fauna.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Block Copolymer–2D Material Hybrid Architectures for Multi-Modal Sensing. This project aims to develop hierarchically engineered block copolymer–2D nanomaterial hybrids that enable true multimodal sensing by simultaneously detecting mechanical, thermal and chemical signals. It addresses the limitation of current single-mode sensors by embedding stimulus selectivity at the materials level through bioinspired hierarchical design and adaptive interphase engineering. The project will establish scalable self-assembly strategies and reveal new structure–function mechanisms governing multimodal signal decoupling. Outcomes include sensor prototypes with high sensitivity, durability and real-time monitoring for healthcare, space and environment, strengthening Australia’s sovereign capability in advanced materials.
national-interest-test-statement: This project aims to develop novel materials that can sense and respond to multiple changes in their surroundings, including pressure, heat and chemicals, at the same time. Current sensors used in areas like health and environmental monitoring, space and aerospace systems are often limited to detecting one type of signal or lack long-term stability. By drawing inspiration from naturally existing structures and using advanced polymers combined with 2D nanomaterials, this research will create lightweight, flexible sensors with superior accuracy, sensitivity and durability. The outcomes of this project will support Australian industries in developing next-generation technologies for health diagnostics, environmental monitoring, defence and space applications. These innovations will strengthen Australia’s position in advanced manufacturing, create opportunities for local industries and contribute to safer, smarter and more sustainable systems. To ensure wide impact, the research will be promoted through collaboration with industry, defence partners and research community, and through public demonstrations and media engagement. Partnerships with technology developers and commercial partners will help translate laboratory discoveries into practical devices, ensuring that Australian science leads to tangible social, economic and environmental benefits.

current-admin-organisation: The University of New South Wales
announcement-admin-organisation: The University of New South Wales
grant-summary: Electromechanics of the cochlear amplifier. Despite decades of work, it remains unclear how the motor protein prestin converts tiny electrical changes into membrane force, or whether that force opens nearby force-sensitive ion channels that shape hearing and cochlear amplification. I will integrate cryo-electron microscopy in native-like membranes, live-cell force sensors and micropillar traction, patch-clamp electrophysiology, calcium imaging, and membrane-mechanics modelling to link prestin’s three-dimensional structure to force generation and channel gating in cells and tissues. This fellowship will refine models of cochlear amplification, clarify species differences in hearing ranges, deliver tools to track outer hair cell motion, and lay foundations to protect hearing.
national-interest-test-statement:
This project aims to uncover how the human ear amplifies sound, a process that remains poorly understood despite decades of research. We will study the molecular machines that detect and boost sound vibrations, allowing humans to hear across a wide range of frequencies and enabling sonar animals to echolocate without visual cues. Using advanced imaging and biophysical techniques, we will reveal what these tiny machines look like and how they work together to convert sound into electrical and mechanical signals that the brain can understand.

Hearing loss affects one in six Australians and is a major cause of social isolation, communication challenges, and reduced quality of life. Understanding the fundamental principles of sound amplification will open new opportunities for treating hearing disorders and protecting hearing health. Given the widespread presence of these molecular machines in other sensory organs, the same mechanisms may also explain how the heart and other tissues sense and respond to mechanical and electrical forces.

This research will strengthen Australia’s leadership in hearing and cardiac mechanobiology, foster international collaboration, and train the next generation of scientists. It will also inspire new biosensing technologies and probes, driving innovation and delivering long-term economic and health benefits for Australian society.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Developing new econometric methodologies to optimise  policy evaluation. Environmental and economic policies need to be able to adapt, over time and across regions, to be effective. Evaluating them requires advanced data-driven methods, yet existing approaches are static and fail to capture dynamic and uneven policy impacts. This project aims to develop new econometric and machine learning tools for adaptive causal inference and policy optimisation that allow complex, long-term policies to be rigorously evaluated and refined. Using Australia’s Green Transition policies—such as renewable energy targets and tax subsidies— as a real-world case-study, expected outcomes include new tools and insights to help policymakers design more effective instruments to foster innovation, productivity growth, and decarbonisation.
national-interest-test-statement:
Australia’s environmental and economic policies particularly those driving the Green Transition, aim to foster innovation and investment while advancing sustainable productivity and reducing emissions. Striking this balance is inherently complex, as policy instruments like renewable energy targets, hydrogen incentives, and carbon pricing continually evolve and interact across varied regions, industries, and communities. Current evaluation frameworks remain largely static, and fail to reflect the dynamic and diverse impacts of these initiatives.
Using Australia’s Green Transition policies as a real-world laboratory, this Fellowship will develop a data-driven framework for dynamic policy learning and causal analysis. It will deliver two key advances: (i) new econometric and machine learning methods enabling policymakers to assess not only whether policies are effective, but also how and why their impacts differ across time, regions, and sectors; and (ii) a user-friendly software platform to evaluate and monitor policy performance in real time. These innovations will position Australia as a global leader in data-driven policy evaluation. 
Findings will be disseminated through workshops, plain-language policy briefings, and open-access software with training resources. The research directly supports Australia’s science and research priorities by advancing analytical tools that foster sustainable growth, innovation, and decarbonisation.

grant-summary: Understanding the Functions of Retroviral Capsids. This project aims to understand the roles played by retroviral capsids during viral infection by building on my recent discoveries showing that they are critical for interacting with the host cell. This project expects to generate new knowledge in the fields of virology, cell biology, and protein science using cutting-edge approaches in microscopy and structural biology. Expected outcomes of this project include understanding how HIV moves through the cytoplasm to reach the nucleus, and how the HTLV capsid engages host proteins to drive infection. This project anticipates making discoveries in fundamental virology benefiting therapeutic, synthetic biology, biosecurity and biotechnology applications in Australia and internationally.
national-interest-test-statement: When a retrovirus enters a cell, it must travel from the cell membrane to the centre of the cell. This is a dangerous journey for a virus, as there are many obstacles and defences within the cell. To protect the viral genome, retroviruses have evolved a capsid – a nano-sized container that not only functions as a ‘shell’ but also interacts with the host cell to direct the virus to its ultimate destination. How the capsid performs these functions is not well understood. This project aims to understand how retroviruses, including HIV, hijack host motors to move through the cell. The project also aims to define the function of the capsid in a poorly-understood group of viruses – the deltaretroviruses - which cause significant disease in livestock and humans, with Aboriginal Australians particularly affected. The knowledge gained will lay the groundwork for advances in the biotechnology, health and biosecurity sectors. It also has the potential to enhance Australia’s international reputation as a global leader in molecular virology, and as a world-class education provider. Researchers and students associated with this project will develop their scientific knowledge, critical thinking, and transferable skills which will benefit Australia in an innovation-based economy. Findings will be communicated widely to researchers in the field via open access peer-reviewed publications and conference proceeding, and to the general public via the university’s social media platforms.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Recalibrating Staffing Assessment Practices for the Age of Generative AI. This project investigates how generative artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping job assessment and staffing practices. It examines (1) how job applicants’ use of AI and employers’ efforts to adapt to this use affect the efficacy of staffing assessments and equity in employment, and (2) how the increasing AI use at work shifts the characteristics that define top talent and the implications of that shift for staffing. The project will generate new theoretical insights into job applicant behaviour and empirical evidence of the characteristics that predict work performance in a context of AI-augmented work. It yields a contemporary evidence base for revised staffing practices, calibrated to improve labour productivity and employment equity.
national-interest-test-statement: This project investigates how generative artificial intelligence can both support and challenge contemporary staffing practices. Generative artificial intelligence is widely regarded as essential to improving Australia’s stagnating labour productivity. This technology, however, can also substantially disrupt staffing if job applicants use it to cheat on employment tests or interviews, or if employers do not adapt their staffing practices to account for how artificial intelligence is changing the way we work. Further, artificial intelligence may exacerbate existing inequalities in employment opportunities, as individuals with higher digital literacy or access to more powerful models gain disproportionate advantages when applying for jobs. Getting the right people into the right jobs is crucial to labour productivity, but current approaches to staffing practice are based on research conducted before generative artificial intelligence was available. This research will benefit employers across Australia, and globally, by providing a necessary, evidence-based foundation to recruit people who are best suited to roles and can use artificial intelligence effectively. The findings will be shared widely through webinars, conferences, blog posts, and presentations to industry groups and peak bodies. An advisory panel of talent acquisition professionals and assessment vendors will ensure the research reaches end-users and will impact practice.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Illuminating Dark Energy In the Nearby Universe. This project tackles one of the greatest mysteries in physics: what is Dark Energy, the unknown force driving the accelerating expansion of the Universe. Through Australian leadership in the two largest international galaxy surveys ever conducted, it will produce the most comprehensive dynamic map of the nearby Universe — ten times larger than any before. Expected outcomes include definitive measurements of Dark Energy’s behavior over the past two billion years, potentially transforming our understanding of the fundamental forces of nature. This project will yield social and economic benefits through public engagement with science and the translation of advanced data-analysis innovations to industry applications in big data and technology.
national-interest-test-statement:
Our best model of the Universe suggests that 70% of its content is an unknown component called Dark Energy, whose discovery earned the 2011 Nobel Prize. Yet, its true nature remains one of the biggest mysteries in science. Recent breakthroughs hint that Dark Energy may have changed over time. If confirmed, this is a discovery that could transform our understanding of gravity or particle physics.

Building on decades of Australian leadership in galaxy surveys such as 6dFGS and WiggleZ, this project will test these groundbreaking claims using data from the largest galaxy surveys ever undertaken. By creating and analysing the most detailed map of our local Universe, we will strengthen Australia’s role at the forefront of global cosmology, deepen collaborations with leading US and European teams, and drive innovation in data science through embedded software engineering expertise.

The project will not only tackle one of the most significant questions in modern physics but also contribute to national capability in big-data analysis, train the next generation of Australian data scientists, and inspire public engagement with science through cutting-edge visualization and outreach — directly advancing the Government’s vision of a science-literate and technology-empowered Australia.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Psychology of Generosity: From Theory to Practice and Back Again. This project aims to test ideas from social psychology in charity contexts. Generosity is important for society. Yet little is known about how psychological theories translate into real charitable giving behaviour. This project involves working with nonprofits to test ideas within actual campaigns. The project will test the impacts of identities and beneficiaries on real giving decisions. Findings can help refine existing theories for the charity context and generate evidence-based fundraising guidebooks to inform nonprofit practice. This project addresses the urgent need to sustain and grow philanthropy in Australia. Insights are expected to help secure funding for essential social services that benefit many Australians.
national-interest-test-statement:
There are 64,000 registered charities and nonprofits in Australia. These nonprofits contribute to society in diverse and meaningful ways. The survival of most nonprofits relies in part on charitable donations. Yet donor numbers are declining in Australia. To address this, the Australian government ordered a 2023 Productivity Commission inquiry to address barriers to giving and harness opportunities to grow it further. The government's stretch goal is to double charitable giving in Australia by 2030.
The current project aims to deliver against this recognised national priority to promote generosity. The project seeks to develop strategies and resources to help Australia’s nonprofits to fundraise more effectively and more ethically. By doing so, the project could help to ensure nonprofits' financial sustainability. This, in turn, can help contribute to a fair and thriving Australian society by ensuring essential community services can be delivered.
Findings will be communicated beyond academia. Fundraising guidebooks will be developed to tell nonprofits about evidence-based approaches to fundraising. Insights will also be shared on a research translation website about donor psychology. Finally, knowledge will be shared through conferences and webinars developed for nonprofit staff.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Procedural Justice for Victim-Survivors of Sexual Violence. Victim-survivors of sexual violence often report poor experiences with police. This project aims to improve these experiences by generating new knowledge about how procedurally just police responses (emphasising fair and dignified treatment, voice, neutrality, and trustworthy motives) can enhance access to justice for victim-survivors. Using an innovative methodology that integrates victim-survivor and police perspectives, outcomes of this project will identify how procedural justice can shape police responses and improve outcomes. Benefits include better interactions between victim-survivors and police, enhanced access to justice, and reduced barriers to reporting for those seeking a criminal justice response.
national-interest-test-statement: Sexual violence affects over two million Australians, yet many victim-survivors face significant barriers when reporting to police. For example, victim-survivors describe experiencing disbelief and negative treatment from police. This leads to re-victimisation and undermines access to justice for victim-survivors. This Future Fellowship aims to address these challenges by better understanding victim-survivors experiences with police and considering how we can improve their experiences with procedural justice. Procedural justice—emphasising fairness, voice, and respectful treatment—offers a promising path to reforming police practices and rebuilding trust with victim-survivors. Through working directly with victim-survivors and police, this Fellowship will advance police practices and reduce barriers to reporting for victim-survivors who seek criminal justice. The research will generate new theoretical insights while delivering tangible social benefits, including enhance access to justice and reduced reporting barriers for victim-survivors of sexual violence. Marginalised populations, disproportionately affected by sexual violence and systemic barriers, stand to benefit significantly. A robust outreach and engagement strategy will ensure findings inform policy, training, and public discourse. By bridging academic research and frontline policing, this Fellowship will help create a more just, supportive, and responsive system for victim-survivors in Australia.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Beyond reminiscence: Benefits of familiarity vs. novelty for older people. This project aims to generate new knowledge about how older people benefit in different ways from familiar versus novel experiences and activities, depending on needs and preferences. The project adopts an experimental approach to compare the impact of familiarity and novelty on mood, identity, and cognition in older and younger people. Expected outcomes include a new theoretical framework mapping overlapping and distinct effects of familiarity- and novelty-based engagement across the lifespan, guiding future research and translation. The project will deliver evidence-based recommendations for aged-care providers, program designers, and technology developers to target and tailor initiatives that enhance engagement for older Australians.
national-interest-test-statement: Australia’s population is ageing rapidly, creating an urgent need to support the wellbeing of older people. This research addresses a critical gap in understanding how different forms of engagement, based on familiarity versus novelty, produce different cognitive and emotional outcomes in later life. Current aged care programs often over-rely on routine and reminiscence, missing opportunities for new experiences that foster curiosity, learning, and growth. By integrating cognitive science and ageing research, the project will reveal how familiarity and novelty each yield distinct benefits, and how age, preferences, and needs determine which works best for whom. Findings will guide the future design of evidence-based programs in both community and residential aged care, helping to reduce disengagement, depression, and cognitive decline. With aged-care spending projected to reach 2.5 per cent of GDP by 2060, even modest improvements in engagement and independence could deliver significant returns. Older Australians already contribute an ~$84 billion/year through volunteering and have more than doubled their workforce participation since 2001. By identifying how to sustain engagement and lifelong learning, this research will unlock social and economic value. Through an existing network of aged-care providers, health districts, and technology developers, outcomes will be translated into recommendations for more effective, better targeted engagement interventions for older people.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Constructing artificial agents operating with unmeasurable uncertainty. The project aims to develop new methods to help digital systems make decisions when there is too little data to rely solely on probabilities. This kind of uncertainty occurs, for instance, where human behaviour or unfamiliar terrain is unpredictable. Expected outcomes of this project include tools for building and checking decision-making systems using ideas from mathematics and computer science. This should provide a unique benefit for the automatic design of systems that do not have access to enormous amounts of data --- a critical aspect that few AI approaches can handle --- and so should support advances in robotics and automated planning, and strengthen Australia’s contribution to foundational research in intelligent systems.
national-interest-test-statement:
Autonomous systems are increasingly important in sectors such as
manufacturing, healthcare, and environmental monitoring.  They are identified
as a Critical Technology in the National Interest, and as an Enabling
Capability in the National Reconstruction Fund.  Yet these systems struggle
when faced with uncertainty they cannot measure, e.g., when they cannot
reliably estimate the chances of different outcomes. This is common in tasks
like exploring remote underwater regions or assisting people in social
settings. This project will develop new mathematics and algorithms to help us
understand how autonomous systems should reason, and to provide assurances
that they will make sound decisions when faced with uncertainties even if 
these cannot be measured.

The research will support innovation in Australia. For example, the
Australian Centre for Robotics could apply these methods to marine
environments and bushfire zones, improving disaster response and environmental
stewardship, as well as their lunar rover project, ensuring consistent decisions.

Result will be shared through open-source tools and industry workshops with
partners, including IBM. This will help to drive adoption, reinforce
Australia’s leadership in autonomous systems, and build public confidence in
responsible autonomy.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: A well-being approach to adaptation in Small Island Developing States. This project aims to transform knowledge about well-being and climate change to improve adaptation policy and practice. By developing community-defined understandings of well-being using a novel psycho-cultural approach in four small island developing states, it will generate new knowledge about the effectiveness of climate change adaptation based on local worldviews. Expected outcomes include enhanced knowledge of adaptation that reflects community priorities, and a methodology for deriving measures of well-being to guide adaptation policies. This knowledge will support local and international actors to design and monitor effective and legitimate climate change adaptation policies and plans.
national-interest-test-statement: Climate change threatens small island states, and adaptation is a key part of managing this risk. Yet current approaches to designing adaptations and measuring their success rely on Western norms of development that do not reflect the needs of Indigenous Peoples. This means donor nations like Australia commit millions of dollars to adaptation without understanding whether these interventions will address what local people value and aspire to, making these investments potentially unsustainable. As a country that invests substantially in adaptation for the sake of its island neighbours and its own strategic interests, Australia needs to ensure these investments work. This project will work with communities in Maldives, Marshall Islands, Papua New Guinea and Tuvalu to articulate wellbeing-based goals for adaptation, and indicators of the effectiveness of adaptation action. This will inform adaptation policy frameworks in island countries, and Australia’s investments in these, through collaborations with national adaptation planning, island governments and local NGOs. As well as helping these nations, this has economic benefits for Australia through more effective and efficient regional investment practices, and environmental benefits through sustainable adaptation practices throughout the Pacific and SE Asia region. This research will position Australia at the forefront of people-centred climate action with tangible benefits for communities.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Oblique impact theory and optimisation framework for crashworthy structures. This project aims to develop an integrated analytical, computational, and experimental framework for designing impact-resistant structures, typically roadside barriers for protection of rapid growing electric vehicles on Australian roads. It addresses the lack of sophisticated design tools capable of predicting the highly nonlinear behaviour of crashworthy systems. By integrating impact mechanics, multi-objective structural optimisation, and artificial intelligence, the project will deliver validated models and efficient design tools for recyclable and cost-effective safety barriers. The methods can be scalable to aerospace, automotive, civil, and marine applications, strengthening Australia’s global position in structural engineering.
national-interest-test-statement:
Australia’s roads are changing fast as electric vehicles become common. These vehicles are heavier and built differently, so they behave differently in crashes. Current roadside barriers were not designed for this reality. The project will fill this gap by creating new science and practical design tools to understand angled impacts and to design safer, more affordable and recyclable barriers. It will combine impact mechanics, computer modelling and artificial intelligence to predict how a vehicle and a barrier interact and to find the best barrier design for local road curves and slopes.

The benefits to Australians are clear: fewer deaths and serious injuries on regional and urban roads; new opportunities for local manufacturing using recycled tyre rubber; lower costs for governments through smarter, longer-lasting barrier designs; and new skills for the future workforce. The methods can also be used in aerospace, automotive, marine and civil structures, extending national impact beyond roads.

Results will be translated beyond academia through close work with industry partners and road agencies to run pilot projects and produce design guides and digital tools for engineers. Findings will be shared with standards bodies to inform future guidance, with data and models released where possible, and through workshops, webinars and public outreach. This approach will speed adoption and deliver safer, more sustainable infrastructure for all Australians.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: An escape act: learning the principles of endosomal escape from nature. . This program aims to harness advanced microscopy to significantly advance both understanding and solutions to cellular delivery via endosomal escape, a process by which lipid nanoparticles or viruses cross the membrane boundary. This project expects to capitalize on foundational infrastructure and expertise to reveal the molecular mechanism in a fundamental biological process. Expected outcomes include new research tools capable of broadly addressing biological questions across multiple disciplines (e.g., from health to food production). This project intends to provide significant benefits, such as enhanced biological knowledge, multidisciplinary training opportunities, and to build Australia's capability in this rapidly advancing field.
national-interest-test-statement: We live in an era of vaccinations where delivery of molecules such as mRNA is life-saving. One of the bottlenecks is cargo delivery of molecules by crossing the single-cell boundary, termed endosomal escape. Past technological limitations have restricted our understanding of this process. This project will leverage cutting-edge microscopy to decipher the mechanisms and biophysical signatures of endosomal escape. The planned research will expand Australia's knowledge base and establish a leading research capability through the development of novel methodologies leveraging on fundamental knowledge generated. This project aims to deliver concrete economic benefits through the direct creation of new start-ups based on licensing and application of the generated intellectual property of cellular delivery tools stemming from fundamental insights gained. The project will provide an excellent research training for early career researchers in a field that is expanding  - advanced microscopy and machine learning/ deep learning based image analytics, and will forge strong links with international leaders of the field, benefiting Australia and positively impacting Australia's reputation in cutting-edge research. The methodologies developed in this project will enable broader collaboration with the biotechnology industry, with drug delivery as major focus, and offer rich venues of commercialization, leading to enhanced economic growth as well as better health benefits through innovation.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Culture, Democratic Resilience & the Challenge of the New Reactionary Right. This Fellowship investigates how the new reactionary right uses culture to build legitimacy and promote anti-democratic politics. It aims to generate ground-breaking knowledge of how cultural preferences, genres and platforms shape the appeal of the reactionary right through examining case studies across Australia, Canada and the United States, and analysing the transnational networks that connect them. Expected outcomes include co-designed, evidence-informed strategies with media and education partners to strengthen democratic resilience and reduce the appeal of reactionary ideas. Anticipated benefits include practical guidance to enhance social cohesion, democratic literacy and institutional capacity for democratic renewal and resilience.
national-interest-test-statement:
This Fellowship investigates how the new reactionary right in Australia, Canada and the United States uses culture - through music, sport, podcasts and influencer networks - to build legitimacy and promote anti-democratic politics. It develops evidence-informed strategies to strengthen democratic resilience by addressing a major gap in how Australia understands and responds to the cultural dimensions of reactionary politics. Current efforts focus mainly on laws, elections and institutions; this Fellowship instead examines how reactionary actors use cultural strategies, who they target, who supports them, and how these tactics can be effectively addressed through new comparative evidence.

The benefits for Australians are social, cultural and economic. Working with media and education partners, the Fellowship will help newsrooms reduce harmful amplification and reputational risk when covering reactionary politics, and support educators responding to platform-driven culture wars. Co-designed resources will lower training costs and help agencies direct investment toward evidence-based strategies that enhance social cohesion and trust in democratic institutions. Public outcomes will include practical tools that strengthen democratic resilience across civic, political and cultural sectors.

Uptake beyond academia will occur through co-design partnerships with practitioners, policy briefings and an open toolkit shared through professional networks and agencies.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
current-admin-organisation: The University of New South Wales
announcement-admin-organisation: The University of New South Wales
grant-summary: Multiscale Reactive Transport Modelling for Safe Subsurface Storage. This project aims to develop high-fidelity modelling frameworks to mitigate risks associated with fluid storage in subsurface reservoirs and to investigate reactive processes in geological formations. The project expects to reveal the interplay of spatial scales in rocks and generate knowledge on reactive transport in porous media by utilising advanced theories, numerical simulation and multimodal imaging. Expected outcomes include novel predictive methods and an enhanced capacity to repurpose underground reservoirs as storage sites for carbon or hydrogen. This will enable energy sector to support Australia in reaching its net-zero target by designing safe, large-scale storage solutions without risk of leakage or groundwater contamination.
national-interest-test-statement: The Australian Government's Climate Change Bill (2022) sets ambitious environmental targets: a 43% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions by 2030 and net-zero emissions by 2050. Averting catastrophic climate change requires an urgent shift to clean energy sources, coupled with continuous efforts to capture and sequester carbon dioxide emissions. Achieving these will require large-scale carbon dioxide sequestration and the adoption of hydrogen as a clean, emission-free energy source. During this energy transition, substantial storage capacity is needed for both hydrogen and carbon dioxide. Subsurface geological formations present significant potential, as they can store large volumes of fluids. However, ensuring effective storage necessitates a comprehensive understanding of the interactions between rocks and injected fluids. It is essential to rigorously model these processes to mitigate risks such as leakage or groundwater contamination. This project aims to develop advanced numerical and experimental methods to help the energy industry identify optimal subsurface reservoirs for hydrogen storage and carbon dioxide geo-sequestration while ensuring safe operations throughout the process. This will position Australia to thrive in a low-carbon economy by enabling the sustainable, safe, and efficient utilisation of subsurface reservoirs. Energy storage and carbon sequestration are two rapidly growing global markets with significant job creation potential for Australia's future.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary:
Transforming Pavement Design: Permeable Pavement Multi Scale Investigation . With increased risk of flooding and growing issues around storm-water management, waterway pollution and urban heat island, the suitability of conventional impermeable concrete and asphalt surfaces for our cities are questioned. Permeable pavements are emerging as a key solution however there is need for creating new knowledge on their engineering design and field performance, given they fall in a cross-disciplinary area of geotechnical engineering and surface water hydrology.

This project aims to create new knowledge, through bringing fields of pavement geotechnics, soil erosion, imaging and advanced instrumentation together. The project outcomes are expected to increase livability and health of our cities facing climate change.
national-interest-test-statement: Urban development has dramatically altered the natural water cycle. As cities expand, conventional pavements—designed to block water from soaking into the ground—have increased surface runoff, reduced groundwater recharge, and contributed to flooding and diminished urban vegetation. Also, they contribute to sediment erosion and water pollution. Permeable pavements offer a promising alternative by allowing water to infiltrate into the ground, helping restore balance to the urban water cycle. However, their widespread use is limited by concerns about long-term durability and water infiltration performance. This project will combine knowledge from pavement engineering, granular material mechanics, and fluid flow in porous media to better understand how permeable pavements perform over time. The outcomes will support the design of pavements that are both structurally sound and environmentally beneficial. Benefits include cooler urban areas, cleaner waterways, improved waste management, and more livable cities with lessened impacts from floods. The project also supports broader national goals by advancing resilient infrastructure and developing practical approaches to help communities and industries respond to environmental challenges. Findings will be shared through workshops, industry user groups, public talks, media, and publications to ensure practical uptake and inform future urban infrastructure planning.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Addressing Cultural Diversity in Healthcare Through Global Bioethics. This project examines how bioethics, the field that addresses ethical issues in healthcare, responds to cultural diversity worldwide and how it can better engage with diverse cultural and moral perspectives. It will study how bioethics is practiced across societies and develop a framework that respects cultural diversity while remaining true to shared ethical values. The project will engage a wide range of stakeholders and create a global platform connecting researchers, healthcare professionals and patients. It will strengthen ethical decision-making, foster cultural understanding, and promote safer and more respectful healthcare and research globally and in Australia, where multiculturalism is a core value for social cohesion.
national-interest-test-statement: This fellowship addresses health as a national priority in Australia and cultural diversity as a defining feature of Australian society, with an increasingly multicultural population. It will help Australia’s healthcare systems better engage with diverse cultural perspectives, foster cultural understanding, and promote culturally safe and respectful care, as well as cultural competency among healthcare workers and policymakers. By studying how bioethics interacts with different cultural contexts, the project will strengthen Australian bioethics, which is currently shaped mainly by Western traditions, by learning from practices in non-Western countries where many Australian migrants originate. The research will enhance social cohesion and public trust in healthcare by improving cultural competence while ensuring ethical responsiveness. It will also build capacity for both Australia and partner countries through global collaboration and shared learning. The fellowship will deliver real-world benefits beyond academia through stakeholder consultations, including patients, public communication, an open-access website, social media engagement, and policy recommendations for the Australian Department of Health and Aged Care and the Australian Medical Association, in addition to international organisations. Its findings will help prevent cultural and ethical tensions in healthcare settings, which can still arise despite Australia’s strong commitment to multiculturalism.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Universal laws for extreme gaps in random structures. This project aims to develop a unified framework for studying extreme gaps in random systems. It focuses on rare, extreme gap events in two fundamental settings: the eigenvalues of random matrices and the zeros of stationary Gaussian processes. By integrating techniques from random matrix theory, Gaussian process theory, and extreme value analysis, the project seeks to create a coherent framework that unifies previously fragmented results and uncovers universality phenomena in correlated systems. It will also investigate the conditions under which these universal laws break down and analyse how such breakdowns are influenced by the underlying correlations within the systems.
national-interest-test-statement:
This project investigates the mathematical principles governing extreme and rare events using extreme value theory (EVT), a branch of probability and statistics that quantifies the likelihood of rare occurrences. EVT provides a foundation for applications across science and industry — including engineering, hydrology, finance, insurance, climate modelling, and infrastructure planning. For example, it underpins estimates of a “100-year flood” in hydrology, quantifies risks of market crashes in finance, and informs the design of resilient infrastructure systems exposed to extreme environmental events.

In addition, the project studies stationary Gaussian processes, which are widely used to model temporal or spatial correlations in complex systems. These processes have important applications in statistics, time series analysis, finance, signal processing, and related fields. For instance, the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process is commonly applied in finance to model the evolution of interest rates or mean-reverting stock prices.

Although primarily theoretical, this research will develop mathematical tools and insights that enable scientists and practitioners to better assess risks, quantify uncertainty, and design more resilient systems across these sectors. By advancing foundational knowledge, the project will strengthen Australia’s research capacity and reinforce the mathematical foundations that drive innovation.
