grant-summary: A new angle on galaxy evolution: connecting the Milky Way and beyond. Due to the complexity of internal and external processes acting on galaxies, many questions about their evolution remain. This project aims to leverage data from a cutting-edge survey using the world’s most powerful 3D spectrograph to directly challenge existing models of disk formation. The innovation is to measure how stars move and what elements they are made of in galaxies viewed at different angles to understand the formation of the Milky Way. By linking Galactic and extragalactic perspectives, this project will build a comprehensive framework for how galaxies evolve. Expected outcomes include a census of bar and spiral properties in Milky Way-like galaxies and new insight into the key physical processes that govern disk formation.
national-interest-test-statement: In tackling the biggest questions of them all - What is our place in the Universe? and How did we get to this point? - this project begins to unlock the detailed history of how our Milky Way Galaxy formed and what that means for us. Using a groundbreaking astronomical survey, this project builds on Australia’s $129 million investment in the Strategic Partnership with the European Southern Observatory, as well as numerous ARC-funded projects that keep Australian science at the global cutting edge. It will fill a major gap in understanding how galaxies like our own evolve by combining the power of the world’s most advanced telescopes with new Australian-developed analysis tools. The benefits of this project will be ongoing. By applying advanced data analytics, programming, and hyperspectral imaging techniques to answer questions in astronomy, the project contributes to a future workforce equipped for disciplines such as agriculture, geoscience, biomedical imaging, remote sensing, and environmental monitoring. Through open data releases, collaboration with international partners, and public engagement activities, the discoveries will be shared widely beyond academia. There is no science that inspires like astronomy, and at a time when engagement with STEM disciplines is waning, astronomy offers a powerful way to inspire students to pursue science and technology careers.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Verifiable Data Deletion for Responsible Knowledge Discovery. This project aims to create new ways to make data deletion verifiable, enabling information to be responsibly removed or updated without harming the quality of knowledge discovery. It expects to advance transparent and efficient approaches for checking whether deleted data truly leaves no trace in analytical systems. The project expects to deliver practical tools and open benchmarks that support organisations to manage, audit and trust their data. These outcomes should strengthen responsible data use, improve compliance, and build public confidence in data-driven innovation.
national-interest-test-statement:
Australia’s growing reliance on artificial intelligence brings both opportunities and risks. As AI systems learn from vast amounts of data, they must also be able to unlearn - to responsibly remove outdated, biased, or private information when laws, ethics, or user needs change. Yet current technologies make it difficult to verify whether deleted data truly leaves no trace in large models, posing challenges for privacy, accountability, and public trust.

This project aims to make data deletion in AI systems verifiable and efficient, enabling organisations to check that removed information no longer influences automated decisions. It seeks to establish transparent frameworks and practical auditing tools that allow AI models to forget and update knowledge safely, without costly retraining.

The outcomes are expected to strengthen Australia’s capability in secure and responsible AI, supporting national priority: Building a secure and resilient nation. By advancing sovereign capability in trustworthy data technologies, the project is designed to help industries and public sectors manage AI systems transparently, reduce reliance on overseas technologies, and build public confidence in data-driven innovation.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Building pre-European reference data for healthy Australian ecosystems. Postcolonial land use and climate change are driving catastrophic wildfire and biodiversity loss across southern Australia. Ecological restoration is a key approach to address these impacts, but it requires reference data that precede colonial disturbance. Current models of pre-European ecosystems rely on limited and inaccurate assumptions that overlook long-term Indigenous management. This project will develop and test methods to generate quantitative pre-European reference data in two threatened systems: the Southwest Australian Bioregion (Noongar Country) and the Gippsland forests (Gunaikurnai Country). The outcome will be a readily applicable set of methods to assess and apply robust ecosystem baselines to guide restoration projects.
national-interest-test-statement: Australia faces accelerating environmental crises, including catastrophic wildfire, biodiversity loss and landscape degradation, which threaten national prosperity, food security and regional stability. These challenges undermine ecosystems that sustain agriculture, water supply, tourism and community wellbeing. This Future Fellowship is a strategic national investment that will generate robust empirical evidence to guide ecological restoration and sustainable land management. Current pre-European ecological models, which underpin major conservation and climate programs, are often inaccurate because they overlook millennia of Indigenous land stewardship and the role of cultural fire in maintaining biodiversity. By integrating palaeoecological data, advanced analytical techniques and Indigenous knowledge, this project will establish reliable ecological baselines for restoration. Research will focus on the Southwest Australian Bioregion (Noongar Country) and the Gippsland forests (Gunaikurnai Country), two regions under acute threat from biodiversity loss and catastrophic fire. The outcomes will deliver practical quantitative tools and partnerships that strengthen Australia’s capacity for sustainable resource management, climate adaptation and reconciliation through shared environmental governance.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Hybridisation in a changing world: building wildlife resilience. Genetic rescue is a powerful but under-utilised conservation tool for enhancing biodiversity resilience. This project aims to increase the uptake of genetic rescue in conservation by addressing uncertainties around the long-term impacts of mixing divergent species on key evolutionary processes linked to viability. This project expects to advance knowledge of how hybridisation shapes persistence over many generations using whole genomes, population viability models and historical samples from a rare natural experiment. Expected outcomes of this project include tools for evidence-based decision-making in conservation. This should provide significant benefits, such as improved conservation outcomes for threatened species and ecosystems.
national-interest-test-statement: The Earth is on the brink of a mass extinction event, threatening biodiversity as well as human well-being. Genetic rescue involves the deliberate introduction of new genetic material from distinct source populations and serves as a powerful strategy to enhance the genetic health and long-term evolutionary resilience of threatened species. Despite its proven potential, genetic rescue remains under-utilised in conservation. This project will strengthen Australia’s capacity to conserve biodiversity under accelerating environmental change by addressing a key barrier to the uptake of genetic rescue: uncertainty around perceived adverse long-term outcomes of mixing taxa that are considered too genetically divergent (e.g. different subspecies or species). This project will generate knowledge of how hybridisation between different species shapes key evolutionary processes linked to viability and generate evidence-based guidelines for managing genetic mixing to enhance species' adaptive capacity and persistence. Close collaboration with relevant management agencies — through stakeholder meetings, workshops, and targeted communications — will ensure the translation of findings into practice. The outcomes of the project will directly inform conservation policy and practice, supporting the recovery of threatened species, strengthening ecosystem resilience, and contributing to Australia's leadership in innovative biodiversity management.

grant-summary: Additive manufacturing of low-cost heat-tolerant high-strength aluminium. This project aims to design and develop a new class of low-cost, heat-tolerant, high-strength aluminium alloys for additive manufacturing. It expects to generate new knowledge on how alloy composition and processing influence microstructure and performance at high temperatures. The expected outcomes of this project include improved understanding of alloy design principles and the production of lightweight, durable components for aerospace, transport and defence. This should provide significant benefits by advancing Australia’s capability in advanced manufacturing, strengthening industrial competitiveness, and training the next generation of skilled researchers and innovators in this critical technology field.
national-interest-test-statement:
This project will develop a new generation of low-cost, heat-tolerant, and high-strength aluminium alloys designed specifically for additive manufacturing. Current aluminium alloys used in Australia’s aerospace, transport, and defence industries are not well suited to additive manufacturing because they lose strength and stability at high temperatures. This project will fill this critical research gap by creating new alloys that can withstand demanding service conditions while remaining lightweight and affordable.
The research will benefit Australians economically and industrially by strengthening local capability in advanced manufacturing and reducing reliance on imported materials and technologies. It will also support new high-value jobs in defence, aerospace, and emerging manufacturing sectors, and train the next generation of engineers and scientists in metal additive manufacturing.
To ensure broad impact, the research outcomes will be shared with industry partners, manufacturing networks, and government agencies through workshops, training programs, and technology demonstrations. Collaborations with international research institutions will also help accelerate translation and adoption. By enabling the design and manufacture of stronger and more reliable Australian-made components, this project will enhance national manufacturing competitiveness and contribute to Australia’s long-term technological and economic resilience.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Uncovering Antarctica’s Hidden Interior through Advanced Seismic Imaging. This Fellowship aims to deepen our fundamental understanding of Antarctica's hidden continent, from surface to deep interior. Using cutting-edge seismic imaging, data fusion, and geophysical inference methods, it will develop the first comprehensive continental-wide model leveraging two decades of multi-million-dollar Antarctic seismic investment. Expected outcomes include unprecedented knowledge of Antarctica’s tectonic structures, volcanic heat, and mantle flow, critical for simulating Antarctica's icy history, tracking ice-solid Earth dynamics, and estimating geothermal heat flux. These insights will lead to more reliable projections of Antarctic ice change and global sea-level rise and shape the next generation of Antarctic science.
national-interest-test-statement: Antarctica holds approximately 90% of Earth’s ice and 70% of its freshwater, meaning changes there have a significant influence on future sea-level rise. For Australia, this is critical: around 87% of Australians live near the coast, and just one metre of sea-level rise is estimated to cause about $345 billion in damage to homes, businesses, and infrastructure. While the melting of ice is influenced by climate, it is also controlled by what lies beneath Antarctica — heat from volcanoes under the ice, the movement of deep rocks, and the slow rise of the land as past ice sheets melt. Yet much of this “hidden continent” remains unmapped because it sits under kilometres of icy cap. This Fellowship will utilise advanced seismic imaging and data from existing Antarctic and Southern Hemisphere seismic networks to create the first comprehensive model of Antarctica’s subsurface, from the surface to a depth of one thousand kilometres. The research will uncover the continent’s temperature, tectonic structure, underground fluids, and mantle rock flow rates. These findings will enhance predictions of Antarctic ice-sheet change and global sea-level rise, thereby aiding Australia in planning for coastal protection, climate adaptation, and long-term national resilience. The project will also strengthen Australia’s leadership in Antarctic geophysics and shape the next generation of Antarctic science. Results will be widely shared through government collaboration, articles and media coverage.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Lifetime-Resilient Underground Infrastructure for Multi-Hazard Environments. Global challenges such as climate change, energy transition, and resource management demand infrastructure systems that are both sustainable and resilient to multiple hazards. Underground infrastructure is increasingly exposed to cumulative deterioration and abrupt dynamic events such as earthquakes, blasting, and induced seismicity. This project will establish a physics-based resilience framework that, for the first time, quantifies, predicts, and enhances the performance of underground structures under multi-hazard conditions. Through world-leading integration of laboratory experiments, constitutive modelling, and multi-physics simulations, it will advance global best practice for lifetime-resilient infrastructure design and management.
national-interest-test-statement: This project addresses a critical research gap in ensuring the long-term safety and resilience of Australia’s underground infrastructure. With tunnelling and underground construction forecast to grow by 25% over the next five years, according to Infrastructure Australia, there is an urgent need to better manage risks such as ground movement, water ingress, and geological uncertainty. The project will develop an innovative, science-based framework to improve how engineers assess and design underground structures, helping them perform safely under multiple hazards and changing environmental conditions. The outcomes will deliver broad benefits for Australia. Economically, the research will reduce repair costs, delays, and financial losses caused by infrastructure failures. Environmentally, it supports sustainability by extending asset lifespans and minimising resource waste. Socially, it enhances public safety and the reliability of critical systems such as transport, utilities, and energy storage. To maximise impact beyond academia, the project will work closely with government agencies, engineering firms, and industry partners to translate findings into design guidelines and best practices. The results will be shared through workshops, technical forums, and collaboration with professional societies, helping shape Australia’s next generation of safe and sustainable underground infrastructure.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Evolution and functional biodiversity of mitochondrial complexes. This project will reveal how the machinery that powers life, the mitochondrial electron transport system, has evolved and diversified across eukaryotes. Using advanced imaging and biochemical methods, it will determine how structural and functional changes in these energy-transducing complexes arose over time. By comparing species from across the tree of life, the research will uncover universal rules of biological energy conversion. The outcomes will strengthen Australia’s leadership in structural and evolutionary biology and build national capability in cryogenic electron microscopy, bioenergetics and high-performance computing for discovery-driven science.
national-interest-test-statement: This Future Fellowship will uncover how mitochondrial energy-transducing complexes evolved across the diversity of eukaryotic life. Mitochondria are essential for metabolism, signalling, and adaptation, yet the molecular basis for their extraordinary diversity remains poorly understood. Using advanced cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM), membrane-protein reconstitution, and comparative evolutionary analysis, this research will reveal how changes in protein structure and lipid environment shape respiratory efficiency, regulation, and resilience across diverse environments. These insights will define universal principles that govern energy conversion in living systems and provide a framework for understanding how complex life arose and diversified on Earth. The project will consolidate Australia’s leadership in structural biology, membrane biochemistry, and molecular evolution by establishing new cryo-EM pipelines for analysing dynamic macromolecular assemblies. It will also build national expertise in high-performance computing for structural biology, an area of strategic importance across the biological and physical sciences. By training early-career researchers, fostering international collaboration, and producing openly shared molecular data, this Fellowship will strengthen Australia’s long-term capability in discovery-driven science and our contribution to understanding life’s molecular foundations.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Monsoon Metabolisms: 20th-Century Energy Transitions in Asia and Australia. The Asia-Australian Monsoon Zone is home to half the world’s population, a growing majority of carbon emissions, and an increasingly erratic climate. Its shift to renewables is vital but complex. To understand this challenge, this project aims to produce the first study of the zone’s 20th century energy transitions. It expects to show how historical forces shaped interconnected energetic systems—climate, fuel, food-labour, plantations, industries—creating unequal socio-ecological impacts that hinder renewable adoption. Anticipated outcomes include a book, articles, interactive maps, op-eds, videos, and a policy brief. These outputs aim to equip stakeholders and policymakers with insights to guide their decisions in climate-vulnerable areas.
national-interest-test-statement: This project will deliver the first history of energy transitions across the Asia-Australia Monsoon Zone, which stretches from Northern Australia through South, Southeast, and East Asia to the Himalaya. Home to half the world’s population and a growing majority of carbon emissions, the zone’s shift to renewables is vital to prevent catastrophic climate impacts and cascading economic and security crises across the Asia-Pacific, including Australia. However, entrenched inequalities, carbon-intensive economies, and climate volatility challenge this transition. While the Australian government has pledged billions of dollars to support Asia’s energy transition and aims to integrate Australian renewables into regional systems, research into the zone’s climate, energy regimes, and their interconnections remains limited. By examining how the zone’s interconnected energy systems evolved and analysing the successes, failures, and legacies of past energy transitions, this project aims to inform future decision-making on energy transition strategies. The outputs will include interactive maps, short explanatory videos, op-eds, a policy brief, and scholarly publications. These will offer context-specific historical, social, and ecological insights for stakeholders and policymakers in Northern Australia and monsoonal Asia. Public engagement will help raise awareness of the zone’s linked climate and energy histories and position Australia as a knowledge leader in regional energy transitions.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: A transmission microscope using cold neutrons for quantum advantage. Slow neutron beams provide unique insights into the structure of materials via quantum effects such as wave reflection and diffraction; however, intensity is limited. This project will develop methods to focus and boost neutron intensity to extract key information about hidden structures in materials under operational conditions such as in batteries, thermoelectrics and quantum magnets. The project will explore a groundbreaking two-stage lens using reflective optics followed by magnetic field focusing. The use of spin-polarised neutrons unlocks quantum focusing mechanisms to achieve sub-micron beam spots. The ability to reveal the invisible has benefits across physics, chemistry, biology, engineering and medicine.
national-interest-test-statement:
Australia has a world-leading neutron source at the Australian Nuclear Science Technology Organisation (ANSTO), widely used to perform critical research into batteries, solar cells, engineering components, drug molecules, food, rare-earth minerals and semiconductors. There is a gap in the knowledge, however, of how to exploit the quantum properties of a neutron to achieve high focusing powers to image sub-millimetre regions of materials to provide missing information. Developing this fundamental knowledge will benefit all of the latter domains, also enhancing non-destructive studies of cultural artifacts and fossils, while simultaneously refining the understanding of targeted neutron capture in medical physics.

This project will address the gap in the foundational science, and scaffold upon existing capabilities to develop the design for a neutron transmission microscope capable of performing studies with high spatial resolution, paving the way for a new generation of neutron instruments in Australia.The project will benefit all Australian and New Zealand users at over 43 universities, and industrial groups. 

In addition to developing the key principles, the project will model, manufacture and integrate prototype hardware and software for tests at ANSTO. 

The project will establish a research hub to train multiple PhD and undergraduate students at the nearby University of Wollongong to work with nuclear techniques on topics aligned with Australian research priorities.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Precision methodologies for unlocking the functions of RNA isoforms. Genes commonly create multiple products, yet the functions of these alternative products are often unknown. This project aims to develop and apply novel methods to characterise the activity of gene products in individual brain cells. Using this innovative approach, this project will generate new knowledge on the functions of genes and their products. Expected outcomes include a better understanding of how the brain forms, strengthened collaborations, increased capacity in bioinformatics and RNA biotechnology and broadly applicable techniques for characterising gene products. This should provide significant benefits and equip the Australian RNA biotechnology sector with the tools to select, characterise and target alternative gene products.
national-interest-test-statement: Genes determine the characteristics of all living things. Most genes have multiple versions, allowing different products to be made from one gene. However, the identify and role of many alternate gene products remains unknown. This project will develop and utilise new precision methods to discover, characterise and manipulate gene products and apply them to advance our understanding of how the human brain forms. By measuring the activity of gene products in individual brain cells and then demonstrating their functional roles inside these cells, this project will identify gene products controlling brain formation in unprecedented detail. This will have benefits for understanding both how brains form and age and, in the future, could provide insights into brain disorders and ways to improve our cognitive abilities. The advanced techniques we develop, including software tools to identify and characterise gene products in individual cells and experimental methods to manipulate which gene products cells make, will be widely applicable and could be of use in agriculture, biotechnology and conservation, for example to improve crops, or create new products and services in biotechnology. This will have economic, environmental and commercial benefits to Australia. Outcomes from this research will be promoted worldwide via publications, dedicated websites and media releases as well as through collaborations with industry partners and participation in national science week.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Revolutionising sewage sludge treatment via high-value products generation. This project aims to develop a transformative sewage sludge treatment technology that reduces sludge volume and produces high-value liquid biofuels instead of conventional methane. These biofuels are easy to collect, store and transport, while eliminating greenhouse gas emission. It expects to shift sludge treatment from a carbon-intensive and costly process to a low-carbon, cost-saving one. The expected outcomes can be readily integrated into existing sludge treatment infrastructure, providing a sustainable, cost-effective, and scalable solution for wastewater industry. This would provide significant benefits by advancing Australia’s leadership in waste management and supporting the nation’s transition toward a circular, net-zero future.
national-interest-test-statement: Australia faces major challenges in managing sewage sludge, a rapidly growing and massive by-product of wastewater treatment that drives greenhouse gas emissions and high operational costs. Current treatment methods are expensive and release methane, a potent greenhouse gas. This project addresses these challenges by developing a cost-saving, zero-methane technology that converts sewage sludge into high-value liquid biofuels, achieving enhanced sludge reduction while minimizing environmental impacts. Benefits for Australians include lower treatment costs and renewable fuel generation, reduced greenhouse gas emissions, and support for resilient, low-carbon communities. By transforming sludge treatment into a cost-effective, zero-methane process, this innovation positions Australia at the forefront of sustainable waste management, driving deep decarbonisation across the wastewater sector and supporting the nation’s circular, net zero future. To maximise impact beyond academia, the project could engage industry partners and government agencies for pilot-scale implementation and policy translation, while public outreach via media, workshops, and professional networks such as the International Water Association could encourage widespread understanding and adoption. This research would advance Australia’s global leadership in sustainable waste innovation and foster a circular economy where waste is minimized and resources are recovered.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Discovery, characterisation and application of defensive toxins from venoms. Our sensory nervous system allows us to detect and respond appropriately to diverse stimuli in our environment. Venomous animals and plants have evolved defensive toxins that target this system, hijacking and manipulating specific components to cause pain. This project will identify and characterise new defensive toxins from venoms and apply them as tools to improve our understanding of the mammalian sensory nervous system. The knowledge gained will advance our understanding of venom function and evolution, and could also provide a foundation for the future development of safer and more effective treatments for sensory nervous system disorders like chronic pain.
national-interest-test-statement:
New knowledge in the biological sciences can have important applications in agriculture, conservation, technology and medicine. In this project I will investigate defensive toxins from venoms that have evolved to potently manipulate specific components of the sensory nervous system of other animals including mammals. Understanding what these toxins are, what they target and the effects that they have, will improve our understanding of the mammalian sensory nervous system. This knowledge could be applied, in future, to improving and/or developing new treatments for sensory nervous system disorders like chronic pain.

The project will build national research capacity in toxinology, molecular pharmacology and neuroscience. The outcomes will enhance Australia’s international reputation in biomedical innovation and could support future advances in health and biotechnology, delivering long-term benefits to the wellbeing and productivity of Australians.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Lighting the dark: shining black holes throughout cosmic time. This project will reveal how the first black holes formed and grew alongside their galaxies in the early universe. Leveraging cutting-edge software developed in Australia, together with privileged access to supercomputers and unique datasets, the project will simulate how black holes produce light and how this connects to the galaxies that host them. These predictions aim to explain striking discoveries from the James Webb Space Telescope, such as overly massive and numerous bright black holes, that challenge our current theories. The results will provide a step change in our understanding of how galaxies and black holes evolved, create open software for global use, and strengthen Australia’s leadership in astrophysics and digital research.
national-interest-test-statement:
This Fellowship will advance Australia’s national capability in high-performance computing, data science, and open research software through a frontier project to explain how the first black holes in the Universe formed and evolved, addressing one of the most pressing mysteries in astronomy. Using Shark, an Australian-developed, open-source galaxy formation model running on national supercomputing facilities, the project will integrate next-generation physics and cutting edge statistical techniques to interpret discoveries from the 10-billion dollar facility James Webb Space Telescope and prepare for data from billion dollar upcoming facilities such as the Square Kilometre Array (SKA).

The research will reinforce Australia’s leadership in astronomy, data science, and high-performance computing-sectors that contribute more than $13 billion annually to the national economy. By training students and early-career researchers in advanced computing and AI-driven analysis, the project will help supply the estimated 160,000 new digital-skills jobs needed in Australia by 2030.

All software, data, and results will be openly released following FAIR principles, ensuring global visibility and collaboration. Outreach through schools, media, and citizen-science platforms will inspire the next generation of Australian innovators. Combining frontier science with open technology, this Fellowship will deliver lasting scientific, educational, and economic gains for Australia.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Quantum Chaos: Analysis, Geometry, and Arithmetic. The theory of automorphic forms is a branch of pure mathematics that has many applications, such as understanding the connection between classical and quantum physics. This proposal aims to greatly expand our knowledge of this connection, by proving new theorems which show that the distribution of a high-energy quantum particle looks like the distribution of the corresponding classical particle. This will result in new, interdisciplinary techniques that combine deep results from analysis and number theory. Benefits include new international collaborations, and developing Australia’s reputation as a center for research in automorphic forms.
national-interest-test-statement: This project focuses on analysis and number theory, particularly the theories of automorphic forms and analysis on symmetric spaces. These are abstract mathematical concepts that connect to several problems with practical applications, including the construction of efficient networks for the transfer of information, electricity, or goods. The specific problems considered by the project include using tools from these areas to investigate the relationship between classical mechanics and quantum mechanics.  This research advances pure mathematics, having direct economic benefits to Australia, contributing to scientific advancement and the exchange of specialised skills crucial to a new economic landscape. Expertise in pure mathematics is highly sought after in the field of data science, as it enables the development of innovative techniques for handling the increasingly large data sets in this industry. The proposal contains high-quality mathematics in a field of global importance, in which the CI is the leading expert in Australia. With the national strategy to build Australia's scientific capacity in mathematics, this investment is a cost-effective way to bring new knowledge to the Australian public as well as the research community. The research findings will be disseminated through online resources, workshops and seminars, and online popular science publications, ensuring accessibility to a diverse audience.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Elastic Energy Storage in Mineralized Tissues: Generation and Functionality. In the biological world, mechanical work is often powered by chemo-mechanical energy, which can be used immediately or stored elastically for delayed functions. The storage of elastic energy is ubiquitous in mineralized biological materials and can mark the boundary between tissue performance and failure. However, it remains a widely underestimated mechanism in the functionality of bioengineered and bio-inspired materials. The core aim of this project is to uncover how elastic energy is generated, stored, and released throughout the lifespan of biogenic ceramics, to explore its interaction with external forces, and to reveal its role in tissue functionality and performance.
national-interest-test-statement:
The pursuit of advanced biomaterials with sophisticated properties drives engineers to tailor material characteristics, often through complex chemical compositions. However, such progress can lead to high fabrication costs and reduced sustainability. In contrast, nature creates multifunctional materials by exploiting physical principles while relying minimally on compositional changes.
This proposal addresses this gap by investigating the generation and storage of internal elastic energy in biological materials—an omnipresent phenomenon critical to material functionality and performance. The project aligns with two of Australia’s key research priorities in advanced materials and manufacturing, offering solutions in biomedical innovation, advanced biomaterials, and biomimetic materials.
It will establish design principles for next-generation biomaterials in which advanced functions can be (i) generated and tailored through internal energy storage, (ii) integrated within the microstructure, and (iii) made location-specific. These advancements will enhance Australia’s global competitiveness by promoting innovation and enabling the development of advanced materials and manufacturing processes. In doing so, they will support critical industries in achieving national objectives such as transitioning to a net-zero future, fostering healthy and resilient communities, and protecting and restoring the environment.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Smart origami: New strategy for energy absorption and structural protection. By integrating origami with stimuli-responsive materials, this project aims to develop transformative, sustainable smart origami for reusable energy absorption and structural protection, with focus on the fundamental mechanics and mechanisms across multi-regime impact velocities. This interdisciplinary research expects to generate new knowledge in origami engineering, structural engineering and impact mechanics. The derived knowledge will significantly advance the design and development of next-generation materials and structures with superior reusable impact performance. This should provide significant benefits to invention of reusable protection systems for sustainability and safety of space and land vehicles against collisions.
national-interest-test-statement: Origami materials and structures have demonstrated exceptional performance of energy absorption and structural protection. However, existing studies on their energy absorption are mostly achieved via the irreversible, plastic deformation, which means that these materials/structures cannot be reused, and thus the engineering systems have to be discarded and replaced after single use. Therefore, this project aims to develop transformative smart origami materials and structures for reusable energy absorption and structural protection, fundamentally moving beyond conventional single-use (sacrificial) protection systems under multi-regime impact velocities. The knowledge gained will drive new inventions of reusable protective structures and materials, offering opportunities for Australian industry (e.g. Defence and Space) to lead the world in design and manufacture of advanced materials and structures for engineering systems against collisions. This research addresses National Research Priority 5 by developing next-generation smart origami materials and structures for extreme impact protection. It also addresses National Research priority 1 by offering a solution to waste issues of structural replacement associated with protective engineering applications. Besides academic presentations and publications, the research outcomes will also be introduced to the public through media and developing industry prototypes to drive utility and adoption.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Harnessing structure in data to solve complex biological problems. The project aims to develop statistical and machine-learning methods that treat shared ancestry, location, and genetics as information, not noise. It will jointly model these structures across predictors and responses to avoid confounding; use grouped-factor methods to compress hundreds of traits into a few interpretable axes; adapt neural networks with clade/region-blocked cross validation to detect genuine nonlinear effects; and combine these with causal diagrams to estimate the impact of interventions given genetic or spatial structure. Expected outcomes are open software, clear workflows, and Australian case studies that inform biodiversity conservation goals and climate-resilient crop design.
national-interest-test-statement: This project builds statistical and machine-learning tools that treat shared ancestry, location and genetics as information, not noise. Current methods often miss genuine biological insights or draw incorrect conclusions because they do not adequately handle these shared structures. By jointly modelling these structures across predictors and responses, the project will deliver a suite of tools for robust scientific inference with capabilities for high-dimensional data, non-linear trends and interactions, and causal inference. The toolkit is highly transferable, lifting analytic capability for Australian researchers and end-users, and supporting data-driven decision making for government, industry and NGOs. Specific gains include stronger evidence for biodiversity conservation (e.g., trait combinations that predict persistence) and improved agricultural productivity and resilience (e.g., climate-resilient trait targets). To maximise uptake beyond academia, outputs will include open software with example workflows and Australian case studies, plus online tutorials and short courses.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Developing sustainable sodium batteries with advanced polymers. This project will design and investigate advanced electrolyte materials that enable safer and longer-lasting sodium-metal batteries, a low-cost and sustainable alternative to lithium batteries for diverse energy storage applications. It focuses on novel, positively charged polymers that combine mechanical strength with good ionic conductivity, addressing key scientific limitations of traditional polymer electrolytes. Using advanced modelling and electrochemical analysis, the project will elucidate molecular mechanisms that underpin sodium-ion transport and interfacial stability. The outcomes will advance knowledge and national capability in energy-storage research, supporting Australia’s net-zero goals via new understanding and training.
national-interest-test-statement: This research will contribute to Australia’s national interest by developing safer, more efficient electrolyte materials for next-generation sodium-metal batteries, a key alternative for large-scale renewable energy storage and achieving national net-zero goals. Unlike lithium, sodium is abundant, inexpensive, and globally available, offering a secure and sustainable foundation for low-cost, grid-level battery storage. The project focuses on new polymer materials that are both strong and highly conductive to overcome major safety and performance barriers that currently limit polymer-based sodium-metal battery development. The outcomes will support Australia’s transition to a clean, reliable, and affordable energy future by improving the storage of electricity from solar and wind. Alongside environmental benefits, the project will diversify Australia’s battery materials base beyond lithium, strengthen domestic research–industry collaboration, and create new opportunities for high-value manufacturing, export, and skilled employment. To ensure translation and impact, the research will be shared with scientific communities, Australian battery companies, manufacturers, and industry partners, while training PhD students and early career researchers in advanced battery materials, modelling, and electrochemistry testing. These efforts will build national capability and reinforce Australia’s leadership in sustainable energy-storage innovation.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Understanding kelp’s carbon metabolism to mitigate climate change. Kelp are major components of coastal ecosystems and economies. Their highly efficient carbon metabolism has sparked interest in kelp-based climate solutions, e.g., to remove more carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. To develop sophisticated kelp strategies, we need to understand why kelp are so efficient and how they differ from related organisms. This project aims to unveil the atomic structure and function of the proteins and cellular components of kelp's carbon metabolism using techniques such as cryo-electron microscopy, and to do detailed biochemical comparisons with other organisms. This will set Australia as a pioneer in kelp molecular biology and help certify kelp forests as blue-carbon ecosystems to meet the 2050 net-zero goals.
national-interest-test-statement: Kelp's efficient carbon metabolism has attracted significant interest as a potential new avenue for atmospheric-carbon sequestration and ocean de-acidification, significant drivers of climate change. However, the almost complete lack of knowledge about the molecular details of how kelp sequester and use carbon and why they are so efficient compared to other organisms is a strong barrier preventing the use of kelp as an effective climate-change solution. This is particularly significant for Australia, which has both extensive kelp ecosystems at risk and strong goals for carbon sequestration, as per the national 2050 net-zero goals. The work from this Fellowship will provide molecular data to certify kelp forests as a blue-carbon ecosystem and create new carbon markets to meet Australia's 2050 net-zero goals. Moreover, by providing knowledge, training in a pioneering field and forming new national and international collaborations, this work will help accelerate Australia's burgeoning seaweed industry to its predicted $1.5 billion by 2040. This work will also help identify climate-resilient kelp varieties for enhanced carbon capture and ocean reforestation, to help repopulate critical kelp forests (priority in DCCEEW's 2022 Threatened Species Action Plan). We will promote our findings to seaweed farmers and general public through public media and talks so that the science is understood and translated into environmental and economic benefits for all Australians.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Shattering the Finite Length Barrier in Extreme Low-Capacity Communications. This project aims to solve the challenge of reliable data transmission in extremely noisy, low-capacity settings, which is essential for emerging technologies like the Internet of Things and quantum security, where conventional theories fail. This research expects to advance fundamental understanding by establishing a new theoretical foundation for these extreme settings, engineering ultra-efficient codes, and devising simple decoding algorithms. Anticipated outcomes include advanced communication techniques that consume less energy and operate more reliably under such conditions. This should provide significant benefits by bolstering the efficiency, security, and resilience of Australia's future digital economy and critical infrastructure.
national-interest-test-statement: This project tackles a major challenge for Australia's digital future: how to reliably communicate tiny amounts of data using extremely weak signals, which is like trying to hear a whisper across a noisy stadium. This capability is essential for new technologies like the Internet of Things, with its billions of low-power devices, and for quantum security, which promises unhackable communications. Our current communication rules break down in these conditions, and this research will create the new science needed to make them work. The research will directly benefit Australians by making our digital technology more efficient, reliable, and secure. This will lead to reduced power consumption, which is better for the environment and lowers costs, and will strengthen our national security by protecting critical infrastructure like energy and banking systems. The outcomes will help grow Australia's digital economy and build a more resilient nation. To ensure these benefits reach the public, the research will be shared in plain English through articles in accessible media. We will also actively translate these new ideas into real-world use by filing patents, creating opportunities for new Australian startup companies, and working with industry to build these solutions into future global communication standards

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Reclaiming Cities from the Sea: Coastal Futures for the Asia-Pacific. This project aims to evaluate land reclamation projects in vulnerable coastal cities of the Asia-Pacific and work with urban and climate advocates to provide improved pathways to resilient urban development. It will generate new knowledge about the economic, social and material relations which sustain coastal cities by producing new concepts and methods, including the analytic of socioecological worldmaking, for understanding the economic geographies of urban climate futures. Anticipated outcomes include alternative models of land reclamation that support the urban majority against climate risks. Outcomes will benefit Australian policymakers, international organisations and international research working towards equitable urban resilience.
national-interest-test-statement: In the vulnerable cities of the Asia-Pacific region, large scale land reclamation promises to extend and elevate coastlines to meet growing populations and escalating climate risks. Although essential for addressing coastal threats, land reclamation also has negative social and ecological impacts. This is the first project to integrate an examination of the economic, environmental and social dynamics of land reclamation through a study of Jakarta, Manila, Funafuti and South Tarawa. The project addresses a critical gap in understanding the multiscalar social and material processes of land reclamation, moving beyond narrow environmental assessments to explore contested urban transformations and community-led alternatives. Working with community groups and climate advocacy organisations, the Fellowship will produce alternative pathways for land reclamation which seek climate justice for the urban majority. The project will identify options for more equitable land reclamation, increasing adaptive capacity, regional stability, partnerships with the Asia-Pacific and Australian leadership in climate resilience.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Defending Democracy: Leveraging AI to Counter Electoral Misinformation . The project aims to address the escalating global threat that electoral misinformation poses to public trust, democratic legitimacy and social cohesion using innovative survey experiments to test countermeasures to reduce misinformation belief and strengthen democratic resilience, including the novel use of AI chatbots. It will deliver the first global systematic study assessing effective ways election authorities can fight election misinformation and distrust. Expected outcomes are new knowledge to position Australia as a global leader in tackling electoral misinformation with outcomes such as policy guidance for governments, authorities, platforms and media to benefit all citizens by safeguarding social cohesion and election integrity.
national-interest-test-statement:
Elections are central to democracy, yet misinformation increasingly threatens public trust worldwide. In Australia, there is no systematic evidence on which strategies most effectively counter electoral misinformation. This project fills that gap by using a range of methods including an innovative AI-driven approach to test whether chatbots can reduce belief in misinformation and preserve trust in Australian elections. It will also produce a global first: a typology and database of strategies used internationally to combat electoral misinformation belief and spread.

The research will benefit Australians by strengthening election integrity, supporting social cohesion, and enhancing political and economic stability. Evidence-based insights will enable governments, election authorities, media, influencers and digital platforms to adopt practical measures that do not require new laws to limit election denialism and the polarising effects of electoral misinformation spread.

To maximise impact beyond academia, findings will be shared directly with electoral authorities and information regulators through a national workshop, disseminated via digital platforms for practical use, and communicated to the public through media coverage. This ensures the research informs policy and practice, promotes understanding, and encourages adoption of strategies that safeguard trust in Australian elections.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: A longitudinal investigation into social cognitive ageing. This project aims to deliver the world's first longitudinal social cognitive ageing dataset, providing novel insights into the developmental trajectory of social cognitive change in late adulthood. This project expects to reveal when, how and why core social cognitive skills change at different stages of late life development, and critically, how these changes contribute to social isolation and loneliness in older age. Expected outcomes include establishing a national research infrastructure that will enhance cross-institutional and international collaboration. This project should provide significant benefits, by generating the foundational data that will inform strategies to help older Australians to remain socially connected for longer.
national-interest-test-statement: Social cognitive function – the ability to detect, understand, and respond to social and emotional cues – plays a fundamental role in social connectedness. Although evidence suggests that social cognitive abilities get worse with advancing age, this is based entirely on cross-sectional studies. As a result, we currently have no knowledge of how social cognition evolves in late life development, or how age-related social cognitive changes contribute to loneliness and social isolation. This project aims to address this gap by establishing the world’s first longitudinal dataset on social cognitive ageing. Using a unique cross-disciplinary approach, this project expects to reveal when, why, and how social cognitive abilities change in older age, identifying novel mechanisms that lead to loneliness and social isolation. The dataset generated in this project is expected to strengthen national capacity to promote healthy and thriving communities by informing evidence-based strategies and policies that enhance social connection, supporting older Australians to live well for longer. Key findings will be made publicly available via a dedicated website, that will provide easy to understand snapshots for promoting healthy ageing. These findings will also be disseminated to government and community organisations, ensuring translation into policy and practice.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Concurrent nano- and macro-ordering to revolutionise additive manufacturing. This project seeks to pioneer a transformative approach to materials design by uniting the disparate fields of nanoscience and additive manufacturing. It aims to develop innovative chemical strategies to direct polymer self-organisation across multiple length scales, unlocking materials that combine programmable nanoscale precision with macroscopic control for unprecedented functionality. Expected outcomes include new fundamental design principles for hierarchical self-assembly, and scalable, high-performance materials for sustainable metal recovery and quantum technologies. This will position Australia at the forefront of advanced manufacturing and train a new generation of researchers to drive the next wave of materials innovation.
national-interest-test-statement: Now is a pivotal moment for Australia to lead in designing and manufacturing advanced materials that will power future industries. The global race toward quantum technologies, clean energy, and sustainable resource recovery demands materials that perform across multiple scales − from the tiniest building blocks to large-scale structures − but current approaches cannot achieve this level of control. This Fellowship will address this urgent need by tackling a grand scientific challenge: understanding and directing how polymers, the building blocks of advanced materials, organise themselves into functional structures across multiple length scales. By uncovering the fundamental chemical rules that allow polymers to self-organise and build increasingly complex structures, the program will establish a new foundation for designing scalable, high-performance materials. Expected outcomes include transformative strategies for creating materials with tuneable properties that enable superior functionality, enabling breakthroughs in quantum devices and sustainable recovery of critical metals. This research will strengthen Australia’s position in advanced manufacturing, clean energy, and circular economy sectors. It will train the next generation of skilled polymer scientists and foster industry collaboration, ensuring Australia captures the economic and environmental benefits of innovation in intelligent materials design at a time when global demand surges for high-performance materials.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Do T cells govern B cell fate and lifespan? This project aims to define how the fate of an immune cell, the B cell, is controlled. B cells give rise to antibody-producing plasma cells, and the signals that program their differentiation are given by T cells. This project will use controlled interventions to tune up or down T cell signalling to define whether these signals amplify differentiation directly or indirectly, and whether the amount of T cell signal dictates the lifespan of outputted plasma cells. Expected outcomes include understanding of what controls plasma cell persistence and B cell fate. The project is expected to provide the framework needed to improve vaccine design against biosecurity threats, diminishing eradication cost and increasing stability of the food supply.
national-interest-test-statement: Australian Cattle, poultry and sheep farming equate to a >$30 billion-a-year industry, but endemic parasite infections and biosecurity threats such as foot-and-mouth put the stability of the industry, and therefore the food supply, at risk. Knowledge of how to improve the effectiveness of agricultural vaccines would reduce the financial costs and overt risk to the food supply of such occurrences, and the main cell type that confers protection in cattle, sheep and chickens upon vaccination is the plasma cell, which is the terminally differentiated form of the B cell. This project examines the mechanisms by which B cells give rise to plasma cells, if the formative environment surrounding a B cell influences the rate at which the cells obtain the plasma cell fate, and if the environment surrounding the B cell dictates the lifespan of the subsequently outputted plasma cells. The project models mammalian immunity in mice, aiming to provide the framework required to improve efficacy of animal vaccines. Key outcomes include knowledge of the means to generate plasma cells with long lifespans, and a greatly improved mechanistic understanding of B-cell fate determination, leading to better agricultural vaccine design. This will ultimately lead to animal welfare and economic benefits in Australia, improving stability of the food supply. Research outcomes will be conveyed to media via EurekAlert and disseminated to the wider public via LinkedIn and BlueSky.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Designing Self-Healing Sodium-Ion Battery Electrodes. This project will develop new self-healing materials for next-generation sodium-ion batteries. It will combine advanced forms of graphene with flexible polymers to create electrodes that can repair small cracks and damage during use. By studying how these materials recover and store energy, the research will deliver longer-lasting, safer and more sustainable batteries made without using toxic solvents. The outcomes will provide design guidelines for low-cost, solvent-free battery materials and support Australia’s transition to clean and reliable energy technologies.
national-interest-test-statement:
This project will help Australia lead the development of safer and more sustainable batteries by advancing sodium-ion technology to diversify national energy-storage capability. Sodium is abundant and inexpensive, offering a secure and environmentally responsible energy source. The research will develop self-healing battery materials that repair internal damage and eliminate the need for toxic solvents, reducing waste and improving safety.

By supporting the Australian Made Battery Plan and National Battery Strategy, the project will strengthen Australia’s capability to design and manufacture advanced batteries from local resources. It will generate new knowledge and transferable technology while fostering partnerships with industry and training future researchers in a growing clean-energy sector. Outcomes will be shared through open-access publications, industry workshops, and collaborations with manufacturers to accelerate translation. This work will enhance energy security, create high-value jobs,  reduce manufacturing costs, and advance Australia’s position as a global innovator in renewable-energy technologies.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Reimagining and Re-embedding the Living Wage in the Digital Economy. Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping work in Australia, accelerating productivity but undermining wage-setting systems and leaving human contributions uncompensated. Combining comparative legal analysis, fieldwork, and design-led methods, this project aims to generate new knowledge on whether and how living wage standards can address co-production and scraping of human outputs by AI. The multidisciplinary outcomes will include legal frameworks for adapting wage-setting institutions and digital regulation, as well as programmable tools for embedding fair compensation into AI. Benefits include stronger protections for workers, more trustworthy digital infrastructure, and enhanced national resilience to technological disruption.
national-interest-test-statement:
As artificial intelligence (AI) transforms the Australian labour market, risks are growing of wage stagnation, economic exclusion, and declining trust in institutions. This project addresses a critical gap for Australia: our wage-setting systems are not designed for an economy where humans and AI co-produce, and where AI uses creative content without payment. The research will directly benefit Australians by developing new legal and technological frameworks to proactively embed fairness and living wage standards directly into the design of these digital systems, rather than just reacting to problems after they occur. It will also guide reforms to ensure our wage-standards established in the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth), National Employment Standards and modern awards remain effective, preventing further wage decline. 

The project aligns with Australian Government priorities around building a secure and resilient nation. By supporting technology design that protects social cohesion and promotes inclusive prosperity, the project will benefit workers, policymakers, unions, and businesses, ensuring all Australians can navigate the future of work with dignity, security, and fairness.

The multidisciplinary outcomes will be disseminated through policy briefs for government bodies, practical toolkits for unions and coding design guides for technology companies, as well as extensive public engagement via mainstream media and public forums across Australia.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: On Borrowed Time: A Sociological Study of Life Expectancies. This project aims to investigate the possibilities and complexities of living with incurable conditions over an extended time from multiple perspectives (people with incurable conditions, families, care providers). Using a longitudinal qualitative design and a strengths-based approach, this research will generate new knowledge about how Australians navigate the challenges of living for years with incurable illness and what enables them to live well. This project will produce a suite of publicly available resources and inform policy to support people with incurable conditions, their families and care providers. This should provide benefits such as better, more inclusive supports for people navigating long-term incurable illness.
national-interest-test-statement: Australians are living longer with a range of incurable conditions, yet many are now navigating the challenge of living for years with compromised health. With Australia’s ageing population, the number of people affected is projected to increase significantly, placing growing demands on healthcare systems, families and communities. There is now an urgent need to ensure that people with incurable conditions are supported to live these additional years well. To date research has been focused on clinical care needs, leaving an important gap in understanding the complex social and financial challenges and uncertainties of living with incurable conditions over an extended period. This project will explore the complexities of living with incurable conditions from multiple stakeholder perspectives (people with incurable conditions, their families and care providers). Importantly this project will examine what is important to people in living well with their conditions, and how they can be better supported. Findings will be translated into a suite of co-created, publicly available resources for people with incurable conditions, their families, care providers, workplaces and consumer advocates. This will address the unmet supportive care and social support needs of this growing population, provide practical resources and inform policy to improve the wellbeing of all Australians affected by long-term incurable conditions.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Entropy-Engineered 2D Materials for Energy Harvesting and Conversion. This project aims to advance knowledge in solar energy harvesting and conversion by developing next-generation high-entropy materials and uncovering how atomic-scale structures influence their performance. It intends to establish scalable fabrication strategies that produce materials with enhanced stability, conductivity, and multifunctionality. The research is expected to deliver new design principles linking atomic configuration with energy efficiency, supporting Australia’s transition to clean and low-carbon technologies. The expected outcomes include strengthening Australia’s capability in sustainable energy manufacturing and contributing to economic and environmental resilience.
national-interest-test-statement:
Australia’s transition to clean and sustainable energy requires new materials that are efficient, durable, and locally manufacturable. Current energy materials are challenging to prepare with precise atomic arrangements, which limits their efficiency, durability, and scalability. This project aims to develop a synthesis strategy regulated by atomic-level entropy, a measure of compositional disorder that improves material stability, to create high-entropy 2D materials with tuneable structures and multifunctional energy-conversion capabilities for solar-driven water purification, hydrogen generation, and clean energy generation.

The expected outcomes will help Australia strengthen its sovereign capability in advanced materials manufacturing, reduce reliance on imported energy technologies, and lower the cost of clean energy and water in remote and high-temperature regions. By integrating photothermal, catalytic, and electronic functions into a single material platform, the project will advance technologies critical to achieving net-zero emissions and resource efficiency.

Beyond academia, the Fellowship will collaborate with national research centres and energy agencies through regular joint meetings, technical workshops, and data-sharing initiatives to accelerate translation into renewable-energy systems. Research outcomes will be disseminated through industry briefings, invited presentations, and collaborative reports to ensure adoption by relevant stakeholders.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary:
Geometric problems in Partial Differential Equations. The study of Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) is a central area in mathematical analysis with profound implications across various domains in both pure and applied sciences.
This project covers a broad range of research and addresses various geometric problems in PDEs, including celebrated long-standing open conjectures and high-impact questions at the forefront of contemporary research, actively pursued by leading mathematicians. It will introduce novel methodologies to tackle these fundamental challenges, aiming to deliver major breakthroughs and disruptive insights that push the boundaries of knowledge far beyond the current state of the art.
national-interest-test-statement: Partial differential equations (PDEs) are a cutting-edge area of mathematics critical to understanding real-world phenomena, such as the way fluids flow and temperature changes. The project aims to solve major geometric problems in PDEs, including celebrated long-standing conjectures and high-impact questions at the forefront of contemporary research. It will leverage a robust network of leading experts across Australia, Europe, Asia, and USA, fostering a fertile environment for scientific advancement, international collaborations, and the training of the next generation of mathematicians. The goal is to deliver major breakthroughs that redefine the state of the art and place Australia at the forefront of this exciting development. The resulting knowledge will provide exceptional cultural benefit, while its far-reaching applications have the potential to yield economic and environmental advantages. For example, the shape optimisation problems investigated in this project include finding shapes which enclose a given volume so as to minimise the surface area (useful to minimise construction costs of buildings), optimise thermal control (crucial to contrast rise of pollution and climate change), or maximise the torsional rigidity (important to reduce wear and tear of bridges). Maximising the impact of the outcomes will involve dialogue with experts in related fields and engagement with broader communities and professionals through targeted outreach including workshops and talks.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Secure and Resilient Digital Infrastructure on the Open Internet. This projects aim to research the fundamental problem of secure distributed computing in open Internet, where network condition maybe unstable and even under attacks. Existing deployed protocols are all assuming certain good network conditions and thus will become vulnerable when moving to the open Internet. The research outcomes will include secure distributed consensus and computing protocols that will remain secure and efficient in open network. With those protocols, all services (including many mission critical ones) now maintained by distributed systems will continue offer security and resilience, and could also enable broader access to new services which now may only be maintained in in-house environments.
national-interest-test-statement:
This research will develop advanced protocols for decentralized systems, enhancing their resilience, scalability, and security under real-world Internet conditions. These improvements are crucial for Australia’s digital infrastructure across sectors such as finance, healthcare, and public services, where uninterrupted, secure operations are essential. By designing systems capable of adapting to network disruptions and dynamic conditions, this project supports the National Science and Research Priority Area 5, dedicated to building a secure and resilient nation, ensuring that vital Australian services are safeguarded against cyber risks.

Aligned with the Digital Economy Strategy 2030, which seeks to position Australia as a global leader in the digital economy, this research will enhance blockchain technology to support a new generation of decentralized applications. By improving blockchain reliability and efficiency, the project opens doors to innovative applications in areas such as supply chain management, digital identity, decentralized finance and gaming, enabling Australian businesses to leverage the full potential of decentralized systems. Making software and findings publicly accessible will also enrich Australia’s technical knowledge base, empowering industries and government to adopt advanced digital solutions that foster economic growth and technological leadership.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: A Novel Philosophical Framework for Australia’s Quantum Future. Quantum theory works, but it fails to provide a clear picture of how and why it works. This project aims to address this problem by building a philosophical framework that places observers inside the scientific picture. Drawing on tools in philosophy and quantum physics, this framework expects to rethink objectivity for the quantum age, and demonstrate practical utility through case studies in optical clock networks and quantum devices. Expected benefits include a transformative new understanding of quantum reality, strengthened dialogue between science and humanities, and reinforced Australian research capacity and leadership in the rapidly growing quantum sector.
national-interest-test-statement:
Quantum theory is remarkably successful, but it fails to provide a clear picture of how and why it works. In everyday science, different researchers safely assume they discuss common objects in the world; in quantum physics, recent results suggest there is no such safe assumption, which creates a puzzle about what counts as our shared reality. This is a philosophical problem that has confounded physicists and that limits our ability to use quantum theory to its full potential. This project aims to fill this gap by building a philosophical framework that places the observer and their instruments inside the scientific picture and sets out when distinct viewpoints can be combined into shared knowledge.

Australia is investing heavily in quantum technologies; clearer concepts should guide smarter research and development choices and help research teams make stronger claims about quantum networks and devices. The project expects to advance foundational knowledge in philosophy and physics, strengthen Australia's research capability at this boundary, and align with the National Quantum Strategy's goal of building a world-leading quantum sector (projected to add around $6B to GDP by 2045). Expected social and cultural benefits include a transformative new understanding of quantum reality and informed debate about our place in the world.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Machine Learning Assisted Design of Ferroelectric Catalyst and Membranes . Artificial intelligence is reshaping materials science, but an integrated machine learning framework for atomic-level simulations remains undeveloped. This project will combine large-scale data mining, accurate quantum simulations, and advanced machine learning to build an automated platform for accelerating the discoveries of ferroelectric catalysts and membranes for renewable energy generation and sustainable water purification. The outcome is expected to produce interdisciplinary knowledge of physics, chemistry and related methodologies. The project will accelerate the transition from material design to real-world use and position Australia as a global leader in artificial intelligence–driven materials innovation.
national-interest-test-statement: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming scientific discovery. Recognising its strategic importance, Australia’s AI Action Plan and the Future Made in Australia Act identify AI-enabled innovation and clean technologies as national priorities for strengthening sovereign capability. This project will develop a machine learning framework to simulate and design functional materials under realistic operating conditions. Next generation electrocatalysts and membranes will be engineered for renewable energy conversion and sustainable water purification. By uncovering the fundamental mechanisms that govern performance, the project will fill a critical research gap, provide theoretical guidance for experimental validation, and accelerate the discovery of durable and low-cost catalytic and membrane materials. The outcomes will contribute to Australia’s clean energy transition, water security, and advanced manufacturing capacity. The developed methodology can be readily adopted by potential industry partners to facilitate technology translation, reduce R&D costs, and enhance Australia’s competitiveness in material science and advanced manufacturing. This project directly supports national priorities in renewable energy, environmental sustainability, and AI-driven scientific innovation, advancing Australia’s leadership in the emerging AI-for-science era.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
