grant-summary: AI and the Housing Crisis. AI will transform the operation of housing systems with potentially vast impacts on housing outcomes. Yet we do not know what these impacts will be. This project will generate world-first, empirically grounded, whole-of-system understanding of the use of AI in housing. It will trace AI's deployment across the system and critically assess its impacts, for better or worse, as it is rolled out. Its novel methodological approach will generate new knowledge of how humans and AI co-shape housing. Outcomes will include empirically-informed recommendations for AI policy and regulation. The project will position Australian research at the centre of international debates and facilitate scholarly and policy knowledge transfer internationally.
national-interest-test-statement: The housing sector is on the edge of a transformative revolution with AI increasingly touted as a solution to global housing crises, through delivering increased efficiencies across the housing lifecycle. Yet AI also poses serious risks. It may entrench existing inequity in the housing system, present privacy risks, and promote private over public interest. Despite AI’s rapid adoption, we know little about the diverse applications and potential impacts across the housing system. A whole-of-system knowledge of AI’s impact in housing is urgently needed. Drawing on analytical, ethnographic and creative research methodologies, this project will track AI’s deployment across different phases of the housing lifecycle to critically assess its impacts. It will deliver evidence to inform regulatory responses to ensure equitable housing outcomes. This knowledge will directly benefit government and the public through insights that will help Australia reach the housing targets set out in the National Housing Accord. It will benefit industry and policy by providing evidence on how to balance innovation and technology's role as components of the housing system, with responsible application and policy. Methodologically innovative in using ethnographic and creative methods, it will facilitate research communication in compelling ways that cut through to critical audiences beyond academia. Continued engagement with policy makers ensures real world impact, providing evidence to inform policy.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
current-admin-organisation: The University of New South Wales
announcement-admin-organisation: The University of New South Wales
grant-summary: Punishment insensitivity: from cells to circuits to behaviour. Some individuals appropriately avoid choices with bad outcomes, while others persist despite ongoing harm. A key knowledge gap is what brain processes cause these differences. This project aims to uncover brain mechanisms for adaptive and maladaptive avoidance, from the whole-brain to single-cell level. By combining an established behavioural task with cutting-edge neuroscience techniques, this Fellowship will reveal how differences in motivation, learning, and choice arise from differences in brain network activity, neurochemical computations, and gene expression within cell types. Outcomes will advance our understanding of learning and choice, reveal new pathways to enhance decision-making, and inform improved artificial networks.
national-interest-test-statement: We all make poor choices sometimes, but many individuals make self-destructive choices repeatedly. Across a variety of domains, from social to financial to legal, the impacts of this are profound. Australians lead the world for gambling-related losses ($32B/year). The majority of scam victims ($2B/year) are repeat victims. Harmful lifestyle choices (risky behaviour, poor diet) cost the Australian economy >$100B/year in productivity losses, and 1.5M years in healthy life lost per year. There is an urgent need to understand how we recognise and learn from our mistakes to mitigate their impact on individuals and the community, yet we know very little about the psychology and brain processes that help us avoid mistakes. This Fellowship uses innovative behavioural, neuroscientific, and molecular tools to map causes for adaptive versus maladaptive choices. It will reveal how the brain supports learning from negative experiences, how motivations for changing versus maintaining behaviour are resolved, and how decisions are made in real time. This Fellowship expects to transform our understanding of brain-behaviour relationships, help position Australia as a global leader in understanding and improving decision-making, and inform the development of new biologically-inspired neural networks.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Chip-Integrated and Tunable Entangled Quantum Source with Layered Materials. This project aims to develop chip-integrated and tunable entangled quantum photon sources using advanced layered materials with strong nonlinear optical properties. These materials enhance light–matter interactions, enabling efficient and controllable on-chip generation of photon pairs. The research will advance understanding of photon creation in nonlinear materials and deliver a high-performance prototype seamlessly integrated into photonic circuits. The outcomes will boost quantum communication technologies, strengthen secure information networks, and accelerate quantum-enabled industries, including computing, precision sensing, and secure data systems, driving innovation and high-value job creation in the quantum technology sector.
national-interest-test-statement: Australia plays a vital role in global sectors such as smart sensing, quantum computing, and communications. To maintain its competitive edge, the country must innovate in lightweight, high-performance quantum light sources, a capability currently underdeveloped. This project addresses this challenge by developing chip-integrated and tunable quantum light sources using advanced nonlinear layered materials. These sources are critical for enabling quantum imaging, secure communication, and future quantum computing, and will support the next generation of portable technologies such as mobile devices, advanced displays, distributed sensors, and wearable photonics. The outcomes will strengthen Australia's manufacturing and design capabilities in novel materials, advanced light sources, and cutting-edge communication systems. The research is underpinned by the strong expertise of Chief Investigator Lu, who has a proven track record of industry translation. Collaborations with global corporations like Toshiba ensure strong academic-industry partnerships, giving confidence that the project will lead to real-world applications, drive economic growth, and secure Australia’s position in future high-tech industries.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Integrated Design Approach to Advanced Thermal Energy Storage Materials. This project aims to develop new materials for thermal batteries that store heat to advance this vital area of renewable energy technology. By creating materials with tailored thermophysical properties, this work addresses a critical barrier to renewable energy uptake: the need for cost-effective, reliable storage. The research will yield fundamental understanding of molecular-level energy storage mechanisms during phase transitions and deliver a library of high-performance materials contributing to Australia's zero-carbon energy future.
national-interest-test-statement:
On average, more solar energy reaches Australia than any other place on earth. Yet renewable sources account for only a small fraction of our electricity generation. The main problem is not with the quantity of renewable energy that can be produced, but rather how it can be tailored to provide power as needed. When the sun goes down and the wind stops, we still need power. Current storage solutions are too expensive and/or rely on imported materials.
This project tackles this by developing new thermal energy storage materials that capture excess energy from solar and wind as heat and release it when needed. Unlike lithium batteries, thermal storage lasts decades with minimal maintenance, making it cheaper over time. The materials will be made from abundant, locally-sourced resources.
The research will use computational modelling and experimental testing to design materials optimised for Australian conditions. By understanding how these materials store and release energy at the molecular level, we can make more efficient and longer-lasting storage systems.
The benefits to Australia are significant: lower electricity bills, faster transition to renewable energy, new manufacturing jobs in regional areas, and reduced emissions.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Atomic-Scale Insights for Next-Generation Hydrogen Storage Materials. Hydrogen stored in solid materials represents one of the most promising solutions for safely and efficiently handling large quantities of hydrogen. However, the influence of complex nanostructural features on hydrogen uptake and release remains poorly understood. This project aims to elucidate the three-dimensional nanostructural characteristics that govern the performance of hydrogen storage materials. By achieving this, the project will generate fundamental knowledge to guide catalyst selection and the design of next-generation hydrogen storage materials. The outcomes are expected to accelerate the uptake of hydrogen as a clean, sustainable energy source and strengthen Australia’s position in the global hydrogen economy.
national-interest-test-statement:
Australia is poised to become a global leader in green hydrogen—driving the nation’s energy transition and positioning it as a key supplier on the international stage. However, the major barrier to unlocking the next generation of low-emission technologies and achieving the goals of the National Hydrogen Strategy lies in the ability to store and transport hydrogen safely, reliably, and cost-effectively at large scales.

This project will generate critical knowledge of the factors influencing hydrogen storage material performance. The outcomes will enable innovative strategies for the design and synthesis of advanced materials capable of safely and efficiently handling hydrogen at scale. Leveraging Australia’s abundant renewable energy resources, the project will create substantial economic and commercial opportunities across the manufacturing, logistics, and energy export sectors. Ultimately, the knowledge gained will accelerate the deployment of green hydrogen technologies, supporting the diversification of global energy sources and reducing carbon emissions. By overcoming key scientific and technological barriers, this research will contribute directly to Australia’s leadership in clean energy innovation and to global efforts in addressing climate change challenges.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Towards Generalisable, Self-Improving Vision-Language-Action Robot Agents. This project will create advanced, generalisable vision-language-action systems that enable robots to learn from Internet videos, imagine actions, and improve themselves through experience. The innovation lies in teaching robots to watch, imagine, and learn autonomously, combining open-world learning, reasoning, and reinforcement to build adaptable, self-improving machines. It addresses the limits of current robots that cannot generalise beyond training data. Expected outcomes include scalable, safe, and efficient robot agents that assist in healthcare, manufacturing, and daily life, enhancing productivity, wellbeing, sustainability, and Australia’s global leadership in artificial intelligence and digital transformation.
national-interest-test-statement: This project focuses on developing intelligent, generalisable robots that can learn from Internet videos, imagine actions, and improve through experience, much like humans. It addresses the current gap in robotic intelligence where most systems cannot adapt beyond training environments. By advancing vision, language and reinforcement learning, the research will create adaptive robots capable of understanding, reasoning, and acting safely in dynamic real-world settings. The potential benefits for Australians are substantial. Economically, the project will strengthen Australia’s leadership in artificial intelligence and robotics, driving innovation and creating high-value jobs across healthcare, manufacturing, logistics, and agriculture. Socially, it will enable human-centred automation that improves care quality and supports independent living for older Australians. Environmentally, the robots’ ability to learn and adapt efficiently will reduce waste and energy use. To ensure translation and real-world impact, outcomes will be shared through open-source frameworks, public demonstrations, and partnerships with hospitals, industry, and government. Outreach through media, exhibitions, and policy discussions will promote public understanding and adoption. The project will help transform automation into a trusted, collaborative technology that advances Australia’s innovation, sustainability, and wellbeing, aligning with national priorities in digital economy, health, and robotics.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Through the Reeds: Archaeology of the Waters of the Limestone Coast. The Limestone Coast is one of Australia’s most archaeologically overlooked regions, but boasts spectacular sites including submerged caves and sinkholes that are time capsules of megafauna and paleoenvironmental data. They hold a clear potential for study of human material culture to address pressing questions in the deep history of Australasia. This project will deliver specialist Australian capacity and research excellence in marine archaeological survey, paleoenvironmental science, and community engagement to survey in and around caves, sinkholes, rivers and lakes as well as offshore. Starting from an aquatic perspective, this project will re-define the investigation of human interactions with Australia’s changing environment.
national-interest-test-statement:
This project investigates the deep-time archaeology of the inland and coastal waters along South Australia’s Limestone Coast to understand how First Nations people have lived with, managed, and adapted to changing freshwater bodies, wetlands and coastlines. Advanced underwater survey methods, environmental analysis and Indigenous knowledge will inform investigation of cultural landscapes now partly submerged beneath sinkholes, lakes, oceans and their hinterlands. New discoveries will deepen national understanding of how people interacted with changing environments.

Benefits for Australia include protection and interpretation of Indigenous cultural heritage and informing water and land management strategies under accelerating environmental change. Collaboration with the local Indigenous community will support cultural renewal, heritage protection and Indigenous researcher training. New techniques in 3D mapping of submerged caves and sinkholes will strengthen Australia’s leadership in maritime archaeology, while innovative methods for studying past human environments will be used on land and underwater, benefitting our heritage, environmental and resource agencies.

Partnerships between Traditional Owners, researchers, cave divers and government will help apply archaeological expertise to sustainable management of Australia’s coastal environments. Results will be disseminated via publications, workshops and media, including engaging digital visualisations of past environments.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Curiosity captured the eyes: investigating attentional information seeking. This project will investigate how learned associations with information value shape attention and influence decision-making. Using innovative eye-tracking methods, the project will examine the environmental and cognitive factors that determine which information sources capture attention and the consequences for choices. The project also investigates how individual differences in attention to information relate to anxious and compulsive traits. Outcomes include new knowledge about how previous experience shapes attention and the consequences for behaviour. Benefits include informing public health communication design and misinformation reduction strategies, and advancing understanding of attention, learning, and decision-making processes.
national-interest-test-statement: In the modern world, we are constantly bombarded with information – news alerts, social media posts, product labels, health warnings. Some information draws our attention, shaping the decisions we make. Currently, we don't fully understand what makes certain information sources draw attention, or why people keep attending to sources that have become unreliable. This project uses eye-tracking to investigate how learned associations with information value influence which sources automatically capture attention. When we learn that certain sources provide valuable information, does this learning shape which sources draw attention in the future? And does this automatic bias influence our decisions? This research will benefit Australians by providing evidence to inform public health policy and communication strategies. Findings will inform food labelling and health warning design to guide attention towards important information and make it easier for Australians to make healthy choices. The research will also inform misinformation reduction strategies by revealing why people struggle to disengage from unreliable news sources, social media accounts, and misleading content. Additionally, it will help understand compulsive information-seeking in anxiety and obsessive-compulsive disorders. Results will be shared through academic publications, conferences, and public science publications, making findings accessible to policymakers, health professionals, and the broader community.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Future Feed:Sustainable Single-Cell Protein through Innovative N Management. The project aims to develop an innovative single-cell protein (SCP) biotechnology using hydrogen-oxidizing bacteria for CO₂ fixation and N recovery under anaerobic conditions. This research will uncover new metabolic pathways and engineering strategies that enhance anaerobic SCP production while replacing O₂ with nitrate as a safer electron acceptor and nutrient resource. By eliminating aeration and leveraging N-rich wastewater, the biotechnology can achieve neutral or even negative operational costs through N-removal credits. The resulting high-protein biomass provides a sustainable feed alternative to soybean and fishmeal, strengthening food security, lowering carbon emissions, and closing nutrient loops within the circular bioeconomy.
national-interest-test-statement:
This project addresses pivotal national challenges and provides significant benefits to crucial Australian industries, including agriculture, wastewater treatment, fish farming, and groundwater management. By pioneering single-cell protein (SCP) production using H2-oxidizing bacteria for CO2 fixation and N recovery under anaerobic conditions, this project offers a groundbreaking biotechnology that reduces the energy and cost burdens associated with traditional O2-dependent processes. This project will advance Australia's net-zero emissions goal by delivering innovative waste management solutions and bolstering the renewable energy sector.
This research offers significant benefits to the agriculture and fish farming sectors, which face challenges from nutrient runoff and the need for sustainable feed. Effective N recovery will reduce eutrophication in Australia’s water bodies and groundwater, while converting N into high-value SCP lowers carbon footprints, cuts feed costs, and improves the sustainability of aquaculture protein sources—key to both economic and environmental sustainability. In groundwater management, this biotechnology will revolutionize the treatment of high nitrate concentrations from industrial and agricultural sources. Integrating this system promises more sustainable and cost-effective operations, enhancing regulatory compliance and supporting national water quality and sustainability goals.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Creating retail food environments that support environmental sustainability. The food system is the single largest risk to environmental sustainability with little progress toward environmentally sustainable diets. This project aims to demonstrate the environmental sustainability of our most impactful retail food environments and the marketing activities that influence them. It will develop the comprehensive evidence base required to support retail-focused policy making by governments as well as supporting voluntary initiatives by retailers. Findings will help address Australia’s number one research challenge of transitioning to a net zero future, with environmentally sustainable retail practices helping to prevent the severe disruption to social, economic and climate systems that will occur if nothing is done.
national-interest-test-statement: The food system is the single most influential driver of environmental harms with 'transitioning to a net zero future' Australia's number one national research challenge. The retail food environment, where nearly all food is purchased, is therefore a crucial setting to address this issue. Despite the potential to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by changing the types of foods they promote and sell, most food retailers address environmental sustainability by focusing instead on operational activities such as transport, recycling and packaging. This fellowship seizes this opportunity to create an environmentally sustainable retail food environment. It will provide the research evidence to support the development of novel government regulation, including understanding for the first time where regulation is required, what the impact initiatives in the retail setting can have on environmental sustainability, and the success factors for the development and implementation of regulation. Evaluation of policy impact and retailer accountability will be supported through the validation of recently created methods for monitoring of retail food environments. Project discoveries will be shared with retail, government and advocacy partners in Australia and internationally through strong existing networks. The research will support retailers to transition to a net zero future, providing a competitive advantage for early adopters and clear environmental and social benefits for all Australians.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Occupying the ice: a history of Antarctic scientific stations since 1945. This project aims to investigate the history of Antarctica’s scientific stations as sites of knowledge production, environmental impact and geopolitical action from 1945 to the present. Using diverse archival, oral history and material sources, it expects to generate new knowledge about human presence in Antarctica and global histories of scientific field sites and environmental ideas in the period. Expected outcomes include long-term and critical perspectives on, and case studies of, human habitation of Antarctica. As station building and growth continues amid geopolitical tension and environmental concerns, this new knowledge will inform national and international policymaking about human actions and cultural and heritage practices there.
primary-field-of-research: 5002 - History and Philosophy of Specific Fields
national-interest-test-statement: Australia is one of 7 countries to claim territory in Antarctica, making significant contributions to global science and environmental protection through its activities there. Australia’s and other nations’ Antarctic activities are shaped by their permanent scientific stations. Yet these stations have not been subject to close historical study. This project aims to understand how these stations work, how they have led to new knowledge, impacted local environments, and expressed geopolitical strategies. This new historical knowledge is needed because the context in which stations are operating is profoundly changing and new directions of action require critical perspectives. New scientific technologies, ongoing geopolitical tension, continuing environmental impacts, and limited government funds demand new research into the physical footprint of Antarctic science. This project will provide cultural and environmental benefits to Australia by generating historical interpretation that will support Australia’s standing in the international Antarctic Treaty System and the Australian Antarctic Division’s and Federal government’s environmental protection efforts and heritage protection obligations. This project will improve public understanding of Australian history through an active program of public outreach to connect with the 75th anniversary of the establishment of Australia’s Mawson Station, the oldest continuously occupied station south the Antarctic Circle.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Literary Criticism and Pluralist Values. This project aims to investigate the neglected role played by literary criticism and theory in advancing pluralist values in modern liberal societies. By introducing the concept of “aesthetic pluralism,” it seeks to show how literary discourse since the sixteenth century has centred upon notions of diversity, freedom, and tolerance, directly impacting the practice of liberal democracy. Intended outcomes include new knowledge about the history of criticism and new understandings of its impact upon pluralist societies and democratic cultures. The project is expected to offer benefits in the form of historically informed guidance for how to enhance trust, civil discourse, and respect for difference in areas of social and aesthetic controversy.
national-interest-test-statement: This project investigates how literary criticism has helped shape the pluralist values—diversity, tolerance, and freedom—that underpin modern liberal democracy. By introducing the concept of “aesthetic pluralism,” it will provide the first systematic account of how ideas about art and taste have promoted coexistence, respect for difference, and civic dialogue from the sixteenth century to the present. In a time of increasing polarisation and cultural conflict, the project offers a new framework for dealing with disputes about censorship, representation, and the expression of personal identity that directly impact Australia’s public life. In order to inform public discussions, educational programs, and policy design, the project will share its findings through speaker series, book publications, and op-eds, as well as through partnerships with the Sydney Policy Lab, the Ethics Centre, and the Australian Public Policy Institute. These activities will help strengthen Australia’s pluralist culture, enrich national conversations about freedom and tolerance, and affirm the social value of the humanities in supporting democratic dialogue and social inclusion.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Uncovering the role of cognition in urban adaptation by Australian birds. This project will address why some birds can successfully thrive in cities while others fail, and how this varies within and between cities. Observations from citizen scientists across Australia on urban bird behaviour will be matched with measures of detailed brain anatomy, social abundance, and high-resolution spatial mapping. Comparisons between city habitats and species will then be used to identify predictors of variation in behavioural flexibility. This will identify when and how cognition helps birds to flexibily adapt to Australian cities, and ascertain limits to this flexibility. These results will improve decision-making on how to maintain urban bird biodiversity under scenarios of accelerating urban sprawl and densification.
national-interest-test-statement: Cities are world’s fastest growing habitat type, and this process of urbanisation is one of the most extreme and challenging forms of change experienced by animals. Studies indicate that intelligence is one of the best defences animals have against changing environments, but we lack mechanistic understanding of how and when intelligence is linked to urban adaptation. This Fellowship will combine behavioural study, detailed brain anatomy, citizen science observations and high-resolution spatial mapping to identify the behavioural mechanisms underlying urban adaptation in birds across a range of Australian cities.  This will be used to create a predictive framework of scenarios for successful persistence by different species. These research outcomes will be promoted beyond academia via direct engagement with citizen scientists and disseminated with public talks and forums to stakeholders, including community action groups. Understanding urban adaptation is particularly timely in an Australian context as 46% of Australia’s threatened animal species are found in our cities, and urban environments are becoming progressively important in conservation decision-making under scenarios of accelerating urbanisation and population growth. Maintaining urban bird biodiversity also provides measurable positive outcomes for residents’ well-being, with both of these benefits aligning with Objective 9 “Enrich cities and towns with nature” of Australia’s Strategy for Nature 2024-2030.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Social Networks & Collaborative Governance for Compound Hazard Preparedness. This project will investigate how social networks help farming communities prepare for and respond to overlapping or consecutive climate hazards like floods, heatwaves and cyclones. It will generate new knowledge about how these networks operate at personal and community levels, and how government systems can support them. The research focuses on disproportionately disadvantaged groups, including culturally diverse households and older people in regional areas. Findings will improve disaster planning and resilience programs, reduce recovery costs, and strengthen wellbeing and connectedness in vulnerable communities across Australia.
national-interest-test-statement:
This project addresses a pressing societal issue: how to support communities in preparing for and responding to increasingly frequent and overlapping natural hazards. Events like floods, heatwaves and cyclones are becoming more disruptive, especially in regional Australia, where farming communities, older adults and culturally diverse households often face barriers to accessing support. While governments increasingly rely on community networks to build resilience, we lack evidence on how these networks function during compound disasters and how governance systems can effectively support them. This project will push boundaries in connecting personal and community-level social networks with institutional arrangements to prepare for compound hazards.

The benefits to Australians are significant. Economically, stronger community preparedness can reduce recovery costs, projected to exceed $40 billion annually by 2050. Socially, the project will improve wellbeing and connectedness in vulnerable communities. Environmentally, it supports proactive risk reduction in climate-sensitive regions. Culturally, it promotes inclusive and locally grounded approaches to disaster planning.

To maximise impact, findings will be shared through policy briefs, toolkits, workshops, a public-facing website and direct engagement with communities, practitioners and decision-makers—ensuring the research leads to practical solutions for a more resilient Australia.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Artificial intelligence-enhanced head injury biomechanics and helmet design. This project aims to use biomechanical modelling, experiments, and advanced machine learning to accurately predict human brain injuries and create the best possible bicycle helmet designs for the prevention of traumatic brain injury. This project expects to generate new knowledge in injury biomechanics, product design, and innovation. Expected outcomes include technologies that enable faster diagnosis and management of traumatic brain injuries for healthcare professionals, and expedite helmet design for manufacturers. Adaptable to other sports and military use, this research can advance next-generation protective equipment, offering widespread safety benefits and improved quality of life for Australians.
national-interest-test-statement: In Australia, up to 200,000 traumatic brain injuries occur annually, many of which are preventable through improved helmet design and a better understanding of head injury biomechanics. This project addresses a key national research gap by combining biomechanical modelling, experimental testing, and advanced machine learning to predict brain injuries and their causes. It aims to develop a rapid, robust framework for designing optimal helmets that significantly reduce injury risks. By uniting world leaders in head injury biomechanics, artificial intelligence, and product design, the project will strengthen Australia’s position in protective equipment innovation. The intelligent computational framework developed will be readily adopted by the multi-billion-dollar sports and defence sectors, enabling next-generation helmets for athletes and soldiers. The outcomes will generate substantial economic and societal benefits by advancing local manufacturing, safety technology, and design capability. Beyond academia, the research will be promoted through partnerships with helmet manufacturers, defence agencies, and sporting bodies, as well as public awareness campaigns and policy engagement. The resulting injury predictor and head impact classifier will empower healthcare professionals, coaches, forensic experts, and safety regulators to make informed decisions on traumatic brain injury management, concussion risk, and product safety, ultimately improving wellbeing and saving lives.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Principles of Impulse-Momentum Exchange in Multi-Robot Systems. This project focuses on foundational research to establish new principles of multi-robot control algorithms that require precise regulation of impulses and momenta, e.g., lifting, pushing, tossing heavy payloads, and hoisting, boosting, and amplifying team members which are crucial skills in manufacturing, and disaster response. To achieve this goal, the project will explore new research in whole-body multi-robot planning and control to investigate how multi-robot systems control the exchange of interactive forces and momenta. The advances will provide insights on leveraging robots as force multipliers and contribute to national priorities of expanding technological leadership in robotics and automation.
national-interest-test-statement: The development of general-purpose humanoid robots benefits modern society by automating dangerous, physically demanding work and supporting national endeavours. Yet as automation demands venture into extreme and remote places e.g., disaster zones and construction sites, many essential activities become difficult for individual robots, driving the need for cooperative multi-robot technologies. This project will contribute to the development of cooperative humanoid multi-robotic systems that can perform labour-intensive and high-risk tasks for construction, infrastructure maintenance, manufacturing, agriculture, and emergency response. The advances of this project will focus on creating new principles for multi-robot coordination and control, enabling teams of robots to amplify force output, expanding the utility of robots in the field. These applications could yield efficiency improvements of 15-30% in tasks involving material handling and assembly, reducing injury-related downtime and associated costs to the Australian economy estimated at $28 billion annually. The outcomes will strengthen national resilience by enabling safer and faster deployment of robotic systems in emergencies and hazardous environments, reducing human exposure to danger. The project findings has the potential to translate research into opportunities projected to add $170-600 billion per year to the GDP by 2030 and contribute to Australia’s future robotics workforce.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Decoding Cell Identity Shifts and Embryonic Circuitry Reawakening in Aging. Transcription factors (TFs) are master regulators of cell identity. My previous work established that aging involves predictable TF network remodeling by hijacking a developmental mechanism. This Fellowship aims to investigate how ongoing chromatin opening during aging leads to aberrant activation of regulatory elements (REs) outside their native cell identities by: (1) characterising age-related activation of these REs and how they are epigenetically repressed in young cells; and (2) exploring strategies to modulate age-opened chromatin to induce/mitigate aging networks. This is expected to generate a framework for predictable age-related shifts in cell identity and knowledge that may benefit by informing future healthy aging strategies.
national-interest-test-statement:
This fellowship aims to investigate the fundamental biological processes driving age-related shifts in cell identity and function. By decoding the molecular process of aging, outcomes expected from this research has the potential to deliver substantial economic, social, and health benefits to Australians. Foundational knowledge from this research, for example, may pave the way for interventions that promote healthy aging, delay the onset of age-related diseases, or improve the quality of life for older Australians. This has the potential to reduce the burden on the healthcare system, support a more active and productive aging population, and contribute to the sustainability of the economy.

This research will support advancing Australia’s intellectual leadership in the field of understanding fundamental aging processes and build important research capacity and skill. An IP protection strategy and established industry collaborators are in place for future commercialization. Research findings will further be disseminated through conferences, publications, and public outreach initiatives aimed at raising awareness of the processes underpinning aging. This is expected to enhance the potential for this work to inform future health aging strategies.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Designer peptides for selective and tuneable modulation of sodium channels. The project aims to investigate the structure and function of sodium channels by utilising venom-derived peptides that specifically target and alter the function of these channels. This project expects to generate new knowledge in the area of neuroscience using an interdisciplinary approach including synthetic peptide chemistry, pharmacology and electrophysiology. Expected outcomes of this project include a framework for the rational design of peptides targeting sodium channels with improved activity and selectivity. This knowledge should provide significant benefits for the advancement of ion channel targeting therapeutics and biodegradable peptide-based pesticides.
national-interest-test-statement: Cell-to-cell communication via electrical signals is critical for regulating nerve impulses, muscle movement, and heart rhythm. Sodium channels are fundamental to this electrical signalling, making them key targets for anticonvulsants, anti-arrhythmics, and painkillers. Disruption of sodium channel function in insects leads to paralysis and death, also making them ideal targets for insecticides. Despite their significance, our understanding of sodium channel structure and function is incomplete. This is due in part, to a lack of selective research tools available to study them. Venom from spiders, scorpions and cone snails has evolved over millions of years to selectively target sodium channels. This project will utilise venom-based molecules to develop a new suite of tools with improved activity at sodium channels. Knowledge from this project can be harnessed in future drug development programs to design safer and more effective anti-convulsants, anti-arrhythmics, and painkillers. Venom-based molecules generated in this project have the potential to be commercialised as safer insecticides for the protection of Australian agricultural industries.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Knowledge-in-the-Loop Learning for Hidden Renewable Energy System Dynamics. While machine learning can effectively fit models to the data, safety-critical infrastructure such as energy systems also demands that dynamic models are consistently transparent and interpretable. This project aims to establish a knowledge-in-the-loop learning paradigm that fuses limited prior physics and partially observed data in a closed loop to deliver expressive, adaptive, and robust modelling of evolving system dynamics, with maintained model interpretability for practitioners. Expected outcomes include an explainable knowledge-data-driven framework with tailored machine learning toolsets. Benefits include enhanced AI responsibility in fostering secure, economical, and sustainable integration of renewables towards Net Zero.
national-interest-test-statement: Australia is one of the leaders in the global shift towards Net Zero, with rapid adoption of renewable power generation technologies to replace fossil fuels. As the energy mix increasingly relies on variational renewables with their dynamic behaviours hidden behind the meters, maintaining endured understanding of energy system dynamics to ensure secure and reliable operation becomes unprecedentedly challenging. Machine learning can learn complex dynamics from data, but typical black-box surrogates are not acceptable for making decisions in such safety-critical infrastructure. This project addresses the interpretability needs in learning-based dynamic modelling and aims to establish a knowledge-in-the-loop machine learning paradigm that fuses limited prior knowledge and partially observed data to adaptively and interpretably evolve the understanding of new dynamics from high levels of renewables. Anticipated outcomes include a closed-loop knowledge-data-driven framework with a suite of machine learning toolsets, designed to enhance dynamic modelling of energy systems, building confidence in the secure integration of renewable energy, and reinforcing Australia’s leadership in AI and low-carbon transition. Outcomes will be shared beyond academia through collaborative, multidisciplinary workshops with key players responsible for running the power grid in Australia, including Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO) and Network Service Providers (NSP).

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Asset Pricing under Complex Historical Dependence: A New Framework. This project aims to develop a more accurate asset pricing framework, examining the impact of complex histories of key economic variables that drive financial markets and investor behaviour. It uses a novel methodology for optimal decision-making under path dependence, a form of mathematical modelling explicitly capturing historical states. It will advance theoretical approaches in economics and offer a comprehensive understanding of how economic trajectories impact future business conditions and asset prices. It expects to deliver more accurate measures of path dependence and sound investment and risk management tools for use by the $4 trillion Australian superannuation industry, business investments, finance regulators, and policymakers.
national-interest-test-statement: Understanding the historical paths of key economic variables, such as production, inflation, and asset prices, is essential for analysing and forecasting future business conditions, particularly during periods of volatility. Yet both economic theory and market practice remain limited in modelling how these historical dynamics shape future outcomes. This project will develop a new asset pricing framework that explicitly incorporates path dependence through an innovative approach to optimal decision-making under path-dependent conditions. By doing so, it will produce more accurate measures of path dependence and enhance investment and forecasting methods by incorporating complex economic histories. Improved modelling is especially beneficial during market downturns, when strong path dependence amplifies the risk of large losses, as seen during the 2020 Australian stock market crash. The project also aligns closely with the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority’s prudential standards (SPS 530 and SPS 114), which require superannuation funds to assess portfolio resilience under adverse economic and market conditions. Building on existing industry partnerships, the outcomes will inform more robust investment and risk management tools for Australian investors, financial regulators, and government agencies, particularly within the $4 trillion superannuation sector, contributing to stronger economic performance and improved quality of life for Australians.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Evolving tempos: how developmental timing shaped mammalian brains. The timing of developmental processes can shape the brain, creating interspecies variation across evolution, as well as in the context of altered timing in neurodevelopmental disorders. However, exactly how timing is linked to specific outcomes, as well as the upstream master regulators of temporal variation, remain unclear. This fellowship will utilise unique methods to compare brain development in placental and marsupial mammals, which present extraordinary examples of variation in developmental timing and brain structure, creating new knowledge about the flexibilities and limitations of brain development. Outcomes include fundamental understanding of how time impacts developmental outcomes across broad biological contexts.
national-interest-test-statement: Understanding the rules that govern how developmental timing in the brain is controlled, as well as the neurodevelopmental consequences of mis-timed processes, are fundamental unanswered biological questions. This fellowship harnesses the advantages of a native marsupial species as a natural example of extreme differences in developmental timing that can provide us with insights about the flexibility and constraints of brain development. The project is built on a strong foundation of pioneering manipulations of gene expression in marsupial mammals and has the potential to reveal fundamental rules of brain development across the animal kingdom, both in health and disease. Potential outcomes of this work may therefore ultimately provide benefits that ensure a healthy start to life for young Australians. In addition, these findings will have potential benefits for conservation of native fauna, as they will outline the requirements for healthy brain development in marsupials. Advancing the innovative in vivo and in vitro methods described in this proposal will further cement the establishment of a world-class critical mass of advanced capabilities, particularly related to brain, stem cells and marsupial research. These enhanced capabilities have the potential to further expand outcomes within and beyond academia, including the biotechnology, neuroscience, environmental conservation and skilled educational sectors, thereby positioning Australia at the forefront of these fields.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Advancing equitable conservation by navigating diverse equity conceptions. Area-based conservation is set to cover 30% of the planet but its ability to benefit people and halt biodiversity loss is undermined by conservation inequities. The project will advance equitable marine area-based conservation by providing the first analysis of how it is understood and operationalised from global to local levels. By revealing how policy, practice, and local actors conceptualise equitable conservation and its levers in diverse sociocultural settings, it will help decision-makers navigate the clashing equity understandings often fueling conservation inequities and conflicts. Outputs will transform how decision-makers operationalise equity, significantly enhancing capacity to advance equitable and thus, effective conservation.
national-interest-test-statement: As a marine nation with more ocean than land, Australia’s coasts and oceans are central to national identity. With over 50% of Australia’s ocean in area-based conservation, it is crucial these areas are equitably governed – that benefits and costs are shared fairly, decision-making is inclusive, and diverse social groups are respected. Equitable conservation will benefit Australians' wellbeing, including by ensuring conservation effectively stems biodiversity loss. But marine conservation inequities are common. This project will generate the knowledge decision-makers need to navigate the clashing equity understandings that often fuel conservation inequities and related conflicts. Revealing how policy, practice, and local actors conceptualise equitable area-based conservation and its levers in diverse sociocultural settings, the project provides the first analysis of how conservation equity is understood and operationalised from global to local levels. Project outcomes include recommendations for the Great Southern Reef study sites, helping to secure its annual total economic value of $11.6B, and advancing Australia’s equity priorities under the Sustainable Ocean Plan and National Biodiversity Strategy. The project’s synthesis – a co-produced equitable conservation roadmap - will provide actionable guidance to help decision-makers account for diverse equity understandings, significantly enhancing capacity to advance equitable, and thus, effective conservation.

announcement-admin-organisation: The University of Notre Dame Australia
grant-summary: AI-Mediated Spirituality in Australia: Protecting Wellbeing, Reducing Risk. This project investigates how generative artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping spiritual practice and belief formation in Australia. Through ethnographic research, surveys and interviews, the project will map how Australians are using AI for spiritual guidance and growth, and evaluate associated risks and benefits. The amalgamation of AI and spirituality represents a new frontier in the study of technology and spirituality, critical as personal growth and development is now the number one reason people use generative AI globally. Through academic and general audience publications, as well as policy briefs and a collaborative white paper, this project will provide tangible resources for mitigating risk targeted to community stakeholders.
national-interest-test-statement: This project will examine how Australians are beginning to use generative artificial intelligence (AI) for spiritual guidance and personal growth, and what this means for individual and community wellbeing. Medical and therapeutic uses of AI are receiving scholarly attention, but the spiritual uses of chatbots in Australia are yet to be understood. While some users report benefits such as a stronger sense of purpose and belonging, others are becoming more vulnerable to misinformation, trapped in online echo chambers, and susceptible to extreme beliefs. By identifying who is using AI for spiritual purposes, how they use it, and what outcomes they experience, the project will provide evidence to support balanced and responsible use. The findings will help educators, health professionals, spiritual and wellness communities, and policymakers design practical responses as AI becomes part of everyday life. The research will be shared beyond universities through open resources, policy briefs, a white paper, public lectures, media engagement, and co-designed materials with community partners. These activities will improve public understanding, reduce harm, and support safer and more informed engagement with AI across Australian society.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Australia’s silent extinctions: how weeds erode native plant biodiversity. Australia is experiencing the fastest rate of new plant introductions globally, yet the contribution of invasive plants to the decline of native species remains unknown. This project aims to investigate how plant invasions erode native plant genomes and reduce their capacity to adapt to future climates. It should generate new knowledge by tracing losses of genetic diversity over the past century across natural and human-altered landscapes. Expected outcomes include better understanding of factors contributing to plant extinctions and new tools for predicting invasion impacts. This should deliver significant benefits, including enhanced capacity to protect Australia’s native flora from the combined threats of invasions and climate change.
national-interest-test-statement: Australia faces the fastest accumulation of new invasive plant species globally, yet the long-term consequences for native biodiversity remain poorly understood. This project should address this major knowledge gap by quantifying how invasions alter native plant genomes and compromise the evolutionary resilience of native flora to future climates. By integrating genomic, historical, and environmental data in novel ways, it aims to identify species and populations most at risk of decline. Findings should inform strategies to maintain ecosystem resilience, protect threatened native flora, and support services such as pollination and carbon sequestration. Social benefits should arise through engagement with land managers and the public, fostering community awareness of the consequences of invasions and stewardship of biodiversity. Economic benefits are expected from supporting knowledge-based conservation and sustainable use of native plant resources. Early career researchers should gain cutting-edge skills in genomics, historical DNA analysis, and evolutionary simulations, building national workforce capacity and strengthening Australia’s global leadership in biosecurity and conservation science. Findings will be disseminated through high-impact publications, open-access datasets, and outreach, ensuring adoption in policy, management, and public engagement initiatives aimed at safeguarding Australia’s unique natural heritage.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Understanding men's pathways to non-violence. This program aims to understand men’s pathways to non-violence and generate innovative, community-led strategies to reduce violence against women across the Northern Territory (NT) and neighbouring Indo-Pacific. Drawing on partnerships in the NT, Timor-Leste and North Maluku (Indonesia), it provides the first multi-country qualitative study of men’s desistance from family violence outside of formal behaviour change programs. Expected outcomes will illuminate the relational, cultural and moral mechanisms to sustain change and inform new theoretical frameworks, practice tools and policy pathways to strengthen prevention, accountability and healing, providing significant benefits to improve safety and wellbeing for women and families.
national-interest-test-statement: Domestic and family violence (DFV) remains one of Australia’s most urgent and costly social issues, accounting for around 5% of the total disease burden among women aged 18–44 and costing over $22 billion annually, with more than $200 million in Commonwealth aid committed to regional efforts to prevent violence against women in the Asia-Pacific. In Australia, the Northern Territory records the nation’s highest levels of harm and the highest per-capita government expenditure on DFV prevention and response. Yet despite decades of investment, little is known about how men stop using violence and what sustains lasting change, particularly outside of formal programs and in remote community settings. This research will generate the first multi-country comparative evidence on men’s desistance from DFV across Indigenous contexts. It will uncover how personal, relational and cultural processes sustain non-violence, and co-create practical tools for early intervention, family support and accountability. These insights will contribute to enhancing safety and wellbeing for women and families, reducing DFV-related justice and health costs, and strengthening Indigenous and regional leadership in violence prevention. Findings will be translated into multilingual practice resources, training materials and policy-focussed outputs with Aboriginal, Timorese and Indonesian partners, positioning Australia as a regional leader in developing community-led solutions to end violence against women.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Ethical Influencers as Mediators of Social Justice in Australia and SEAsia. This project investigates the emic values and vernacular practices of Influencers to understand how the sector defines its own ethics, focusing on ‘ethical Influencers’ in Australia and Southeast Asia (Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia). Moving beyond current foci on commercial concerns, it develops a contextual, nuanced, and ethnographic understanding of Influencers’ beliefs and practices surrounding ‘ethical influence’ and their potential to mediate social justice cultures. This anthropological approach prioritises lived experience, addresses the lack of independent Australian research, promotes healthier internet cultures, and strengthens digital literacy within a sector that rising numbers of young Australians aspire to enter.
national-interest-test-statement: In a time of information saturation, Influencers are critical gatekeepers of online attention, being visibility experts who amplify and suppress public interest in wide-ranging issues. Over 73% of 15-40yo Australians follow Influencers for opinion leadership, including climate change, anti-racism, and poverty reduction. Yet, the industry is under-regulated with errant ones peddling misinformation and harm. To inform governance and enhance positive outcomes from Influencer partnerships in the longterm, this ethnographic project will produce original ethnographic insights on how ‘ethical Influencers’ formulate their values and norms, and develop and maintain ethical practice to guide content production, especially on social justice issues. Evidence from Southeast Asian (Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia) ecologies with a history of mobilising Influencers for social justice issues will guide critical understanding of ‘ethical Influencers’ as important opinion leaders who cultivate citizen interest in informed ways. Open Access resources and public events will improve digital literacy about the Influencer industry.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Unifying the Ethics of Health Security:Bridging Politics, Policy & Practice. This project aims to develop a comprehensive, unified ethical framework for decision making in Australian health security covering preparation for and responses to naturally occurring disease pandemics, biological weapons, and laboratory containment failures. The project expects to generate new knowledge in bioethics, using innovative and interdisciplinary methods to identify ethical responses during public health crises, and understand Australians' beliefs about government preparation and responses to those crises. Expected outcomes of this project include novel bioethical frameworks in public health, improved trust in Australian pandemic response, and ethics guidance for Australian public health and national security policymakers.
national-interest-test-statement: COVID-19 killed ~20,000 Australians, cost $55.9 billion in health care, and will cost billions more from “long COVID.” The next pandemic could be worse. Viral outbreaks may also result from biological weapons, or a laboratory-based outbreak of a genetically modified disease. Responding to any of these threats involves complex ethical decisions, and measures like quarantine may harm individuals and communities in the name of public security. However, there is no unified framework that enables Australia to prepare for and respond to these growing "health security threats," and this lack may impair government response, harm Australians, and undermine trust in government and public health. This project addresses that lack by combining bioethical and experimental methods to develop an ethical framework to guide health security decisions in Australia. This framework will form the basis for ethical decision making, legislation, and policy for future pandemics and other biosecurity threats. It will generate the knowledge and capacity to face new challenges to Australia's health, help shape legislation and policy domestically, and support Australian leadership internationally at venues like the United Nations.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Higher representation and character theory . This project develops a unified framework for higher representation and character theory, integrating higher categorical and homotopical methods. It generalises the classical theory of group representations and characters in multiple directions, encompassing its transchromatic analogue and the deep relations between them, with applications to the far-reaching chromatic redshift philosophy. The expected outcomes will include foundational results published in top peer-reviewed journals, new computational tools, training of students and young researchers, strengthened international collaboration, and will position Australia at the forefront of the rapidly developing field of modern homotopy theory.
national-interest-test-statement: This project develops new methods in frameworks of pure mathematics for studying fundamental symmetries of complex systems. These frameworks are driving major recent developments across topology, algebraic geometry, number theory, and mathematical physics, providing unified foundations and language for diverse areas of contemporary mathematics. Australia already holds a leading position in higher category theory; building on that strength, and combining it with powerful homotopical methods, the project aims at providing significant new findings. In doing so, it positions Australian researchers at the centre of an international network of activity and aligns national expertise with key directions of current mathematical research. The project will expand Australia’s research capability and train early-career mathematicians in frontier theoretical techniques. By fostering exchange and visibility, it will consolidate the country’s standing as a hub for high-level mathematical collaboration and attract leading researchers seeking an active environment for fundamental work. In the long term, the new techniques developed by the project have downstream applications in materials engineering, finance, coding and data management, all of which have potential economic and commercial benefits for Australia. The results of the project will be communicated with the public through general interest seminars and media articles.

scheme-information: schemeCode: FT   ^ program: Discovery ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 1 ^ schemeRound: FT26 Round 1
grant-summary: Fracture-Guided Design for Intelligent 4D-Printed Adaptive Structures. This project aims to establish a fracture-guided design framework for adaptive structures fabricated through 4D printing. By integrating advanced structural optimisation, embedded sensing, and smart manufacturing, the project will enable structures to detect damage and adapt their shape or behaviour in real time. The research will open new pathways in materials design, digital manufacturing and structural health monitoring. Expected outcomes include novel design methods, adaptive structures, and integrated manufacturing workflows, leading to safer, more reliable and more efficient components for Australia’s aerospace, biomedical and defence industries, reinforcing its global leadership in future manufacturing.
national-interest-test-statement: This project will strengthen Australia’s capability in intelligent and sustainable manufacturing by developing adaptive structures produced through 4D printing that can autonomously detect damage and respond in real time. By integrating fracture-guided design, embedded sensing and advanced manufacturing workflows, the research addresses a critical gap in creation of lightweight, self-monitoring components for the aerospace, defence and biomedical sectors. The research aligns well with the national priorities in sovereign, high-value and environmentally responsible manufacturing, supporting Australia’s long-term economic resilience and technological competitiveness. Australians will benefit from safer, more durable and more energy-efficient products, reduced material waste, and lower maintenance costs. The project will also train the next generation of engineers with advanced digital design and computational optimisation skills essential for tackling challenges in Industry 5.0, fostering a skilled workforce for the nation’s manufacturing future. Through collaboration with industry and manufacturing hubs, it will accelerate technology translation, strengthen supply-chain security, and expand high-tech export capacity. By demonstrating world-leading expertise in adaptive materials, smart structures and intelligent fabrication, this research will help position Australia as a global leader in future manufacturing, delivering enduring economic, environmental and societal benefits.

scheme-information: schemeCode: LP   ^ program: Linkage ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 2 ^ schemeRound: LP25 Round 2
grant-summary: Wellington Caves: a unique archive of faunal evolution and ecosystem change. The project aims to investigate how the mammal fauna of eastern Australia changed over the last four million years using the uniquely rich, diverse and historically significant megafauna locality of the Wellington Caves. The project will analyse faunal and vegetation change over different timescales on the back of an intensive field-, museum- and lab-based program. New knowledge on the ecological impacts of major climatic changes and megafaunal extinctions will provide improved historical benchmarks to guide biodiversity management. With its strong citizen-science / community-education focus, the project is expected to benefit regional tourism and local schools, and provide improved training opportunities for young First Nations People.
investigators: Prof Gavin Prideaux; A/Prof Lee Arnold; Prof Andy Herries; Dr Kale Sniderman; Dr Matthew McCurry
national-interest-test-statement: Australia’s animals are renowned for their uniqueness, but prior to 40,000 years ago, the fauna was even more peculiar, including >70 giant species. Fossils of ‘megafauna’ were first collected by Europeans in 1830 at the Wellington Caves in central western New South Wales, yet 195 years later, our understanding of these species and how their ecosystems changed over time remains poor. This hinders our ability to establish ecological benchmarks to guide ecosystem restoration. As one of only three locations in the world with vertebrate fossil sites that span the last four million years, the Wellington Caves are uniquely placed to address this deficiency. The project will study existing collections and conduct new excavations with the help of citizen science. This will allow identification of the ecological impacts of aridity and seasonality, climatic warming and cooling, and megafaunal extinctions. The work will incorporate Wiradjuri knowledge of megafaunal species and provide training opportunities for young Aboriginal people. Positive impacts are expected via increased regional tourism, enhanced school education programs, rejuvenated exhibitions at the Caves and Australian Museum, high-profile scientific publications, and a Megafauna Festival in the bicentenary of the original discovery.

scheme-information: schemeCode: LP   ^ program: Linkage ^ submissionYear: 2025 ^ roundNumber: 2 ^ schemeRound: LP25 Round 2
grant-summary: Improved wheat and soybean for the Australian agrifood sector. This project aims to develop high-yielding, nutrient-dense wheat and soybean crops tailored to the Australian food and feed industries and builds on multiple discoveries arising from a previously awarded ARC Linkage project. The project will employ innovative plant breeding methods to boost levels of naturally occurring phytonutrients that enhance iron and zinc uptake in plants and improve dietary absorption in animals. Expected outcomes include novel health claims for bread, improved livestock feed formulations for poultry and pigs, and crops with stacked nutritional traits. The benefits encompass higher-value food and feed products, greater returns for Australian growers and stronger national resilience to global supply chain disruptions.
investigators: Mrs Lesley Gillespie; Prof Alexander Johnson; A/Prof Hafiz Ansar Rasul Suleria; Prof Enzo Lombi; Dr Elad Tako; Mr Luke Farrell; Dr Jesse Beasley; Mr Richard Devlin
national-interest-test-statement: Australia consistently ranks among the world's top three exporters of wheat, however, nutrient-poor soils often limit the growth and nutritional quality of Australian wheat crops. Conversely, Australia is a net importer of soybean and heavily reliant on other countries to secure sufficient soybean meal and flour for livestock feed and food applications. This research will improve the nutritional quality and yield of Australian wheat and soybean using innovative breeding methods that have quick paths to market, resulting in increased productivity and sustainability of the Australian cropping, livestock feed and breadmaking industries. The research findings will be promoted to the grains industry through Living Farm, a Western Australia-based R&D company with deep connections to a wide range of agribusinesses throughout the Wheatbelt, and to the livestock feed industry through the biotech startup company 121SEED. The research will also be shared with millions of bread consumers by Bakers Delight, Australia’s most successful bakery franchise, through the development and promotion of novel bread types containing high levels of bioavailable iron and other essential nutrients. The project will provide invaluable opportunities for an established team of higher education researchers at the University of Melbourne, University of South Australia and Cornell University to translate several recent discoveries in crop and food nutrition into tangible products for the agrifood sector.
